Śrī.
The Śrīnetratantra (Mṛtyuñjayabhaṭṭāraka),
accompanied by the commentary titled Netrodyota composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja.
The First Section:
"The Illumination of the Net.
The lords of the gates reside in the nine apertures; Vāstu and Gaṇeśa reside in the heart; and the mind resides there as well.

We praise that Netranatha, whose greatness consists of Sound and the other [tattvas] as his gurus, the ten vital winds (samīra) consisting of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), the conscious God (ciddeva) accompanied by the power of self-reflective awareness (vimarśaśakti), the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), the assembly of limbs, and the lords of the worlds as his instruments. || 1 ||
That which is the leader of the garland of mantras, which is one's own inner and outer virility,

which bestows prosperity upon embodied beings through the instruments [of yoga], and which effects the protection of the universe— that light is the supreme, consisting of the highest nectar, the universal self, the fourth state (turya), and the Trika.
I bow to the Eye, consisting of five and seven [syllables], the singular hero Mṛḍa, who belongs to Śiva and Śivā. || 2 ||
He who, instantly perceiving the universe within, brings it to identity with his own self through the goddesses who rule the senses; he who, having ascended the stream of supreme bliss,
likewise manifests as the surging form of his own self even externally due to his fullness.
Victorious is that certain, unprecedented, and secret Guru, who is the radiance of awakening! || 3 ||
The light of consciousness, which illumines all appearances, which is pure, autonomous, and radiant;
which consumes the fuel of duality, surging with the nectar of supreme non-duality;
which dispels the darkness of the views of both duality and non-duality, and is the single essence of the three abodes.
The eye of Śiva shines forth from beyond for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world.

O passionate ones, for the sake of pacifying the latent impressions of this worthless saṃsāra, savor the fragrance from me, whose heart-lotus has blossomed through the radiance of the sun of ever-new awakening. || 5 ||

Here, a certain introducer of the Tantra, whose mind is intent on bestowing grace and who has been awakened by the Goddess of Supreme Consciousness, offers a salutation to those worthy of salutation in accordance with this teaching, which seeks to bring down the secrets of all the Agamas.
He said: "The Powerful One, assuming a threefold form in three states, brings about the emergence, maintenance, and withdrawal of the entire universe through his power. (1.1)
Salutations to that Creator, whose nature consists of pure nectar;
to Śiva, the Supreme Self who transcends Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.

Salutation to that Śiva, the Supreme Self, whose nature is the supreme good consisting of the mass of consciousness and bliss; through the humble surrender of the limited self—comprising the body, vital breath, and so forth—I enter into Him. Of what kind is He?
He is superior to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, extending from Brahmā up to Anāśrita.

And [salutations] to the one who performs its protection and fulfillment. The word *īśa* (Lord) generally denotes [the categories] from Rudra up to Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Anāśrita. Because of His supreme nature, He is pure (*śuddha*), untainted even by Mahāmāyā, and therefore consists of nectar (*amṛtamaya*) and is the very soul of the bliss of the universe. His *ātman* is His own essential nature.
For it is precisely such [a nature] that will be described by him in the *Paramātmaprakaraṇa*:
"The nature of the Supreme Self is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
consciousness is said to be the form of the Self in all the scriptures" (8.28).

Thus [it is asked]: "For what purpose? To this he says "In three ways," and so forth. He who is empowered and independent, by means of his power—namely, the power of autonomy (*svātantrya-śakti*)—within the three states (the external, consisting of the cosmic egg of Brahmā, Prakṛti, and Māyā;
and the internal, consisting of the waking state and others beginning with the heart), because those very states have been manifested by him alone.

Assuming and taking on the threefold form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, he— who is characterized by that nature— performs, as appropriate, the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this entire world consisting of Māyā; likewise,
he exists in three ways within the three states known as dissolution, authority, and enjoyment.

Relying upon the nature of Īśvara, who is the *sadāśiva* that is non-dependent, he ordains the simultaneous emergence and other states of the entire universe— which consists of the pure path— as appropriate;
[he does so] through dissolution and grace, which are essentially specific forms of maintenance and withdrawal, [the latter] being [included] within maintenance and withdrawal themselves.
"In [the act of] acceptance," [it is said]; thus the God of gods is the performer of the five acts.
And the subsequent passage, which conforms to these two interpretations, states:
"I, who possess three bodies, perform creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (1.31)

Thus it exists. Furthermore, he who, assuming the threefold form known as action, knowledge, and will within the three levels—the supreme, the intermediate, and the inferior—effects the processes of emergence and so forth; as he will say:
"In this way, my power is called will, knowledge, and action" (1.29).
Thus:
"By the power of action (kriyā-śakti) he creates; by the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the maintenance of the world; and by the power of Rudra (rudra-śakti), dissolution. (21.43)

Thus it is said. Furthermore, he who, assuming a threefold form through the divisions of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva, ordains the emergence and other states of the entire universe during the three supreme stages which consist merely of the object of knowledge and the means of knowledge—
what will become of him?
"All mantras, according to the rule thus stated, [arise] from the three principles; they become [manifest] everywhere and in every respect. (21.57–58), and so forth. Moreover:

Assuming a form ending in *sa* (sānta) through the threefold division of the imperishable (*akṣara*) across the three states consisting of emission (*uccāra*), sacrificial offering (*havana*), and rest (*viśrānti*), [the Lord] stands above the entire universe, from the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) up to the final digit (*caramakalā*).

He is the ordainer of the emergence of the true nature of existence, which consists of consciousness, fire, internalization, light, bliss, and being; as he will declare: "The Praṇava is the life-breath of living beings. (22.14)

This continues from the beginning up to the end of the passage "by the Full One" (22.17). Furthermore, having assumed a threefold form— consisting of the moon, sun, and fire— within the three internal regions of left, right, and middle, as well as externally in the states consisting of night, day, and twilight, [the breath] proceeds through the specific movements of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* channels.
He who is the ordainer of the emergence and other states— such as nourishment, illumination, and combustion— for the entire universe;
he who shall command the sun and moon, and the fire, through the arrangement of the three abodes.
The conceptualization of my three eyes is seen here for that purpose.
"By that [process], I perform both burning and nourishing, as well as illumination. (1.30.31).

In this sūtra, the word *avasthā* (state/condition) should be understood according to the context as being derived either from the sense of "being" (*bhāva-sādhana*) or from the sense of "locus" (*adhikaraṇa-sādhana*). Thus, having observed this authentic reading, [the text reads]: "He who [exists] in three ways in the three states..."
And having read [the word] "vidadhāti," those who attempt to explain it as "yat-tat" (that which) are indeed objects of ridicule. || 2 ||
Having thus paid homage to the chosen deity, the introducer of the tantra begins to state the sequence of its transmission:
[He beheld] Hara, the Great Lord, the God of gods, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, sporting together with his attendants and accompanied by Pārvatī. (1–3)
Seeing the God delighted by his desire for the welfare of living beings,
Pārvatī quickly descended from his lap and grasped his feet.
Having gratified the Supreme Lord, he questioned him with supreme devotion—
the one called Maheśvara, the God and Sovereign of the gods beginning with Brahmā,

the divine one whose true nature consists of luminosity and other qualities, who is Hara because he removes the darkness of all dualistic distinctions and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And it is said:
"He who removes the bonds from the bound souls (paśu) and leads them upward is Hara.
Thus, [he refers to] the Supreme Śiva, the Lord of Umā, who dwells on Kailāsa, accompanied by Pārvatī. Therefore...

Even while playing with external groups, he is in reality constantly engaged in the play of creating the universe and so forth together with his own multitude of rays; and thus, through the excellence of resting within the circle of his own rays, he is intensely delighted, being a mass of supreme bliss.

And for this very reason, she is "Ke," the shimmering *elā* (cardamom) power in the head; she is the one who knows the opportune moment (*avasara-jñā*), having perceived and ascertained that [the Lord] is seated there—in the highest peak (*śikhara*), the most exalted abode whose nature consists of *vyāpinī* and *samanā*. This [Lord] is composed of the expansion of the supreme reality (*unmanā-paratattva*).

The Goddess, out of modesty, quickly released the mass of rays from her lap and, having first grasped his feet, satisfied him with devotion intent on worshipping his supreme form; then, desiring to favor him as if he were her own life-breath, she questioned him. || 4 ||
He shows what she asked:
the venerable Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the world, Master of the universe! (1-5)
O God, that great wonder which you have performed is a cause of amazement for the entire world; yet, O Supreme Lord, it is nothing at all to me.
This secret is difficult to understand, difficult to attain,
and has not been revealed even to Kārttikeya, nor to me, nor among the gods or the Gaṇas.
Not even for the mistresses of yoga, nor for the Mothers, nor for the sages, nor for the yogis [is such power].
Therefore, O Lord of the World, O Master, if you are pleased with me today— || 1.8 ||
I pray; having taken refuge in you, you ought to explain everything without remainder.

O Blessed One, endowed with the excellence of knowledge, sovereignty, and other qualities; O Lord and Master of the gods of worship, Brahmā and the rest; O Protector and Master of the worlds; for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal—
"O Lord sought by the worlds, O Protector of the entire universe, O God devoted to divine play and other such activities,

O Supreme Lord, O Embodiment of Paramaśiva"— these forms of address, through the contemplation of both the manifest (*sakala*) and unmanifest (*niṣkala*) natures, are intent upon proclaiming the Lord's universal identity (*sārvātmya*).
In order to bring [the Lord] face-to-face with oneself by manifesting an excess of devotion: that great marvel performed by You,
which consists in the manifestation of the eyes that effect both the dissolution and the nourishment of what is yet to come and what was previously seen;

That is not mine alone, but it causes wonder for everyone; and since that secret is known with difficulty, is ascertained, attained, reached, and entered, it has therefore not yet been revealed to anyone. The *yogeśvarīs* are the external ones, such as Khecarī and the others; the *mātṛs*...

Brahmā and the others, the sages of intense austerity, and the yogis who worship the Lord through the six-limbed yoga and other means—this is a marvel. "To me" refers to one who partakes in devotion to You. "Gracious" means that through the pacification of the turbidity of *māyā*, there is internal purity.

[The word] "gone" [is used]; because the term "Lord of the World" (*jagannātha*) occurs within another part of the sentence, it is not a redundancy. Since you are the Lord of the World, therefore I, having sought refuge and being solely intent upon your worship, entreat you:
you ought to tell this in its entirety to me, who have taken refuge in you. 8.
Here, the introducer of the tantra establishes the connection:
having heard these words of the Goddess, he spoke with a smiling face. (1.9)
"Aṭṭahāsa" refers to one whose face and speech possess a preeminent laughter that involves an immersion into the state of devouring others.
[As stated: "From Śiva, the supreme cause, who is tranquil and whose form is unseen, the scripture has emerged in the form of sound..."
Because it is so stated in the sacred traditions (āmnāya); and furthermore, because his face was blossoming due to the emergence of the sattvika-bhāva of laughter. ||9||
To the question "What did he say?", it is said:
The Blessed Lord spoke: "O lady of beautiful hips, tell me what, what secret resides in your heart."
"I shall tell you everything without doubt, O sinless one, for I have been gratified by you."

"Since I have been gratified by you through your knowledge of the proper occasion and your inclination toward wishing to favor others, I shall therefore declare to you the entire secret without any doubt. Tell me, what is it that resides in your heart?"—having spoken thus, he encourages the Goddess with a specific inquiry. And furthermore:
That secret which is situated within your own heart is merely unopened. In the reading "you speak," the meaning is clear. || 10 ||
Thus, in order to strengthen what had been promised by the Lord in general terms,
the venerable Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who set in motion wondrous marvels!"
I have never heard of such a wonderful and beautiful thing; now I am hearing it.
O All-pervading One, with a serene countenance, you who bring about supreme bliss;
O Blessed One, out of your lack of envy, please explain this to me.

"Such as this" refers to that which resides in my heart and is about to be made manifest; "not heard" means that its true nature has not yet been determined—I hear it now, and I desire to master it. || 12 ||
This clarifies that which is seen everywhere: that the divine eye is composed of water;
therefore, how did the fierce fire, the burner at the end of time, arise? || 1-13 ||
By whom, indeed, was Mitrāyu reduced to ashes merely upon being seen? O Lord, what such terrible deed has been done by you, who are like fire and time desiring to consume all?
The entire world, from Brahmā down to the stationary beings, was set ablaze;
likewise, O Supreme Lord, Kāma was consumed by you as if in play.
O Lord, that fire from the eye of Krodha which was seen by no one—what has been done by the God of gods is truly a cause for great wonder! (1.16)
O Lord, whose fire is visible within the eye except for yours?
Or rather, how is it that the eye itself is not perceived as being composed of fire? || 1.17 ||
O Lord of the World, with that very eye which consists entirely of nectar, you instantly nourish the entire expanding universe.
O Lord, you gladden me with a gaze that is indeed gracious—
pure as the form of nectar and bringing nourishment to the world.
Therefore, from what does fire arise that resembles the fire of cosmic destruction?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this to me in brief.
That which is seen as the "eye," appearing as a physical orb and perceived by all, is water because of its abundance of white color.
"O Goddess, the water of my eyes... [and so forth].
And because it has been stated by the Lord in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra* (10.174–175): "The Gaṅgā has issued forth in ten ways," [the eye] is of the nature of water (*ap*).
Although the logicians infer that the eye is of the nature of fire (*tejas*), nevertheless, that which is actually perceived is as follows:

Because of the reason stated therein, it is indeed formless; for this very reason, there is no *maya*—for *maya* is violence—and thus how could a contradictory fire that burns with time (*kāladāhī*) arise? What was that fierce act performed by you, the illuminator of the world, out of your sovereignty, for the sake of burning away Time, Desire, and the rest? Or rather, what is this?

Since that which was raised up at the occasion of his anger is not seen by anyone else, it must surely have been done by the God of gods, who illuminates the wheel of power of all the senses and who is ever-victorious; and because it is seen nowhere other than in you, it causes great wonder. Or rather—what else could it be?

If fire is the eye because it conforms to effects such as burning at the [proper] time and because others likewise accept it as such, then why is it not seen— just as a lamp or other sources of illumination for other things are seen? Or, even if it is not seen in that way,
how is it that you, spreading forth as this fire, nourish the world and gladden me?

And [He is] of the nature of nectar (*amṛtākāra*). Therefore, for this reason, [the author asks]: "How is it that from this cause, which is the source of the arising of nectar, there has arisen this [fire] which is like the fire of time (*kālāgni*) and burns time, desire, and so forth? How can this appear as something contradictory?"—O Supreme Lord, please explain how this is possible. || 20 ||
Questioned by the Goddess, the Blessed Lord said:
"O beloved, you ask this because you are overcome with great curiosity; listen."
Having addressed the Goddess by saying "Listen," he makes a formal declaration in order to establish a specific certainty: "That fire which is within my eye, and that unsurpassed nectar... || 1-21 ||
I shall tell you all of that through the method of yoga; listen, O beloved!

That which was previously described as the unsurpassed secret—the pair of fire and nectar within my eyes—is therefore the burner of the fetters (pāśas) and of Time (kāla), consisting of an immersion into the supreme abode (paradhāma), and the nourisher of the universe.

"By means of yogic method, through the penetration into the expansion of the supreme non-duality, I shall speak; you too should listen in that very way and reflect within. This is the opening statement.

Herein, the subject matter to be expressed is the secret of the Eye, which is the nature of the nectar of the supreme fire (paravahni). By the qualification "supreme" (anuttama), [its excellence is indicated].

The status as a means toward the two goals known as worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) has been indicated. The sixfold relationship, beginning with *parā* and ending with *adivya*, is indeed well-established. || 21 ||
He clarifies the name "Netra" (the Eye), which was proposed because it expresses the reality of the Eye, by stating:
"That whose own nature is innate, pure, all-pervasive, and facing in every direction. (1-22)
Abiding within all beings as the life-force in all living creatures,
it is attainable through yoga, difficult to approach, and hard to reach for those of unrefined self.
One's own individual power is to be personally realized; it is my very supreme state.
That power is the power of all powers, and it is indeed the strength of the strong.
All that is the vigor of vigors— eternal, immovable, and constant—
is my supreme will, the power endowed with power, born of its own nature.
Like heat in fire, or like the rays of the sun, one's own power, which is of the nature of the cause, should be understood as belonging to the entire world. (1.26)
The qualities such as omniscience and others abide therein, both manifest and unmanifest;
she herself is the will, whose nature is knowledge, and who is expanded by the qualities of action and the rest.
Indeed, those six qualities beginning with knowledge, being established therein, become manifest;
she is considered to be the single, abiding power of action (kriyā) whose form is great activity. || 1-28 ||
She brings about and transforms the eight qualities, beginning with *aṇimā*.
Thus, my power called *icchā* (will) is said to be the power known as *jñāna* (knowledge) and the power known as *kriyā* (action).
The sun, the moon, and fire constitute the conceptualization of the three abodes;
for my sake, the conceptualization of the three eyes is perceived here for that purpose. (1.30)
By means of that [power], I effect both combustion and nourishment as well as manifestation.

That which is one's own—meaning one’s very self—is the nature of the universe consisting of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower; because no specific [external] material cause is required, it is the conscious self (cidātmā) which is the cause of all arrangements.

It is pure by its very nature, all-pervasive, and while it manifests the universe within its own ground, it is not covered by the universe, like a mirror; it is that from which powers radiate in every direction,
and which consists of all cognitions of blue, pleasure, and so forth.
In accordance with the principle stated in the *Vijñānabhairava* (6.20), "The Śiva-nature is here called the mouth," [the Lord] is one whose "mouths" are the means of attainment (*prāptyupāya*).
Furthermore, in every respect, He is the primary cause of all things, from the stationary beings up to Brahmā.
It manifests as the form of the Great One (Mahantā) abiding within all beings;

it is the life-force in all living creatures whose forms are manifested as vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, having assumed the stages of *prāṇa* and the rest according to the principle that "first consciousness is transformed into *prāṇa*"; and therefore, by means of yoga—
It is to be reached by the cessation of the subjectivity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth; it is to be attained with difficulty,

for according to the principle that "this is not obtained unless Śaṅkara is propitiated," it is accessible through instruction only to one who possesses the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), and it is acquired with great hardship.

"Even when [the reality] has somehow been perceived, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) does not arise"— according to this principle, it is attainable only by certain diligent practitioners in their final birth, but not by those of unsteady intellect; for it is one's own power (*svavīrya*) of the self, which is the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).
Power is the nature of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that creates the universe; it is the venerable *Kālīkula*.
As it is said: "Of that supreme deity of deities, whose very nature is transcendental consciousness, reflective awareness is the supreme power, all-knowing and endowed with wisdom."

Thus: "It is my own," meaning self-cognizable and self-luminous; it is the supreme state (*pada*) of mine, Umāpati. The word *va* (in *mamaiva*) is displaced [from its position]. It is the potency (*vīrya*) even of all potencies, such as the various mantras, mudrās, and so forth. It alone is the strength of the powerful winds and other elements. It alone is the vital energy (*ojas*) of all vital energies.
As it has been said:
"The engagement with the possible and the impossible without regard [to their distinction] is called 'splendor' by the wise; such is the nature of the wind of consciousness."

Thus [it is said]. And all that is the universal self, eternal, non-evolving, immovable, unchanging, fixed, and constant. That "She" (seti) is my supreme power (parā śaktiḥ), which is related to me and has attained the form of will (icchā). What kind of will? Born of its own nature (svabhāvajā).
It is endowed with innate power (*sahajā śakti*), which means it is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is non-different from the entire range of cosmic powers contained within it.
And it is said in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara): "That power of the Creator of the world which is declared to be inherent (*samavāyinī*)."
"That goddess assumes the state of desire for him who wishes to create," and so forth (*Mālinīvijaya Tantra* 3.5).
By the term "inherent nature" (*svabhāvajā*), she clarifies that she is like the heat of fire or the form of the sun's rays;
and by the phrase "endowed with power" (*śaktiyuktā*), she reveals her nature. By the word "of all" (*sarvasya*), she is shown to be the causal essence of the entire universe.

The "creator" (nirmātrī) is her own inherent power (śakti), which is connected to the nature of consciousness and bliss (cidānanda-svarūpa), and not something separate. As for "omniscient," those qualities such as omniscience and the rest also abide within that very will (icchā); whether manifest or unmanifest, they exist there in a state of being merely indicated (āsūtrita-rūpa). That [will] itself is the will.
"The power of will itself, making it known with perfect certainty in this world that 'this is so, and not otherwise,' is called the power of knowledge. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.7)

Thus, according to the previously stated principle, having attained the state of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), it is said: "When [the will] arises again, thinking 'let this object become thus,' then, by making it so, it is here called the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.8)

Thus, by way of this state, the power of action (kriyā-śakti) is perfected. Of what nature is it? It is expanded by all the qualities (guṇas) and has attained extension through all effects in the form of attributes (dharmas). As for "knowledge and so forth" (jñānādi), those [qualities] such as omniscience (sarvajñatva) and others which were previously mentioned in the context of Will (icchā) as being merely sketched out, they are present therein.

Established in the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), they become manifest in the state of the venerable Lord (*īśvarabhaṭṭāraka*) and thus prevail and expand. Indeed, because this is so, it was rightly stated previously that they are "manifest and unmanifest. That very [power] is the Great Action (*mahākriyā*); it is the power of action whose nature is the venerable Lord, and it is that very [power] which is action itself.
In the creation of the universe, the Lord’s power is considered to be one and non-dual in its causal form.
It is that very power which effects, generates, transforms, sustains, and withdraws the *aṇimā* and other [siddhis]—this is the meaning.
Thus, according to the stated principle, my power, whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), is said to consist of the triad beginning with will (*icchā*).

Regarding the term "Sūrya" (the Sun): it is precisely within the three powers of Will and the rest (*icchā-ādi-śakti-traya*) that the conceptualization of Fire, Sun, and Moon occurs in the central, right, and left channels. Both internally and externally, the Sun and the others are nothing but the expanded manifestation (*sphāra-rūpa*) of the powers of Will and the rest. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:
"This power of knowledge of the Lord shines in the form of the sun;

... the power of action shines in the form of the moon" (Svacchandatantra 10.498–502), and so forth. Regarding the "three eyes," the conceptualization of three eyes is for the sake of manifesting my own form to me.

Here, in the opening of the three eyes, that [reality] is perceived; and that too is for the purpose of manifesting the triad of powers presiding over the three determined abodes. As it is said in the *Bhārata* as well:

"When the three goddesses constantly attend upon him, he is then to be known as Tryambaka... Thus, because the supreme abode itself has been described by the stated reasoning as being of the nature of the Eye (*netra*), it is called "the burner" (*dahana*).
Whatever I do—whether it be the destruction of time, the burning away of desire, the nourishment of the world, or its illumination—that is entirely appropriate;
for what indeed is impossible for the all-powerful abode of consciousness? This is the sense.
Therefore:
And as one possessing three bodies, I perform creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
I alone am that one consisting of pure consciousness, whose three bodies are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; through them, I perform creation and the other cosmic functions in succession.

Furthermore, having assumed the forms of Āśrita, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara, I effect creation and the rest—indicated by the word "and" (ca)—as well as dissolution and grace, within the sphere of the paths supported by my own foundation.
"I alone perform the fivefold acts and so forth; there are none whatsoever who act apart from me.
Those who, disregarding such a clear literal meaning, assert that the Lord's agency in creation and the rest is through the presiding of Brahmā and others, are indeed deluded. (1.31)
Moreover,
that which is filled with vigor and augmented by my own splendor,
consisting of will, knowledge, and action, is the unsurpassed nectar of the eyes. (1.32)

That light of mine—which is filled with the vitality (*vīrya*) consisting of the power of absolute freedom (*svātantryaśakti*) proclaimed by Him; which is nourished by the nature of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*); which is all-pervasive and performs functions such as satiation; and which consists of the state of equilibrium among the triad of powers beginning with Will (*icchā*)—that [light], it [is].

Because it possesses the nature of protecting the eyes and so forth—as will be described—and because it consists of imperishable supreme bliss, it is called *amṛta* (the nectar); and since there is nothing else superior to it, it is called *anuttama* (unsurpassed). ||32||
Moreover, what is that supreme abode of vigor which consists of the highest nectar;
that which is that very supreme bliss, and this which is the supreme state? || 1.33 ||
This very [reality] is partless knowledge, the pure and supreme eye;

it is that aforementioned vitality (*vīrya*) whose essence is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*). It is the supreme abode because it acts as the illuminator of the sun and other luminaries, and it consists of the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*) because it is imperishable by virtue of its nature as consciousness. That which is "that" is this.

Brahman is of the nature of supreme bliss. That which is "this"—ever self-luminous—is the supreme, most excellent state (*pada*) or abode (*dhāma*), because it is the locus of the foundation for the entire universe, both external and internal. "That which is this" refers to that very reality through the demonstrative pronoun *tat*, which functions as a clear, direct reference.

That which was previously touched upon everywhere is now made manifest; by the word "this" (*etad*), together with the word "that" (*tat*), he demonstrates the recognition whose object is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). It is partless (*niṣkala*), having emerged from all parts (*kalā*), and that from which the parts have emerged is likewise pure (*viśuddha*).

That consciousness which is the supreme non-dual self is called the "eye" (netra); it is not, however, the form of Aghora, Gopāla, or the like as suspected in the text of the question, nor is it the form of the eternal, inferable Taijasa witness-consciousness. || 33 ||
Since this has been thus proclaimed by Mṛtyujit, it bestows liberation upon all.

This [text] grants the attainment of that supreme deity who bestows liberation from all suffering; the particle *ca* is used in the sense of "and. By means of that form, which is the partless conscious self (*niṣkalacidātman*), this "Conqueror of Death" (*mṛtyujit*) has been described; and this is also a sūtra-like indication of the future methods for conquering death. For all...
By the phrase "bestowing liberation," the eligibility for the daily rites (*nityakarman*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is indicated. And he will say:
"All living beings, beginning with Brahmins, who are afflicted by the fear of all defects..."
"By the mere remembrance of which, they are indeed liberated... (Ne. 2.16).

By the word "of all," it is meant that through the pervasion of the supreme non-duality to be described hereafter, this applies to those who worship various deities well-known in all the [religious] currents, from Viṣṇu down to Sugata.

It is indicated that the ground of liberation is indeed equal [to all]. "Bestowing its accomplishment" is an introduction to the subsequent section on accomplishment (*siddhi*). By the phrase "the supreme deity," the immersion into the essential nature of the reality of illumination and so forth is hinted at; as he will state:
"If he is perceived in a mere blink of an eye, from that moment on he is liberated and shall not undergo rebirth again. (Netra Tantra 8.9).
For this very reason, for those who have entered into the supreme existence, apart from the state of being a subject limited by the body and so forth—
Because it prevents contact with future suffering, it grants liberation from all suffering. ||34||
The god who removes all diseases, the auspicious one who removes all ailments.
It eternally pacifies poverty, conquers death, and faces in all directions;

it removes all various mental anxieties, physical ailments, and diseases such as fevers through the diverse forms of mantras, yantras, and other methods to be described in the sixteenth and fifteenth chapters.

And for this reason, *śiva* is of the nature of the supreme good (*śreyaḥ*). By the phrase "the pacifier of poverty," the ritual procedure beginning with the worship of Śrī Mahālakṣmī, which will be described in the eighteenth chapter, is introduced. By the phrase "eternally the conqueror of death" (*nityaṃ mṛtyujit*), the supreme [deity] mentioned in the eighth chapter is indicated.

The method for conquering death (*mṛtyuñjaya*) has been indicated. By the phrase "having made [the deity] all-facing" (*sarvatomukhaṃ ca kṛtvā*), the method of conquering death based on subtle meditation (*sūkṣmadhyāna*) found in the seventh chapter is pointed out;
likewise, the methods arising from meditation, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth are also suggested. As he will state:
"When one is overcome by diseases or has even reached an untimely death,
then one should worship with white offerings or with milk and ghee."
"By performing a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds or with milk-soaked sacrificial fuel, one attains peace," and so forth. (6.37.38) || 35 ||
Moreover, it is unfailing, stainless, peaceful, the giver of all, and the liberator from everything. || 1-36 ||
Even the combined brilliance of thousands of millions of suns and tens of thousands of millions of fires is not worth a sixteenth part of his splendor.
Since it consists entirely of splendor and is unassailable by gods or asuras,
I shall surely consume everything in an instant with that fire from my eye.
By that very [means], I further effect its nourishment and manifest its luminosity.

Because it consists of the ultimate fruit whose nature is supreme bliss, it is unfailing; because it shines constantly in all states, it is stainless; and because differentiation has ceased, it is tranquil—thus it is of the nature of pure consciousness alone. Nevertheless...

He is the giver of all; although he is the creator of the universe and the agent of its emanation and so forth, because his sole intent is to bestow grace, he grants liberation from everything as well as long life, strength, and other such qualities. As he will state:
"Longevity, strength, fame, joy, fortitude, intelligence, beauty, and prosperity..."
"His supreme sovereignty over the lords of the earth proceeds entirely [from that]," and so forth (Netra Tantra 6.46).

Whatever is conceived through imagination—whether it be equal to the splendor of countless suns, fires, and so on—that too exists only because it is a mental construction. "Of him" refers to the aforementioned Great Radiance (*mahādhāman*).

It does not merit even a sixteenth part, nor is it comparable in even the most subtle degree, because its nature is solely that of the non-constructed supreme subject (*akalpita-parapramātṛ*). It is invincible and unassailable. Since it says, "I burn everything," what need is there to mention Time and Desire at the onset of the great dissolution? This is certain and settled.

By that very means, I shall again effect nourishment and illumination for all objects at the end of the kalpa; what need then be said of nourishing beings whose elements are exhausted, or of illuminating the hopes of those whose eyes are veiled by wind and other such afflictions?
And by this, the emission (sṛṣṭi) and so forth occurring in the twenty-one chapters have been introduced. || 38 ||
Moreover, nothing else more supreme than that is seen anywhere as a source of vigor. (1.39)
That very [power] consists of weapons, is fierce, and is the supreme means for the rescue of living beings;
this indeed is the supreme virility. As he will say:
"Indeed, infinite millions of mantras exist, established as both manifest and unmanifest."
"All these grant success because they are constricted at the initial and final *tuṭis*. (Ne. 14.9).

By this, the supreme nature of all mantras found in the fourteenth and twenty-second chapters is indicated. Therefore, it is the fierce weapon that cuts through duality, consisting of the *astra*, and having the form of the sword of knowledge for all individual souls (*aṇus*).
This is the supreme means of deliverance for living beings. || 39 ||
Likewise, this is proclaimed to be a weapon that brings about the destruction of all enemies. || 1-40 ||

That which sustains the life-span of all beings is called *āyudha* (a weapon); it is called *śastra* because it is the cause for the destruction of all enemies, for the root *śas* has the meaning of "to injure.
As he will state:
"It brings victory to kings who are terrified by foreign kingdoms" (Ne. 17.6).

[The word] "of all" refers to the fourteen classes of beings, beginning with the immobile; it sustains their life-force (*āyus*) and vital breaths (*prāṇa*) because its nature is solely that of pure, autonomous consciousness (*svaccha-svatantra-cideka-rūpatva*). And that is the weapon.
Because no distinction is stated, everything [is included], since it consists of great heroic power. || 40 ||
Thus it is said: "That single potency is spread out in many ways, diffused through the infinity of its divisions. (1.41)
It has spread forth through an infinite variety of divisions and manifold diversities. || 41 ||
He clarifies this very point:
"The Mahāpāśupata [weapon] belongs to me; that Sudarśana belongs to Viṣṇu;
the Brahmadaṇḍa belongs to Brahmā; and for all others, there is their own respective weapon. (1.42)
"Mahyam" means "for my sake"; the remainder is clear. || 42 ||
And this weapon, which exists in many forms and varieties,
is my own heroic power bestowed upon the gods in their respective individual forms.

Whatever manifold weapons belong to all the gods in their various forms and essential natures, that is my own power which has been surrendered; it means that it has appeared in such and such a variety of ways. || 43 ||

Now, an objection has been raised by the proponents of dualism: "Śiva is one and changeless, and his power is likewise; therefore, they two are not capable of existing in manifold ways, or else [they would be so] because they would be subject to modification if deprived of consciousness. How then can this [position of yours] be maintained?
By the power of yoga, however, this entire universe is pervaded by that Lord of Yoga.

According to the principle stated in the sacred tradition (Āmnāya): "His own inherent yogic powers flash forth on all sides," the power—that is, the capacity—of the yogic energies such as Vāmā and the others, [is what is meant].

By her, the entire universe is pervaded, woven warp and woof in every part—that is to say, through identity with her. As it is stated in the *Śivasūtras*: "The universe is the accumulation of his own powers" (Śiva Sūtra 3.30).
Thus [it is said].
Moreover, for those who are afraid, it is the supreme protection; for those who are terrified, it is the ultimate fearlessness.
It is the supreme and certain bestower of liberation for those afflicted by enemies;

it is the ultimate protection for those who are afraid— namely, those mentioned in the nineteenth chapter to be described, who are oppressed by various defects of their own reflections (*chāyā-doṣa*), spirits (*bhūta*), planets (*graha*), *yakṣas*, *śākinīs*, and so forth— as will be explained in that specific section.
It is the supreme unsealing; and for those who are terrified, it is the supreme fear. As he will say:
"He provides protection for all and the deliverance for those whose minds are terrified" (22.11). "Terror" (*trāsa*) is a violent striking of the heart, as well as the affliction caused by enemies.
It is the supreme terror. As he will say:
"At the time of battle, she who dwells upon the blade of a sword, like a leafy creeper, should be meditated upon;
she certainly bestows victory and becomes the destroyer of the enemy's pride. (18.86)
This king of mantras is dedicated to Mahālakṣmī; it is certain and definitive that it bestows supreme liberation—this is its primary essential nature.
"What is the use of speaking at such great length or repeating yourself again and again, O beautiful one? (1.45)
Whatever is most intense, fierce, glorious, or indeed powerful—
that very thing is indeed grace, the bestower of boons, the highest good, and manifestation.
That object of knowledge is immeasurable, and that wisdom is the great power of mantra;
it is the protector of all beings, and it must always be kept secret and hidden by you.
O Goddess, that has been told to you today; what more do you wish to ask?

It accomplishes even the most intense, the instantaneous, and the seemingly impossible; it is fierce, the destroyer, glorious, possessed of great majesty, powerful with extraordinary strength, exceedingly pure in its grace, and the bestower of boons.
It bestows whatever is desired; it is the essence of the highest good, consisting of the repose within one's own self after all afflictions have been stilled.

It is light itself that is the object to be illuminated, appearing in the form of luminaries such as the sun, moon, and fire. "Whatever there may be" means everything whatsoever that exists within the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan); all that is indeed this very [light].

By the phrase "whose essential nature is a mass of light and bliss as previously described," the Lord Netranātha’s state of being composed of the entire universe and his absolute preeminence are stated. The particle *hi* (for/indeed) indicates the logical connection: since this is so, what is the use of further elaboration?
And by this revelation of his universal self-nature...

The true nature (*satattva*) of all conduct, which will be demonstrated in the sixteen chapters, has been introduced. That very reality, because it is the most excellent of all (*viśvottama*), is to be known; and because it is the universal self (*sārvātmya*), it is both possible and worthy to be known.
Furthermore, it is immeasurable knowledge, whose nature is uninterrupted consciousness (*anavacchinna-saṃvid-rūpa*), and not [the object] of anyone else.
It is the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it is said in the *Trikahṛdaya*:
"Just as a dog seeks to leap over its own head's shadow, yet its head cannot be at the place where its feet are; so too is this *bindu*-kalā."
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"Of the variegated painting of the manifold universe" (2.3.15).
The great power and supreme vigor of the mantras, numbering in the tens of millions—this and...
This has been introduced in the fourteen, twenty-first, and twenty-second chapters as that which will come to pass.

And this is radiant with the *tāra* [syllable] because it protects (*trāṇa*) all beings through a manifold display of grace; since it is protection (*trāṇa*), it is *trā*, and by that it is *tāra*. Because it is thus, it is a supreme secret well-guarded. Therefore, it must be concealed.

"This must be protected by you and revealed only to those upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has occurred, and not to others. And these [disciples] are worthy of this; it was told to them at the occasion of their desire to know the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*) through an extremely intense descent of power.
[The phrase] 'What more do you ask? is used to grant space for the subject matter (*prameya*) that is yet to come."
This is for the purpose of reconciling the *Pāṭalika* [tradition]; may there be auspiciousness.

We worship the glorious Eye of Īśvara, beautiful through its aesthetic harmony with the universal selfhood of the entire universe without exception, and consisting of a mass of consciousness and bliss.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Netrodyota*, a commentary on the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the venerable and preeminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 1.
The second chapter,
"The Illumination of the Net":
That which is praised as the eightfold form, the universal form, and the formless.
We bow to the mantra-form, the eye of the Great Lord, which is the embodiment of that consciousness.
Having been granted the opportunity by the words, "What more do you wish to ask?",
and having first restated the reality already understood, the Śrī Devī spoke, desiring to favor the world and wishing to bring down the nature of the mantra.
If it is thus, O Lord, that supreme tranquility, the abode of immeasurable virtues, and the energy that benefits all has been heard by me from your own mouth. (2.1)
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who act for the benefit of the worlds;
all this, born from the three wombs—whether among animals, humans, or gods—is [your creation].

Agitated by the fear of mental and physical ailments, afflicted by the dread of poisons and malevolent spirits, beset by hundreds of untimely deaths, and possessed by fever, cough, and consumption. (2–3)
In the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Mānuṣa, living beings such as Brahmins and others are beset by hundreds of miseries and defects; O Lord, whence can there be happiness for them? (2-4)
According to the measure appropriate for their respective ages,
those endowed with strength and augmented by your own splendor and power will seek to destroy them according to their own standards.
Greatly afflicted by hundreds of various types of diseases and divisions, for the sake of favoring them and for the benefit of living beings, [I have composed this] out of compassion. (2-6)
O Lord of the World, [teach] the means of speech by which [beings] are liberated from everything.

The vocatives are as before. If it is so, according to what has been said, then that supreme vigor—characterized by tranquility and other qualities—which was determined in the previous section, has been heard from Your mouth.

O Blessed One, it is all-encompassing; it is the benefactor of the universe. It concerns the fourteen-fold creation of beings, which is beset by diseases and other afflictions, as well as the Brahmins and others in the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Mānuṣa, who are overwhelmed by innumerable sufferings and defects such as passion and hatred. And for them—
Even a lifespan measured according to the [duration of the] Yugas is increased by your splendor and power;
yet, Śākinīs, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, Grahas, and the like, along with diseases, desire to destroy it.
Therefore, out of compassion for all those living beings, instruct us in the beneficial means by which these [may be protected].
All those who were severely oppressed are liberated, freed from all calamities, and attain final release. || 6 ||
And thereafter,
by whatever means— through the yoga of knowledge, through mantra, or otherwise— (2.7)
"O Lord of Gods, tell me the means for whatever you perceive.
O Lord of Gods, O Self, relying upon the mantras of the yoga of knowledge, tell me the means for that perceived welfare— be it by whatever means, whether gross, subtle, or supreme."
Speak.
In this context, the introducer of the tantra establishes the connection:
having thus heard the words of the Goddess, Śaṅkara laughed and spoke. (2–8)

"Having laughed"— this is because it was commanded that "I shall speak through the application of yoga," and so forth; thus, having laughed due to the immersion in the supreme vibration (*parasphurattā*), and furthermore, having let out a loud laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*) due to the immersion in the awareness of *nāda* according to the principle previously described, what is that which belongs to him?
Having smiled, [he thought], "This is impossible for the Blessed One to accomplish. || 8 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
O Goddess, you ask me this question out of being possessed by great compassion;
I have never been questioned by anyone, nor has anything ever been told by me to anyone.

Since I have been questioned here by you out of great compassion, whereas I have not been questioned by anyone else, I too have not declared this to anyone, in accordance with the maxim: "One should not speak to anyone unless asked.
Therefore:
Among all mantras, it is proclaimed to be the very eye;
yet within my heart, it has not been perceived by anyone, for it is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Today I shall explain to you the supreme, eternal [teaching] of three kinds,
which is accessible through mantra, yoga, and knowledge, and which is the bestower of liberation and the excellent attainment of perfection.
As for that which you asked regarding the nature of the "eye" (*netra*): among the three and a half million mantras existing as the most preeminent, and among the objects of sense, it is the "eye.
Just as the eye is the primary organ among the other senses, so it is the foremost among all existing entities.
And it is likewise proclaimed as the illuminator; as he will say:
"The Lord is common to all, bestowing the fruit of all accomplishments, since he is remembered as the very life-force of all mantras. (13.44)
Thus it is said. And at the time of teaching all the scriptures, this [truth] which resides within my own intention was not understood by anyone;

for it is extremely difficult to attain, being the supreme non-duality that is the self of all, which is indicated in all the scriptures through cryptic expressions and is hard to discern by those conditioned by the sense of duality.

Because it is accessible through the knowledge of this mantra-yoga, I shall today certainly declare to you, who are worthy, that which is attained through the gross, subtle, and supreme means— threefold, eternal, constant, and bearing the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation; thus, once again, there is the presentation of the reality of the object along with its means and purpose.
He makes a specific promise, because this matter is of the utmost importance to be adopted. || 11 ||
In this regard, I shall first describe the mantra-form, which is endowed with the threefold accomplishment,
complete with its limbs, joined with its own mudrā, and supremely protective in every respect. (2.12)

That supreme form which was introduced is such that its essential nature is mantra, because awareness has *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) as its core; it possesses the threefold accomplishments (*siddhi*) distinguished by their being future, terrestrial, atmospheric, and celestial.

Accompanied by the six limbs beginning with the heart, joined with the future Padmāmṛta-mudrā, the performer of universal protection and the bestower of grace upon all—I shall speak; this is the formal promise of authority regarding the subject matter of the mantra. || 12 ||
Furthermore, [he is not disturbed] by hosts of spirits, yakṣas, those possessed by madness, śākinīs, and yoginīs;
nor by sisters, mothers of Rudra, ḍāvis, ḍāmarikas, and the like.
Even if they are sealed by many *rūpikās*, by *apasmāras*, and by *piśācas* in great numbers, or by *brahmarākṣasas*, *grahas*, and so forth, by the tens of millions; (2.14)
Overcome by untimely deaths and sought to be slain by the nooses of Time, kings, princes, and royal consorts have indeed perished in great numbers. (2.15)
I shall tell you that by which all living beings, beginning with Brahmins, who are afflicted by the fear of all defects, are indeed liberated merely through its recollection. (2.16)

If those who have been sealed by the Bhūtas and other spirits, those who have encountered untimely death and are sought to be slain by the nooses of Time, those such as kings who protect the subjects and have reached their destined death,
and those such as Brahmins who are protected by them— all these [are freed from] whatever fear there may be from all defects, such as diseases and the like.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "I shall tell you the nature of that mantra by which those afflicted by them are liberated simply through its recollection. *Bhūtas* are those residing in places such as empty wells, solitary trees, and crossroads.
*Yakṣas* are powerful classes of sentient beings. *Grahas* include the *bālagrahas*, *ratigrahas*, and so forth.
*Unmāda* is the manifestation of various mental states such as incoherent prattle, causeless anger, and desire.

*Śākinī* is she who draws forth animal blood and other substances for the purpose of transforming physical form. The *yoginīs* are goddesses born from the sacred seats (*pīṭha*). The *bhaginīs* arise from portions of Brahmā and the other [deities]. The *rudramātaraḥ*, however, are Brahmāṇī and the others.
In the *Śrīsarvavīra*, it is said: "The Ḍāvyas and Ḍāmarikās possess the knowledge of entering another's mind and effecting the transformation of form;
she who is greedy for nectar should be known as Rudraḍākinī."
Having begun thus:
"And such women are to be known as ḍākinīs, who delight in secret conduct and worship;
they taste [the offerings] but do not kill, though they are intent on seeking out faults."
But others are to be known as ḍāmarīs, whose minds are absorbed in the mantra;
they partake of the supreme nectar and cause human beings to be carried along.

"They roam the entire earth, assuming various forms"—thus they are characterized. The *rūpikās* are harmful female spirits. Epilepsy (*apasmāra*) causes sudden falls, loss of consciousness, frothing at the mouth, and so forth. They dwell in cremation grounds and similar places.

The *ulkāmukhas* are *piśācas*; the *brahmarākṣasas* are a specific class of *rākṣasas*; and the *grahas* are Mars and other planets that have attained an unfavorable aspect. We shall explain their true nature in detail later on. (16)
Now, regarding the extraction of the mantra, he describes the procedure:
on a level and pure plot of ground, smeared with sandalwood and agallochum, rich with the fragrance of camphor and perfumed with the scent of saffron. (2.17)
But the teacher, with a serene mind, anointed with sandalwood and agallochum,
adorned with ornaments such as the uṣṇīṣa, is one of great intelligence.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus, one should inscribe the *mātṛkā* thereon.

"In the pure" means in unmixed colors. "With sandalwood" (*candana*) means worshipped with sandalwood and other substances as the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*). "Serene" (*prasanna*) refers to one whose self has attained the purity resulting from immersion into Śiva. "Candaneti" [is the vocative].
Having performed his daily obligatory rites, he was possessed of great intelligence and knew the true nature of the *mātṛkā*s;
for "mother" (*mātṛ*) is unknown, while the "matrix" (*mātṛkā*) is the mother of all mantras and other such things without exception. (18)
To the question "How?", he says:
"Having placed the three bodies in the middle, one should write the groups [of letters] starting from the east. (2-19)
One should contemplate the Oṃkāra three times in the center of the pericarp, and the consonant groups beginning with ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya,
and śa, in order, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.

Having written it in this manner, one should worship with supreme devotion according to the sequence of recitation, using extensive offerings of flowers, incense, and so forth; O Goddess, one should then extract the Mother of Mantras, the deity of the mantra.
"Should extract" means immediately after the worship. || 20 ||
He states the extraction:
"Beginning with Viśva, ending with Viśvarūpa, and having Viśvahā as the sprout of nectar;
Light, Sound, Supreme Power (Parāśakti), and Śiva are established together in one place. (2.21)

The first letter of the universe (*viśva*) is the vowel *a*; the end of the *māyā* whose form is the universe (*viśvarūpā*) is the vowel *u*; and *viśvahā*, meaning time, is represented by the syllable *ma*. Furthermore, the first creator of the universe is Brahmā, and because it denotes him, it is the vowel *a*; likewise, [it refers to] Viśvarūpa.

That whose final determination is Viṣṇu is the letter *u*; since Rudra is the destroyer of the universe, the letter *ma* is likewise so called because it denotes him—thus the extraction follows the meaning of what is expressed.

The nectar (*amṛta*) is the point (*bindu*), which consists of the knowledge of the non-difference between the entire world of objects of cognition; the sprout (*kandala*) is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).

The *jyotirnirodhikā* consists of a clear line; the resonance (*dhvani*) is the nature of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is non-different from all denoters; the sound (*nāda*) takes the form of *ha* and *ka-lā*; and the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), situated between the two points (*bindu*), is the clear line. Here, by means of *nāda*, the end of sound (*nādānta*) is subsumed.

By means of the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), the powers of Aparā and the others existing on lower levels—namely the powers Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā—are internalized. Śiva, whose essence is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of non-difference from the aforementioned universe, is to be perceived as standing above all else in the form of the supreme sound (*paranāda*). Thus it is said.
The Sequence of the Dissolution of Dust:

"The manifestation of the unity of Brahmā, Upendra, Hara, Aṇḍaja, Umā, and Vāk, which reaches the end of the obstruction of the crescent moon of one's own knowable objects as they dissolve, serves for the ascent to the ground of Nāda."

"When the object of knowledge has dissolved within the two states of the knower of sound (nāda) and the level above it (tala), then that state of non-conceptualization (amananā), which is the stage of the pervasion of the touch of the clear internal resonance, is the *unmanā* of the principles (tattva)—to that we offer praise.
Thus is the sequence of the piercing of the heart (*hṛdbheda*). This is because of the statement: "established in one place."
The fact that the entire collection of categories has the single syllable *praṇava* as its essence has been demonstrated. || 21 ||
He describes its greatness:
"By this [tantra] everything is strung together like clusters of gems upon a thread;
from it have arisen seventy million mantras for those who are qualified. (2.22)

"Grathita" means strung together, that is to say, pervaded. Regarding the statement "seven crores of mantras," it was only during the first creation that there was authority for that many; however, immediately thereafter, "as soon as the world was born... [the rest follows].
"Three and a half crores of mantras were appointed by Śiva;
having graced the multitude of individual souls (aṇu), they have gone to the state free from affliction.
Since this is stated in the *Śrīpūrva* [Mālinīvijayottara Tantra], three and a half crores are authorized. (22)
He extracts the second seed-syllable:
it ends with the word *citrabhānu*, has the interior of a crescent moon within it, is placed above a goad (*aṅkuśa*), and is joined with a downward-pointing [hook] and an upward-pointing [hook]. (23)

The word *citrabhānu* (the sun) refers to the letter *pa*, which belongs to the lotus (*pādma*) and is the leaf of fire (*āgneya*). Within that is the letter *ṅa*, which is associated with the *ka*-group (*kavarga*).
That [letter *ṅa*] has within its belly or center (*udara*) a digit of the moon (*śaśāṅkaśakala*), namely the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
Following this method of extraction, the letter *ja* arises as having the nature of both fire and moon (*agnīṣoma*). Of that, the goad is the vowel *u*.

"Upward" (ūrdhva) means that which is to be placed above should be performed. Likewise, there is the wind moving horizontally on its petal; the "end" (anta) with respect to the labial class (*pavarga*) is the letter *ma*. By that, it is joined upward, meaning it has a conjunction in the form of a bindu. And here, the bindu is intended for the purpose of outlining the objects of knowledge such as the half-moon and so forth. || 23 ||
He speaks of its majesty: "This is that supreme abode; this is that supreme nectar.
The meaning is that it is a mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaghana*).
He extracts the third,
which is designated as the supreme nectar, renowned throughout the world.
That which is endowed with a digit of nectar and resembles the radiance of the full moon—

being self-evident through the flashing forth of its own true nature and because it involves the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of the actual existence of the bliss of immersion— is designated as the supreme nectar (*amṛta*).
"World-renowned" means that it is well-known in the world as the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*), consisting of the letter *sa*.

It is joined with the supreme power of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśakti*) called the sixteenth digit of nectar (*pīyūṣakalā*) or *Amā*, because it brings about the state of being composed of supreme nectar for the entire existence of the universe; thus, it is equal to the radiance of the full moon.
Since the greatness of the third seed-syllable has been stated by the expression "that which is designated as supreme," he now declares the greatness of the Lord of all Mantras:
"This is that supreme abode; this is that supreme state. (2.25)
This is that supreme vigor; this is that supreme nectar.
It is the highest splendor among all splendors, the most excellent light among all lights. (2.26)
The Lord is the God, the supreme cause of the entire world;
he is the creator, the sustainer, and the destroyer, and there is no one as powerful as him.

For this is the abode of mantras and the locus of all the qualities of accomplishment (*siddhi*). These words are used for the purpose of identifying its essential nature: the supreme and unsurpassed *dhāman* is the light of consciousness; the *pada* is the ground of rest; and *vīrya* is the power.

Amṛta is bliss; the God of all— that is, of the world consisting of the six paths— is the shining, supreme cause independent of material causes and the like, [residing] upon the wall of His own consciousness, [and presiding over] the splendors of the fires such as Kālāgni and the luminaries such as the sun, moon, and pole star.
He is the illuminator of the universe, which, though not distinct from Him, appears as if distinct; therefore, He is powerful and capable.

There is no one equal to Him in performing the fivefold cosmic acts, such as creation, because He alone is a single, pure, and autonomous mass of consciousness. This is not the case for Sadāśiva and the others.

For it is precisely by His will that those who have been illumined by this [Light] perform the acts of creation and so forth, through being sprinkled with a drop of this sovereign power (*aiśvarya*). And He will say this:
"Indeed, by His power, the Lord performs everything because of His omnipotence."
The deity is the efficient cause, just as the sun is the cause of the activity of a sun-crystal.
"But that power, when agitated through conjunction, is grasping (*upādāna*). (21.50–51).

We shall explain this very point in that same place. It is called "the abode of mantras" because it is the essence of the potency (*vīrya*) consisting of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*), and because it is the source of all the desired accomplishments (*siddhi*) sought by practitioners.
And he is the locus, the support, of the qualities such as omniscience and the rest.
Now,
I shall describe the auxiliary limbs (aṅga), equipped with which one attains success.
The "limbs" (aṅgāni) are the heart and so forth; "bound" (saṃnaddhaḥ) means having undertaken [the practice] in the daily obligatory rites (nitya), occasional rites (naimittika), and so on;

the practitioner (sādhaka) and others "attain success" (siddhyati), meaning they obtain enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti); as for the teacher (ācārya), he bestows [these] upon his spiritual sons (putraka) and others by implication. And by this [verse], which introduces the future daily rites and so forth, the sequence of the text (pāṭalika) [is established].
The connection has been shown. || 28 ||

Therein, the heart-mantra, which bestows all accomplishments, consists of the middle letter of the end-maker (kṣ), followed by the king of vowels (a) and the fifth note (pa), with the end of the wind (ya) at its head. || 29 ||
The second mantra consists of the middle letter of the *ca*-group (*ja*) belonging to Kṛtānta situated in the southern half;
the fifth letter of the *ava*-group (*u*), which is the Lord of Vowels (Indra), follows it and is positioned below it;
and the letter at the end of Prabhañjana (*ma*), in the form of a bindu, is placed upon its head. Thus is the second mantra.
This very seed-syllable is determined to be the heart; through its possession of great majesty, it bestows all supernatural attainments. || 29 ||
He states the head-mantra: joined with that which begins with fire (RA) and ends with Soma (SA), and conjoined with the Praṇava (OM);
this is the head...

The letter *va* is at the end of the group [of letters] situated in the directions starting from the Moon (the North). It is joined with the first letter of the Fire-god—that is, the letter *ra*, which is the color of fire—and is mixed with the *praṇava*. Thus, through the unification of these three—*va*, *ya*, and *om*—this is the "Head," the *Śiras-mantra*.
Then,
the *māyā* [syllable] joined with the end of *anila* is known as the *śikhā*.
Māyā is *ī*, with the end of *anila* (the letter *ya*) as before, joined with the *bindu*; thus, according to the uninterrupted tradition, it is known as the *śikhā*. || 30 ||
Regarding the armor (kavaca), he says: "Ending with Īśa and above Īśvara, joined with the twelve and half-above; then conjoined with Śiva, Śakti, and Nāda—that is the supreme armor. (2-31)
The letter *ha* ends the group of letters beginning with *īśa* (the letter *i*) and ending with *ga*; this is because the letter *kṣa* is treated as a separate "peak-syllable" (*kūṭākṣara*).
Alternatively, it may mean that *īśa* refers to the face of Īśāna, and that which has *kṣa* at its end;
thus, *īśvara* refers to the venerable Lord Īśvara, whose head is above, consisting of the *bindu*. This is the half of the twelve.
The sixth seed-syllable, *u*, is joined above [the previous one]; by the phrase "Śiva and Śakti," all that is to be measured by the upper mantras is expressed; *varma* means armor. || 31 ||
He states the Eye-mantra:
preceded by Bhairava and others, with the Praṇava and situated at the head of Sadāgati;
this Eye-mantra is most formidable and destroys all sins. (2-32)

Bhairava is the designator of Jhāṅkārabhairava; his first letter is *ja*. That which exists together with the first letter of Bhairava is the form of the *praṇava* (Oṃ), situated upon—that is, above—the head of the letter *ya*, which is the syllable of Vāyu. Thus, it consists of the unification of this triad. [The term] "Mahogra" [is explained as follows].

Because all differentiation has been burnt away by the fire of Bhairava, which is agitated by the power of Śakti, it therefore burns away all sins. The word "ca" (and) conjoins the quality of bestowing ultimate repose. || 32 ||
Regarding the weapon-mantra, he says:
"This weapon-mantra is proclaimed as being conjoined with the 'ajīvaka'.
Since no living being (*jīva*) exists therein, it is the letter *pha*, which is the syllable of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*). That—

And this [syllable] is joined with the letter *ṭa*, which is lifeless (*ajīvaka*), breathless (*aprāṇa*), and boneless (*anacka*), being perfectly endowed with the essence of withdrawal (*saṃhārasāra*).
The word *ajīvaka* is to be repeated twice.
He summarizes: "The sixfold limb of the king of mantras, which bestows accomplishment, has been fully explained. (2.33)

Right effort has been declared to be the essence, meaning that it bestows accomplishment upon those who practice; by this, the connection to the subsequent section is indicated. May there be auspiciousness! 33.
[Salutations] to the Eye of the Lord, who is the light of a single mass of perfect and beautiful consciousness, joined with limbs consisting of the sixfold qualities such as omniscience,
and who performs the fivefold cosmic functions in their entirety.
We pay homage to the Mantra, the sole Great Lord of all mantras.

Thus ends the second chapter, the Extraction of Mantras (*mantroddhāra*), in the *Netrodyota* commentary on the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 2.
The third chapter,
titled "The Illumination of the Net," begins, by the illumination of which the daily rites of the great-souled ones proceed.
We praise that Nīlalohita, the leader who dispels all afflictions without exception.

Having stated that it "bestows success," the Blessed One spoke in order to reveal the daily rites (*nityakarman*) for the purpose of establishing authority through the fulfillment of the procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*):
"Now I shall describe the sacrifice by which the king of mantras attains success."

"Now," [meaning] when the nature of the mantra being propitiated has been revealed; "sacrifice" refers to the internal and external sacrifice; it "is perfected," meaning it becomes the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
Since one who has not bathed lacks the qualification for sacrifice,
one should first perform a bath that destroys all sins.
"How so? he says:
"O Goddess of gods, having extracted the clay with the Astra-mantra, the knower of mantras, having performed the appropriate purification, should thereafter commence the bath. (3-2)

The connection [of the text] is as follows: having performed physical purification according to the rules prescribed in the Smṛti scriptures, one should take up earth with the Astra-mantra and begin the bath. || 2 ||
Therein, first, according to the sequence of dissolution, one should wash the feet, the calves, the hips, and the thighs—starting from the beginning—with three portions of earth each;
"having washed" is the understood ellipsis, and the word "with three" involves a change of grammatical gender. The same should be understood for the other parts as well.
To the question "What is meant by 'without interruption'?", he says:
"by means of a threefold intervening practice.
This refers to the practice of washing being performed three times with an interval between each instance; having washed both feet by means of that connection with the cleansing of the hands.
One should wash the hands; then the shanks, then the hands; then the thighs, then the hands;
then the hips—this is the meaning here.
Having acted thus, one is purified again by means of the seven.
By means of the earth-clods taken for the purpose of washing the hands; this is the implied meaning. || 3-3 ||
Then,
having consecrated the clay seven times with the Astra-mantra, the knower of mantras should heat it before the face of the sun and subsequently smear it upon his body.

"Mantravid" means one who knows the power of the weapons that burn away the aforementioned sins; "arkamukhām" means she whose face is shown as the sun, or, when that is not seen, she who is touched by the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa); and this anointing is his own intended [action]. || 4 ||
For the sake of pacifying obstacles,
having washed his body with water from the ..........., he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
For the purpose of purifying the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times with the *praṇava*, wipe the lips twice, and touch the door-frames.
Having described the impurity-bath for the sake of ritual sipping, he now describes the formal bath (*vidhisnāna*).
One should cause three portions of fine clay to be made upon the palm of the left hand.

The clay is praised as being soft; "three parts" refers to those situated in front, on the left, and on the right, according to the method prescribed in the Śrī-Svacchanda-tantra and other scriptures. || 5 ||
There,
one should cast that which has been consecrated with the weapon-mantra in the directions,
[and likewise] the portion situated at the front.
One should fashion the *tīrtha* at the root;
the meaning is that one should fashion the *śivatīrtha* with the left side [of the hand] over which the root mantra has been recited (*japta*).
Having touched his body with its limbs and washed them, he should mutter [the mantra] while submerged within the water. || 3-6 ||
"With the limbs" means with clay from the southern side that has been consecrated by reciting the six-limbed mantra;
"within the water" means inside the water. || 6 ||
As for what one should recite and how much, he says:
"The root [mantra] according to one's capacity..."—
one should recite the root mantra according to one's ability.
Then,

having emerged from the water, one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyā) in due order; and according to the method taught in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra* and other scriptures, having consecrated one's head with the jar-mudrā (*kalaśa-mudrā*), one should emerge from the water.

The downward scattering of drops of water held in the left hand with the branches of the right hand while reciting the weapon-mantra (astramantra), and the upward scattering with the root-mantra (mūlamantra) and those beginning with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra), and so forth, constitutes the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana).
Furthermore,
having tied the topknot and having recollected the topknot, one should then perform the libation for the mantras.

Having recollected the *śikhā-mantra* and tied the topknot (*śikhā-granthi*), and having likewise bound the topknot as the central power (*madhya-śakti*), one should remain there and perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for those mantras whose essence is their vital potency (*vīrya*). || 7 ||
Then,

having gratified the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and human beings along with all living creatures, and having taken possession of the sacred bathing place, he should enter the sacrificial hall according to the prescribed rule.

Having satiated all the mantras, and having caused the Śiva-tīrtha to dissolve into one's own self through the mantra and meditative visualization, one should enter the sacrificial hall according to the procedure to be described. || 8 ||
He states that ritual procedure:
one should worship Āśā, Mātṛgaṇa, Lakṣmī, Nandin, and Gaṅgā;
then one should worship Mahākāla, Yamunā, and the Dehalī.

One should worship the Mothers of the outer directions; above the door, Gaṇapati and Lakṣmī; on both sides, Nandin and Gaṅgā, and Mahākāla and Yamunā; and on the left, one should worship the threshold (dehalī) by joining it with the syllable *praṇava*, the dative case ending, and the word *namaḥ*.
According to the Siddhānta view, because this [threshold] is all-enduring (*sarvasaha*), Nandin and Gaṅgā are to be worshipped on the right.
In the Mahākāla-Yamunā [tradition], [the goddesses] are on the left; likewise in the Vāma-srotas, but with the addition of Meṣāsya and Chāgāsya on the right and left respectively.

In the Bhairava-srotas, because of its predominance of withdrawal (saṃhāra), Mahākāla and Yamunā are on the right, while Nandin and Gaṅgā are on the left. However, in the Trika (Ṣaḍardha) tradition, Diṇḍi and Mahodara are the additional ones.

Then, having recited the Saptavārāstra mantra seven times over a radiant flower, one should cast it inside by means of the Nārācāstra, thereby effecting the expulsion of obstacles and performing the binding of the directions with the Kavacāstra.

Having expelled the obstacles residing in the netherworld (pātāla) and other regions by means of the weapon-mantra (astra), using sounds such as the striking of the heels, clapping, and high-pitched tones,
one should bind the directions with the armor-mantra (kavaca) so that those expelled obstacles cannot re-enter.
Then,
for the sake of one's own seat, one should likewise fashion the auspicious power known as Ādhārikā.

Having sat down, one should then perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) in due order. For the sake of providing a seat for one's own conscious self (*cidātman*), one should contemplate the auspicious Supreme Lord’s power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which takes the form of a foundation because it supports the entire path of the universe on all sides. *Oṃ*.
Having thus conceived, "Salutation to the Support-Power (Ādhāra-śakti)," and having sat down, making oneself the locus of that [power], one should,
through the sequence of forceful exhalation, inhalation, and retention, effect the burning of the body for the sake of touching the power of Śakti residing at the *dvādaśānta* of the self.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) in order to produce variety. || 10 ||
Then, having first performed the ritual placement for the purification of the hands (karaśuddhinyāsa),
one should begin the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) here simultaneously through the processes of drying and so forth.
One should meditate there upon the six-sheathed impure body as being incinerated;

and within the body, one should meditate upon the earth-dhāraṇī, which is yellow, square in nature, marked with a vajra, and characterized by firmness; and likewise the water-dhāraṇī, which is white, half-moon in nature, marked with a lotus, and characterized by nourishment.

Having reflected thus, one should meditate on its drying up along with the retention of the wind element (vāyavya-dhāraṇā), which consists of a black circle marked with six dots and the letter *ya*; such is the meaning of the first [verse]. When this has been done, the impure body—consisting of skin, flesh, blood, marrow, bone, and semen—[is purified].

One should contemplate the burning away of the sense of ego (ahaṃbhāva) through the meditation on the fiery dhāraṇā, which is marked by the syllable *ra* and consists of the red triangular power (*ātmaśakti*), by means of the Kālāgni arising from the big toe. || 11 ||
Then one should contemplate consciousness alone as empty there, all-pervading. (3-12)
When that body has been contemplated, one should remember all-pervading pure consciousness, because the object of knowledge is empty.
Thus, through meditative absorption,
there is neither "I" nor "another," and here no object of meditation is found;
the mind has become absorbed in the state of bliss and has attained a state of equal flavor.
