Thinking that "I am not" refers to the limited subject, "another" refers to external objects such as blue, and "the object of meditation" is nothing at this juncture because it consists of internal mental representation— thereby, when the state of atomic limitation (aṇutā) has subsided through immersion in the expansion of Śakti, one becomes absorbed in the plane of bliss.
The mind, having entered the state of equanimity, became the nature of pure consciousness alone. || 13 ||

Thus, immediately after the deposition of one's own form (*ātmamūrtinyāsa*), he describes the subsequent deposition of the forms of the mantras consisting of both the manifest (*sakala*) and unmanifest (*niṣkala*) aspects, preceded by the deposition of the appropriate seat:
"Thereafter, one should contemplate one's own seat as being established upon the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*)."
The nurse-mother, the ocean of milk, and the lotus illuminated by the lunar disc.

Thereafter, one should sprinkle it with the nectar arising from the collection of time-measures (kalās), and one should likewise fashion the three principles (tritattva) as having become embodied by means of the root mantra alone. || 3-15 ||

"Subsequently" means immediately after the purification of the body and so forth. The "lotuses in the ocean of nectar of the *dhātrī*" refer to the successive pervasions of the principles (*tattvas*) of earth, water, and fire; and since that [fire] is conjoined with space, it extends up to the Foundation Power (*ādhāraśakti*).
Thus: "Earth, water, as well as fire, air, and space itself..."
"These five principles, by which the entire universe is pervaded" (Kālottara 8.1.2).

In accordance with this principle, one should place as a seat for one's own self, by means of the *praṇava*, these five principles which encompass the entire expansion of all the paths (*adhvan*). Upon that—

One should thoroughly sprinkle the Lord— who possesses a complete form whose essence consists of the three principles beginning with the Self, and whose body is fashioned for the upcoming meditation by means of the thirty-eight digits (kalās) beginning with Nivṛtti— with the root mantra,
using the true nature of the stainless pervasion that consists of the nectar of supreme bliss.
One should perform the visualization. || 15 ||
Then, one should again project the limbs upon the body with both hands.
The word "again" (punar) means that within the partless self (*niṣkala-ātman*), the six limbs— which consist of attributes such as omniscience and so forth—
are manifested through the reflective awareness of the two powers whose nature is expanding knowledge and action, resulting in the emergence of the partless self-nature (*naiṣkalātmyonmajjana*).
The intended distinction here is that one should "imagine" [the deity]; and through the yoga of meditation, one should contemplate the mental conceit (abhimāna) associated with the mantra. || 3-16 ||
One should enter with one-pointed concentration into the contemplation of the mantra, which is the essence of the power of that which has been explained and that which is yet to be explained.
Then, for the purpose of bringing [the deity] near, having bound either the Amṛta-mudrā or the Padma-mudrā,
one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods within oneself, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Resembling a pure pearl, with a luster like that of a mountain of crystal,
resembling the jasmine flower, the moon, cow’s milk, and the snowy mountain— [they beheld] the all-pervading Lord.
Adorned with white ornaments such as pearls,
elephants, and moonstones, his limbs are smeared with white sandalwood paste and greyed with camphor powder.
Surrounded by the vast and abundant waves of the shimmering nectar of the moon,
[he] stands in the center of the lunar mandala, with one face and three eyes.
Seated upon a white lotus, established in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana),
four-armed, with large eyes, and with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Holding a jar that resembles the full moon, pure and filled with nectar itself, he is indeed the one who brings nourishment to the world. (3.22)
One should visualize a full moon in his left hand;
due to the arrangement of the left hand with the thumb raised and the little finger bent across and touching the top of the right [hand],
it is the Amṛtamṛtakalaśa mudrā, which, because of its excellence in being filled with supreme nectar, is described elsewhere as follows:
Placing the right hand above the left,

with the fist loosely formed and the thumb pointing upward, they call this the *kālaśī* mudrā; or else, one may form the *padma* mudrā by joining the two hands, closing them into a bud-like shape, and then opening them out while the thumbs remain joined.

Having fixed one's intention upon the nature of one’s own self, which expands the entire universe without exception, one should meditate on the Lord within that very self as one's own essential nature. Thus, the light of consciousness itself—free from all limiting adjuncts—by virtue of its own sovereign majesty, manifests the entirety of the universe upon its own screen; it is the most joyful form, white and pure as the moon, delighting the whole world.
One should contemplate the form: "the moon shining" means that here the moon is held in the hand; it has one face due to its union with an extraordinary, independent power (*svatantra-śakti*);
it has three eyes due to its union with the triad of powers—will (*icchā*) and the others—as illuminated by its own majesty; [it rests upon] a white lotus.

The lotus of power is his vehicle due to the binding of the *padmāsana* posture; the deity possesses four arms because of the excellence of the expansion of the powers beginning with *Śāntā*, which are non-different from him who transcends *Śānti*; and he has large eyes because of his intention to illuminate the universe.

The hands hold the *vara* (boon) and *abhaya* (fearlessness) mudrās and a jar full of nectar like the moon, in order to manifest the unfolding of one's own true nature, which consists of the knowledge and action that bestow success and uproot all fears.
Having meditated on him in this form,
one should recollect him as worshipped with entirely white offerings.
*Upacāra* is that by which one performs worship; it refers to flowers, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. || 23 ||
Thus, what is the use of saying much more here?
For this Lord, being filled with supreme bliss...
...the ocean of nectar in person;
and this is indeed fitting.
For from this very source arose the nectar that sustains the entire world.
The supreme Śākta potency, which has arisen and is radiant, is nectar. || 24 ||
With the intention that "In what form indeed does this God not manifest himself for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who are to be graced," he says:
"Then one should meditate upon [the deity] resembling a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) according to the differentiation of states (bhāva). Of the state...
By means of the piercing—that is, the shattering—of the mental disposition (āśaya) that is defiled by passion and the like.
And that [face] was gentle, fierce, as well as terrible and deformed, according to the distinction of its emotional states.
[He manifests as] Sadāśiva, Tumburu, Bhairava,
Vīranāyaka, and Kuleśvara; the meaning is that he appears in various forms as the bestower of grace, according to the diversity and distinctions of the practitioner's disposition and state of being.
As it has been said:
"In whatever form the practitioner constantly contemplates him,
the Lord becomes identical with that very form, like a wish-fulfilling gem."
Because of his compassionate nature. || 25 ||
Having meditated thus, one should worship the deity with auspicious mental flowers.
In the heart-lotus, for the sake of all accomplishments, [one should worship] with mental offerings appropriate for each respective accomplishment. || 26 ||
Having thus explained the subject matter concerning the practitioner, he speaks generally:
"... afterwards, one should worship externally.
Following the mental worship, [one should worship] with the droplets from the *argha* vessel, which has been purified by the circle of mantras.
Considering that worship performed with flowers and other offerings becomes superior, one should first perform it mentally;
moreover, that worship which is performed with mental flowers is regarded as being characterized by goodness (sāttvika) and stable. (3.27)
It is unwithered, supremely pure, bestowing liberation, granting perfection, and auspicious;
for here, through the constant vision of the offering to Brahman based on the universal appearance of all things as being of the nature of consciousness (cidātmatva).
Therefore, with every effort, mental worship is indeed certain. (3.27–28)
First of all, [the preliminary rite] must be performed...

Then, having worshipped the lineage of gurus (gurupaṅkti), and having received permission from all of them for the manifestation of the state of Śiva, afterwards [one should worship] with extensive ritual substances.
In one's own home, in a temple, at a meeting place, or on a mountain peak. || 3-29 ||

The logical connection is that the sacrifice (yajana) should be performed on a highly praised, beautiful plot of land marked by lotus clusters; the phrase "on a plot of land" (bhūbhāge) is to be understood as applying to every instance.
First, in that regard:
One should draw a variegated maṇḍala adorned with white lines.
It has four gates and four corners, perfectly level and beautiful; endowed with primary and secondary ornaments, in its center is a lunar mandala.
Resembling the full moon and endowed with a garland of rays,
in its center is an eight-petalled lotus, brilliantly white and like the moon.

The procedure for the mandala, which is endowed with variegated filaments and possesses a supreme golden pericarp, will be described further ahead in the *Śrīyāga*; therefore, it has not been elaborated upon here.
Now...
In the center of that, one should bring down the Lord of the Gods from His own abode.
From its own place—the inner sacrificial ground of the abode of consciousness—one should cause [the deity] to descend for the sake of grace;
one should contemplate it as descending in the form of an external manifestation and, by way of the process of emanation, project it externally. || 33 ||
Having placed the two palms face upwards with the two thumbs positioned between them,
this is the *āvāhanī* or invocation mudrā.
Then one should invoke the deity conceived as having three bodies.
One should cause [the offering] to flow everywhere, even outside, for the sake of bestowing grace; one should contemplate the three bodies (*trideha*) as the support for the foundation of the refuge.

These consist of the three bodies—the supreme, the subtle, and the gross—which are the essence of the partless (*niṣkala*) and so forth, existing in a state of mutual pervasion and being pervaded, respectively, through the form known as the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) by virtue of pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*), and through the state of being external.

"Even though the Supreme One is of a single nature, He, being liberated through His sovereignty, creates by His own freedom a self that is non-dual in essence, and having fashioned it through volitions such as those of Īśvara and others, He engages in worldly transaction. (Ri. Pra. 1.5.16)
Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, the meaning is that [reality] is divided into a triad. || 34 ||
Having displayed the *liṅgamudrā* with the thumbs and fists raised for the sake of the presence of the invoked deity,
and having then displayed the *niṣṭhurā mudrā* with the thumbs and fists placed inside [the palms] for the sake of confinement, even beyond that—
One should assign the limbs upon the petals according to the divisions starting with the southeast:
the four limbs beginning with the Heart in the directions of Agni (SE), Īśa (NE), Rakṣas (SW), and Vāyu (NW); the Weapon in the four directions starting from the East; and the Eye in the pericarp.
All that is to be worshipped with white offerings, including flowers, garments, and ointments.

With various and wonderful food offerings, and with pure incense that has been well-fumigated; and with various heart-pleasing drinks—having thus performed the fumigation, is the meaning. The rest is clear. || 35 ||
The practitioner should worship [her] according to the different states of being. || 3-36 ||
In that regard,
O Dear One, one should worship with white offerings for the sake of pacification;
for the sake of nourishment, one should sacrifice with abundant and mixed materials well-prepared.
By means of mixed [colors], such as white, red, and transparent forms. || 37 ||
Then, as an ancillary part, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation according to one's inclination:
the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) with sesame seeds and clarified butter, while the seeker of enjoyment (bubhukṣu) with the materials to be employed.
Where? He says:
"In a place that has three ridges, is circular, square, and very beautiful. (3.38)

"In a pit of at least one cubit" (*hastamātre 'ntataḥ kuṇḍe*) refers to the case of a "large-scale fire sacrifice" (*sthūlahoma*). In the case of a pit measuring two or four cubits and so forth, it will be [the case of] a "future [sacrifice]" (*bhaviṣyat*).
And for this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the upper girdle (mekhalā) is one-sixth [of the height];
the middle is two [parts], the fourth is four [parts], and the lowest shall be twelve parts. (3-39)
Its length and width are likewise [one cubit]; it is three finger-breadths at the middle and the tip.
The upper girdle is four finger-breadths wide, being one-sixth of the cubit;
the middle [girdle] is two [finger-breadths], meaning it is four-eighths or three finger-breadths; the lower [girdle] is...

Twelve parts shall be two finger-breadths [in height]. The excavation (*khāta*) below is empty. The lip-girdle (*oṣṭhamekhalā*) is a specific internal part visible within the interval of the excavation. The navel (*nābhi*) is like an *aśvattha* leaf and shaped like a womb (*yoni*); the navel is a specific part at the front, [measured] by its length.
And that [line] which is nine finger-breadths on the sides, six finger-breadths in the middle, and three finger-breadths at the tip. || 39 ||
And this pit has been described for a *sāhasrika* homa— that is to say, one consisting of a thousand [oblations].
And it is held that at ten thousand [recitations], the merit is doubled.
*Caṣṭvaḥ* means in the sense of "cast" (thrown). *Ayuta* means ten thousand (*daśasāhasra*). || 40 ||
When the homa consists of fifteen thousand oblations, that [measure] is prescribed as double;
for a lakṣa-homa, a sacrificial pit endowed with the proper characteristics is recommended.

In a *homa* of thirty or fifty thousand oblations, it is double [the previous size], thus four cubits (*hasta*). In a *lakṣa-homa*, it is double even that, thus eight cubits. The term "double" functions like the eye of a crow (applying to both preceding cases). It should be endowed with the proper characteristics, with the measurements for the girdle and other features being appropriate according to the measurement of the cubit.
Furthermore, for rites that are obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires, as well as for pacification and nourishment,
a circular [mandala] is used; for the attainment of all perfections it is praised, and for those desiring prosperity, a square one.
The former measurement is praised for the general rule, while the remainder is indeed prescribed according to the distinction of the ritual action:

in the case of the *nitya* (obligatory) rite, the perpetual one; in the *naimittika* (occasional), such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), the festival days (*parvan*), the purificatory thread (*pavitraka*), and so forth; and in the *kāmya* (optional) rite, consisting of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*). Thus, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is circular. However, regarding matters concerning the desire for prosperity (*śrīkāma*):

It is square; and that measurement is according to the previously stated number of oblations (*homasaṃkhyā*), meaning it follows the prescribed count. However, in the case of other [rites], such as the accomplishment of all goals (*sarvasiddhi*) or rites like the expulsion of the body (*dehoccāṭana*), the remaining [shapes]—namely the triangle, hexagon, and so forth—are used. || 42 ||
Then,
the consecration of that vessel must indeed be performed with the weapon-mantra.
He said to them:
"Digging below, extraction, casting away the debris, filling it up, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and likewise smearing. (3.44)

Digging is the excavation of earth from the ground; lifting is the raising [of it]; removal of impurities is the discarding of pebbles, charcoal, and the like; filling is the act of filling [the pit];
sprinkling is the application of water with a ladle (*mekṣaṇa*) or similar tool immediately thereafter; and pounding is the act of trampling.
The powdering of the hard portion [of the sacrificial post], the sweeping of the pit, its leveling, the smearing [with cow-dung], and the sprinkling with cow-dung. || 44 ||

At the time of accomplishing these eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras), and even for that which is already accomplished, one should perform the ritual preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by means of the sword of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) using the syllable Om (praṇava).

Conceptualization is performed by way of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*); as for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and striking (*tāḍana*), these will be explained immediately thereafter by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*). From the words "sprinkling" (*ukṣaṇa*) up to "the conceptualization of the sacrificial pit" (*kuṇḍakalpana*), the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*) by means of the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) is to be inferred.
Now, here at the crossroads or the enclosure for dice, the construction of the house of Vāgīśī is described.
With the sword...

[he performed] the placement of Vāgīśī at the crossroads with two *darbha* blades facing east and north, because of obtaining the center; and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), previously with three [blades] facing east.

With the single [mantra] *saumyānana*, one should perform the work of the vajrī-maker; and for the sake of enduring the auspicious fire, one should perform all this—the spreading of darbha grass toward the upper direction and the enclosure of the axle-pit—with the *vāgīśī* mantra and the *astra* mantra, saying, "for the abode. || 45 ||
...Or rather, O Goddess, the invocation of Vāgīśī should be performed with the *praṇava* alone, and the worship should be performed with the three *tattvas*.... The invocation is:
"O Vāgīśī, be present here. Worship is performed by joining the dative case with *namaḥ*.
"Tritattva" refers here either to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) or to the root-mantra. || 46 ||
He states the completion of the previously mentioned consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) [with the words]:
"as well as sprinkling" (verse 3.46).
Having consecrated [the disciple] according to the prescribed ritual, one performs the striking with the Astra-mantra;
then, by means of Kauṇḍalī, who is the very embodiment of the power of action (kriyāśakti), the preparation of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is performed. || 3-47 ||

"By Kauṇḍalī" means by the pervasion of the Śaktikuṇḍalinī; or else, one should perform the mental construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) consisting of sprinkling, striking, and Kuṇḍalī within the very womb of Vāgīśī. || 47 ||
Then,
one should prepare there the fire whose nature is the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti).
How?
Taking the fire placed in a vessel and consecrated by the five purificatory rites (pañcasaṃskāra), || 3-48 ||
He tells them these five [steps]: inspection and so forth with the Astra-mantra, veiling with the Kavaca-mantra,
and offering five oblations with the Praṇava for the purification of the flesh-eating (kravyāda) element.
Thereafter, one should perform the universalization of the fire (*viśvāgnīkaraṇa*) and rotate it three times.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), sprinkling and striking are included; this constitutes the first [rite]. The state of being a flesh-eater (*kravyādatva*) and the state of being associated with the cremation ground (*śmāśānikatva*); their purification is the third [rite]. Universal fire (*viśvāgni*) is the essence of the fire-principle (*agnitattva*).
The production of the Śiva-fire is performed by circling it three times with the Praṇava alone. || 49 ||
Moreover,
from that seed-form, one [perceives] the fire, the Self, the Supreme Lord.

One should contract Vāgīśī, who is Māyā herself, by agitating her within the *yoni*; having visualized her at the end of the word "Vāgīśī" as being made circular, one should contract her by means of a threefold whirling.
Whatever the reality is in this matter has been shown in the *Śrī-svacchandoddyota*. (50)
Then, [one should perform] the worship in the Viśvāgni with the Praṇava. || 3-51 ||
That [offering] should first be placed in his mouth, and afterwards the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) should be performed in the fire.

With the intent of destroying [impurities] through the heat of the Śiva-fire, one should perform the purificatory rites—which manifest through the purification of the self and worship—by reciting "Obeisance to Śivāgni. || 51 ||
He spoke of them:
the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
The conceptualization of the faces, the emergence [from the womb], and the conceptualization of the neck and so forth;
likewise, here [are] the birth-rite, the emergence, and the naming. (3.53)

The six limbs beginning with the heart should be performed in successive order. "Sīmantonnayana" (the parting of the hair) is a qualifier for this [rite], as is "the fashioning of the faces" and so forth. The "fashioning of the faces" refers to their non-manifestation; "emergence" means manifestation, which is the fashioning of the major and minor limbs. In this regard:

In the middle, by the word *sīma*, the conceptualization of the locations of the mouth, heart, and feet through their threefold pervasion is indicated. "Departure" refers to the sight of the sun. And here, having worshipped the fire with the heart-mantra, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds with that same mantra, saying: "I perform the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite), svāhā!"

This sequence and so forth should be sought in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra* and other sources, because this ritual is concise and depends upon related scriptures; the same applies hereafter as well. || 53 ||
Furthermore,
those [rites] beginning with the *cūḍā* and ending with the *bāla*, which were previously [performed], are [accomplished] by means of a single *pūrṇāhuti*.

One should also offer all those purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) into the fire with the root mantra. Regarding the rites such as marriage that occur at the end of childhood for one observing celibacy, there is an adaptation (*ūha*) here: "I perform all the purificatory rites beginning with the tonsure (*cūḍā*) in the fire, svāhā. (54)
Then,
the knower of the ritual procedure should visualize there [the two deities] consisting of Śiva and Śakti.

Those two, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, should be made firm and produced from a milky tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*). The procedure will follow immediately. A "milky tree" refers to the white *arka* and others of that kind. || 55 ||
Furthermore,
those [offerings] produced from auspicious trees are praised for rites of pacification and nourishment.
[The two] arising from Śrīparṇī, Bilva, and so forth. || 56 ||

"Except for the distinction of specific intentions, the two effects—pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*)—should be performed according to the nature of the rite, primarily for the sake of practitioners by the Blessed One Amṛteśa; this is stated by his own mouth in various places. As for the other [effects], they were previously indicated through general statements."
He shows the measurement: the sacrificial ladle (sruc) should be thirty-six finger-breadths in measure, or else the length of one's arm. || 3.57 ||
An *aṅgula* consists of eight barley grains. Regarding the measurement of the arms: "The upper arm and forearm [are] eight and nine *kalās*; the joint is half a *kalā*.
Likewise for the hand and forearm..."
Thus, according to the method stated by me, [the measurement] is from the base of the arm to the end of the forearm;
and in this context,
the rule "one-ninth of the length of twelve parts (twelve finger-breadths) is one finger-breadth" refers to one's own finger-breadths.
The specific distinction is that it measures thirty-six finger-breadths. || 57 ||
And its staff, rising from the *kumbha*, has a circumference equal to one-sixth [of the total height].
"Circumference" (*pariṇāha*) refers to the measurement of the perimeter; the *kumbha* is a specific configuration at the base shaped like a jar (*ghaṭa*).
And that staff has a seat four fingers wide at its tip, and it is four fingers [in thickness] all around. || 3-58 ||

The pedestal (*pīṭha*) is in the shape of a four-legged stool; that pedestal should be made like the interior of a lotus at the front of the handle. Here, by the word "handle" (*daṇḍa*), the entire ladle (*sruc*)—which has the nature of the vital-force-handle—is intended. Regarding its division as well:
The jar and the staff are sixteen finger-breadths each. The four-legged stand is measured by four finger-breadths.
Since the neck and mouth of the pedestal are sixteen [finger-breadths] in their upper portion, the measure for the middle part—the seat—is four [finger-breadths]. || 58 ||
And on that pedestal, there is a lotus, two finger-breadths long and round. (3-59)
The height should be half a finger-breadth, with various decorative patterns made of finger-breadths;
having left two finger-breadths on both sides for the purpose of making tilaka designs, it means that two finger-breadths should be made in the middle. "Samutsedha" refers to height. || 59 ||
In front of this, an altar eight finger-breadths high, square, and very beautiful, should be constructed. || 3-60 ||
But [the altar] resting upon the lower lotus...
and of this altar... five finger-breadths in length above.
The excavation should be made three finger-breadths deep, and above that, it should gradually become circular.

Above the back part of the altar, having set aside one and a half finger-breadths on each side of a platform measuring eight finger-breadths in length, a place for the clarified butter (ājya) should be made in the center, five finger-breadths long and three finger-breadths deep. Above that, by means of a rotating cord (sūtra), [the outline] is drawn through rotation.
It becomes circular. || 61 ||
Furthermore,
it is adorned with sectarian marks (tilakas) measuring half a finger-breadth in size,
and its four sides are provided with four corners.
And that is the manifold arrangement of the craftsman’s technical knowledge.

On the side of that circular pit situated in the middle, the one and a half finger-breadths located on the pedestal (vedikā) should be divided into three parts; in the middle portion, there are tilaka-marks measuring half a finger-breadth.

[The suffix] *kārya* [is used]. *Racanā* means the act of arranging. *Suracana* refers to something being beautifully arranged, such as a decorative leaf-pattern (*patrāvalī*) and the like. However, the term *suracita* is clearly [used in the sense of "well-arranged"]. || 62 ||
At the front of the altar-railing,
a neck one finger-breadth wide should be made, divided into three parts.

On the two sides, however, it is one finger-breadth in length; in width, it is likewise [one finger-breadth]. Having thus divided the measurement of the eight-finger altar into three parts, and having partitioned the two sides and set aside two parts—
The meaning is that it should be made with a measurement of three middle parts. || 63 ||
At the tip of the neck, which is one finger-breadth [in width],
the auspicious face should likewise be made seven fingers in length.
The mouth is a field for the falling stream of clarified butter; it is auspicious when graced by the arrangement [of the sacrificial ladle].
...its sides, however, are eight [units]...
its face; the meaning is that on the sides, the base is equal to the altar (vedikā).
And of this, one should gradually reduce two parts. (3.64)
The tip of the mouth is one-third of that [width], and two parts are on its sides.
One should fashion the front portion of the mouth by dividing it into three parts, [measuring] eight finger-breadths, with the middle part being on both sides.

Having stretched two threads in the two eastern corners, one should delineate two side-sections and mark them according to proportion; then, one should diminish and cut away those very [sections]. In this way, the tip of the face becomes one-third of the measurement of eight finger-breadths.
Furthermore,
one should pierce that [point] with a measure of the little finger.
In the middle, for the falling of the stream of clarified butter. || 65 ||
One should make that [surface] sloped, increasingly lower, up to the interval between the tips of the openings;
from the tip to the middle of the opening, one should make a short, low-lying cavity.
Moreover, on both its sides, an auspicious and variegated design should likewise be fashioned.
Regarding the *sruva* ladle, he says:

one should make the *sruva* one cubit in length; its base should have three prongs, the middle and top bases should be marked with lotuses, and the neck should be well-rounded and one finger-breadth in circumference. (3.67)
One should have it made four finger-breadths long, with two well-rounded layers at the tip,
and hollowed out like the joint of a thumb, shaped like a cow’s hoofprint.
Measuring one *kaniṣṭhā* finger-breadth for each branch,
one should fashion it as circular, arranged with the proper design, and its mouth filled with *karṣa*.

Its base-platform (*mūlapīṭha*) is square in its arrangement. Its branches, which rise from the base-platform, are praised for being measured by the tip of the little finger and extending across three [units]. Likewise, both the middle and the front platforms are marked with lotuses; and on the front portion of the front platform—
"One finger-breadth at the neck" means it is well-rounded at the neck;
its length is four finger-breadths. "Two-fold" refers to that whose tip has two sides divided by a line in the middle; it is well-rounded.

It is beautiful according to its proportions; for this very reason, it has the shape of a cow's hoofprint (*goṣpada*), meaning it possesses a hollow whose boundaries are defined by the joint extending from the middle line of the thumb to its tip. And thus, the mouth—the location of the oral cavity—is filled with a *karṣa*.
If one should make the *sruva* ladle of such a kind, it will not determine the measure of the clarified butter in the *sruk* ladle. || 69 ||
It should be full of four palas...
[the text] states the pervasion of the *sruk* and other implements:
"The *sruk* is indeed Śakti, while the *sruva* is Śiva."
The power of action (kriyā-śakti) is indeed the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is likewise the fire.

Because the intention here is that the supreme consecration consists precisely in the pervasive non-difference from Śiva, the two consecrations for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are not mentioned in this context.

Having thus accomplished [the preliminary rites] according to the rule, one should thereafter commence the fire-sacrifice (*homa*). "Accomplishment" (*niṣpādana*) means the contemplation (*vimarśana*) through the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti. "According to the rule" (*vidhivat*) means in accordance with the pervasion of vitality (*vīrya*), that is, according to one's capacity, [reciting] the root mantra a hundred or a thousand times.
One should offer one-tenth of that [number] as oblations for the ancillary rites during the daily ritual.
Regarding the rite for specific desires, he states the rule for the materials:
"By means of oblations of sesame seeds mixed with milk, combined with sugar and ghee... (3.71).
Great peace shall arise at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
Having spoken thus in connection with this topic, he states the subject at hand:
"First, one should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya), and after that, the fire-oblation (homa). (3.72)
To them he said:
"First is placing [the vessel] on the fire, then removing it, stirring, and setting it down;
thereafter is inspection with the weapon-mantra, and after that, the lustration (nīrājana). || 3-73 ||
The circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), as well as the rising and falling (utplava-saṃplavau),
[are performed] with the Astra-mantra alone...
the pouring from the vessel into the receptacle, the placing above the fire, [and the purification] of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Sprinkling water three times around [the fire], placing it within the *yoni*, causing it to become composed of supreme splendor (*paratejomaya*) through that splendor,
illuminating all directions with a *darbha* torch, casting the burning *darbha* into its interior,
and thrice pushing it upward with both hands using the *pavitra* held by the thumbs and ring fingers.
The three downward thrusts; such is the nature of the acts beginning with placing [the vessel] on the fire.
Having performed these nine purificatory rites (saṃskāras) with the Astra-mantra, [one should perform] worship with the Mūla-mantra as well as the rite of nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa). || 3.74 ||
The Amṛta-mudrā should be displayed here. || 74 ||
Then,

one should arrange the darbha-grass mats and the seats (viṣṭara) with the weapon-mantras (astramantra). Upon the darbha-grass mat, the seats are prepared through the pervasion of various kinds of weapons.
Having established the guardians of the world (lokapālas) for the purpose of protection,

one should set up branches measuring one cubit in length, accompanied by mantras, as enclosures (paridhis) to extend the protective wall of weapons (astraprākāra) outside; these three [elements] are situated outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, having placed two blades of darbha grass into the vessel of clarified butter,
one should visualize the sun and the moon on the outside with the syllable Om.

Having prepared the three abodes within the clarified butter using the root mantra accompanied by the *praṇava*, and having filled the *sruva* ladle from the left, right, and middle [parts] in sequence, one should perform the oblation with the words "To Soma, Svāhā! To Agni, Svāhā!
To Agni and Soma, Svāhā! preceded by the root mantra; through this offering, the threefold nature of the fire should be conceived during the bright fortnight.

In the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), however, one should follow the procedure taught in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra*: from the left [hand], "Svāhā to Sūrya"; from the right, "Svāhā to Agni"; and from the middle, "Svāhā to Agni and Sūrya.
Now, regarding the fire:
One should meditate upon the nine-tongued [fire]...
[It is] the source of sovereignty, the producer of burning [fever], the giver of death, and the destroyer of enemies;
it is the subjugator, the eradicator, the bestower of wealth, and the giver of liberation.

"Bestower of all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhipradā*)— tongues of fire with such names should be arranged at the beginning, middle, and end of the fire, using the modification: "I arrange the tongues of fire."
...one should pour out the full oblation with the root mantra.

Having thus consecrated the sacrificial pit, the fire, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should thereafter worship that mantra together with its limbs (*sāṅga*) as situated in the center. || 3-76 ||
The practitioner, however, having performed [the preliminary rites] in this manner, should offer oblations with the mantra according to the specific ritual action.
"Having performed in this manner" means at the conclusion of the daily rites (*nityakarman*).
In that case, nourishment becomes eternal through milk mixed with ghee. || 3-77 ||
By means of the oblation, [success comes] for the practitioner. || 77 ||
By means of an oblation of ghee and guggulu, one whose desire is for long life certainly attains a full lifespan.
One who desires prosperity should offer lotuses drenched in ghee and milk.
One who desires a kingdom should offer *bilva* fruits smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) into the fire;
by offering fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from milk-producing trees, one shall obtain health through the oblation.
By performing oblations with excellent fuel-sticks in a fire fed by wood of even more excellent origin, one attains all desires; this is indeed the truth, and not otherwise. (80)
By performing seven oblations with *vrīhi* rice, one who seeks wealth shall become a possessor of wealth.
This is clear. || 80 ||
Having thus described the fire-offerings (homas) that yield auspicious results, he speaks with ease regarding the fire-offerings that yield results such as eradication (uccāṭana):
"Aiming for the desired object, one should perform the desired fire-offering. || 81 ||
Regarding the oblation appropriate for this mantra, he says: by performing the oblation with milk alone, one will certainly conquer death. (82)
Because this Lord is the conqueror of death, all is auspicious.

I bow to the form of Śiva and Śivā, which illuminates the entire world, which possesses a radiant portion of compassion flashing like hundreds of moons, fires, and suns, which is joined with a flowing supreme nectar,
and which has the appearance of a beautiful, natural, and wonderful tilaka mark.
Victory to the one with false eyes, who effects creation, dissolution, and maintenance.

Thus ends the third chapter, concerning sacrifice and other rites, in the *Netrodyota*, a commentary on the *Śrīnetratantra* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. 3.
The Fourth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Eyes.
Casting a glance toward liberation with a gaze fixed upon the upper and lower corners of the eyes.
The glorious eye on the forehead, together with its enjoyment, conquers the divine eye.
With the intention that the occasional (naimittika) rite follows immediately after the daily (nitya) rite, the Blessed Lord said:
"Now I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā), which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Initiation for enjoyment is divided for the practitioner according to the distinction between Śiva-dharma and worldly dharma."
The cause for attaining the principle of Īśvara, however, is the initiation into liberation (*muktidīkṣā*) for the initiate (*samayin*);
it is both seeded (*sabīja*) and seedless (*nirbīja*), as both apply to the teacher (*ācārya*) and the spiritual son (*putraka*),
since they are authorized up to the end of the maṇḍala as taught in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra* and other scriptures regarding the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
By means of thirty-six principles, or half of that, or even by five. || 4.1 ||
It should be performed with either three or one [mantras] for the sake of supreme and non-supreme manifestation.

There are thirty-six principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva; half of that is eighteen principles: the five elements, primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual soul (puruṣa), and attachment (rāga).

[Niyati, Śuddhavidyā, Kāla, Kalā, Māyā, Vidyā, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śakti]—and Śiva [is the tenth]. Half of that [nine] is also ninefold: Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Niyati, Kāla, Māyā, Vidyā, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śiva. Then there are the five [tattvas], beginning with Earth.

Like the *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*, [the principles] are all-pervasive. There are three called *bhuvana*, *śakti*, and *śiva*, which are pervaded by *māyā*, *sadāśiva*, and *śiva* respectively. However, the single *śivatattva*, beginning with *viśva*, is entirely [all-pervasive].
The supreme and non-supreme manifestations—liberation and worldly enjoyment—are to be accomplished and are undifferentiated everywhere. (1)
Having thus indicated the sixfold initiation into reality (tattva-dīkṣā), he now also indicates the initiation by means of the [five] kalās and so forth:
"Or else, the initiation may be performed by means of the five kalās, or again by means of the words (padas). (4.2)
Alternatively, by means of the fifty phonemes (*varṇa*), or by means of the mantras, or likewise by the worlds (*bhuvana*);
[there are] the *kalās*: Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śāntā, and Śāntyatītā.
According to the system beginning with "Śrī" and following the sequence of the *Mātṛkā*, [the phonemes are]: kṣa, ha, sa, ṣa, śa, va, la, ra, ya, ma, bha.

Ba, pha, pa, na, dha, da, tha, ta, ṇa, ḍha, ḍa, ṭha, ṭa, ña, jha, ja, cha, ca, ṅa, gha, ga, kha, ka—these are the nine words; however, because it is the locus of the rest of the universe, the tenth word consists of the visarga and ends with the letter *a*.
According to the perspective of the *Śrī Svacchanda*, however:
The eighty-one words beginning with *ū* (ūkārādi), as taught in the *Navātmaprastāra*,

are, however, according to the system of the *Śrīsvāyambhuva* and other scriptures, related to the *Vyomavyāpin*. The thirty-four phonemes from *kṣa* to *ka* are the designators (*vācaka*) of the categories from Earth up to Sadāśiva.
The sixteen [phonemes] beginning with the visarga and ending with the letter *a* are the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) of the non-duality between the principles of Śakti and Śiva.

According to the tradition of the *Śrīpūrva*, these words, which take the aforementioned forms through the operation of the intermediate speech (*madhyamā-vāk*), are *mantras* by virtue of the operation of the visionary speech (*paśyantī-vāk*), wherein the predominance of the reflective awareness of both difference and non-difference is subtly manifested. This is according to the system of the *Śrīsvacchanda*.

However, the limbs are indeed the Heart, Head, Crest, Armor, Weapon, and Eye; these are the mantras of the faces beginning with Sadyojāta, which contemplate the entire path (adhvan) through the sequence of pervasion by the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti. These are the mantras.

Due to the absence of mantras for the speaker according to the procedure (*prakriyā*) presented here, there are only the limbs (*aṅga*s). As for the worlds (*bhuvana*s), however, they number one hundred and eighteen according to the procedure previously described by Śrī [Abhinavagupta], but according to the perspective of the *Svacchanda*, they consist of two hundred and twenty-four; such is the view of this scripture.

Because it comprises all currents [of tradition], there is no contradiction with the sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*) through the conceptualization of the division of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) as taught in various scriptures. || 2 ||
In that regard, when it is possible, initiation should be performed by all these aforementioned methods;
otherwise, however...
Or indeed, one or another [of these] should be performed. || 4-3 ||
And in each individual mode as well, initiation must be performed by means of all six paths collectively.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"By means of the nature of power and manifestation,
having purified one or another path, [one pervades it] through its manifest form and its all-pervasiveness."

The meaning is that, having relied primarily [on the central channel], one should contemplate the five paths situated within it as being pervaded by the nature of Śakti. As it is said in the *Śrī Svacchanda*: "Thereafter, the observation of the paths occurs through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader. (4.95)
And so forth.
And this entire initiation must be performed by the most excellent teachers according to the extent of their available wealth. || 4.4 ||
For those possessing wealth, [the offering is made] with great collections of materials; for others, even with dūrvā grass, water, sprouts, and so forth.
Thus, through diligence and freedom from desire, the excellence of the teachers is established. (4)
Therein, first, having performed the hanging of the thread of bonds upon the body of the disciple, the joining of the paths (adhvan), the presentation of the paths,
the worship of the paths and the fire-oblation (homa), the contemplation of the three bonds within the paths, the placement of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), and so forth;
The worship of Vāgīśī should be performed...
[beginning] with the invocation and ending with the fire-oblation (homa), as is implied by the sense.
Then, having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and striking (tāḍana) and having seized the consciousness (caitanya), he should unite the bound soul (paśu)— the disciple— within that [womb],
for the sake of producing the fourteen-fold variety of bodies which serve as the substrata for experience, as is possible under the influence of the fetters of karma.
And for this [soul], there are conception, birth, qualification, and likewise dissolution. (4-5)
Enjoyment, the acquisition of karma, and immediately thereafter its expiation must be performed with the root mantra...
[The internal sprouting of various bodies is conception (garbhādhāna); their external emergence is birth (janana).]

*Adhikāra* is the attainment of increased prosperity suitable for enjoyment; following that is the acquisition of *karman*—which has its means of fruition ripened by the majesty of the mantra—in the form of a readiness to bestow experience; and following that is *bhoga*, which consists in the attainment of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Then, even when enjoyment has ceased, for some time there is a dissolution (*laya*) of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of enjoyment;

thereafter comes expiation (*niṣkṛti*), which consists of the complete exhaustion of all [karmic] acquisitions regarding caste, lifespan, and enjoyment—all this should be performed with root-mantra oblations (*mūlamantra-homa*) numbering three hundred and so forth; however, the expiation itself consists of one hundred oblations, and at its conclusion:
One should contemplate the attainment of the state of the twice-born and the attainment of the portion of Rudra.

When enjoyments have come to an end, having produced the latent impression (saṃskāra) known as disjunction, which consists in the absence of being an enjoyer... such is the severance of the bonds (pāśaccheda) as it is traditionally taught. || 4-6 ||
With the *astra-mantra*...
then, having performed the cutting of the cord of the noose— which is remembered as occurring immediately after the separation— with that very *astra-mantra*, [one should perform] that of the noose.
...but the burning [of the body] must be performed.
Even beyond that,
[it exists] in the state of reduction to ashes;
"reduction to ashes" is the pacification of the bonds (pāśas) devoid of residual impressions by means of the weapon-mantra alone.
But "established therein" (tatsthitam) means that, having contemplated the unification with the root [mantra] of the disciple’s consciousness whose entire body has ceased,
its state of being established consists in bringing it to reside within the disciple's heart by first leading it from one's own heart to the *dvādaśānta*; thus it is called "established therein."
It is established through etymological derivation.

Immediately thereafter, having performed the invocation, worship, fire-oblation (homa), the offering of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka) and its constituent parts, the proclamation, and the dismissal (visarjana) of Brahmā and the other deities, and having accomplished the purification of all the paths (adhvan) preceded by the contemplation of the sequence from the Kalās up to the Tattvas;

"Then one should perform the cutting of the crest (śikhāccheda) and the fire-oblation (homa)..."— the meaning is that, having cut the crest by means of the pervasion of the crest which is the form of the vital energy (prāṇaśakti) resting upon the entire path (viśvādhvan), one should offer it as an oblation.

Then, following the fire-oblation for atonement which may be required due to the possibility of failing to perform the ritual correctly, one who possesses the yoga of knowledge and knows the true nature of the fifteen categories of objects taught in the *Śrī Svacchanda*, beginning with the words: "Having known the measure of the movement [of breath], as well as the circulation of the vital breaths" (4.231).
The excellent teacher should unite the disciple, whose bonds have been stilled, with the Root [Mantra] itself. 4-7.
"Having abandoned mental activity, one should unite with pure consciousness alone;
then, like a bound soul (paśu), one attains the state of Śiva and is liberated from the ocean of existence. (4-437).
According to this view stated in the *Śrī Svacchanda*, through the method of immersion into the supreme reality, [the self] becomes one in form with Paramaśiva.
One should perform [it]. || 7 ||
Therefore it is said:
"Having joined [the disciple] to the supreme reality, one should cause him to remain established therein;
thus he shall become identical with that."
Now, for the sake of the teacher's authority, he states the division of those who are joined [to the path], as they abide in the state of the higher and the lower: || 4-8 ||
One should know that for those seeking the state of Śiva, initiation (dīkṣā) takes place in Sadāśiva;
likewise, for the "son" (putraka), it is in the Supreme Reality (parama-tattva), and for the "vow-holder" (samayin), it is in Īśvara. || 4-9 ||
Regarding the state of Śiva in the supreme and non-supreme levels,
it is according to the principle stated in the *Svacchanda-tantra*: "Established here, however, Śiva acts as the supreme cause" (10.1258).
After the union with Paramaśiva, the union with Aparaśiva must be performed for the Ācāryas;
however, for the Sādhakas, after the union with Śiva, the union with Sadāśiva must be performed;
for the Putrakas, it is in the Supreme Reality (Paratattva) alone; and for the Samayins, it is in the Lord-principle (Īśvaratattva)—such are the divisions. || 9 ||
Thus, initiation has been described by way of summary; the detailed account is found elsewhere. 4-10.

By the words "in brief" and "from another [source]," he instructs that although this procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*) is extensive, because it has been indicated here only in extreme summary, it must be understood thoroughly and applied by expanding upon it according to the *Śrī Svacchanda* and other scriptures; thus all is auspicious.
Victorious is the eye of the Great Lord, which burns away the entire flood of bonds for those possessed of devotion and bestows entry into the supreme abode.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on Initiation, in the *Netrodyota* commentary on the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. 4.
The Fifth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Eyes.
He consecrates [the disciple] for the sake of enjoyment and liberation with the great [nectar] flowing from his own body.
We worship this supreme eye of Śiva and Śivā, which consists of cascades of the highest nectar.

Then, in order to consecrate the teachers and practitioners who have been initiated with the "initiation with seed" (sabīja-dīkṣā) as taught in other scriptures and indicated in this scripture, and who are endowed with learning, virtue, and proper conduct, the Blessed Lord said: "I shall proclaim the consecration (abhiṣeka), how and to whom it is given here. Regarding the word "how":
The promise is: "I shall explain the initiation (abhiṣeka) in such a manner—by means of which procedure it is given, and to whom it is given, namely to the teacher or the practitioner."
In that regard,
eight jars should be given to the preceptor according to the prescribed rule.

The ritual procedure in the northeastern direction involves one who is seated upon a throne of śrīparṇī wood and other materials situated within a maṇḍala such as the svastika; who has performed the prescribed nyāsa; who is worshipped as Amṛteśa;
and [who performs] the dismissal [of obstacles] by means of a lamp and a jar filled with sour gruel, rice, clay, cow dung, dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, and so forth.

Then, for one whose obstacles have been pacified, [the rite] consists of the pouring of water from the vase upon the head, accompanied by the contemplation of the essence of the stream of supreme nectar flowing forth from the expansive immersion of the supreme mantra. || 1 ||
And those pitchers are said to be the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras), together with the oceans and their contents.

The meaning is that they should be visualized as being filled with the waters of the eight oceans, pervaded by the expansive [power] of the venerable Amṛteśa-Bhairava, and presided over by the Lords of Knowledge beginning with Ananta. "Together with their contents" (sagarbhagāḥ) means...

These are endowed with jewels, medicinal herbs, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth; this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, according to the scriptures, regarding the subject of consecration for one who has been consecrated, [the ritual is performed] with mantras applied individually, each empowered by one hundred and eight recitations of the root mantra.

Everything taught in the Āgamas— such as the bestowing of the *uṣṇīṣasaṃhitā*, the parasol, the sandals, the *karaṇī*, the *kartarī*, and so forth, which serves as the means for expanding the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*)— must be followed.
He states another alternative regarding the subject matter of the *kalaśa* [vase] with five verses:
"Or else, by means of those numbering five elements, or by means of three whose nature is the *tattvas*. (5.2)
By means of those [principles] known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva— even by that single Śiva-nature—

there is the complete manifestation (*samyak-khyānam*) of the elements from earth up to space; this is the illumination (*prakāśa*) of those [beings] through the contemplation of the pervasion of the *kalās*, beginning with Nivṛtti, by means of the principles (*tattvas*) starting with Ātman.

Those for whom there is form, transformation, and discernment; those whose manifestation is through identity with that [reality], being proclaimed on all sides by the knowledge of the Self and by Śiva. || 2 ||
And this consecration is for the sake of authority in the case of the teacher, while it is for the sake of the desire for accomplishment in the case of the practitioner. (5.3)

The objective concerning the teacher (*ācārya*) should be performed with the sole purpose of benefiting others; the objective concerning the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should be performed with the intention that, through the propitiation of the mantra, he may attain accomplishment (*siddhi*) regarding his own self.
In this matter as well, the entire procedure as taught in the *Śrī Svacchanda* and other scriptures is to be followed. || 3 ||
Then this practitioner, having been consecrated and authorized, should indeed perform the mantra-attainment;
he must not remain indifferent.
Therefore, he observed that vow, practiced those rites, was devoted to them, and took them as his supreme refuge. || 5-4 ||
Devoted to the practice of purifying food, eating lightly, and with senses restrained,
he should dwell in solitude in a sacred field or within the precincts of a holy shrine.
The practitioner, whose mind is freed from all attachments, should begin the recitation (*japa*).
In this very context, "vow" (*vrata*) refers to the restraint of speech and mind, while "conduct" (*samācāra*) consists of worship (*pūjā*) and fire-oblation (*homa*).
The rest is clear. || 5 ||
There,
the practitioner of mantra, endowed with prior service, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
By that, the common rites of the practitioner are accomplished;

furthermore, it is stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda* that during the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), recitation (*japa*) should be performed with greater repose starting from the rising of Pisces (*mīnodaya*), and likewise, that the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed with excellent and other materials using one-tenth of the number of recitations.
The common rites are those such as subjugation, summoning, and so forth.
Furthermore,
by reciting it ten hundred thousand times, one attains the accomplishment (siddhi) pertaining to the earth.
And one attains the celestial realm... the meaning is that one obtains the power of movement through the netherworld and the sky.
... Certainly within fifty lakhs [of recitations].
The practitioner attains divine accomplishment; there is no doubt about this.
Divine, consisting of the attainment of the status of the Lord of the World;
likewise, by performing ten million recitations, one shall obtain the sovereign *siddhi*.
Having become all-pervasive Śiva, one becomes capable of both restraint and grace. (5–9)
He performs everything according to his will; he can sustain and intensely withdraw [all things]. He certainly becomes all-pervading, the creator of all, and omniscient. (5.10)
By the words "pervasive" and so forth, the accomplishment of the Goddess (Īśvarī-siddhi) has been made clear: [she is] all-pervading and the self of all.
And all this the practitioner attains while remaining within this very body; thus all is auspicious.
He extends the entire universe through the distinct forms of the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— those auspicious and most gracious manifestations of Śiva— and yet he does so non-differently;
furthermore, he here consecrates his devotees with the supreme nectars.
Victorious is this eye of Śiva and Śivā, which bestows all accomplishments.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Consecration," in the *Netrodyota*, a commentary on the *Śrīnetratantra* composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 5.
The Sixth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Eyes.
That which extinguishes the fires of the defects of disease, misfortune, old age, and so forth, by means of the supreme nectars;
I bow to that Hara whose eye is turned upward, who sprinkles and performs worship, oblations, meditation, recitation, and so forth.
By way of restating the meaning already understood from the preceding chapter, the Śrī Devī spoke in order to introduce another deity:
"O Mahādeva, I have heard [the teaching] on Mṛtyujit, the bestower of accomplishment and liberation;
now I wish to hear [the teaching] endowed with the threefold accomplishment. || 6-1 ||
The high-souled Amṛteśa is the life-force within all living beings;
he bestows success upon people in this world and acts for their welfare. (6.2)
It pacifies the evils previously mentioned, destroys untimely death, nourishes the body, and bestows auspicious peace and prosperity. (6.3)

Furthermore, I have heard that Mṛtyujit, who consists of the mantras characterized as the signified and the signifier as taught in the first and second chapters, bestows liberation through the obligatory and occasional rites taught in the third and fourth chapters, and generally bestows supernatural accomplishments (*siddhi*) through the optional rites taught in the fifth chapter.

But now, that very Amṛteśa— who bestows terrestrial, celestial, and atmospheric accomplishments, who is the life of the universe, the Great Self— bestows whatever accomplishment is attained and in whatever manner it is attained; he grants this everywhere in the world,
especially to those afflicted by diseases and other ailments, according to the perspective described in the second chapter on the creation of beings.

I wish to hear that which brings benefit to human beings. The quality of being a benefactor has been clarified by the previously mentioned [passage] beginning with "hitaṅkara. Peace (*śānti*) is the cessation of afflictions such as those caused by malevolent planets. Nourishment (*āpyāya*) is the restoration of moisture to what is parched. Prosperity (*puṣṭi*) is the state of having all limbs complete. Auspiciousness (*śubha*)...
It removes poverty and other such misfortunes. || 3 ||
Thus questioned, the Blessed Lord said:
"Listen, I shall fully declare this most wonderful secret,
by which men submerged in the ocean of suffering cross over."
People are overcome by hundreds of untimely deaths, beset by poverty,
agitated by the fear of mental and physical ailments, and tormented by floods of sin.
And how they are all liberated from the aforementioned terrible [sins], O beloved—that means is threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme. || 6-6 ||

Just as human beings, being urged by the state of being preeminent objects of compassion, cross over [suffering] so that they do not become partakers of pain and the like, and just as they are liberated— that is, released— from cruel spirits and other such beings,
so too is that essential reality which conquers death, consisting of the secret of the ultimate truth and the essence of the aforementioned power, the very means for that purpose.
That which I shall fully declare.
In that regard,

the King of Mantras intensely performs gross acts such as sacrifice, fire-oblation, recitation, meditation, and the collection [of materials], as well as the mechanical devices for delusion and so forth. (6–7)
The king of mantras performs the sacrifice and other rites, and it also remains through its own power. The mudrās here are those previously mentioned.

"Subtle" refers to that yoga which occurs through the conjunction of the wheels (*cakras*) and so forth, as well as through the arising of the channels of the *kalās* (*kalā-nāḍī-udaya*). By "the arising of the channels of the *kalās*" is meant that which indicates the divisions of time such as the *muhūrta* and so on; it is primarily characterized by those [divisions]. The yoga consists of the six wheels and the sixteen supports (*ādhāras*) that arise within the sevenfold domain of authority (*saptamādhikāra-bhāvin*), beginning with the six wheels and the sixteen supports. Through that [yoga], as well as through the arising of the channels of the *kalās*—where *kalā* is intended as an indicator for the parts of time such as the *muhūrta*—[it is subtle]. It is primarily characterized by that.

The meaning is that the King of Mantras, impelled by the unification of the external, internal, fierce, and otherwise [designated] times as taught in the *Śrī-svacchanda* and other scriptures through the arising of the channels (*nāḍī*), effects the destruction of diseases and so forth by means of a subtle method through the expansion of His own potency.
Furthermore, it is the soul of all, the bestower of liberation, and the conqueror of death.
Because he is the embodiment of the power of the mantra of the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya), the Lord Mṛtyujit is described in this way:
he is the supreme non-duality that is the self of all. This will be determined in the eighth chapter.
In that regard, he begins to explain the gross means:
"O Dear One, when one is seized by Time and has fallen under the power of death, then, for the sake of countering that, one should worship Amṛteśa. (6.9)

Then, by means of entirely white offerings according to the previously stated procedure: *mṛtyu* is untimely death; *kāla* is great death (*mahāmṛtyu*); and *vidhāna* refers to the sacrifice and other rites described in the third chapter.
And thus,
for whomever one intends by name, one should worship the Lord Mṛtyujit.

"One will quickly cross over death; this is my truth, not a false word. [The word "this one" (asau) refers to the practitioner. By saying "truth," one should not doubt here on account of the presence of a subject characterized by illusion (māyā-pramātṛtā), because certainty alone is the cause for accomplishment. || 10 ||
With sesame seeds mixed with white sugar and saturated with ghee and milk. || 6-11 ||
In a fire fueled by wood of meritorious trees, within a circular pit with three ridges,
one should perform oblations according to the rite of great protection while uttering the name of the person for whom it is intended.
There shall quickly be great peace even for one who has gone to the abode of Yama.

"Merit" refers to fuel such as *palāśa* wood and the like, which serves as the means of kindling. "The ritual of great protection" consists of the visualization of weapons, ramparts, and so forth, as well as within the sacrificial hall.
The protection against the entry of the wicked; "by name" means by the utterance of the end of the mantra; "the abode of Yama" means the house of Yama. || 12 ||
Or else, with milk mixed with sugar, or with milk alone.
Through this oblation, one shall quickly conquer death; there is no doubt that he becomes the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyujit).
This is clear. || 13 ||
By means of an oblation of fragrant ghee in a fire made from the wood of milk-exuding trees, || 6-14 ||
When satisfied, he destroys death; there is no doubt that he is the conqueror of death (Mṛtyujit).
This refers to the person by whose name [the rite is performed]. 14.
By offering oblations with fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees, one destroys fever in an instant.
The fuel-sticks should be the size of a span, with their bark intact, as thick as the little finger, fresh, and from branches. || 15 ||
Sesame, rice, sour gruel, clarified butter, and milk combined—
this is the oblation of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), which destroys all that is evil.
By the grace of the King of Mantras. || 16 ||

O lady of excellent vows, by offering oblations of guggulu resin in pill form, each three times smeared with clarified butter and in the measure of a chickpea, one whose body is emaciated quickly attains nourishment.

From an oblation of guggulu incense pills, each the size of a chickpea and smeared with the three sweets—clarified butter, milk, and honey—nourishment (*puṣṭi*) arises. According to the principle stated in the *Svacchanda-tantra*, "The *vaṣaṭ* [exclamation] is recommended for nourishing," the *vaṣaṭ*-class [of mantras] should be employed here in all cases. || 17 ||
When a man is seen to be weak, overwhelmed by hundreds of diseases, then by reciting his name while joining the palms together, he is liberated. (6.18)
By means of the root mantra; this is the implied meaning. || 18 ||
Furthermore,
whatever mantra a wise person recites while encased within the *amṛteśa* [mantra],
that [mantra] is quickly mastered by him, even if he should be devoid of fortune. (6.19)
The recitation here is according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual. || 19 ||
Having stated this as a digression, he speaks of the subject at hand:
"O Goddess of gods, for one whose limbs are wasted, the medicine is the encapsulation with mantra.
O Goddess, when it is given, that person instantly attains nourishment and becomes strong. (6-20)
"Bheṣaja" means medicine; "mantrasaṃpuṭam" means that which is employed by being enclosed within a mantra. || 20 ||
Having placed the individual soul (jīva), located in the center of the heart-lotus and within the orb of the moon,
obstructed by the vowel 'a' and the following consonants, one crosses over death completely.

He who performs or meditates upon the life-force (jīva) of himself or another— situated within the lunar orb and obstructed by the seed-syllable of fire (Hūṃ), the syllable *svāhā*, the visarga, the letter *sa*, and the *praṇava* (Oṃ), which have sequentially emerged from near the life-force and extended outward, having been visualized as occupying the eight directions— is [liberated].
"He transcends death. The sense of the causative (*ṇij*) is also implied within the root *kṛ*. || 21 ||
Having caused it to be obstructed by the *sādyarṇa*, the knower of yoga should meditate upon it within the body;
he shall become liberated from all diseases—of this there is no doubt. (6.22)
This is the practice of obstructing the living body. || 22 ||
Situated in the midst of a lotus in the Ocean of Milk, agitated by waves of nectar,
it is enclosed above and below by the moon and encapsulated by the vowels beginning with 'sa'.
With a highly delighted mind, he meditates upon himself or upon another,
whose body is pure both internally and externally, as if filled with nectar.
With an undisturbed mind and free from exertion, one is liberated from all diseases;
[he is] seated upon the moon situated in the pericarp of a white lotus in the midst of the Ocean of Milk,
being sprinkled by the nectars of the upward-facing moon, with the Ocean of Milk overflowing from the mass of lunar radiance.
One whose body is intensely meditated upon as being filled inside and out with waves, pure white, and encapsulated by the King of Mantras according to the stated method, becomes free from disease.
Combined with *rocanā*, saffron, and milk.
In the center of an eight-petaled white lotus, he is enclosed by the syllable *sā* and surrounded by a lunar disc; he is afflicted by all manner of diseases. (6.26)
One who has entered a four-cornered city marked with a vajra, bearing a vajra, is liberated from the affliction of all diseases; of this there is no doubt. (6.27)

Having drawn a white lotus on birch bark or similar material with *gorocanā*, saffron, and milk, and having inscribed the mantra according to the prescribed method upon each petal, one should enclose it— meaning the target (*sādhya*) whose name is written at the gateway of the pericarp— with a sixteen-part lunar disc surrounding it on the outside.
Standing in the four-cornered city together with Vajra, even one overcome by disease is liberated from the affliction of all diseases.
When "Vajradhara, O Vajra! is uttered, he instructs that one should meditate upon the vajras as being empowered.
In the great sixteen-spoked wheel, adorned with the sixteen vowels...
By means of the union of the initial and final mantras, one should write the name in the middle.

Having enclosed it on all sides with the Lord of Nectar (Amṛteśa) for every syllable— [the mantra] which has *jīva* at its beginning, the end of the vowels (*sānta*) in its middle, and is protected by the end of the consonants (*varṇānta*).
In the center, upon all the petals, [is the deity] situated within a lunar disc;
on the outside, however, is a double lotus arranged in the sequence from *ka* to *sa*.
As before, the mantra-practitioner should write [the syllable] obstructed by the letters beginning with *pra*;
within that syllable is the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and on the outside is a solar mandala.
One should surround it on all sides from below with *purandara* and *pura*,
combined with white sandalwood and through the application of *rocanā* and milk.
Having written the King of Mantras, grey with powdered camphor, this great rite of protection bestows nourishment and good fortune. (6.33)
O Great Goddess, one should worship this wheel with white flowers;
with all-white offerings, one should place it in the midst of honey.

By this very procedure, one becomes a conqueror of death within seven days. Having placed the name of the person to be accomplished— enclosed by the mantra— within the letter *sa* (the letter of life) at the pericarp of a sixteen-petaled lotus, and having positioned it inside the letter *ha* (which ends in *s*), [one should conclude] with the final letter.
One should provide protection by means of the letter *kṣa* situated both inside and outside. For each mantra,

one should write the name encased within the *Amṛteśa* mantra, surrounded by the letter *ṭha*, and placed sequentially in the midst of the vowels beginning with *a*, writing it facing toward the central mantra.

One should draw thirty-two petals outside the sixteen-petaled lotus, and there one should place the thirty-two letters from *ka* to *sa*. Within those, for each letter, it is encased by the mantra according to the previously stated method of being "constrained by the initial letter" (*sādyarṇarodhita*); that [mantra] is the one previously placed.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the middle of the interior, one should draw a solar disc (*arka-maṇḍala*) outside of all this—

that is, the syllable *ṭha*— and outside of that, one should construct a square arrangement marked with a thunderbolt (*vajra*), which is the city of Indra (*purandara-pura*). Regarding the phrase "obstructed by the letters beginning with *pra*":
The phrase "and even those separated" indicates that the word *varṇa* is connected with the word *prati*, which is separated [from it].

Having written this entire wheel with white sandalwood, gorocana, and milk, and having worshipped it with white flowers, camphor, and other offerings, [the wheel], when placed in the midst of honey, brings about nourishment and good fortune.
And [the mantra] placed in honey for seven days is the conqueror of death.
Furthermore, why should this ritual for the protection of kings be made public to rulers? || 6-35 ||
At the time of battle, it becomes a granter of boons that destroys the pride of enemies;
each of the nine principles (tattvas), beginning with Śiva, is a lunar orb.

When one is beset by hundreds of diseases or hundreds of untimely deaths, the practitioner, beginning from the center and proceeding toward the northeast and so forth, [should perform the rite] with the mantra of Amṛteśa.
Then, having worshipped with white offerings or with milk and ghee,
one attains peace through the performance of oblations with sesame seeds or with milk-soaked sacrificial fuel.

In a nine-square grid formed by four lines arranged lengthwise and crosswise, each square being marked with a lunar disc, one should place [the following] starting from the central square and proceeding in order from the east to the end:
Śiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyā, Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, and Prakṛti.
Having enumerated the principles of the Puruṣa by name, when the practitioner performs worship with this white-colored ritual service (sitopacāra) using this mantra,

and offers oblations according to his capacity with milk and ghee, or with sesame seeds soaked in milk, or with sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) soaked in milk, then— even if [the person] is beset by hundreds of diseases, untimely deaths, and the like— [he is liberated].
The body of the one to be healed attains a state of well-being. || 38 ||
Having thus worshipped the jar, which is endowed with all medicinal herbs, from which white lotuses emerge, and which is filled with water containing gems; 6.39.
One should indeed perform an ablution upon his head with the sound of all auspicious chants;
he who is afflicted by every disease is liberated from it, without a doubt.
Having thus meditated upon and worshipped the nine principles beginning with Śiva in the water-pot (kumbha) according to the stated reasoning,
whoever is consecrated on the head by that [water] is liberated even if afflicted by all diseases.
The compound *sitapadmairmukhe udgāra āmodaḥ* means "one whose exhalation from the mouth has the fragrance of white lotuses."
Having meditated upon the supreme nectar, which is eternal, perpetually manifest, and free from ailment,
one should bring down that nectar situated within the ritual process from the supreme Śiva.
The support of the four and nine nectars, filled ninefold,
eternally agitated by fifty, and endowed with six, five, and one.
It is as deep as the infinite foundation and adorned with thirty-eight [attributes],
or else, for the sake of establishing [the teaching], it is complete with five [attributes] and thus uninterrupted.
Thus, the preceptor, intent on mantra and devoted to meditation, having agitated the jar of nectar—both external and internal—within the crown of the head, [bestows it]. (6.44)
For one who stands upon the stage of the state of grace should be consecrated with diligence;
he is liberated from the difficult-to-cross cycle of existence, of this there is no doubt. (6.45)

Having meditated upon—that is, having contemplated through the method of *samāveśa*—the nectar of the supreme reality (*unmanā-paratattva-amṛta*) which resides within the process of emanation (*prakriyā*), extending as far as the end of the path at *samanā*; which is eternally manifest, consisting of the form of unobscured conscious light; which is eternal and indestructible; and which is such that no affliction (*āmaya*)—namely, *māyā*—exists therein—from that very Paramaśiva.
Thinking "it is nectar"— that is, the bliss of Śakti— and having visualized it as having descended onto the head of the disciple,
one should uplift the jar filled with supreme nectar, which has been worshipped with its mantra; thus,
one remains intent on the meditation upon both kinds of nectar.

The preceptor, intent on the realization of the King of Mantras and desiring to bestow grace, should sprinkle this nectar—both externally and internally—upon the head of the disciple; he certainly attains liberation.
To the question "Of what nature is this nectar?", he says: "In the fourth [state], nine, thirty-six"—that is to say, the principles (*tattvas*). These very [principles] are [the nectar].

And according to the principle that "even in each single *tattva* there is the nature of all thirty-six *tattvas*," these nectars constitute their support (*ādhāra*) or substratum; likewise, it is filled by the eighty-one words (*padāni*), which are ninefold through the procedure beginning with the *navanavātmavyoma-vyāpī*.
It is completely pervaded; likewise, it is agitated and pervaded by fifty letters from *a* to *kṣa*; and it is perfectly endowed with six limbs, five faces, and one root.

It is complete with the collection of mantras for the rites to be accomplished as taught in the *Śrī-Svacchanda* and other scriptures; likewise, it is profound and immeasurable, being filled with the infinite foundational worlds beginning from Kālāgni and ending with Anāśrita, which are visualized within;
and it is adorned with the thirty-eight faces and five kalās.

By the word "tena" (by that), it is meant that [the reality] is continuously filled by these sixfold paths; therefore, its purpose or objective is *siddhi*—that is, the preeminent accomplishment characterized by worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). || 45 ||
And therefore, for one who is consecrated by this [rite],
longevity, strength, victory, luster, fortitude, intelligence, physical form, and splendors—
all these proceed forth.
It exists in a state of excellence; the meaning is that it flourishes.
In that same way...
the supreme sovereignty of the mountains.
It proceeds. || 46 ||
Moreover, one afflicted by suffering becomes free from suffering, and one who is diseased becomes free from disease; a barren woman obtains a son, and a maiden finds a husband. (6.47)
The meaning is that through this consecration with the water-pot (kalaśābhiṣeka), everyone attains their desired fruit. || 47 ||
As it has been said:
"Whatever desires one may strive for, one shall certainly attain them all"—
thus it is.
Now, the greatness of the consecration as prescribed by the ritual rules.
O Goddess, this has been told to you by me out of a desire for the welfare of all beings,
