through the ritual application of other scriptures and through the practice of other treatises. || 48 ||
Thus, by means of this consecration, the one to be accomplished shall become the secret for the pacification of all things. || 6-49 ||
In place of the word *arhat*, this word *araha* occurs.
Concluding this, he introduces another topic:
"Thus has the gross procedure been set forth; now hear the subtle one as well. (50)
By this heading, gross meditation has been explained; however, subtle meditation will be discussed by the upcoming seventh [chapter].
Thus all is auspicious. || 50 ||
We praise the eye of Śaṅkara, which shatters all suffering, brings about every prosperity, and generates the supreme liberation.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the "Procedure for Sadhana," in the *Netrodyota*, a commentary on the *Śrī Netratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 6.
The Seventh Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Eyes" (Netrodyota).
[It describes] that which is crowded with the wheels (cakras), supports (ādhāras), voids (vyomas), targets (lakṣyas), knots (granthis), channels (nāḍīs), and so forth.
I remember the Lord with upturned eyes, sprinkling his own body with nectars.
Then, in order to determine subtle meditation (*sūkṣmadhyāna*), the Blessed One said:
"Henceforth I shall proclaim the subtle, unsurpassed meditation;
for there exists no other meditation superior to this subtle meditation, yet beyond even this, there is something more excellent."
It will come to pass.
He begins that [teaching]:
"The wheel of the seasons, supported by the vowels, having three targets and five voids. (7.1)
It is joined with the twelve knots, endowed with the three powers (śaktis), traversing the path of the three abodes (dhāmas), and provided with the three channels (nāḍīs). || 7-2 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, having understood that the body is enveloped by seventy-two thousand channels and three and a half crores [of hairs], || 7.3 ||
Overwhelmed by a multitude of channels, defiled, and enveloped by diseases,
[the body] is purified only by the supreme nectar of subtle meditation that has arisen from the Other.
The yogi brings about nourishment for himself and for others;
he becomes possessed of a divine body, free from all diseases. || 7-5 ||

The six seasons are the seats of birth, the navel, the heart, the palate, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*; they are called the wheels (*cakras*) because they are the supports for the expansions of the channels (*nāḍīs*), *māyā*, and so forth—namely, the piercing, the blazing, and the quiescence. Therein reside the sixteen vowels at the thumb, the ankle, the knee, the penis, the anus, and the *kanda*.

It is that in which there are supports— namely the channels, the belly, the heart, the tortoise-channel, the throat, the palate, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, the aperture of Brahmā, and that which is called the "end of the twelve"— serving as the bases for the individual soul; or else, according to the Kula method, because this system endures everything.
Below the penis is to be known as Kula; in the middle, it is designated as Viṣa;
but at the base, it is called Śākta, which, through awakening, sets [the flow] in motion.
Above that, at a distance of four finger-breadths, is the one called Agni;
below the navel, in the support of the wind, is the one called Ghaṭa located at the navel itself.
On the path between the navel and the heart, that which is known as "all-desires" (sarvakāma) is situated;
it is called by the name Sañjīvanī and resides in the center of the interior of the heart-lotus.
The tortoise is situated on the chest, and that which is called the "trembling" (lolā) is said to be in the throat;
above the lambhaka is the "support of nectar" (sudhādhāra), which consists of nectar.
Relying upon that very root, the gentle one, enveloped by the digits of the moon,
resides in the expanse of the sky between the eyebrows, known as the lotus of knowledge.
Raudra has its support at the base of the palate and is presided over by the power of Rudra;
it is known by the name Cintāmaṇi and resides at the crossroads.
In the center of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) at the crown of the head is the support of the fourth state (turyādhāra);
it is the supreme, subtle support of the channels (nāḍī), which awakens one to the pervasive density [of consciousness].
Thus have been described the sixteen supports (*ādhāra*)....................................
Thus [it is said]. Wherein there are three objects of perception (*lakṣya*)—to be characterized—which possess the nature of being internal, external, and both;
because of their nature as being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "enduring that which is called birth" (7-27),
there exists therein a pentad of spaces (*vyoma*) consisting of those about to be described: birth, the navel, the heart, the bindu, and the nāda.
Furthermore, as will be stated [in the verse], "But at the root of birth is that which is called Māyā" (7-22),
the knots— which are the causes for the obscuration of consciousness— are known as Māyā, Pāśava, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Indhikā, Dīpikā, Baindava, Nāda, and Śakti.

That which is bound by those fetters; that which is perfectly endowed with the triad of powers beginning with Will (icchā) and so forth, as it proceeds toward objects to be sought and the like; [that which moves] by way of the three abodes in the form of Moon, Sun, and Fire, through the left, right, and middle vital breaths.
It is presided over and endowed with the triad of channels known as *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*, which serve as the substrata for the vital winds;
and because it is joined by *gāndhārī*, *hastijihvā*, *pūṣā*, *yaśā*, *alambusā*, *kuhū*, and *śaṅkhinī*,
there are ten channels that constitute its paths.
It is completely surrounded— that is, woven warp and woof— by those known as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya;
and by the seventy-two [nāḍīs] which have become the manifestation of the ten channels situated in the ten directions.

It is completely pervaded by thousands [of channels] through intermediate pervasion, and by three and a half crores through great pervasion, along with the multitude of *nāḍīs*. It is defiled by its association with the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika* nature; for even among yogis, it is said: "That by which this [world] exists is indeed [experienced] through enjoyment."
Thus, having realized that the body is necessarily embraced by its state of persistence, the yogi nourishes—
whether it be his own self or that of another— the [body] with the nectar of subtle meditation that arises immediately thereafter, becoming manifest even while not abandoning its supreme nature.
He who does so becomes one whose diseases have departed and whose body is divine; thus, he becomes a manifestation of Śakti, emerging from the nectar of subtle meditation. || 5 ||
Regarding what was stated— "by the supreme nectar of subtle meditation alone, which has been brought forth"— he clarifies that [state] along with its preliminary stages:
"that whose nature is self-verified, established in itself, and arising from its own pervasion."
But the supreme power (parā śakti) spoken of by oneself is situated therein; the auspicious one (śivā) resides within its womb.
One should carry that [mantra] in the middle breath, which is constant between the prāṇa and apāna;
having become that [mantra], one should then [place] the mantra situated therein, firmly within its womb. || 7-7 ||
O lady of excellent hips, having performed that act of identification with the movement by means of the movement as previously taught, one should deposit it into the place of birth.
By means of the differentiation of states, one should join that [energy] to the mūlādhāra from its place;
one should pierce it through the application of the needle of sound (nāda) by means of subtle yoga.
Having pierced the sixteen supports as well as the twelve knots,
one who has ascended the path of the central channel should pierce the supreme, immutable point.
Having entered that and become established therein, Śiva is all-pervasive;
through the abandonment of all afflictions, he possesses partless and unshakeable power.
Having filled it again by that same path into the interior of the heart,
one should meditate upon the elixir as soon as it has entered there.
Having attained the experience of rest, one should cause that entire nectar to flow from that place; one should expel it everywhere with forceful speed. (7.13)
Having completely filled his own city with the supreme, infinite nectar through the differentiation of infinite channels and by means of the yoga of infinite meditation; 7.14.
Then, O Dear One, having become free from old age and death, both internally and externally,
everything is thus filled by Mṛtyujit through subtle meditation.
Therefore, O Goddess, he attains success quickly; this is the truth and not otherwise.

That which was indicated in the first chapter as the "vital power (*vīrya*) of the supreme abode" is the "own-nature" (*svarūpa*) of everything, because no specific [entity] is designated; it is self-cognizable and self-luminous, and not [otherwise].
He is the object of knowledge for self-awareness and other means of valid cognition;
"for that God of gods, there exists no dependence on another. Because he depends on nothing else, he is therefore established as independent."
Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Kāmika*, because this Blessed Lord transcends the sphere of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
He abides solely in His own independent Self and not elsewhere, for there exists nothing else distinct from Him;
on the contrary, the entire universe, being pervaded by Him, can only exist as being identical with Him— so he says.
"Whose manifestation (*saṃbhava*) occurs through its own pervasion (*svavyāpti*)," meaning whose emergence as the form of the universe (*viśvarūpatayā*) takes place by means of its own pervasion.

Furthermore, the supreme power (*parā śakti*) of this Lord, which consists of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), is "its own" (*svā*)—that is, non-deviating—and "arisen" (*uditā*), meaning it is of a throbbing nature; and it abides precisely within that form of the Lord, not elsewhere.

And it is not by way of the relationship between container and contained, but rather through identity (*sāmarasya*), as he says: "she who dwells within that. For this reason, she is *Śivā*, because her nature is non-different from the ultimate Śiva. Having thus revealed the supreme form as the foundational ground, he begins to explain subtle meditation with the words "her" (*tām*) and so forth.

One should carry that supreme power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) into the central breath—the *udāna* vital energy known as the Brahman residing in the *suṣumnā*—and, having submerged the pervasion of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, one should contemplate it in its state of emergence. How? By becoming the "I" (*ahaṃ*).

The meaning is: having entered into the full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) by means of the pacification of the subjectivity associated with the body and so forth. Then, having made the root mantra—which possesses the pervasion of the powers already mentioned and those yet to be described, which resides therein and is contained within it, and which thus consists of the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*)—into the form of the universal vibration (*spandana*), that is, the nature of general pulsation;

How? By means of the pulsation (spandana) uttered by oneself, through the stabilization of the non-vital breaths (aprāṇa) and so forth. Having thus contemplated the essence of the potency of the mantra (mantravīrya), one should deposit—that is, firmly establish—in the foundation-base (janmādhāra), which is the wheel of bliss (ānandacakra), that very self-potency consisting of that extraordinary aesthetic wonder (camatkāra). How?

By means of the differentiation—that is, the pacification—of "being" (*bhāva*), which consists of the conceit (*abhimāna*) limited by the body, vital breath, and so forth; then, even from that state, one should fix that conceit within the *kanda* at the *mūlādhāra* by means of the very differentiation of being, thereby making it firmly established.
Furthermore, by means of the needle of the vital breath (*prāṇasūcī*) of the Lord of Mantras, whose nature is throbbing and unfolding, he who has been [prepared]...

By that yoga, which consists of an upward ascent through increasingly exalted stages; likewise, "by means of subtle yoga" refers to the excellence of the intensification of the emerging and vibrating [consciousness]. Having ascended the path of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), one reaches the sixteen supports (*ādhāra*) prescribed in the previously mentioned Kula scriptures and other texts.
Likewise, having pierced the twelve knots that have been approached and are about to be resolved, one should pierce and enter the supreme,
eternal abode of the *dvādaśānta*. Having entered that very place,
through the abandonment of all bondage— including every affliction up to and including *mahāmāyā*— one remains right there.

Abiding in the fixed state (*dhruvapada*), having become all-pervasive and of one form with Supreme Śiva— being in a state of aesthetic identity (*samarasa*) with the eternally manifest supreme power (*parā-śakti*)— one fills the center of the heart by means of that very central path (*madhyama-mārga*) which has extended inward from the *dvādaśānta*, and having suffused it with the flow of supreme bliss (*parānanda*), therein...
As soon as that elixir, whose nature is supreme bliss, has entered the heart, one should meditate upon and contemplate it until rest is attained therein;
thereafter, one should cause that nectar to overflow from the heart.

One should direct [the breath] toward various streams. Then, having completely filled one's own body, both internally and externally, with that very nectar— which has flowed through the channels of Ananta and been meditated upon through intense meditation— one should thereafter [expel] all that nectar with force.

With a rapid flow, one should exhale through all the pores of the body throughout the entire field of perception, impelling it in an uninterrupted stream. When the yogi thus contemplates that everything is filled by the Blessed One, the Conqueror of Death, who is the essence of supreme virility, through the meditation on the subtle bliss of Śakti as taught [by him].

Then, having become free from old age and death, he quickly attains perfection and achieves the state of the Lord Mṛtyujit; no doubt easily accessible to an ordinary subject should be entertained in this matter. || 15 ||

Having thus explained subtle meditation according to the divisions of the *ādhāra* and so forth as taught in the Kaulika method— which consists of relying upon the path of Śākta bliss— he now begins to explain subtle meditation consisting of the contemplation of the surging waves of the full, dark nectar (*pūrṇāsitāmṛtakallola*), following the sequence of gross practice and according to the divisions of the *ādhāra* and so forth as taught in the Tantric method.
Having resorted to the place of birth, one should take hold of the central digit situated at the point of vibration.
Having established oneself as being situated in that, one should take refuge in the Fire of Time (Kālāgni);
having gone there and grasped the consciousness, one should deposit the vital energy (vīrya) right there.
The power called Kriyā, filled with that vigor, is middling and supreme;
having pierced upwards by means of consciousness and through the breaking of knots by means of will.
Having relied upon the root-throb and then abandoned the two flows, one should take recourse in that which flows through the middle path, known as Suṣumṇā. (7.19)
Relying on that very [state], one should desist from the domain of all the senses;
then, by means of consciousness in which illusion has completely subsided, one proceeds further upward.
Having gradually abandoned the causal agents beginning with Brahmā,
and having reached the six empowered [centers] ending with the one called Kuṇḍalinī, which is the obstructress,
[one attains] the five voids beginning with the heart through the piercing of the knots beginning with Māyā.

Previously, the organ of bliss (*ānandendriya*) was described as the place of birth; here, however, it is the bulb (*kanda*). There, having resorted to the middle digit—the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*)—which is characterized by vibration (*spanda*), she has blossomed hundreds of times through the contraction and expansion of the locus of the scent of intoxication (*mattagandha*).

Having seated oneself within the subtle vital energy (*sūkṣmaprāṇaśakti*), and having at that moment made the self and the mind abide therein, intent solely upon its contemplation, one should go to the "Fire of Time" (*kālāgni*) which has its support in the big toe, and take refuge there— that is, one should occupy it through meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*). And in that very place, one should grasp the realized knowledge (*vijñāna*).

"Vīrya" refers to the potency consisting of the vibration of Śakti (śāktaspandātma) attained from the ground of the bulb (kandabhūmi); one should deposit this and make it manifest through the intensification of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā). Thus, "filled with that potency"—meaning filled by the aforementioned potency—and having attained its rise, the power of action (kriyāśakti), whose nature is the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspandātma), emerges with the highest excellence.
It becomes the middle; that is, it arises having reached the navel, which is the center of the entire body.

How? By means of the will (*icchā*), through the effort of ascending upwards by the process of contraction, and through discernment (*vijñāna*) and contemplation (*bhāvanā*). "Upwards" refers to the sequence beginning from the upper [parts], namely the ankles, knees, genitals, the root-center (*kanda*), and the navel.

Having pierced—that is, having broken through—the knots by means of the activity of piercing, one ascends those very upper stations. The root *bhid* (as in the expression *bheditā māṇḍalikā bhūbhujā*) is used here in the sense of acceptance (*svīkāra*). Now, regarding the phrase "having resorted to the root-vibration" (*mūlaspandam*):

Having blocked the locus of the scent of intoxication (*mattagandha*) by means of a succession of expansion and contraction— and this is intended as an illustration of the divine instruments (*divyakaraṇa*) taught in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra*— one should then abandon and bypass the two flows, namely the two lateral channels (*pārśvanāḍī*). From there...

By means of the method of firm reliance upon the previously taught will and knowledge, one should properly take recourse in the channel named Suṣumnā through the previously taught power of Brahman, which flows along the central path as the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having taken recourse in that, one should then desist from the objects of all the senses resulting from that [practice].

One should remain with all the senses turned inward. At that time, one is such that *māyā*—the manifestation of the self as primarily consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth—is cast down and rejected. By means of knowledge whose nature is light and bliss, one [perceives] the causal principles, such as Brahmā, which are the very essence of the consciousnesses of emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and the rest located in the heart, throat, and other centers.

Having gradually abandoned [the elements], together with the five voids of the heart and so forth through the piercing of the knots of Māyā and the rest as will be described hereafter, one [proceeds] above the six causal deities known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śiva.
Having reached the power called *samanā*, which resides above as the power known as *kuṇḍalī*—
abiding in the form of a coil whose nature consists of the womb of the entire universe from the end of the void (*śūnya*) up to the beyond-void (*atiśūnya*)—
one should desist from further upward movement by means of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).

The connection with the distant [verb] is: "one should enter into the state of being whose self is the supreme reality beyond the *unmanā*. The word "should cease" (*viramet*), which occurred previously, is to be applied here as well.
In that regard, he first indicates the nature of the knots (*granthi*) and so forth, which are difficult to pierce, in successive order:
"But at the root of birth is the knot called *māyā*; in birth is the *pāśava* [knot]. (7.22)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five residing in the causal state are thus declared to be the knots. (7.23)
The knot known as Indhikā is Śiva, who pacifies the two paths; above that is the one named Dīpikā, and above that is indeed the Baindava.
The great knot called *nāda* follows, and beyond that is the knot of *śakti*.
The root of birth is the organ of bliss; it is the cause for the arising of the body and is known as the "knot of *māyā*" because it takes the form of *māyā*.
At the time of birth, within the *kanda*, it is the "knot of the bound" (*pāśava*) because the power of vision of bound souls (*paśus*) is contracted.
This is the first stage of the manifestation of the pāśyas— the support, the various channels, the vital breaths (prāṇas), and so forth.
Because Brahmā and the other causal deities residing in the locations of the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows,
and the forehead act as obstructors toward the bound soul (paśu) by exercising their agency over creation and the rest, they take the form of knots (granthis).

The five knots situated therein are to be suppressed above; for it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, and Urdhvagā are the powers of Nāda. These very [powers] are mentioned here.

The knots are so called because they have the nature of obscuring the light of the consciousness of others. Among them, the knot known as Indhikā is called "the pacifier of the two paths" (*dvimārgāśamana*);
it is the cause for the complete pacification of the flow in the left and right channels once they have been touched by Nirodhikā. For this very reason, it is Śiva.

Because it ascends the single path above, it is of the nature of the supreme good (*śreyas*). Above that is the knot (*granthi*) called the Lamp (*dīpikā*), because it is the cause of a slight radiance; beyond even that is the Bindu-knot (*baindava*), because it is the cause of a slightly greater light. The knot is of the nature of the power (*śakti*) described elsewhere as "the Illuminating" (*rocikā*). Above that is the one called Nāda.

Regarding the term "Great Knot" (*mahāgranthi*): elsewhere, two powers are mentioned, namely *mocikā* (the liberator) and *ūrdhvagā* (the upward-moving). Among these, *ūrdhvagā* is identified as *nādāntā* (the end of sound), and it is precisely there that she is said to have the liberator (*mocikā*) included within her. That very power is what is called the "Great Knot" known as *nāda*. Its greatness arises precisely from its inclusion of the other knots. Therefore:
The knot situated at the location of the supreme power is the "knot of power" (śaktigranthi).
When it has been thus determined,
one should enter the supreme state after piercing through that group of twelve knots.
In the abode that is the self of the supreme reality beyond the *unmanā* state. || 25 ||
In this context, he states that by the very breaking of the knots of the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, one should dissolve the locations such as the heart presided over by them,
as well as the location of Śakti through the breaking of the knot of Śakti, and above that, the abode of Vyāpinī and the abode of Śiva.
One should likewise pierce Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, as well as Sadāśiva, Śakti, and the abode of Śiva.
The word "place" (*sthāna*) at the beginning is used to indicate that the words for Brahmā and the others also signify their respective locations.
Now, he demonstrates the previously mentioned five voids (*śūnyapañcaka*) and the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*): "The infinite space called Janma is in the navel; the second void is [there]."
The third is in the location of the heart, and the fourth is in the center of the bindu.
Now the six cakras, beginning with that called Nāda, are described;
the cakra of the channels (nāḍicakra) is in the [cakra] called Janma, while the supreme one called Māyā is at the navel.
The yogic wheel is situated in the heart; that which is situated in the palate is known as the piercing [wheel].
That which is situated in the bindu is the wheel of light, while that which is situated in the nāda is called the peaceful [wheel]. (7.29)
It is infinite because it is the support of the infinite universe; it is called "Sound" (nāda) because it is the substratum of sound;
and because it is the cause for the expansion through the channels, there is knowledge of the bodily array at the navel-center. (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 3.25)

According to this principle, the reasons for [the practice] beginning with the wheel of channels (*nāḍicakra*) are, in sequence: because it is the cause for the manifestation of the entire phenomenal world of *māyā*;
because it bestows one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*) upon yogins; because it is to be pierced through effort; because its nature is radiance (*dīpti*);
and because it bestows peace (*śānti*). These are the voids (*śūnya*).
Because they bestow the immersion of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-āveśa*), whereas the wheels (*cakras*) are to be abandoned because they are the cause for the proliferation of duality,
one should pierce all those previously mentioned along with them using the spear of knowledge (*jñāna-śūla*).
According to the previously stated method, these are the foundational knots and so forth; the "spear of knowledge" is the vibration of consciousness that constitutes the potency of mantra.
He states the reasoning for kindling the lance of gnosis: "Having ascended, one should gradually press upon its root, which is called the support of birth. (7.30)

Having firmly established the ground of the *kanda* through one-pointed concentration of mind and vital breath— its root being the location known as *mattagandha*— one should, by means of the practice of contraction and expansion, gradually press [the area] once the emergence of the *śakti* is perceived, so that the *śakti* becomes directed upwards. 30.
Now, as an incidental digression, he speaks of the synonyms for the locus of birth well-known in various scriptures:
"O lady of beautiful hips, listen further to the synonyms of the locus of birth;
the place of birth is called the *kanda*, and there are five locations known as the *kūrma*. || 7-31 ||
Likewise, it is here called Matsyodara and also Mūlādhāra;
because it is the cause of the arising of the vital breath (marut), because it has the form of the cavity of the central channel (madhyanāḍī), because it is shaped like a tortoise (kūrma),
because it is the locus of the five elements beginning with earth and ending with space, and because it vibrates like the belly of a fish (matsyodara).
And because it is the fundamental cause, birth and the rest are so designated.
Thus, because of its great majesty, it is described in the Tantras as the root-ground;
the knower of yoga should indeed find the mudrā called Khecarī situated therein. (7.32)
O Goddess, when the self is indeed sealed by that mudrā,
then it shall gradually ascend upwards through higher knowledge.

The yogi may obtain that which is "situated therein"—the power (*śakti*) vibrating from the ground of the *kanda*; the "seal" (*mudrā*), so called because it releases the bonds through the resonance of joy (*mudaḥ*), because its nature consists of piercing and liquefying, and because it seals the wealth of supreme consciousness; and [he obtains] the one known as Khecarī because she moves in the sky of awakening (*bodha-gagana*). And when, by means of that which has been obtained—

When the self has been sealed and brought under its control, then, by means of the consciousness whose nature is the vibration of the power of that mantra, it should expand and pervade upward as far as the limit of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta). || 33 ||
He clarifies this very point:
"One should pierce, one should pierce the supreme station until it is honored by the excellent vowels;
having reached that very station, the yogin becomes of equal flavor. (7.34)

Having attained the partless state, the all-pervading Supreme Śiva [resides] in the supreme station, the End of the Twelve. By the repetition [of the verb], the expression "should pierce" is clarified as occurring sequentially. Thus it is said: "in a state of equal flavor."
Because everything belonging to the lower path has attained a state of identification with that [Supreme], it is "Paramaśiva";
however, it is not of the nature of a liberated Śiva who is distinct [from the Absolute] as asserted by the proponents of duality (bhedavādin).

Now, restating the pervasive presence of non-difference from Paramaśiva by means of half a verse, he begins to teach the pervasive presence [of Śakti] through the process of descent: "Having thus become all, equal, motionless, and eternally arisen. (7.35)
From that, there proceeds a power that is free from affliction and devoid of an external object;
it is designated by mere will, having the nature of knowledge and consisting of action. (7.36)

That single [reality], existing through its differentiation by means of the differentiation of states (*bhāva*), has become so; here the sense of the causative (*ṇij*) is internalized. Thus, everything up to the *samanā* level, by ascending to the *dvādaśānta*, becomes equal (*sama*), i.e., of one flavor (*samarasa*), motionless (*niḥspanda*), and with its waves stilled (*praśāntakallola*).

Having contemplated— that is, having accomplished— the state of being eternally arisen as the unity with the light of the supreme consciousness (*paracitprakāśa*), from that very source, namely the abode of the *dvādaśānta*, there proceeds the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), which is the effulgence of the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*) and other powers, characterized by a supreme vibration devoid of any objective referent (*lakṣyahīnā*) and from which all affliction (*āmaya*) has departed.
The meaning is that it "opens up," which is to say it unfolds sequentially in the form of will, knowledge, and action.

For that very reason, it is "one"; yet, by virtue of the differentiation of states belonging to Him—namely Paramaśiva—consisting in the variety arising from the manifestation of the objects of desire, the objects of knowledge, and the objects of action, it exists in a state of differentiation.
Because of the manifold variety of desires and so forth that have been grasped;

since the Power (Śakti) proceeds spontaneously from Paramaśiva in this way, therefore, having filled [the space] by means of the Khecarīmudrā, [one should contemplate] there, everywhere, up to the end of Śakti. (7.37)

As long as the moon has not yet risen, so long does that which is subtle, stainless, graspable through meditative state (*bhāva*), free from doubt, abandoned by all conditions, and supreme [remain hidden]. (7-38)
O fair-faced one, yogins become that pervasive, sovereign, incomparable, and painless state when they have ascended to it.
In that regard:
"Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), the yogi should place the Lord of the Eye at the navel;
he should lead it, rod-like in form, as far as the three voids."
"Having restrained [the breath] there, one should quickly impel it through the three voids (*kha-traya*).
Having bound this, the great yogi attains movement in the sky (*khe-gati*). (7.15.17).
Thus, by means of the aforementioned *Khecarīmudrā*, characterized in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*, up to the end of *Śakti*—

Until, having filled [the body] in every way and in every manner, the downward breath (*apāna*) has been impelled there as the "moon"— at that time, when the yogi has ascended upon it and entered the station of its power,
[he perceives that which is] subtle, beyond the senses, stainless, unobstructed, graspable through meditative state (*bhāva*), and self-luminous.
It is free from doubt, its essence being self-reflection; it is abandoned by all states such as waking and the rest;
it is superior to the state of universal equilibrium (*sāmarasya*); it is all-pervasive because it is not delimited by directions or locations;
it is the Supreme Lord, autonomous; it is incomparable due to its non-duality; and there exists no affliction (*āmaya*) [in it].

Since the severance of the great illusion occurs for those who possess devotion, that is the stainless [state]; the meaning is that they become one with that supreme abode, they are born as being composed of it. || 39 ||
Thus, for the yogin who has attained non-difference from the supreme reality, that which was described by the phrase "that power proceeds"— the supreme power (*parā śakti*) unfolding—
is the womb (*yoni*) of all the gods and of all powers in manifold ways.
The womb consists of Agni and Soma; from it everything proceeds.
In that state, the mantras woven together indeed become possessed of power;
it is the dissolution of all things, and that alone is the supreme state.
Therefore, having attained the incomparable nectar and having playfully agitated the *bindu*, one agitates the supreme Śiva and from that the creation proceeds. (7.42)
Then, when the rising of the moon is proclaimed, one should there contemplate that supreme and most excellent nectar—an infinite wave of thick nectar. (7.43)
Therefore, having attained the pure nectar, one should draw it up by means of one's own power; O fair-hipped lady, one should pierce the causal centers and so forth by way of the central channel.
One should perform the act of nourishment (āpyāyana) at each respective stage in due order;
therefore, one should nourish [the elements] from below until the state of Brahman is reached.
One should cause it to proceed into the fire of time (kālāgni) by way of the path of its place of origin;
then, having filled it from all sides, one should contemplate the city as completely full.
One should contemplate the entire [body] as completely filled with the nectar of the Suṣumṇā, [spreading] from there through the infinite channels and the pores of the skin in every direction. (7.47)
Having emerged and become all-pervasive, [the yogin] is immersed in the ocean of nectar,
which is agitated by waves of nectar and overflowing with the ocean of nectar.
Above that is indeed the ocean of nectar, flowing forth, all-pervasive, and auspicious;
thus the nectar has become of one flavor, facing in every direction.
Having attained Śiva, whose nature is that of will, knowledge, and action, and who is one's own true self, free from all affliction, one should contemplate Him through direct personal experience.
Having attained the subtle state of Amṛteśa, one indeed becomes immortal;
having thus become immortal, one conquers death—of this there is no doubt. (7.51)
Time-conquering, fortunate, and steadfast—death does not afflict him.

"Of all the gods" refers to Anāśrita, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Ananta, Rudra, and the others; "of the powers" refers to Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and so forth. And because that power is the womb consisting of Agni and Soma, for that very reason...
She is preeminent as *soma*, because from her everything proceeds and arises;
therefore, the universe—which is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of the power of Agni and Soma—is composed of Agni and Soma alone.
And thus, the knowers of reality say that even fire gladdens and even snow burns. Furthermore:

In that regard, the mantras—which are strung together within the abode of the power whose nature is Agni and Soma, and which are uttered as the very essence of its vitality—are possessed of protection and bestow both accomplishment (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*). Thus, it is stated that power is the cause of persistence.
That very [power], because it is of the nature of fire within the power whose essence is Agni and Soma, also possesses the quality of being the destroyer. In this way...
Having demonstrated that Śakti is the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, he states the subject at hand with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).

Since this Śakti is of such a nature, therefore, having agitated the Supreme Śiva by descending through the stage of Samanā and thereby making Him intent upon creation, [one realizes] therein that which is beyond comparison.

Having attained the nectar consisting of supreme bliss— that abode which is the nature of great luminosity and has ascended to the *samanā* level— one agitates it through "play," that is, through the sport of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), making it oriented toward the flow of emanation. Then, when the rising of the moon— the arousal of the *apāna*— is known to have occurred, [the process proceeds] from that very abode of Śakti.

One should meditate upon that which has arisen as the supreme nectar, preeminent with the essence of bliss, possessing dense waves of nectar and the spreading of pure white ambrosia—such is it; one should contemplate that which is infinite and uninterrupted. From that rising of the moon, having obtained the pure nectar by means of one's own power turned inward, [one should proceed].

One should draw [the breath] through the middle path and cause it to descend further and further. By that means, one should pierce and sprinkle all the causes—namely Brahmā and the others—and by the word "etcetera," the previously mentioned centers such as the wheel and the support. This very process has been clarified by the passage beginning with "This is nourishment" (etadevāpyāyanam).

From the heart-center, which is the abode of Brahman, until that [state] becomes attained as the nectar (*amṛta*), one should then pour it down from there into the place below the navel; having filled [the body] up to the end of the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*), one should contemplate the body as completely full on all sides. Then, spreading forth through all the pores of the skin, one should effect a pervasion both internally and externally.

One should contemplate oneself as the stainless Supreme Śiva-nature, whose form is the supreme nectar that has become one in essence with the flooding of the ocean of nectar pervading all directions, and which is radiant with the powers of will, knowledge, and action. Thus, through subtle meditation, having conquered death and attained supreme auspiciousness, [one abides] in the immortal—
He becomes equal to Śata. || 51 ||
I have revealed to you this subtle method for cheating death. || 7.52 ||
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, I have not explained this to anyone except for you.
This has been thus revealed by you alone, whose sole vow is the supreme favoring of others.
I praise the lofty eye of the Great Lord, which floods everything with the playful surges of nectar arising from subtle meditation.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Subtle Meditation," in the *Netrodyota*, composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja, on the *Śrī Netratantra*. 7.
The Eighth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net" [of the Vidyās].
It is beautiful with the swaying of vibration, which brings about an abundance of intense bliss.
Victory to the Eye, the self-luminous, the great light of consciousness, the conqueror of death!

Immediately after the subtle meditation (*sūkṣmadhyāna*), for the sake of determining the supreme meditation (*paradhyāna*), the Blessed One said: "Now, O beloved, the eternal and supreme *mṛtyuñjaya* (the conqueror of death) is being described;
having attained which, one would no longer proceed within the threefold cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). (8.1)

The word *atha* (now/then) serves to indicate the immediate succession to subtle meditation (*sūkṣmadhyāna*). And that which is eternally the conqueror of death (*mṛtyuñjaya*), the devourer of time (*kālagrāsin*), the supreme and unsurpassed nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśa-svarūpa*)—it exists in three forms:
as *bhava* (existence), *abhava* (non-existence), and *atibhava* (transcending existence), corresponding respectively to the limits of Māyā, Sadāśiva, and Śiva. || 1 ||
Furthermore, the yogi shines as all-pervading, all-seeing, all-doing, and auspicious;
I shall explain that, for there exists nothing other than it. (8.2)
Having attained that state, one indeed becomes ageless and immortal through identification with it;

for this supreme yogin, because he is untouched by the sense of being a subject (pramātṛtā) regarding the body and so forth, there is no talk whatsoever of old age, death, or the like— this is the meaning.
He begins to explain this very point:
"That which speech does not constantly speak, and that which cannot be seen by the eye. (8.3)
That which is not heard by the ears, that which the nose does not smell, that which the tongue does not taste, and that which the organ of touch does not feel; (8.4)
It is not to be conceived by the mind, being devoid of all colors and tastes;
yet it is endowed with all colors and tastes, immeasurable, and beyond the reach of the senses.
O Goddess, that which yogis attain by means of great practice, supreme dispassion, and [the grace of] the Supreme One, they indeed become free from old age and death. || 8-6 ||

O beloved, through the abandonment of passion and hatred, the destruction of greed and delusion, the relinquishing of intoxication and envy, and the exhaustion of pride, arrogance, and darkness. || 8.7 ||

That which is eternal, constant, auspicious, immutable, and supreme is attained—even though primordial speech, consisting of the three forms, beholds it, she does not speak it; and that which is beyond the range of the external and internal organs, [is described as follows]: "they describe it" are the *varṇas*, meaning the denoters, for they are themselves described (*varṇyante*).

The phonemes (varṇas) are the denotable; "abandoned by all those phonemes and their aesthetic flavors (rasas) and expansions" means that its nature is neither the denoted nor the denoter. And yet, because it is the self of the universe, it is endowed with all of them; therefore, being beyond the senses, it is not an object of knowledge (prameya), but rather—
It is concluded that [the Self] has the singular nature of the supreme subject; having attained and entered into such a reality, [it is said]:
"They desire yoga as oneness," Mālinīvijayottara Tantra (4.4).
Thus, by abiding in this state, yogins who possess the singular supreme reality become, in truth, free from old age and death. Therefore, through great practice:
"Those who, fixing their minds on me, worship me with constant discipline... (Bhagavad Gītā 12.2).
Thus, through supreme effort in constant immersion and through supreme dispassion—
the absence of craving for all enjoyments from the Earth principle up to the Unattached (Anāśrita), as perceived through both direct experience and scripture—
and precisely because of this, through the pacification of all defects such as attachment and aversion, [the goal] is obtained from the honor of Śaṅkara by means of pride (māna).

Through its destruction, there arises that which is eternal, irreversible in nature, constant, supramundane, auspicious, consisting of supreme bliss, imperishable, and unchanging; and for these reasons, it is the highest, being the most excellent of all.
And yet this vast expanse of his is perceived in the mere twinkling of an eye. || 8-8 ||

From that time forward, he is liberated and shall not undergo rebirth again. The word "by anyone" (*kenacit*) is to be supplied in the middle [of the sentence]. He is "perceived," meaning he is fully absorbed. "From that time forward" means not at some other later time. "Liberated" means rendered free from qualities (*aguṇīkṛta*), even while the body and vital breaths remain. And... [the text continues].
Upon the abandonment of that body, he does not undergo rebirth or attain connection with another body; rather, he becomes none other than Paramaśiva himself.
And then the yogi shall attain [the goal] through the eightfold yoga, and not from anywhere else.
The Lord sequentially teaches that eightfold yoga, which is distinct in form from what is propounded in other treatises:
"Constant detachment from worldly existence is declared to be the supreme *yama*."
But cultivation (bhāvanā) regarding the supreme reality is called constant restraint (niyama). || 8-10 ||
This is clear. || 10 ||

Resorting to the middle breath (madhyama-prāṇa) in the interval between the paths of prāṇa and apāna, and taking hold of the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), one shall obtain the seat situated therein.
Having resorted to the *udāna*— the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that moves upward, which exists in the middle channel (*madhyanāḍī*) between the left and right paths of *prāṇa* and *apāna*—
and through the submergence of the pervasion of *prāṇa*, there arises the emergence of the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*).

Having taken hold of—that is, having firmly grasped—consciousness in the form of the unfolding and throbbing radiance of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the yogi obtains the very seat situated therein; the meaning is that, seated upon the seat of his own power of knowledge, he becomes the Great Lord (*Maheśa*) of consciousness. || 11 ||
But having abandoned the gross state of the vital breaths and so forth, one then attains the subtle, internal, and supreme vibration which transcends even the subtle. || 8-12 ||
That is designated as *prāṇāyāma* from which one does not fall away again.

Having abandoned—that is, having cast off—the gross state or nature consisting of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and so forth, which occurs in relation to the vital breaths such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *samāna*; "then" (*atha*) refers to that which follows immediately after this gross *prāṇāyāma*.
Having abandoned that which is subtle and internal— consisting of the forms of exhaling, inhaling, and so forth by means of the middle path—

from which [path] even that which is subtle is transcended as the supreme, namely the vibration whose nature is the pulsation of the insentient [elements] such as breath; therefore, that alone is the supreme vibration, which is He Himself.

The regulation (*niyama*) of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), which possess the distinction of being gross and subtle, consists in the cessation of the manifestation of their primary [individual] nature; this has been described and established as the most excellent.
For, by attaining this *prāṇāyāma*, one does not fall back again from the state of being composed of the conscious subject (*cit-pramātṛ-mayatā*).
Sometimes it abandons [it].
That which is the functioning of the qualities such as sound and so forth is indeed experienced by the mind. || 8-13 ||
Having abandoned that [external world], one should enter that supreme abode with one's own mind;
this is declared to be *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal), which severs the bonds of worldly existence.

Having abandoned— that is, having cast aside with indifference— whatever state or condition of the qualities such as sound and touch, which consist of *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, is experienced by the mind through consciousness;

for it is precisely by means of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of conceptual consciousness within one's own mind that there is entry into the abode of supreme Consciousness (*paraciddhāma*), because [that abode] is the ground of Consciousness (*citibhūmi*).
Pratyāhāra consists in bringing back the outward-tending mind to its opposite state; therefore, it is the cutter of the bonds of worldly existence. || 14 ||

Having transcended the qualities of the intellect (dhī)—such as *sattva* and the rest—and having meditated upon the object of meditation that is beyond thought, imperishable, and all-pervading; that meditation which is self-realized is what the wise know to be true *dhyāna*. (8.15) Having transcended the qualities of the intellect (*dhī*), that is, the *buddhi*, by means of total absorption and thereby pacifying them...

"Nirdhyeyam" means that which has emerged from the objects of meditation—namely, those things characterized by fixed forms, shapes, and so forth—and from which those [objects] have emerged. It is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), omnipresent (*vyāpaka*), imperishable (*avyaya*), eternal (*nitya*), self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*), and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). It is "dhyeya," meaning worthy of meditation, and yet also "adhyeya," meaning that which is to be studied.

It must be contemplated and remembered; having meditated upon and reflected on the Supreme Lord—who is, by implication, a mass of consciousness and bliss—those wise ones who know reality understand that "that" (tat) is precisely the nature of that reflective awareness (vimarśa);
they know meditation (dhyāna) as an uninterrupted succession. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of *eva* (indeed). || 15 ||
That by which the state of the Supreme Self is always maintained is designated as *dhāraṇā*; it is the destroyer of the bonds of worldly existence. (8.16)

For that yogin by whom the state of supreme selfhood— consciousness— is always maintained and sustained through immersion, his meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*), which consists of the reflective awareness of consciousness,
is designated as the cause for the destruction of the bondage of worldly existence, being distinguished from other forms of concentration.

Having thus established the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), postures (āsana), breath-control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), and concentration (dhāraṇā) from the perspective of the supramundane view, he also teaches samādhi— which has the supreme essential nature as its object— and which is attained through the means of the individual (āṇava), the empowered (śākta), and the divine (śāmbhava), as well as the "means-less" (anupāya).
The establishment [of the self] equally in all beings and the restraint of the mind—this is declared to be *samādhi*; otherwise, it is merely worldly hypocrisy. (8.17)

The restraint of the mind consists in the application of the mind toward all living beings with equanimity, by means of suppressing the practice of partiality; this is also called "concentration" (*samādhāna*). Contemplating the equality of others with oneself is what is declared to be concentration. Otherwise, [it would not be so].
That composure which is the opposite of this, consisting of such methods as closing the eyes and so forth, has as its sole purpose the deception of the world. (17)
This is the *samādhāna* (concentration) pertaining to the means of *āṇava* [yoga], which employs meditation; that pertaining to the means of *śākta* [yoga] employs pure conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Thus it is said:
"One whose intellect is equal toward all beings, whether situated within oneself or outside, in this world..."
"I am Śiva, I am without a second; that is remembered as the supreme samādhi. (8-18)
"I alone am all this"—

this supreme *samādhi*, which consists of the ascertainment arising from pure *vidyā* through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "I" and "this," is traditionally known by way of lineage. || 18 ||
Now, he teaches the ever-arisen samādhi, which, although attainable through a single means, is yet "without means" (anupāya) due to its independence from any means;
it is to be realized as one's own true nature, consisting of pure consciousness, and born of one's own innate being.
And they know that the state of meditative absorption, whose nature is self-cognizable, is supreme.

That which is to be experienced through the means of a single, perfect application—that which vibrates as the innate nature of consciousness, shining as the abode of *cit*—is the self-evident nature of one's own being; thus, it is self-luminous, eternally arisen, and a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) without emergence from it. || 19 ||
Having skillfully investigated the state through the two heaps of consciousness and insentience, he speaks of the Śāmbhava samādhi, which is the means free from conceptualization;
the wise know that samādhi to be the eternal and perpetual form. (8.20)

The mass of the insentient (*jaḍarāśi*) consists of the worlds, objective entities, bodies, and so forth. The mass of consciousness (*cidrāśi*) is the group of subjects known as the Sakala, Pralayākala, Vijñānākala, Mantra, Mantreśa, Mantramaheśa, and Śiva. From between these two, the "middle" (*madhya*) is the plane that is the locus of the foundation of the universe; it is subtle.

Having reflected deeply and deliberated, those who know reality understand that the state of composure is that form which shines forth as eternal, indestructible, perpetual, devoid of transformation or evolution, and ever self-luminous. || 20 ||
Concluding what was introduced with the words “by means of the eightfold yoga,” he applies it to the present subject:
“Thus, having perceived by means of the eightfold yoga the supreme, eternal [Self] abiding in its own nature, one deceives Time—the supreme, all-pervading Lord of Immortality. (8.21)

O Goddess, he shall become a conqueror of death, and Time shall not be able to calculate him; this is according to the form thus described, and not by means of non-violence, truthfulness, and so forth as taught in other scriptures—
[he who worships] the Supreme Lord of Deathlessness, the Master of Consciousness (Cinnātha).
Having seen the Lord of all causes, who is without support and whose end is infinite, one deceives Time;

one becomes a single mass of consciousness-bliss, untouched by time. Therefore, in reality, he alone is the "Conqueror of Death" (*mṛtyujit*) because of his shattering of death, which consists of contraction. However, one who has merely made the body stable for a very long time is not [the Conqueror of Death].
In reality, the underlying intention is that he is Mṛtyujit (the Conqueror of Death).
Furthermore, [this occurs] through the abandonment of the thirty-six principles and the avoidance of the infinite worlds. || 8-22 ||
Indeed, beyond the eighty-one syllables and above the fifty letters, it is all-pervasive within all mantras and is truly the life-force of them all. (8.23)
But above the thirty-eight kalās is that which is within all and situated in the midst of all;
its beginning, middle, and end cannot be found by anyone. (8.24)
Having attained that immeasurable and incomparable [state], nothing remains to be acquired.

Having abandoned the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva, as well as the worlds (*bhuvanas*) beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Anāśrita— according to the system of the *Navātman* and others, through the fifty letters beginning with 'A' which constitute the words beginning with *praṇava*— [one attains the goal].
Above the thirty-eight kalās, beginning with Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, and so forth, it pervades all mantras;

thus, it transcends the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan). Consequently, it is the life-force of all, existing within all as their prior and posterior limits, for the entire universe is composed of that very essence.

It is situated at the center of all, yet its beginning, middle, and end cannot be found by anyone because it transcends directions, time, and so forth; therefore, it is immeasurable, and because it is non-dual, it is incomparable; having reached it, yogis attain it by transcending the body, vital breath, and other elements composed of the sixfold path.
"Everything"—meaning the entire expansion of the paths—is not found, nor is it attained; therefore, as before, it is not concealed.
However, by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), the sense is that "everything is not not found," but rather it *is* indeed found;
the meaning is that the state of Amṛteśa-Bhairava, which is the self of all and everything, exists.
Likewise, by that single [element], which is immeasurable, the entire world is filled. || 8-25 ||
Having known that, and having ascertained it with firm conviction, one is swiftly liberated from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra.
Moreover,
it is free from the three principles, eternal, immovable, and constant.
Having seen [the truth] through the divine path of yoga, one is not born again; it is liberated from all sense faculties, unknowable, and free from affliction. || 8-27 ||

The triad of principles known as Nara, Śakti, and Śiva is eternal; like the theory of vivarta (illusory manifestation), it does not assume unreal or distinct forms. It is immovable, unchanging, fixed, and constant.
Being free from the senses, it is untainted—that is, unobscured by *māyā* and the senses—and is unknowable by [ordinary] means, yet [knowable] through the divine.

By means of the path of yoga—through the method of sustaining non-conceptual awareness as it emerges through the abandonment of conceptualization—one sees [it] directly; having realized it, one does not return to birth again. || 27 ||

Thus, it is stated that the supreme reality (para-tattva), attained through the means of Āṇava, Śākta, and Śāmbhava, which bestows liberation, is not only to be accepted here [in this system], but in all scriptures as well; for he says:
"But the nature of the Supreme Self is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi)."
Consciousness is declared in all scriptures to be the nature of the Self. || 28 ||
That consciousness which is specifically devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and delimiters (*avacchedaka*), being uncontracted by such limitations, is the nature of the Self as the subject;
that very same thing is the essential nature of the Supreme Self, Paramaśiva, and not something distinct from it, as the proponents of duality (*bhedavādin*) maintain.
They think thus; for this very reason, it is stated at the conclusion of the determination of the ultimate samādhi: "I am Śiva, I am non-dual.

This is taught in all the scriptures and not merely in some of them; by this, it is established that even within the established doctrines (siddhāntas), the secret essence of non-duality exists internally.
For those whose latent tendencies toward the duality of worldly existence are deeply rooted, this [truth] has not been made manifest. As it is said in the venerable *Kulapañcāśikā*:
"To say that something exists which does not exist for all the world is a contradiction."
O Goddess, when that which is proclaimed does not take root in the heart, [it is said to be so].
"For this reason, O Goddess, it has been carefully guarded by the deities.
Therefore, O Mistress of the Gods, what is there on the surface of the earth that cannot be accomplished through that Siddha?
Thus, [it is said] in the Śivasūtras, which consist of a compendium of the essence of all the Śaiva scriptures:
"It is consciousness that is the Self"—this was stated at the very beginning [of the work]. || 28 ||
Even though this form of one's own self is thus constituted, O Goddess, it would not be stainless as long as it has not been awakened by Śakti.
Here, the mouth of Śiva is said to be [the means]. (20)

Thus, according to the principle taught by the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka and others, by means of the power of the Supreme Lord Himself, the individual soul (aṇu)— which consists of the manifestation of that power— submerges its state of limited individuality (aṇutva) through the entry into its own inherent radiance (sphurattā),
and its state as the Supreme Śiva (paramaśivatva) is made manifest.
One might object: "Even though they have become Śivas through initiation (dīkṣā), are not the liberated Śivas still distinct from Paramaśiva?
Therefore, how can it be said that the consciousness of the self (ātmacaitanya) is identical with the nature of the Supreme Self? To pacify this doubt, [the author] states:
"By means of initiation, knowledge, and so forth, one purifies the self and makes it stainless. (8.29)
Those who speak thus and do not find the other, the supreme Śiva—they are worshippers of the self within the Śaiva tradition and do not reach the highest state. (8.30)

Those who, through initiation, knowledge, yoga, and conduct, claim that the self being purified becomes something stainless and distinct—separate from Paramaśiva and different from his manifestation—do not find Paramaśiva; they do not attain the nature of Paramaśiva. They are worshippers of the self (*ātmopāsaka*), those who venerate the principle of the pure self (*śuddhātmatattva*) within Śaivism.

The "supreme state" is the state of Supreme Śiva; they do not go to it, that is, they do not attain it. However, if they should ever—due to the intense descent of power (tīvra-śaktipāta)—attain it, it is only through Śaiva knowledge, namely the non-dual knowledge imparted by Śiva, and not by any other knowledge; this is to be construed with the seventh and third [verses] of the Tantra. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīsvacchanda*, at the occasion of determining the pure Self situated within the level of *samanā*:
"Those who, without knowing the supreme reality, have merely imagined Śiva-nature for themselves—those worshippers of the self in the Śaiva system do not reach the Supreme Śiva. (4.392)
Thus [ends the section]. || 30 ||
He clarifies this very point by means of another formulation:
"Or rather, the Supreme Śakti, endowed with qualities such as omniscience and the like, being stainless, would not expand [further] once she has expanded from the soles of the feet upward. (8.31)
Until then, indeed, the Self is not stainless; at that time, it is said to be bound in the Śiva-state.

In view of the word *tāvat*, the word *yāvat* is to be supplied. Therefore, from the feet up to the big toes, through the expansion [of consciousness] by means of the immersion of the predominance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

As long as the supreme power— which consists of omniscience, omnipotence, and absolute freedom— is not unfolded, nor made manifest, by the grace-bestowing power in the form of initiation, knowledge, and so forth, which causes the predominance of consciousness to emerge, the self remains a *jīva* and is not stainless. And when this occurs, then...
In the Śaiva tradition, this self is said to be truly bound because it has not attained liberation while living.
He shows the nature of the expanded power:
"Abiding therein, the person knows everything—past and future. (8.32)

Having fully restrained the collection of the senses, when the yogi attains a stable state within that reality characterized by *śakti*— which consists of the falling away of the moments (*tuṭi*) and abides in the initial unfolding (*ādyonmeṣa*)— he knows everything, including the past, the future, and so forth; that is the nature of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*).
Reality is characterized by power.
Likewise, wherever there may be desire, knowledge also proceeds. || 8-33 ||

Alternatively, that very reality characterized by power (śakti) consists of action (kriyā), which is the essential nature of what is to be done (kṛtya). Wherever— be it at whatever opportunity— an uncreated, non-conceptual will, cognition, or action whose nature is not something to be produced (niṣpādya) but rather its own essential nature (svarūpa), proceeds as a vibration (sphurattā), therein [resides that reality].
In that context, the reality of the self, which consists solely of the pure will and so forth uncolored by those objects of desire and the like,
is characterized as *śakti*.
Likewise, O Goddess, because the all-pervading Self, whose nature is consciousness, is Śiva. (8.34)
That power which spreads forth as wondrous bliss is known as the Supreme.

For the yogin who contemplates his own self as consisting of all-pervading pure consciousness, that power—which is of the nature of wonder and consists of bliss—spreads forth and unfolds from Śiva; she is remembered as the Supreme.
The meaning is that this very reality is characterized by power (śakti).
Thus, by expanding that self through the manifestation supported by the powers thus characterized, he becomes the possessor of qualities through such attributes as omniscience and the rest. (8.35)

O Goddess, Śiva, the supreme cause, is said to be "with appearance" (sābhāsa) by virtue of his qualities such as omniscience; for, having expanded himself through the reflective awareness (vimarśana) of that [divine nature], there arises the "great bodiless state" (mahāvideha), which is an unconstructed mental modification directed outwardly, whereby the veil over the Light is destroyed—according to the Yoga Sūtra (3.43): "The great bodiless state is the external, unconstructed mental modification, because it results in the destruction of the covering of the Light."
The yogi who, through stability, has blossomed and become endowed with those very qualities such as omniscience and the rest,
is called Śiva-with-appearance (sābhāsa-śiva) precisely because of his reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the appearances of omniscience and so forth.
He clarifies this very point:
"For he whose awakening is indeed beginningless is omniscient and completely satisfied. (8.36)
For he who is independent, undecaying, and possesses infinite power—the possessor of qualities—experiences his own qualities through the differentiation of those qualities. (8.37)
One should contemplate here the manifoldness [of objects] through their various distinctions and divisions;
that [subject] is called "with appearance" (sābhāsa), while the one without appearance (nirābhāsa) is described as follows.

He is completely satisfied through the absence of desire, a mass of consciousness and bliss; he is beginningless, yet not produced by mental cultivation; he is independent, yet unlike a limited Lord (bhedeśvara) who depends on the ripening of the impurity of karma and so forth;
he is unimpaired, yet unlike Brahmā and others who are obscured by states such as sleep; and he possesses infinite power.

"In accordance with the principle that 'His powers are the entire universe,' he has the whole world as his body in the form of rays; he is the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān), having manifested the nature of the Supreme Power as it is defined; [and he is] of the qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—"

Through differentiation— that is, through the tearing apart [of duality] arising from the immersion of the state of being a subject (pramātṛtā) such as the body and so forth into the ground of consciousness— one attains one's own qualities, such as omniscience and the like. And by means of those very qualities, one becomes the possessor of qualities (guṇin),
which is the state produced by the exclusion of various distinctions— such as omniscience and other specific attributes— according to the perspective explained.

That which would reflect upon the self as having a distinct differentiation—that is, as a state of manifoldness consisting of various appearances—is said to be "with appearance" (*sābhāsa*). However, that which is without such reflection is called "without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*).
He said to him:
"I am not, nor is there another; at that time, one becomes free from appearances (nirābhāsa).
That state is declared to be the supreme state of Śiva, the Supreme Self. (8.39)
He has emerged from the appearances that consist of the reflective awareness of the grasped and the grasper;
he whose supreme reality is solely the reflective awareness of consciousness. As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"But [the Lord] is entirely filled with the flood of infinite categories merged within him."
"Śiva is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme imperishable. (4-1|14) || 39 ||
And regarding the yogin who has entered this state, he describes such a vibration as follows:
"I do not exist, nor does another exist; and here no object of meditation is found.
The mind is dissolved in the state of bliss, having attained a state of equal flavor. (8.40)
"I" refers to the grasper, consisting of the body and so forth; "other" refers to objects such as blue, which are distinct from me;
and "the object of meditation" is that which is presented by the intellect as the benefactor [of the self]. || 40 ||
To attain this state, the Lord teaches the Śāmbhava means:
"One should not employ meditation above, nor below, nor in the middle;
nor in front, nor behind, nor at either of the two sides. (8.41)
One should not contemplate [the object] anywhere within the configuration of the body, nor outside;
one should not bind the focal point in space, nor should one cast the gaze downward. (8.42)
One should not blink the eyes at all, nor should one fix the gaze upon anything; one should not contemplate that which is supported as unsupported, nor that which is unsupported as supported. (8.43)
Having abandoned everything—that which consists of the senses, the elements, and sound, touch, taste, and so forth—one should remain established in samādhi and become solely absorbed in That. (8.44)

Above, at the *dvādaśānta*; below, at the *kanda* and so forth; in the middle, at the heart and so forth; in front, behind, and on both sides—therein resides the form of Tatpuruṣa, Sadyojāta, and the others. Regarding "within the body":
"From the root [of the *kanda*], it has the luster of rays, being subtler than the subtle."
"One should contemplate her as subsiding at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], the arising of Bhairava.
(As in the *Vijñānabhairava*). "Not externally" means:
"While another object is being perceived, there is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) regarding all objects of knowledge."
"By meditating on that very [object] with the mind, one becomes tranquil even though [the object] is known"—
just as in this case, when the sky is variegated by light from the sun, a lamp, or other sources, it is not [perceived as] "not-space."
By fixing one's vision right there, one's own true nature shines forth— just as in the *Vijñānabhairava*: "Not downwards" means by standing in a great pit such as a well and looking upwards.
"As for one whose mind is free from conceptualization, the dissolution of the mind occurs clearly and immediately" (Viśvabhairava-tantra 115).
Nor is there a closing of the eyes; rather, in this very manner, having first closed the eyes, one should [visualize] that which has the luster of black ink before oneself.

"Having extended the Bhairava-form, one should become absorbed in that while meditating," as it is said [in the *Vijñānabhairava*, verse 88]. "Not with the gaze fixed" means that one should cast the gaze toward a place devoid of trees, mountains, walls, and the like.
As it is said: "When the state of mental objects has dissolved, one becomes devoid of mental fluctuations" (Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā 60).
That which is supported is the support—the form of the object of meditation;
when that state is abandoned, the restrained consciousness itself does not proceed toward another state.
"Then, through that state of being in the middle, supreme contemplation blossoms," as it is said [in the *Vimalaprabhā* 6.2]. "Without support" (*nirālamba*) means that,
having known both states in their cognition, one should take refuge in the middle.

"Just as when both [extremes] are simultaneously abandoned, reality shines forth in the middle" (Viśvabhairava-tantra 61). Knowledge exists together with its object; it is "with an object" (*sālamba*) and "with a form" (*sākāra*). As it is said: "When desire or knowledge has arisen, one should settle the mind [upon it]."
"In that state, one should become single-minded through the intellect; from that, the vision of the Self arises"—as it is said [in Viṣṇu-bhāgavata 6.9.8].
Having abandoned everything according to the method taught in the chapter on various *dhāraṇās*—namely, "neither the senses nor the elements"—one remains established in *samādhi*.

Thus, by virtue of not thinking of anything at all, he is intent on the contemplation of his own true nature; being absorbed in that, he consists of the knowledge of the state of *samarasa* (flavorful union) merged in the plane of bliss (*ānandapada*). || 44 ||
This state which is thus constituted is declared to be the supreme condition of the Supreme Self;
that is the signless state, and having attained it, one does not return.
One abandons the worldly condition. || 45 ||
And therefore, he who should thus meditate upon the Self through the power of self-meditation shall go to the supreme, peaceful, and utterly stainless Śiva. (8.46)

One should cultivate that which is the power of the cultivation—the realization through the elimination of conceptual constructs—of one's own non-conceptual self-awareness; by means of that power, which is the firmness of reflective awareness, one should bring it to fruition. || 46 ||
Moreover,
that single reality which exists everywhere is Śiva, the conqueror of death;
it is the supreme Amṛteśa, the third and most excellent state.
It has been explained to you, O Goddess of gods; what else shall I tell you?

Throughout all things, from the earth up to the Unmanifest (Anāśrita), that alone is the one without a second—the ultimate reality, the essential nature, the auspicious form of supreme well-being, which conquers death.
The word "third" is used in relation to the two previously mentioned types of knowledge, the gross and the subtle;
"to you" refers to one whose sole intent is grace. The meaning is: "What else shall I tell?"—that is, there is no further secret remaining to be told beyond this.
He summarizes this as follows: "Thus, having meditated upon everything as pervaded by the Conqueror of Death, one is liberated. (8.48)
The yogi. || 48 ||
And this,
O beloved, is said to be the deception of time at all times,
because of the instruction on entering the abode of consciousness which is untouched by time.
Having concluded the current topic, he brings back the previously introduced subject:
"Thus, O Goddess, these three kinds have been revealed by me to you. (8.49)
This practice known as the "deception of time" is a yoga that is extremely difficult to attain.
Moreover, by means of this yoga of practice, a person becomes a conqueror of death. (8.50)
Not only for oneself,
but by this very yoga and through the desire to favor the world,
the yogi becomes the conqueror of death among all living beings at all times. (8.51)
The meaning is that one who is established in this knowledge is capable of bestowing grace upon the entire universe.
Furthermore, regarding the supreme knowledge mentioned here in this context:
"This is known as the conqueror of death, eternal, supreme, and immutable."
There is nothing higher than this; I declare this to be the truth.

With the intention that the disciples may develop firm confidence in this matter, he respectfully restates the point he has already taught— because it is so highly worthy of being adopted— again and again.
That which is the nature of supreme nectar, described by me as being threefold—
by practicing that, a person becomes either the Self or the Supreme.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that one becomes equal to Amṛteśa and a conqueror of death;
moreover, in whatever manner and wherever one may remember this Lord Mṛtyujit.
By that very state, that yogi becomes a conqueror of time;
"by whatever" means by the individual (āṇava), the empowered (śākta), or the divine (śāmbhava) means; "wherever" means that there is no restriction here regarding place, time, state, or the like.
And wherever this yogi may be situated, or by whatever vow he may abide; || 8-55 ||
"By whichever yoga and by whichever distinction of state one succeeds"—
by whichever yoga as taught in the *yogapāda* of those respective *saṃhitās*,
and by "the distinction of state," that is, by a particular form of meditation (*bhāvanā*) fixed upon reality (*tattva*).
And this supreme reality known as Amṛteśanātha, O Goddess—though it is one, when meditated upon in many ways, it indeed bestows accomplishment. (8.56)

Whether it be in the dualistic, non-dualistic, or mixed [traditions], or in the Ekavīra or Yāmala [systems], it shall always bestow accomplishment according to the methods of all the scriptures. (8.57)
"Single" refers to the reality of supreme non-dual, autonomous consciousness; therefore,

the meaning is that when meditated upon in its manifold forms— as the venerable Sadāśiva, Tumburu, Bhairava, Kuleśvara, and so forth, which are manifested through that very autonomy as will be described in the subsequent chapters— it certainly bestows accomplishment (siddhi).
Furthermore, because this Lord has the nature of supreme non-duality,
there is no contradiction in his encompassing all modes of existence, such as duality, non-duality, and so forth. And he will state this in the twenty-first chapter:
"Non-duality, free from conceptual construction, a mass of consciousness. (21–23) || 57 ||
Furthermore,
just as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) in the world bestows the fruits of whatever object is thought of,
even so does this king of mantras bestow the fruits of whatever object is thought of. (8.58)
The meaning is "one belonging to this place. || 58 ||
Furthermore,
he is the supreme and most powerful repository of the seventy million mantras,
because even those possess the singular heroic power of the ultimate non-duality.
Moreover, those mantras that are devoid of essence, lacking power, or obstructed; || 8-59 ||

Those who are devoid of both color and measure, lacking the transmission of the Guru, fallen from the tradition and bereft of it, and those who are obstructed by having abandoned the Āgama; || 8-60 ||

O Goddess, when those [mantras] that are desired have not been accomplished even after being recited thousands of times—those which are unaccomplished, hostile, and devoid of all their constituent parts—[they do not succeed]. (8.61)

O Goddess of the Gods, they are enclosed by this mantra Amṛteśa, which consists of the initial syllable conjoined with the encapsulation of the beginning and the end; thus they are restored to life. || 8.62 ||
For when recited, these desired mantras are accomplished without effort; there is no doubt.
When meditated upon, O Goddess, they bestow everything; this word is not false.
Those devoid of meditative cultivation (bhāva) are ignorant of vigor; those devoid of power are possessed of impurity (añjana). As it has been said:
"Those possessed of impurity, situated within the egg (aṇḍa), consist of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
They are "pinned down" (kīlita), meaning their syllables and words are inverted, and they are deprived of the oral tradition (āmnāya) of the Guru by the disciples.
Those who have grasped [the teachings] from books by themselves, whose oral tradition has fallen away, who do not know how to restore the *saṃhitā*,

and who have perished for that very reason; those who, abandoned by the *āgama*, are constantly obstructed by the employment of petty supernatural powers (*kṣudrasiddhi*) and overcome by impediments— these are the enemies who remain unvanquished.
