If one counts the syllables of the mantra from the syllables of the name according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā*, by repeatedly rotating through the four finger-joints— if it touches the first joint,
then [the mantra] becomes *siddha*; if it touches the second joint, then it is *sādhyasiddha*.

That is explained as follows: if it touches the third joint (*parvan*), then it becomes well-accomplished (*susiddha*). If, however, it touches the fourth joint, then it is obstructed for him. All the *aṃśakas*—those known as *bhāva*, *svabhāva*, *puṣpa*, *pāta*, and so forth—are to be understood in this manner from the *Śrīsvacchanda-tantra* and other sources.

Thus, even such mantras as these, when encapsulated by the Lord of the Eyes (netranātha), become bestowers of all accomplishments when desired, meditated upon, and recited. By stating, "There is no doubt" and "These words are not false," he instills confidence even in those who were previously lacking it. || 63 ||
Thus it is concluded; everything has been fully explained as the supreme secret, O beloved.
Whatever supreme secret was questioned in the first chapter has been fully explained according to the perspective thus stated; may there be auspiciousness! || 64 ||
Victorious is the glorious abode of Śaṅkara, a mass of consciousness and bliss, the supreme nectar that conquers death and uplifts the world through its own immersion.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Netrodyota*, a commentary on the *Śrī Netratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 8.
The Ninth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Eye.
The eye of consciousness, which is pure and autonomous, [acts] for the sake of bestowing diverse graces.
The Lord triumphs, manifesting through forms such as Sadāśiva and others.
Then, establishing the connection for the subject matter, the venerable Goddess said:
"O God, I have heard all the majesty of the Lord of Mantras.
Now I wish to hear that which was spoken by the All-pervading Lord to me."
It bestows accomplishment through the application of all scriptures and the differentiation of internal states,
whether according to the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Siddhānta, Saura, Vaiṣṇava, or Vaidika traditions.

O Lord of the Gods, tell me of that deity who grants the accomplishment of one's desires through the application of conduct according to one's will, and which brings about the fruit of the wish-fulfilling gem.
"All that has been stated" refers to what was taught in the eight chapters [of the *Tantrāloka*].

It is said in the eighth chapter, beginning with "By whatever yoga, by whatever distinction of state... (8.56) and ending with "...bestows success" (8.57). The verse beginning with "Vāmā... and so forth serves as a preliminary outline for the subsequent chapters. As desired...
The conduct (*ācāra*) of the respective deities of those [specific] currents is well-established and not mixed; as he will state:

"In whichever scriptures I have taught such-and-such conduct, that same [conduct] should be observed in those currents, especially in the case of sacrifice (*yāga*) and fire-oblation (*homa*)" (16.21).
Thus, for from it the arising of results occurs, as if from a wish-fulfilling gem or similar object. || 3 ||
To provide certainty regarding this, the Blessed Lord said:
"Listen, O beautiful one; I shall tell you the ultimate truth in its true essence," meaning, regarding the matter you have asked.

In this regard, although this Blessed One is the ultimate reality of supreme non-dual pure consciousness, his nature as various individual deities is nonetheless established; thus, he teaches them in succession:
"By means of the ritual of Amṛteśa, Mṛtyujit has been described by me. (9–4)
That which was taught at the beginning of the first chapter is thus:
the supreme deity, the immortal Lord, free from ailment;
that is declared to be one's own nature (svabhāva)—all-pervasive, eternal, and constant.
Neither form nor color exists for him in the ultimate sense, because the auspicious God is omnipresent and consists of all scriptures. (9.6)

It is the pervader of all mantras and the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). That which has been determined as the Great Heroic Power (*mahāvīrya*), the Lord Amṛteśa—the nature of the universe because no specific [limiting] material is taken up—is that which has been correctly taught; its future form, such as Sadāśiva, or its name, does not exist.
But even from the ultimate perspective,
it is said: "For this very reason, he should make himself an object of knowledge."
"By His own sovereignty, the Lord, having fashioned from His own non-dual nature through volitions such as 'I am the Lord' and so forth, causes the liberated Self to engage in worldly transaction.
(Pratyabhijñā 1.5.16). According to the principle indicated here, it is logical that [the world] has been manifested in such a way for the sake of bestowing grace upon individual souls.
For this reason, the Lord consists of play and so forth; He goes everywhere, meaning He manifests as all forms.

Precisely for that reason, He takes the form of various scriptures consisting of both the taught and the teacher, because all scriptures are of a single nature in the Lord, whose essence is reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), by virtue of being a single syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*). And therefore—
It is auspicious, consisting of the supreme non-dual bliss; it is merely that wherein that state of the Supreme Lord consisting of supreme reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not manifested,
they— failing to perceive the unity of the sentences concerning the mere functions of emission and so forth— [remain as such].
Those disciples of the scriptures who possess limited comprehension rest content with the meaning of individual intermediate sentences.

Therefore, by the reasoning already stated, the Lord consists of all the Āgamas; for that very reason, He abides pervading all mantras without distinction, and consequently, He is the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
He illustrates this by means of an analogy:
"Just as a stainless crystal [appears colored] when strung upon a white or other [colored] thread. (9.7)
For whatever thing colors it everywhere, that very thing it displays to others; it is not colored by its own intrinsic nature.
In that very same way, the Lord of Gods, who is established in all the scriptures,
bestows fruit upon all practitioners from every side.

"Let it reflect" means that it should receive a reflection; "not by its own nature" because its form is purely transparent. Being joined to all scriptures because it is the self of all, it is meditated upon as having the form of the deity taught in each respective scripture for the sake of all practitioners.
It yields fruit.
Since this is so,
therefore, like a radiant wish-fulfilling gem within all the streams [of tradition],
when meditated upon according to the distinction of one's disposition, it bestows the fruit of all the scriptures.
Śiva, Sadāśiva, Bhairava, and likewise Tumburu—
the all-pervading Lord assumes the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
Shining and radiant within all the channels (srotas), Śiva—

when meditated upon according to the distinctions of one's disposition and the suitability of one's inner intent in the forms of Sadāśiva and so forth— bestows the fruits prescribed in the scriptures of the Siddhānta, Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and other traditions. || 11 ||
And this is appropriate, as he says:
"Since the Lord consists of knowledge (*jñānamaya*), and knowledge exists in many forms;
it is the protection for those who are restrained and bound, and thus it is called the Eye. (9-12)

The Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, consists of knowledge and has pure consciousness as his ultimate reality. That knowledge, through its absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), manifests contraction and remains assuming multiplicity; therefore, for those who partake in this manifestation of contraction, [the Lord] becomes the cause for the unfolding of their own true nature through various forms of vision and worship.
It is a protection for the gods; therefore, from the perspective of etymology (nirukta), it is called "netra" (the eye), but not by virtue of being the physical eyeball.
And because he alone delivers one from death, he is called Mṛtyujit;
likewise, because he bestows immortality, he is remembered as Amṛteśa. (9–13)
Death arises from the state of restless flux involving the body, vital breath, and so forth; immortality is the immersion into the power of Rudra.
Thus, O Goddess, the omnipresent God, who possesses many forms like a gem,
is worshipped by all who desire the fruit of their own spiritual accomplishments.
The Lord is the bestower of fruits for all, the fulfiller of requested aims;

this is according to the principle stated as "evam" (thus). "With the desire for the fruit of one's own attainment" means by way of being intent upon that fruit, which has been grasped through His will. || 14 ||
Since this is so, therefore the practitioner, established in the means of accomplishment, should act in accordance with the nature of reality. 9-15 ||

By whatever state of being [one approaches him], he becomes the bestower of that very fruit; [that is,] in accordance with the state of being, which is to say, in conformity with the disposition and the mode of contemplation. 15.
And thus, the practitioner who always meditates upon the inner and outer sacrifices in the form of Sadāśiva. (9.16)
O Goddess of the Suras, his body becomes like that of Sadāśiva;
he becomes the body of Sadāśiva and assumes the form of Sādāśivī for the sake of bestowing grace. || 16 ||
And this is appropriate, as he said: "For he is the one who bestows favor upon all those [beings]. (9.17)

And for this reason, in accordance with the venerable Aghoravaktra, it remains to be understood that "this [deity]— Sadyojāta, Vāma, Aghora, and the forms of Puruṣa and Īśāna— is to be meditated upon."

And because this king of mantras, being of the nature of supreme non-duality, is the self of the universe, he states that the limbs, the seat, and so forth are to be deposited by means of this very [mantra]:
By means of this, O fair-faced one, the heart-mantra and the others should be deposited.
One should prepare one's own seat with this very mantra.
By this specific statement, the supersession of the previously mentioned limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) is shown.
The particle *eva* (very/only) expresses the state of being neither deficient nor excessive. "Beautiful" (*sva*) means that which abides through non-dual pervasion.
And the seat of Anantānta is one's own seat. As it is said in the Śrī Kālottara:
"The seed-sprout [is established] by the Supreme Power (parā-śakti), and thereafter the seat of Ananta;
O Six-faced One, one should make Ananta reach the end in due order."
And so forth.
He describes the meditation on the form of the Blessed One as Sadāśiva: resembling a mass of moons and like a collection of snow mountains. (9.19)
He has five faces, wide eyes, ten arms, and three eyes;
he wears a serpent as a sacred thread and is clothed in a garment of tiger skin.
One should meditate upon the Lord seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), standing atop a perfected lotus.
Furthermore, what are his trident, lotus, arrow, rosary, and water-pot?
Thus, on the right hands— and likewise on the left, as one listens further— he holds a spheṭaka,
a mirror, a bow, a mātuluṅga fruit, and a water-pot.
The spheṭaka and the udyamanaka. || 22 ||
Furthermore,
one should meditate upon the Lord, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel and is yellowish-green in color from his eastern face.
And its right [side] was black, terrible, fierce, fanged, and distorted-faced.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, he causes terror to the world;
his western face has the luster of snow and kunda flowers, and his left face has the radiance of a red lotus.
O Maheśānī, one should contemplate the upward-facing [face] as having the luster of crystal;
this is clear.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord of Gods, one should worship him according to the prescribed ritual.
The method is the procedure stated in the established doctrine. || 25 ||
Where one should worship, he says:
"In one's own form, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in a liṅga, or in water upon a lotus.
One's own form is that which was mentioned previously in the passage beginning with "the primary [form] is one's own."
And there,
one should worship Īśāna and the others, ending with Sadyojāta, in their respective directions.
One should worship [the faces] in the directions starting from the northeast with the root mantra itself, following the sequence of the enclosure of the faces beginning with Īśāna. || 26 ||
One should place the heart-mantra and the others at the front of that [mandala], starting from the southeast (āgneyī) and so forth, according to the ritual of worship.

For the purpose of the rite of worship, the heart, head, crest, and armor [mantras] are to be placed in the intermediate directions of fire (southeast), the lord (northeast), the rakṣas (southwest), and the wind (northwest).
One should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) as follows: the Weapon (*astra*) in the four directions starting from the East, and the Eye (*netra*) in front of the deity.
As it is stated in that very same source:
"One should place the Heart (*hṛdaya*) in the Southeast, and likewise the Head (*śiras*) in the Northeast."
One should place the *śikhā* mantra in the southwest and likewise the *kavaca* in the northwest.
"One should then assign the weapons to the directions and Sadāśiva upon the pericarp. (Kālottara 7.7).
Because the Eye is preeminent due to its nature as light, its place is at the tip of the pericarp. As it is said in the venerable Svacchanda:
"The eye, resembling the form of light, is situated in the center. (2.111) |||
And when anyone should worship in this manner, then they will succeed without a doubt; I tell you this truth. (9.27)
Thus ends the section on the group of those who have attained success; may there be auspiciousness.
Victorious is the glorious, non-dual eye of Śaṅkara, which has the form of Sadāśiva, is intent upon the desire to favor others, and conquers death.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the illustrious Netratantra, in the Netrodyota commentary composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net.
The southern body, which is Aghora, is unfailing and skilled in swallowing the multitude of fetters.
Victorious is the eye of Śaṅkara, the protector of the minute, which takes refuge in Bhairava for the sake of bestowing grace.
In order to determine the nature of the Blessed One as Bhairava, as previously indicated, the Śrī Bhagavān said:
"Now I shall proclaim that which is distinguished by the Bhairava Āgamas—resembling a mass of crushed collyrium and having the nature of the fire at the end of an aeon. (10.1)
Five-faced, mounted upon a corpse, ten-armed, and terrifying;
resembling a host of night-demons, he roared with a fearsome sound. || 10-2 ||
With a face made terrifying by fangs and eyes curved with a frown,
he was seated upon a lion-throne and adorned with necklaces of serpents.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, with a gaping mouth and a massive body,
he wears a cloak of elephant hide and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
The god holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, carries a sword and a shield, and has hands that grant boons and fearlessness. || 10-5 ||
Having worshipped Bhairava— the great hero who holds a vajra in his hand and a battle-axe as his weapon— one should then contemplate her seated upon his lap.
Having a form like the fire of universal dissolution, with the luster of lac-dye and vermilion, with hair standing erect, massive-bodied, hideous, and most terrifying. || 10-7 ||
She has a large belly and five faces, adorned with three eyes;
she has claw-like nails, sunken eyes, and is decorated with a garland of severed heads.
The goddess whose arms were described by Bhairava, who bears the weapons of Bhairava,
who is renowned as the Power of Will (icchāśakti), and who moves upon the lap of Svacchanda.
One should meditate upon her bearing this form, renowned as Aghoreśī;

she is differentiated within the Bhairava Āgamas arising from the Rightward Current (*dakṣiṇasrotas*), such as the Svacchanda, Caṇḍa, Triśirobhairava, and others, by virtue of her being the destroyer of duality.

I shall describe the essential nature of the Blessed One, the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyujit), as it has been taught through his blazing and extraordinary form. By the words beginning with "bhinna" (divided), his state of being exceedingly black and intensely radiant is expressed by virtue of his role as the destroyer of differentiation. Here, the corpse is Sadāśiva.
As it is stated in the Śrī Svacchanda:

"One should conceive of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna ending with the corpse" (1.39). "Roaring" refers to the supreme awareness of the *nāda* (the primordial sound). "Torn" means whose mouth is wide open.

"Clad in elephant hide" means one by whom a garment has been made from elephant skin. The passage beginning with "skull," etc., is intended to determine the ten-armed nature [of the deity] according to the sequence of left and right. Regarding the word "having worshipped": it is by this very mantra, together with the heart and other limb-mantras, according to the manner already stated and to be stated hereafter, because this [mantra] alone has authority in all instances.
"Koṭarākṣī" refers to one whose gaze is directed outward while the internal object of focus remains within.

By the term "icchā-śakti," it is stated that although she possesses form, her essence consists of supreme pervasion (*paravyāpti*). Those [energies] for whom no "ghora" (terrible) form exists—that is, a form characterized by duality or primarily consisting of both difference and non-difference—[are the Ghoras].

One should remember— that is, meditate for the purpose of worship upon the Mistress (Īśī), the Sovereign of those Aghorā powers which consist of rays and act as bestowers of grace by means of manifesting the abode of supreme non-duality. Whatever secret is contained herein regarding the form of Bhairava, that has been shown by me in detail in the *Svacchandoddyota*.
The same should be understood regarding other forms as well; the rest is clear.
And this, which is the stainless nature of Bhairava consisting of the power of will— namely, Svacchandabhairava and the others, whose essence is the Supreme Consciousness— I [have taught].
And it has been taught in all the tantras, yet kept concealed and not made explicit. || 10-10 ||
For even within the established doctrines (siddhānta), there exists the pervasion of the Supreme Lord, who is partless and autonomous.
Because it is entirely hidden, my intention therein has not been perceived by anyone on earth; it is difficult to find.
For those of coarse vision are not capable of grasping a secret.
And likewise, in the Śrī Kālottara it is said:
"That which is called Nāda is the supreme seed-syllable...
(1.5), and so forth.
"However, these five principles by which the entire world is pervaded," (8.2),
and "Having understood this, O Mahāsena, one should initiate even outcastes"—
if such extremely secret [teachings] were explained otherwise, they would be contradicted.
Having stated this as a digression, he speaks of the subject at hand: "For the sake of the destruction of those sins such as the suppression of disease... (10-11).
One should always perform sacrifice for the sake of protection, pacification, and nourishment regarding cows and Brahmins.
"Affliction caused by disease" refers to suppression, assault, and so forth—the word "etc. including mental anguish and the like.
For the pacification of such evils, and for the purpose of protection, pacification, and nourishment, one should worship this Bhairavayāmala.
The locative case endings ending with "gobrahmaṇeṣu" are used in the sense of the genitive.
Or else, [one should meditate on her] possessing a luster equal to snow, the kunda flower, the moon, and a pearl.
One should meditate upon the Bhairavayāmala, which resembles ten million moons and is like a mountain of crystal.
Resembling the conflagration at the end of an eon, it is like the hibiscus or the kiṃśuka flower.
One should visualize him as having the appearance of ten million suns and red in color;
or else, with the luster of a ruby or the brilliance of yellow orpiment. (10.14)
Anticipating the objection, "How can that which is one be manifold?", he says:
"The God who assumes forms according to His will, who bestows the fruit of the accomplishment of one's desires—
He is indeed the Bhairava of Consciousness, [appearing] by His own will through the disposition of various practitioners who desire those respective accomplishments."
The meaning is that it assumes those respective forms.
And therefore, in whatever form the practitioner should recollect him, [in that very form he should do so]. || 10-15 ||
One should worship such a form that bestows corresponding auspicious accomplishments (*siddhi*).

One should meditate upon and worship the Lord according to the prescribed rite in the form described as "ten million moons" (10.13) and so forth—not, as before, mounted upon a corpse, but rather seated in the center of a lotus. (10.16)

The procedure consists of the offering of appropriate food, flowers, incense, and liquor to the Lord, as well as the rites of *vidhi*, *nirodha*, and the presentation of the *argha* water. As it is stated in the *Śrī Svacchanda*: "Thereafter, the *argha* should be offered with well-scented wine. (2.136)
And so forth; it follows the meditative absorption (dhyāna) according to its corresponding form. 16.
Facing the aforementioned Bhairavayāmala, he sequentially assigns to the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions the goddesses named Siddhā, Raktā, Śuṣkā, and Utpalahastā;
[he first] instructs [on] the goddess who resembles cow’s milk and possesses a luster like the laughter of a pearl necklace. (10–17)
Resembling a perfectly pure crystal, as stainless as the kunda flower, the moon, or the moonlight;
she has four arms, three eyes, and is adorned with one face.
The goddess, clad in white garments, adorned with white necklaces,
seated upon a deer-throne, holding a vajra in her hand, and possessed of great strength.
The goddess, holding a noose and a goad, resounding with the ringing of a bell,
stands in the eastern direction facing the God of gods.
But that man who meditates with a disciplined mind attains success quickly. Indu means camphor; sāraṅga means deer; "toward the gods" refers to the eastern direction.
Having described the Siddhā, he speaks of the Raktā:
"She has a brilliance equal to ten million suns, with a radiance like blazing fire. (21)
Resembling a heap of vermilion, having the form of lightning and terrifying,
she has three eyes, a fearsome face, a stout body, and a large belly.
She has a protruding belly and large breasts, is mounted upon a corpse, and possesses great strength;
she is adorned with a garland of skulls and wears a tiger skin around her waist.
She has an elephant hide as her upper garment, is adorned with a garland of severed heads,
shines like a great meteor, and illuminates the quarters of space while remaining naked.
One should meditate upon her situated in the southern direction, having four arms and one face, holding a sword and a shield, and bearing a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff. (10.25)
"Clad in the directions" (digambarām) implies, by the sense of the context, the alternative of having an elephant hide as an upper garment (gajacarmottarīyām). || 25 ||
He spoke of her as withered, blackish-red, greatly radiant, fleshless, and distorted-faced;
she was extremely emaciated, with sunken eyes, a single face, and four arms.
She has three eyes and a terrifying face, adorned with a necklace of serpents;
her hair stands upright, her body is massive, and she is decorated with a garland of severed heads.
Her limbs were bound with cords of sinews, her loins covered by a human skin,
she wore a tiger-skin garment, and she carried a sword and a shield.
One should visualize her in the western direction, holding in her hand a sack filled with intestines, blood, and flesh, and tearing apart the great entrails.
She was seated upon a Kumbhīra (crocodile) throne, facing the God of gods;
her limbs were bound together by cords of sinews due to extreme emaciation, and she held a *piṭaka*,
a particular type of vessel.
Regarding the crocodile (kumbhīra) mentioned as her seat, it is now described as follows:
"It has the neck of a camel, the shoulders of an elephant, the ears of a horse, and the face of a rhinoceros. (10.30)
With a form like the shanks of a serpent, with claws resembling the weapon of Vajra, with a back like a tortoise and a tail like a fish, he is proclaimed to be a *kumbhīra*. || 10-31 ||
One whose face is like that of a ram (huḍa) or a sheep; one whose claws are like the weapon called the thunderbolt (vajra).
[31] She who holds a blue lotus in her hand, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, resembling the autumnal sky—[he addressed her].
She has three eyes and one face, and is adorned with blue garments. || 10-32 ||
Mounted upon the back of a lion, with bow and arrow raised in her hands and a spear in her hand, the Great Goddess, when meditated upon, bestows desired fruits. (10.33)
Siddhā, Raktā, Śuṣkā, and Utpalahastikā—
these goddesses stand in the four directions, O Mother of Bhairava’s hosts.
Furthermore, having stationed the female messengers (dūtīs) in the intermediate directions from the southeast to the northeast:
Kālī, Karālī, and likewise Mahākālī. (10.35)
They are renowned as Bhadrakālī, established in the form of goddesses;
yet these goddesses, in their sequence, are two-armed and seated upon lotus-thrones.
All of them indeed bear the *kartikā* and the *muṇḍa*; the *kartikā* is the blade of the hero.
Furthermore,
the servants [stand] at the gateway;
in sequence, they are at the four gates.
Krodhana, Vṛntaka, Karṣaṇa, and Gajānana; || 10-37 ||
They have two arms, distorted faces, and hold swords and shields in their hands;
this is the form described for the eight goddesses and the servants (*kiṅkara*s) as they constitute the retinue of the primary *Bhairava-yāmala*.
Regarding the subject of optional rites (*kāmya*), however, he says:
"But all white [substances] for the sake of pacification...
[The compound] *sarve ca sarvāśca* is an instance of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member).
...or form, according to the differentiation of karma. || 10-38 ||

One should meditate on these [colors]: "red for subjugation (*vaśya*), yellow for immobilization (*stambha*)," and so forth; furthermore, the retinue ending with the *kiṅkara*s is to be worshipped with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). This is understood from the upcoming ritual of protection (*rakṣāvidhi*). || 38 ||
Regarding this, he says: "Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the protection of the king according to the ritual procedure;
one should write the name in the center, joined with the encasement of the mantra. (10.39)
Above that, O Dear One, one should worship the god Bhairava, Amṛteśa;
likewise, the goddesses are placed upon the petals, joined at the beginning and the end by that very [mantra].
In this manner, the female messengers and the servants are commanded by means of the root mantra;
one should then draw a very bright lunar disc outside the lotus.
Outside of that, it should be four-cornered and marked with the insignia of a vajra,
using yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron, milk, and likewise white sugar.
Having written it down, one should worship for the sake of pacification with entirely white offerings,
along with appropriate food offerings, snacks, balis, and fermented liquors.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished— enclosed by the Netra-mantra as before— within the center of a lotus pericarp drawn with *gorocanā*, saffron, milk, and white sugar, and situated upon a lunar disc; one should then worship Amṛteśabhairava along with his Goddess on its surface using the Root-mantra itself, according to the present context.

Having written down the names of the goddesses and the female messengers (dūtīs) on the petals according to the previously mentioned sequence of directions, enshrined within the mantra, one should worship them. Likewise, having written down the servants (kiṅkaras), enshrined within the mantra, at the tips of the four petals in the cardinal directions, one should draw a square outside marked with vajras, and [proceed] in order.

This mantra-wheel, for the purpose of protecting the king, one should worship with all-white offerings and great preparations; the connection is that it is with food offerings (*naivedya*), along with those *bali* offerings, and with spirits (*āsava*). || 43 ||
Having performed worship in this manner, [he should offer] rice grains and sesame seeds mixed with white sandalwood, greyed with powdered camphor,
along with unbroken rice and white sugar.
One whose intellect is focused on effort should offer oblations combined with ghee and milk;
that is, one whose mind is intent on effort for nourishment and other such purposes, and who possesses the consciousness of meditative visualization.
For whatever purpose one should perform the fire offering,
for that there shall be great peace, even if one has already been seized by death.
Even if one who is to be accomplished is overtaken by death, peace will surely come through the worship of the protection wheel and the performance of fire oblations; may there be auspiciousness!
I take refuge in Cinnatrabhairava, the divine medicine for diseases, the root-cutter of mental afflictions,
and the crusher of calamities.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Netrodyota*, the illumination of the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 10.
The Eleventh Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net," the vomiting forth of the enjoyment of all auspiciousness, the vision of the Left.
I bow to the eye of the Trident-bearer, which reveals supreme bliss.
Having demonstrated that the nature of Lord Mṛtyujit consists in the practice of the Right Current (dakṣiṇasrotas),
the Blessed One spoke in order to show that his nature also consists in the Left View (vāmadarśana).
Now I shall proclaim the supreme and most excellent *uttara-tantra*;
with this mantra, one should perform sacrifice for the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments.
Its supremacy is due solely to the principle of the pervasion of this mantra, which is the essence of the supreme non-duality. || 1 ||
Therein,
O Goddess, for the sake of pacifying all calamities, one should [place] the god Tumburu in the center of the previously described eight-petaled lotus maṇḍala.
Having placed the ten-armed Lord of the Gods, who has five faces and three eyes,
upon the seat consecrated by the root mantra, one should fashion his faces with the very body of Sadāśiva using the root mantra itself.
By the root mantra alone. || 3 ||
And he [saw] Him with a crescent moon upon His head, seated upon a lotus throne,
white as snow, jasmine, or the moon, resembling the snowy mountain.
He has a serpent as his sacred thread, is adorned with ornaments of snakes,
is endowed with all types of jewelry, and has a tiger skin around his waist.
Clad in an elephant hide, mounted upon a bull, and possessed of great strength;
the God bearing a sword and a shield, adorned with a *ṭaṅka* and a *kandala*.
The god holds a noose and a goad, has a discus in his hand and carries a rosary;
he grants boons and fearlessness with his hands, and is the destroyer of all sins.

One should meditate [as follows]: the lotus-seat by the pervasion of the lotus of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*); above that, the bull by the pervasion of the power of Sound (*nāda-śakti*); and above that, the Lord whose form is Consciousness (*cinmūrti*). The *ṭaṅka* is a specific type of weapon;
the *kanda* is a skull. || 7 ||
And the goddesses are situated in all directions, starting from the east, as well as the female messengers (dūtīs); likewise,
the servants (kiṅkaras) are in the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast, at the locations of the gates.
He enumerates the female messengers (dūtīs) and attendants (kiṅkaras) by name:
Jambhanī, Mohanī, Subhagā, and likewise Durbhagā; these are declared to be the female messengers. Now hear further concerning the attendants.
One should place Krodhana and Vṛntaka, as well as the mighty Gajakarṇa,
on the left and right sides of Tumburunātha, and install Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī [on either side].
Then, one should place the hook (aṅkuśa) above and the māyā [syllable] immediately after that.
Regarding the phrase "immediately after that," the kiṅkaras are outside the entire wheel of mantras (mantracakra).
Thus, in this sequence...
All of these should always be joined with the root mantra.
Regarding their meditative absorption, he says:
"The goddesses are indeed white, red, yellow, and black, and they have four faces;
from among these..."
She has four arms and three eyes, and she holds a chisel and a lotus bud.
Holding a staff and a rosary in her hands, she shines resplendent upon a hungry ghost (preta).
The goddess Jayā, however, as well as Vijayā, are red in color and possess four arms.
The goddess has four faces and three eyes, holds a bow and arrows, and carries a sword and shield; she is seated upon an owl. (11.14)
Ajitā, Padmagarbhā, Caturvaktrā, and Caturbhujā; the goddess holds a spear and a bell, and she carries a shield and a paṭṭiśa.
The Great Goddess, mounted upon a horse, adorned with all ornaments,
is Ajitā Jayantī.
Resembling a split sapphire, she has four faces and is adorned with ornaments. || 11-16 ||
She has four arms and three eyes, and likewise holds a noose and a goad;
she carries a jewel-vessel and a mace in her hands, and is well-seated upon a divine throne.
Clad in golden garments and adorned with golden ornaments—
[meaning] Aparājitā and the others.
Established in their own directions, these beloved ones, when meditated upon, bestow the fruit of accomplishment.
In the intermediate directions, however, are the female messengers (dūtīs) who assume those same forms, but are adorned with only one face;
they have two arms and three eyes, and are adorned with a severed head and a razor. || 11-19 ||
Their seats, respectively, are the fish, the tortoise, the crocodile, and the frog.
Furthermore:
And the servants have two arms, carry swords in their hands, and wear shields. || 11-20 ||

Having one face and three eyes, with glances curved by frowning brows, they grant the fruit of accomplishment when visualized according to the distinctions of colors such as white and so forth. || 11-21 ||
By the word "white" and so forth, red, yellow, and black are included.
Gāyatrī has the luster of a red color and is adorned with a single face;
she sits in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) with her eyes opened in meditation.
Sāvitrī is white in color, with her eyes fixed in meditation;
likewise, the limbs of the goddess are [described]...
likewise, the limbs [of the goddess are described], meaning that the goddess has one face and four arms, but—
Holding a noose, a goad, a book, and a rosary in her hands—this goddess is Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī.
Furthermore, ...
Māyā is dark-complexioned and four-armed. || 11-23 ||

From the pair of hands joined in the form of a casket (*saṃpuṭa*) while embracing the Great Cloth (*mahāpaṭa*): by means of the "Great" (*maha*), which is explained as being spread out and all-pervasive, the cloth—held in the two hands like a noose and a goad at the sides—is placed upon the head and necessarily conceals or covers the universe; thus it is said.
She is characterized by her two hands joined slightly in the form of a hollowed cup, which encompasses and pervades the covering of the universe within. || 23 ||
Furthermore,
the all-pervading Lord has the form of Bhairava, holding a noose and a goad.
Bearing a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, greedy for fat, blood, and flesh,
he has a terrifying form with a face made formidable by frowning brows and protruding fangs; thus it is said in the *Śrīnandiśikhā*:
"He has one face and is most terrifying," so it is said. Likewise:
"[... resembling smooth coral..."

"With its head shaped like a noose and a goad, it is the supreme means for attracting the object of practice (sādhya). Since this is stated in that very same source, it should be visualized in such a form. || 24 ||
He speaks for the purpose of performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seat for the wheel of mantras that has been described and will be described:
"The boat, the ocean of milk, the earth, and the auspicious foundational power (ādhārikā-śakti). (11.25)
One should employ a white lotus for the purpose of the seat and for the sake of pacification.

By means of the pervasion of the void (*vyomavyāpti*), there is the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*); above that is the Earth (*urvī*, *pṛthvī*); above that, by means of the pervasion of the principles (*tattvavyāpti*), is the Ocean of Milk; and above that, by virtue of the properties of floating and movement...

The boat [of the lotus] is formed by the pervasion of the two elements, fire and air. And this much is the root-ground of the white lotus, which possesses the pervasion of the principle of Śuddhavidyā. As it is stated in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara):
"First, however, one should visualize the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti) four finger-breadths below the navel."
"The fourfold [foundation] consists of the earth, the subterranean water, the boat, and the bulbous root. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 8.55).

Having thus described the meditation on the seat, mantra, and wheel, he states the specific detail regarding this very [practice]: "But all of them, O Mistress of the Gods, being perfectly white (suśukla), bring about pacification. (11-26)
They should be visualized as red, yellow, and black according to the distinction of the ritual action, due to the variety [of rites] such as subjugation and so forth. || 26 ||
Just as at the conclusion of the previous section, he here states the procedure for protection:
"Now I shall fully explain another, the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja), which possesses great power."
Possessing great power, it is unimpeded in pacifying and other such rites. || 27 ||
There,
one should write the name in the middle using the very same enclosure of the beginning and end;
one should then install the god, the goddess, and the female messengers according to the procedure as before.
The wise one,

having written the name of the person to be protected— enclosed within the mantra— in the center of the lunar disc within the pericarp of the lotus drawn with the previously mentioned substances such as *gorocanā* on the petals, sub-petals, and everywhere else, [he should place] above it the *Sāvitrī* together with the *Gāyatrī*.

Having meditated upon the deity, one should worship him with white offerings. Having written the names of the four goddesses, Jayā and the others, on the petals in the cardinal directions starting from the east, and the female messengers, Jambhanī and the others, on the petals in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast— each name being enclosed by the mantra— one should [place them] outside the lotus in the four cardinal directions.

The summary meaning is as follows: having drawn the *kiṅkaras* outside of that, then the two *māyāṅkuśas*, and outside of those, the arrangement of a square marked with vajras, one should worship the entire mantra-wheel with white offerings; this is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the female messengers" (*dūtīśca*), which includes the *kiṅkaras*.

And there are two *māyā-aṅkuśas*. "Elsewhere" means that the placement of the *kiṅkara*s and others occurs in the outer directions from the lotus-field. By the word "everywhere," the four-cornered city outside the *māyā-aṅkuśas* is indicated.
And this protection wheel [should be worshipped] with appropriate food offerings for the sake of abundant peace for oneself. || 11-29 ||
Or it may be applied to another; having written it, worshipped it, and bound it [to the person], [it should be used].
Furthermore,
having prepared an outer maṇḍala, one should perform the sacrifice for the rite of pacification.
Here, he describes the oblation according to propriety:
with sesame, rice, honey, clarified butter, milk, and sugar. (11.30)
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) as before in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) kindled with excellent fuel;
this is for the purpose of satisfying the circle of mantras (*mantracakra*), which is the implied meaning. "As before" means in a circular [pit]. || 30 ||
When this is done, great peace shall arise for the one to be protected; my word is true, not false.
And these goddesses, who grant excellent accomplishment, are to be worshipped according to the stated lotus-arrangement in all rites of protection. || 31 ||
He says that even by another sequence in the external sacrifice:
"Or one should worship the goddesses standing in rows, and the god Tumburu in the center. (11.32)
The practitioner who has restrained his senses and whose mind is one-pointed attains all forms of prosperity.
Or, by employing it for another purpose, one conquers; of this there is no doubt. || 11-33 ||
In this world, Śiva is victorious—he who exists in supreme excellence through the attainment of all desired goals. || 33 ||
Through the sequence of worshipping the wheels of the leftward-flowing stream of vomit,
the glorious Netra, overflowing with the nectar of Śakti, conquers death and bestows all supernatural powers.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Netrodyota*, the illumination of the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 11.
The Twelfth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net" (Netrodyota).
That which, though bringing an end to desire, uniquely fulfills the desires of infinite multitudes of beings;

We praise that eye of Śarva— the supreme refuge of the three worlds— which brings an end to all things, which is the destroyer of Death himself, which is stainless and undisturbed, and which belongs to the true lineage; it is the universal effulgence arising from the shattering of all dualities, the protector of the three realms, the guide to one’s own abode, and the essence of the three lights.
Having revealed the nature of the upward, right, and left currents,
and in order to demonstrate that Lord Mṛtyujit is also composed of the Kula tradition whose essence is non-differentiation from them,
the Blessed Lord said: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain..."
The demonstration of the family tradition (kulāmnāya), by which one may accomplish all sacrificial rites (yāga), fire offerings (homa), and recitations (japa). || 1 ||

I shall correctly explain the ritual activities— such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and fire-oblation (*homa*)— which are illuminated by the traditional teachings of the lineage (*kulāmnāya*), so that by means of them the practitioner attains all worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
First, [one should worship] Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, the Guru, and the others, starting from the northeast and ending in the northwest direction.

One should worship, preceded by the mantras of this tradition, those ending with the feet [of the deities] in the east, south, and west: namely, the lords Śrīkhagendra, Kūrma, and Meṣa, together with their messengers and lineages; and in the north, the six royal princes beginning with the venerable Śrīmacchanda and Kuṅkuṇāmbā, together with their messengers.
The meaning of the term *kulāmnāyadarśana*. || 1 ||
Now, Bhairava, as previously enjoined, is to be worshipped in the center of the lotus at the end of the row of the Guru of the Yuga;
for the eight goddesses naturally reside upon the petals situated in the directions starting from the east.
And [they possess] the forms, weapons, and vehicles of the deities beginning with Brahmā;
"of Brahmā and the others by their very nature" means by their own form which performs their respective functions such as creation.
Those [goddesses] whose forms, weapons, and vehicles belong to Brahmā and the others are thus described.
He shows them by name: Brahmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. || 12-3 ||

Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Bahurūpiṇī—these four primary goddesses are situated in the directions starting from the east and south; the others are in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast and northwest. Thus, the teachers maintain that there is an inclusion of the sequence of emanation and reabsorption through both direct (anuloma) and reverse (pratiloma) orders.
He clarifies the distinction between their forms, weapons, and seats—from Brahmā down to Bahurūpa—as well as their respective forms and vehicles. (12.4)
And the own weapon of all [the goddesses] is adorned with their own respective forms;
that very form which belongs to Brahmā and the others—such as having a ruddy complexion and four arms—is their [form].
And their vehicle is indeed the same vehicle, and that too...

The mounts of Vārāhī—swan, bull, peacock, Garuḍa, Airāvata, crocodile, and the form of a preta—are not seen. Her weapon alone constitutes her vehicle, and that takes the form of a staff, trident, spear, discus, thunderbolt, and sword; and this is held in her right hand.
And all this, beginning with the seat, is shining by its own intrinsic nature.
Elsewhere, regarding the three cubits [of the image], he states the rule for the common ritual:
"They hold a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, with their hands raised in the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness. (12.5)
The left hand displays the gesture of granting boons. || 5 ||

Having described the placement (nyāsa) according to the sequence of directions, he also speaks according to the sequence of rows: "Or one should worship the goddesses residing in the rows, who bestow all desired fruits.
This means there are four [goddesses] on each side—left and right—of the deity.
And why? Because these [mantras] are for the sake of the peace of all living beings by one who desires their welfare. (12.6)
One should perform the extensive sacrifice according to one's desire;
the meaning is that in rites such as pacification (śāntika) and so forth, it should be performed in the form of white and other colors.
O Goddess, they should especially be worshipped by the practitioners, even for kings.
The meaning is: "by means of a great accumulation. || 7 ||
For it is by the grace of these very [goddesses] that all kings enjoy a kingdom free from thorns, being truly fortunate upon the surface of the earth.
And this is logical, as he says:
"Because this entire world is born from the very nature of the goddesses;
O Dear One, these [goddesses] are the womb-forms of the world of gods and so forth. (12.9)
All of them remove the flood of all sufferings for living beings who love them; like mothers, they always protect and sustain the world.
The meaning is that because they are the cause of the universe, they protect the creation of beings by their own nature like the universe itself; how much more so when they are worshipped? || 10 ||
Moreover,
O Dear One, just as farmers [preserve] their power in the form of the world within their storehouses,
so too do they sustain it during the dissolution and create it here once again.

Just as farmers, at the time of dissolution during the month of Pauṣa, store the world in its stationary form— remaining only as seeds in the state of potential energy— within their granaries, and then create it again by making it ready for sowing, so too do the Goddesses.

At the times of the dissolution of the universe, which is the soul of all, they bring about that which remains as mere latent impressions (saṃskāra) and once again prepare it for the purpose of creation. || 11 ||
And just as farmers sow seeds at the proper time for the sake of fruit, so too do those who grant fruit [the gods], desiring to bring forth a new Brahma-kalpa.

"Time" refers to spring. "Bestowers of fruit" refers to the goddesses. Regarding "Brahman": the *kalpa* of Brahmā consists of his own day; it is by means of the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) that exists therein as the cause [of manifestation]—the term "Brahma-kalpa" being intended to indicate the entire period ending with the day of Sadāśiva—that [the goddesses act]. For the goddesses themselves are indeed...
They perform creation and the other cosmic acts through the presiding influence of the respective causal deities, beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Brahmā.
As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "The power of the All-pervading Lord is called 'Brahmī'; wherever He wills, there He causes [the effect] to fall."
Thus it is said; likewise:
"Viṣṇu is remembered as being [contained] within the Vaiṣṇavī [mudrā]," and so forth. || 12 ||
Since they pervade the world at the beginning of the eon, during its middle, and at its end,
they are therefore beneficial in every way for the sake of peace.
O Goddess, they are to be worshipped, to be offered oblations, and to be meditated upon by one desiring accomplishment (*siddhi*).
"To be offered oblations" means they are to be gratified through the fire-sacrifice (*homa*); "by one desiring accomplishment" means by one who has the desire for accomplishment.
Furthermore, [one may offer] sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets, or auspicious *śrīphala* fruits, containing all the seeds. || 12-14 ||
With highly praised flowers, or with other well-offered fruits, these goddesses grant all perfections and bestow the fruits of all desires. (12–15)
The meaning is that because its intrinsic nature is the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*), it grants all fruits of desire.
And in this regard,
a fire-oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter is praised as the bestower of all desires.
For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of wealth through grain, one should perform oblations of ghee and guggulu.
"Extensive accomplishment—whether inferior, middling, or superior—is born [therefrom].
One shall obtain prosperity by means of white lotuses and bilva fruits smeared with clarified butter.
(2.280–281) One should follow such passages as these spoken in the *Śrīsvacchanda*; may there be auspiciousness! 15.

Victorious is the glorious Akula, the singular Bhairava of Consciousness, who, through his inherent natures such as the creation of the universe and so forth, proceeds from the lineage of the families beginning with Iñci.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Netrodyota*, the illumination of the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 12.
The Thirteenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net. Having filled [the body] with floods of the flowing essence of supreme nectar, one becomes identical with that.
I take refuge in the Eye that reveals the entire world to those who possess devotion.
Having established the connection through the context of authority, the Blessed Lord spoke in order to introduce the subject matter:
"Thus indeed has the Kaulika procedure for the King of Mantras been enjoined;
I shall now further proclaim another ritual injunction which bestows its fruit. (13.1)
By means of this universal pervasion, it bestows both full enjoyment and liberation.
Therein [he saw] Nārāyaṇa, four-armed, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
resembling an *atasī* flower, with one face and two eyes. (13.2)
The god is adorned with all ornaments— the conch, discus, mace, and lotus—
and wears divine garments, graced by celestial flowers.
One should always remember Him as He stands risen, adorned with a network of tiny bells from the rubies in His shimmering crown, and wearing divine earrings.

The compound means "the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, as well as all the ornaments. Regarding the word "should remember," it implies that he should contemplate them while reciting the mantra pertaining to this [deity]. || 4 ||
Alternatively, [one may meditate on the deity] seated upon the king of birds, exceedingly white and beautiful,
possessing three faces with gentle countenances, and adorned with boars and lions.
One should meditate on Him endowed with six arms, granting boons and fearlessness; in His lap, one should contemplate Śrī, who possesses the same complexion and bears the same weapons as He.

"Resembling the beauty and splendor of the God of Gods, facing him"— this refers to what was previously mentioned regarding the granting of boons and fearlessness, as well as the excellence of the conch and other attributes. "Lāvaṇya" and "kānti" refer to the arrangement of the limbs and the beauty of the physical form.
By means of this method of the enclosure, one should worship the goddesses stationed in the four cardinal directions and the limbs in the intermediate directions. || 13-7 ||
The arrangement of the limbs is as before. || 7 ||
The Goddess said:
"One should indeed worship Jayā, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and Māyā in the cardinal directions;
and those..."
The goddesses hold nooses and goads, with their hands granting boons and fearlessness.
In the presence of the God, one should meditate upon the auspicious Varnas who possess beautiful forms;
their limbs are identical to those of the God, and they bear weapons of the same color as His.
Because they resemble the Lord and because they are his inner limbs, worship is performed first for them.
Having spoken thus according to the perspective of the *Śrījayāsaṃhitā*, he further speaks according to the position of the *Māyāvāmanikā*:
"Alternatively, [one should worship] the eight-armed Lord, yellow in color and most beautiful."
O Goddess, he is seated upon a ram, clothed in the directions (naked), and possessing an erect phallus.
He describes the placement of two hands, which are distinct from the previously mentioned six hands holding weapons and so forth:
"And grasping the horn with one...
[referring to] that which belongs to the ram; the meaning is that it is situated [there].
Likewise,
one should constantly worship him in the form of a child, playing with groups of women, with his hands raised in joy. || 13.11 ||
And situated in its four directions are goddesses, beautiful in their sky-clad attire:
Karpūrī, Candanī, Kastūrī, and Kuṅkumī. (12)
And these goddesses, assuming those forms, bestow the fruit of the accomplishment of one's desires;
or else:
What is the use of saying more here? One should indeed meditate upon Him as the Universal Form, with a multitude of many faces and likewise many weapons in His arms.
Or else, [one should worship him] as lying on his bed, as standing at the time of marriage, or likewise as endowed with half of Lakṣmī.
One should meditate solely upon Narasiṃha, or Varāha, or Vāmana;
or else Kapila is to be worshipped, or even the unmanifest (avyakta) and partless (niṣkala) one. (13–15)
He is known by the name "the Unmanifest," and he is partless, his essential nature being perfectly tranquil. || 15 ||
Moreover, in whatever manner one might recollect a particular state of being, one attains identity with that; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (13–16)
The phrase "having reached the abode of Mṛtyujit" follows from the sense of the context. || 16 ||
Now, he describes the propitiation of Mṛtyujit even in the form of deities such as the Sun, as seen in the Saurasaṃhitā, the Vedas, and other texts, saying: "Therefore,
I shall describe that which consists of light, by means of which success shall come to men."
Having a form resembling a red lotus, with a radiance equal to liquid lac.
Having the hue of a mass of vermilion, with a luster equal to a ruby, resembling the color of safflower, and possessing the brilliance of the pomegranate flower. || 13-18 ||
Having a single face like the fire at the end of an eon, with three eyes,
four arms, and great-souled, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should meditate upon the Sun. || 19 ||
And he should hold a vajra with one hand and a ray of light with the other.
And that...
Mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, with a serpent as his sacred thread.
Wearing red garlands and garments, and anointed with red perfumes;
or else, O Goddess, he has eight arms and is equipped with the weapons of the world-protectors.
One should always worship him in the center of the lotus—three-faced, with a formidable countenance, three-eyed, and with a distorted face—mounted upon a horse. (13-22)
The weapons of the world-protectors are the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, the banner, the mace, and the trident.
He should worship the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eyes, and the weapon as the protective enclosures of the Blessed One.
One should perform the placement of all the limbs as before; this is the intended meaning.
And here,
one should worship the deity in the center of the lotus, and the eight planets in the second [circle].
The six beginning with the Moon, along with Ketu and Rāhu, are the planets; these are in the second enclosure. || 23 ||
In the third [circle], however, the constellations are to be worshipped three by three according to their respective order;
on the tips of the petals, a triad is to be worshipped, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the fourth.

In the fifth lotus-arrangement, one should worship the eight weapons. The twenty-seven constellations (*nakṣatras*), divided into groups of three, are worshipped upon the eight petals starting from the east; specifically, twenty-four are on the petals and three are at the tip of the eastern petal. This is the third enclosure, the *nakṣatra*-enclosure, followed by the world-guardian (*lokapāla*) enclosure.
The fourth is the enclosure of weapons; the fifth—
He has also stated another method:
"Or else, one should visualize [the deity] standing alone, with two arms, and endowed with rays of light. (13.25)
Or [he may meditate on] the Lord of the World, who is the very embodiment of Viśvakarman, possessing a universal form,
the Great-Souled One with four arms, bearing an axe and a book.
One should visualize him holding a pair of tongs with his left hand and a thread with his right, while being praised by gods, siddhas, and gandharvas. (13.27)
Holding a pair of tongs. || 27 ||

One should perform worship on dry land, in fire, in water, or on a mountain peak— indeed, everywhere as previously described and to be described hereafter; or wherever it pleases the mind, for that bestows the fruit of the fulfillment of one's desires.
In this Blessed One, there is no fixed rule regarding his physical supports (āśraya), just as there is none regarding his deities; the locative case in "citte" is used in the sense of the dative.
Furthermore,
one should contemplate him as having the form of Rudra, white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, possessing three eyes, and mounted upon a bull in the form of Sādāśiva. (13.29)
The great-souled Lord has four arms, is endowed with the trident and the gesture of fearlessness, holds a mātuluṅga fruit, and is the master who bears a rosary.
"He is mounted upon a bull and has four arms"—this is the distinction from the form of Sadāśiva. || 30 ||
In this very way,
one should likewise meditate upon the Lord, the many-armed deity, standing in the midst of a dance,
bearing Umā on half his body, or else bearing half of half of Viṣṇu.
One should meditate on Him as being present at the wedding, or one should worship Him when He is nearby;
"nearby" means in the presence of the goddess Umā.
Furthermore, Brahmā has four faces; he is gentle, red in color, and possesses beautiful eyes.
With a long beard, possessing great splendor, mounted upon a swan, and four-armed;
holding a staff and a rosary in his hands, and bearing a water-pot and the gesture of fearlessness.
Endowed with the four Vedas, he bestows the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Regarding the phrase "with the Vedas," it means [the Vedas] are present at his sides in embodied form.
Furthermore:
The Buddha is seated upon a lotus throne, with his earlobes and monastic robes hanging down. || 13-34 ||
Lotus-eyed and marked with the lotus sign, adorned with jewels, he is the benefactor of the world;
established in samādhi, the great yogi has his hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The god who bears a rosary, holds a lotus in his hand, and possesses beautiful eyes—when meditated upon and worshipped in this manner, he bestows the fruit of liberation upon women. (13.36)

One whose eyes are like lotuses; one who has a lotus as a mark or sign upon his hands and so forth. In the compound *maṇibaddha*, the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is placed after the first member according to the rule governing compounds beginning with *āhitāgni*.
Or rather,
O beautiful one, what is the use of saying much here again and again?
[They are] Kārttikeya, Kāma, Sūrya, Soma, and Vināyaka.
Likewise, all the world-protectors (lokapālas) and those others born of divine origins [are present] everywhere—
in the Gāruḍa, in the Bhūtatantre, and in all the rules for the employment of speech.
In the various systems such as Nyāya, Arhat, Yoga, and Vaidika, and in the Yāmala, Ekavīra, and Navaka [Tantras] according to their threefold divisions; || 13-39 ||
And in the case of equal division, [the offerings are made] to the one called Devī, the one called Durgā, Vindhyavāsinī, Caṇḍikā, and the four others, as well as to Maheśvara who is self-manifested.
Or in an image already consecrated, or one joined with a seer or a human, or in various weapons, and everywhere in the seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭhas).

O you of excellent vows, by means of this mantra, all the powers within the *pātāla* tantras, among the *nāgas*, and among the Drāmiḍas, as well as the infinite [powers], are indeed [subjugated]. (13.42)
When worshipped according to the prescribed rite, all of them without exception bestow the fruit of every accomplishment;
they are all unfailing—truly this is my word, not false.
"Sūrya" was previously mentioned as existing within the *saṃhitā*, but here it refers to the external [deity]. "The others" refers to those ending with Dhruva.

As for the gods beginning with Kārtikeya, and the goddesses who are the Śaktis in the [tantras] beginning with the *Gāruḍa* and ending with the *Drāmiḍa*, all of them [are worshipped] by this very mantra, according to the prescribed rule (*vidhāna*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: when worshipped according to the specific variations of ritual procedure (itikartavyatā) well-known in their respective scriptures, they become bestowers of the fruit of all accomplishments (siddhi). In the Nyāya system, the deity is Maheśvara, who is distinct from human beings and possesses qualities such as omniscience; among the Ārhata [Jainas], it is Arhat; in Yoga [it is Śiva].

A specific person untouched by afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like; those Vedic rites among the Puranic and historical ones in which deities such as Agni appear; "Yāmala" refers to the *Brahmayāmala*, *Rudrayāmala*, and so forth; and "Ekavīra" refers to the *Parātrīśikā*, *Mata-triṃśikā*, and so forth.

"In the *Navaka*" refers to the *Navātmamantra* and so forth; "in the *Trika*" refers to the systems of the *Ṣaḍardha*; "and in the *Samabheda*" refers to the systems of doctrine known as the Equal and the Unequal; "called *Devī*" refers to the divisions such as the *Mahāghorā* and *Jayā*;
"as *Vindhyavāsinī*" refers to that which propounds the deity bearing this name; and "in the group of four beginning with *Caṇḍikā*" refers to the same.
In the right and left currents, which set forth the propitiation of those respective groups of four deities,
[there is] that Maheśvara who has arisen as the self-existent one in the form of the *liṅga*; therein,
[one should worship] the specific deity who is the presiding authority, established by tradition according to the descent of the respective principles (*tattva*).
In the phrase "prākpratiṣṭhite ṛṣimānuṣayojiti," the two locative cases are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

"Vividhe" refers to various forms such as the sword (*khaḍga*) or iron arrows (*nārāca*); "nāgeṣu" refers to the specific forms of those respective *nāgas*; and "drāmiḍeṣu" refers to forms of deities established by the undisputed renown of the Drāmiḍa and other peoples. "Avitathāḥ" and so forth...
As before. || 43 ||
Moreover, this deity is common to all and bestows the fruit of all accomplishments,
because he is remembered as the very life-force of all mantras. (13.44)

Then, during the installation and worship, as well as at the auspicious throne, the arghya vessel, the consecration of the fire, and during the placement [of mantras], meditation, and the invocation; 13.45.
No conceptual differentiation (vikalpa) should be made at all, since [the deity] is common to all;

"vehicle" refers to the seat. Regarding "differentiation," one should not entertain doubt here on the grounds of the various types of pervasion taught in dualistic and non-dualistic scriptures, because this Lord [is present] through the aforementioned supreme non-dual pervasion.
It is common to all; the meaning is that it is like a level wall-surface for the variegated painting of the manifold diversity of the universe.
And for this reason, no confusion shall arise here; therefore, one should abandon all doubt.
The meaning is that, unlike elsewhere, there is no confusion whatsoever here regarding the mantras and so forth.
This too is the majesty of this king of mantras:
that when recited once, it resides within the body; when recited once, it is placed in the argha vessel;
when applied once to the hands, it is achieved through a single mental recitation.
Stationed outside, one should worship [the deity] once; once in the forms of the moon and sun;
once in the fire-oblation (homa); once in the recitation of mantras (japa); and one should sacrifice once in water.
One should worship the Supreme Lord everywhere, doing so repeatedly;
this has been stated thus because He is eternally manifest.
Therefore, [the practice of] breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth, as well as the yoga of gestures (mudrā) and concentration (dhāraṇā), are merely afflictions. || 13-49 ||
O you of virtuous vows, nothing indeed is of use for this king of mantras;
all acts such as the worship of this Blessed One must be performed with resolute determination, otherwise it will not be at all...
The meaning is: by means of entering into the power of the great mantra that is an easy method, and not through affliction.
But if the exertion of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth were to be resorted to, then this very [point] is the refutation here. || 13-50 ||
It comes to be.
But when performed with perseverance, it becomes flawless for the sake of increasing the kingdom of the king, the foremost of practitioners.
Thus it is auspicious.

I bow to the eye of Śiva, the conscious self, which is simultaneously both common to all systems and unique to its own system, for which there is no distinction that can be imposed by anything external, and which is the shattering of constraints, eternally manifest.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Netrodyota*, a commentary on the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 13.
The Fourteenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net.
Having manifested by means of his own splendor, he causes the wheel of mantras to flash forth by his own splendor alone, [revealing] his own Self.
We pay homage to that divine eye which, for the sake of bestowing grace, presides over the two eyes for the purpose of pacifying dualistic vision.

Thus, by this collection of topics, the nature of the King of Mantras as the supreme non-dual reality—the great secret that is the essence of all philosophical systems—has been determined in accordance with the question. Then, anticipating the uselessness of other mantras, the venerable Goddess said: "O Lord, if the mantra described as supreme is indeed the best..."
Of all the tantras and of all the deities in every respect.
For this king of mantras is the supreme heart that bestows all accomplishments; tell me, what is the use of reciting other principal mantras, even those that are desired? || 14-2 ||

In this verse, the word "tarhi" (then) should be supplied at the beginning of the phrase "kimiti. Furthermore, the particle "ca" (and) conjoins the phrase "kimiti" with the various modes of worshipping Him. The word "sva" (one's own) is a separate term. || 2 ||
Thus questioned, the Blessed Lord said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Maheśānī! Since I have been asked by you, O sinless one, I shall fully declare that which is the supreme, eternal essence."
I shall explain correctly that matter about which you have questioned me, for this is a supreme secret, certain and eternal. || 3 ||
He begins to describe that [reality]:
"In the beginning, this [universe] existed as Śakti—beyond comparison, free from disease, auspicious, all-pervading, pure, inconceivable, and beyond the senses. (14.4)
The phrase "this" refers to whatever appears as an object of "this-ness" in relation to a subject such as the body;

in relation to the supreme subject— the consciousness of the other which is not entered by the body and so forth— that same thing is of the nature of power (śakti) and non-different from that supreme subject.

And therefore, according to the principle stated in the *Rigveda-prayoga* (2.1)—"Thus, for the Immeasurable One, all entities appear full by their own nature, just as the Self appears by itself"—the nature [of the Lord] is beyond comparison and the like. The remainder has already been largely explained. || 4 ||

And therefore, O Goddess, desiring to create by his own will, this first Lord of Gods, Śiva— who is all-knowing, all-pervading, and whose nature is action— is endowed with the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti). (14.5)

The God who is the self of all things is the initiator of the primordial creation. Since the universe existed as the form of His power (*śakti*), due to the identity of power with the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), He is this first one, the primary cause, and the original source. He is "the all-of-all" (*sarvasarva*) because everything is His; "self" (*ātman*) means His essential nature.

For one who possesses such [a nature], by his own will, through the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) having attained that very form, he— being of the nature of action (*kriyātmaka*) and having taken up the plane of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*)—
[acts] by means of that which manifests as Anāśrita, Sadāśiva, and so forth.
He is the initiator and the one who causes the manifestation of the primordial creation, which encompasses the entire manifold of infinite intermediate creations and dissolutions.
Having thus brought forth such creation, thereafter, within that very realm, the creation of mantras was indeed performed by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Just as various forms are fashioned through distinct systems of differentiation, so too is the Supreme Lord of Gods, who is the self of all and everything. || 14.7 ||
When the Lord of Mantras is common to all as the designator of them all,
then indeed he is the self of all and remains untainted.

"From that" means from that very substratum. "In accordance with" means by way of conformity, through the predominance of consciousness whose nature is autonomous light. "By means of the arrangement of differentiation" refers to the intention of manifesting the variety of grace bestowed upon those to be graced.
Just as the creation of various mantras was fashioned by Śiva, so too is the creation of mantras [described here].
With the intention that "May the supreme non-dual pervasion not leave me desirous," [the Lord] is the one who consists of all things as his own self;

he is the supreme one who effects the protection and fulfillment of the mantras of the universe; he is the common one, whose nature is the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya); and for this very reason, like the word *sat* ("being"), he is the designator of all things, such as jars and the like.

He is one whose awareness is his own non-differentiated majesty; he is fashioned by Śiva alone, the Supreme Self, and manifested through His own great power. And since this is so, he is the self of all;
for because it is thus, therefore he is untainted.

It is not smeared, nor stained, nor grasped by the pervasive duality of mantras such as those of the Vedas, Vaiṣṇava, Gāruḍa, Siddhānta, and so forth; for those things considered to be "smearers" lack substantiality apart from being of the nature of the potency of the Great Mantra, whose essence is the light of that Consciousness.

And therefore, tens of millions of mantras—both manifest and unmanifest—are established; all of them grant accomplishment when they are brought to cessation by means of that which has no beginning or end. || 14-9 ||
When recited by means of this *saṃpuṭa* method, they bestow the fruit of accomplishment;
for that purpose, O fair-hipped one, I have revealed them to you out of affection. (14.10)
"The supreme secret truth...
[they are] innumerable with respect to their retinue; they are manifest and unmanifest, having both differentiated and undifferentiated forms;
[they are] 'beginningless and endless' by enclosing the creation within them," according to the tradition of the *Pārvatī-tantra* (Pa. Trī. 3).

That very abode of consciousness (*ciddhāma*), which is the primordial ground and the essence of the power (*vīrya*) of the Great Mantra, unfolds the wheel of mantras upon its own screen and permeates it with the light of consciousness alone; thus, what is intended here is the meaning of "stopping" (*nirodha*) through the predominance of power (*vīrya*), whereas the "encapsulation" (*saṃpuṭīkāra*)— [...is as follows: (The remainder of the sentence is not provided in the source text.)
By means of the method of reciting the mantra.
And because this is such a supreme secret,
it must not be told to just anyone whose stain of the latent impression of duality has not been removed.
For this reason,
O Goddess, when secret it bestows perfect accomplishment, whereas when manifest it destroys accomplishment.
Excellent accomplishment is enjoyment that culminates in liberation. || 11 ||
Therefore, the oral tradition (*mukhāgama*) must be kept strictly secret.

That which has its origin (*āgama*) and dissemination (*prasaraṇa*) from the mouth—that is, from the face of Paraśakti—is this very [tradition] whose essence is the explained secret; having duly considered the most intense descent of power (*tīvratama-śaktipāta*), it is bestowed upon one who possesses it.
Thus, this tradition must be kept strictly secret and well-established within oneself; may there be auspiciousness.

Having established within its own abode the King of Mantras— resplendent with the power of its own vitality that vibrates from beginning to end— and causing the host of Śambaras to flash forth with a power equal to its own,
the Śāṅkara [power] carries out on all sides the playful activity of various acts of grace.
I bow to the Eye, which is intense with the nectar of supreme bliss and all-encompassing power.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Netrodyota*, the illumination of the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. 14.
The Fifteenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net. Radiant with the throbbing expansion of all-pervasive consciousness, which shines as the self of all things.
We worship the eye of Śarva, which destroys Rākṣasas, provides all protection, and bestows prosperity.
Having thus determined the majesty of this king of mantras, the Blessed One spoke in order to determine its nature as a cause of protection as well:
"Henceforth, I shall explain how it effects all forms of protection."
The Lord of Mantras [offered] the most fierce incense, which is prescribed for the destruction of demons.
"Yathā" means by which method, such as the procedure of fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth; "mahogram" refers to incense that pacifies all calamities.
Likewise, I shall proclaim that substance designated by the term "rakṣoghna" (demon-destroyer) because it is taught as being destructive of demons.
This is also an illustration for flowers and other such items. || 1 ||
For when this mantra has been consecrated seven times and given to someone, it destroys the Rākṣasas;
and whoever [receives] it...
One should always wear it on the head; by doing so, one is liberated from all defects.

Now, explaining the names of the Rakṣoghna [mantra], he demonstrates its majesty for the purpose of destroying all the Daityas, since the Brahmā spoken by me performed an *abhicāra* rite against all those who were full of envy. (15.3)

Therefore, he is called *sarṣapa*; because he protects (*pāti*) and guards (*rakṣati*) from all sides those who are envious and full of jealousy, such as the Dānavas and others— meaning he protects them from the envious (*serṣyebhyaḥ*)— it is for this reason, based on the similarity of syllables, that his name is *sarṣapa*.
When all the Rākṣasas had been slain and put to flight. || 15-4 ||
Then, O Goddess, she was called by me "Rakṣoghnā" (the slayer of Rākṣasas), meaning that she became renowned on earth as "Rakṣoghnā" because she slays the Rākṣasas.
And in all battles with the Daityas, along with the foremost of the gods.
Appointed as destroyers of the wicked for the sake of accomplishing the destruction of enemies, their purpose was fulfilled;
therefore, they are known on earth as Siddhārthakas.
O Goddess, you are renowned as the destroyer of the pride of beings with wicked minds;

for when the gods were appointed to the task of destroying their enemies so that they might achieve their own self-perfection, and when the purpose and aim of those gods was accomplished through them, [then you appeared].
Then they became known as Siddhārthakas, at which time all beings were terrified on every side. (15.7)

O Dear One, the practitioner of mantra, intent on providing protection, should offer oblations marked with the [target's] name into the fire according to the rite of *nīrājana*, with a mind full of wrath. (15.8)
Then, the *nīrājana*—renowned as the supreme bringer of all prosperity—is [performed].

For those who are terrified by dangers on all sides and afflicted by internal defects such as mental anguish and the like, it is performed by means of the *nīrājana* procedure, which will be described below;
"nīrājana" means a complete (*niḥśeṣeṇa*) illumination (*rājana*) or kindling (*dīpana*). This...
The object known as a mustard seed is well-known and famous.
And this Rakṣoghna [mantra], which consists of the white [syllables] and so forth, exists according to the distinction of the Yugas; it is powerful in bestowing grace. || 15-9 ||
According to the divisions of the Kṛta and other yugas, he manifests in white, red, yellow, and black forms, and being powerful, he proceeds toward bestowing grace.
In that regard, the white [sandalwood] is renowned as bestowing everything; the red is the giver of sovereignty;
the yellow is declared to be the provider of protection; and the black is the destroyer of enemies. (15.10)
Thus, in the ancient age (purākalpa), there was a distinction of duties based on the distinction of castes.
But now,
