throughout all the four ages (caturyuga), there are two forms, yellow and black; [the others] are known as rājasa, white mustard-seed, and fair-complexioned.
The black mustard seed is *rājikā*; "gaura" means yellow.
Having become twofold in form, he vanished, O beloved.
It is of two forms, white and red; however, the meaning is that today it does not circulate because of its supreme nature. || 11 ||
Having spoken thus as a digression, he states the subject at hand:
"When one has fallen under the power of death and is assailed by all beings, then [one should take] cow's milk mixed with ghee and white sugar. (15.12)
Having mixed [the offering] with sesame seeds, one should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*), which grants all peace.

The word "gone" (*yāta*) refers, by implication, to the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The word "having made" (*kṛtvā*) refers to the mustard seed (*sarṣapa*) mentioned in the context. The oblation here is performed with the root mantra.
The best rājasarṣapa is combined with black sesame seeds. || 15-13 ||
One should offer oblations that have been triple-anointed; this immediately bestows the fruit of all peace.
"Triple-anointed" means sprinkled with the three sweets (trimadhu).
Having consecrated this very [substance] with this [mantra], it is placed into the hand of [the recipient].

Incomparable good fortune arises for him; there is no doubt about this. "By this" refers to the root mantra. The particle *eva* (only) indicates the absence of any modification (*ūha*) in its application. "This" refers to the substance, namely the *rājasarṣapa* (black mustard seed).
Having recited this mantra seven times, the knower of mantras [should act].
Upon whose head one should cause it to fall, he is liberated from all defects.
This applies everywhere for one who knows the mantra and understands its potency; "one should cause it to fall" refers specifically to the mustard seed.
In order to determine the object previously indicated and characterized, he says:
"Having consecrated the garments and the medicinal herb... (15–16).
Or, when [the food] is consecrated with the *samālambha* mantra, it becomes a slayer of whomever it is given to. (15–17)
For the non-violent one indeed commits no violence whatsoever.
The word *vā* has the sense of *eva* (indeed). The meaning is that those [beings] do not at all cause him harm when he has entered the forests. || 17 ||

For the sake of protecting one who is self-restrained, one should recite [this mantra] in the cardinal and intermediate directions, whether by day or by night, whether sleeping or even while awake. (15–18)
That man remains on earth unslayable by all beings;
"a mustard seed" is the intended meaning.
Thus, I have revealed this ritual procedure for the protection of kings. || 15-19 ||
Out of affection for you, I shall speak this excellent secret that grants all perfections.
Since the king protects when he is favorable toward his subjects, the entire universe becomes protected; thus, by virtue of being the primary locus [of protection], he is called "Rāja" (King).
"Thine" refers to [the compassion] consisting of the desire to favor.
And for this reason, [the same applies] to kings, queens, and their sons, in relation to the twice-born and others. (15–20)
He who acts as an Ācārya, bestowing grace upon all, whether he be a knower of mantras or a practitioner (sādhaka), is in every way worthy of worship as a lord. || 15-21 ||

"By means of various honors and manifold extensive gifts"—this refers to providing protection according to the perspective of what has been said and will be said; "the practitioner who knows the mantras" refers to one who has perfected the mantra through the propitiation prescribed in the *kalpa*; because of his equality with a teacher (*ācārya*), [he is so designated].

"This initiation of retention (*dhāraṇādīkṣā*) must indeed be performed here by a yogin, or else, O Goddess, it becomes truly well-performed when done by one who has attained mastery over mantra. Since this is stated in the *Śrī Svacchanda*, the teacher must be satisfied in every respect.
This clarifies the point by means of a primary illustration:
just as the word *svāhā* joined at the end of a mantra is praised in the case of a fire offering (*homa*). || 15-22 ||
Likewise, one who is skilled in all rites and always knows the mantras shall immediately bestow fruit; he is auspicious and grants all peace. || 15-23 ||

"At the end of the mantra" means uttered as joined [with the following]. "Svāhā" refers to the word *svāhā*. "Dakṣitaḥ" means gratified by the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). "Fruit" refers to liberation and supernatural powers (*siddhi*); thus it is in the subsequent [verses] as well. || 23 ||
Furthermore, just as *sudhā* is for the *nāgas* and *svadhā* is for the ancestors, so too is *namaskāra* for the gods; *vauṣaṭ* is praised for rites of pacification (*śānti*). (24)
Likewise, for those who know the mantras, constant giving and the highest honor quickly yield fruit and bestow all accomplishments. (15.25)
"svadhā" refers to the word *svadhā*. The rest is clear. || 25 ||
He establishes this very point:
"Mantras reside in the power of knowledge, and that knowledge resides in the mind; when that mind is honored and satisfied, it shall always become characterized by sattva. (15.26)
Prosperities are eternally established in *sattva*, and *lakṣmī* herself resides therein; by the destruction of *rajas* and *tamas*, mantras abide in the arising of *sattva*. (15.27)
They quickly become bestowers of accomplishment because they are exceedingly pure;

since their nature consists of protecting through reflection (*manana-trāṇa-dharmaka*), mantras abide in the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), meaning that their essence is that potency. And that knowledge, whose self is potency, abiding in the mind, is the contemplation of that potency (*vīryānusandhāna*).
It is based on the supreme consciousness, and that mind is "worshipped," meaning it has been propitiated with a weight of devotion;
and thus, through the blossoming of a transformation arising from the gaze of the intensity of devotion, the sattvic state comes into being.
Among the emotional states (bhāvas) which take the form of one's own limbs, there is both the knowledge and the activity of the Lord.

According to the principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, "In the third [state], Māyā, those very [powers] become for the bound soul (*paśu*) the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*," it attains the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), which is the emergent essence of *sattva*.
When a being has become such, all forms of prosperity— the fortune of great enjoyments— reside within him,
and the fortune of liberation likewise abides right there. Therefore,

through the destruction of the *rajas* and *tamas* that consist of flickering and contraction, and through the arising of *sattva* characterized by the aforementioned expansion, [liberation is attained].
The mantras are exceedingly pure; thus, through the great power of the self consisting of the attained capacity for gnosis, they swiftly and always bestow all accomplishments.
Therefore, for this reason, one should strive with every effort; for this is the command of the Supreme Lord. (15.28)

"It must be protected with effort" means that it is the command (ājñā) determined as such through every possible exertion. "This" refers to the form [of the teaching] that the propitiation of the teacher must be performed in every way.
For one who protects this [discipline] with such effort,
perfection and liberation are not far off;
the meaning is that they will come quickly.
Concluding the matter concerning the office of authority, he demonstrates its secret nature:
"But one should not bestow the ritual procedure of the Unsurpassed upon one who has been initiated by another. (15.29)
One should bestow [the initiation] upon one's own disciple who has been initiated; otherwise, it does not succeed.
This is because one initiated by another is a dualistic disciple and has not entered into non-duality. May there be auspiciousness!
I take refuge in that eye of Śiva, which is the supreme, full nectar arising from the reflective awareness of the initial and subsequent contemplation, and which spreads auspiciousness everywhere.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the illustrious Netratantra, in the Netrodyota commentary composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, the illustrious Kṣemarāja. 15.
The Sixteenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net.
The fruit of various forms, accumulated through diverse modes of conduct.

We praise that eye of Śarva, which bestows the undifferentiated manifestation of the self-nature of the one consciousness; its own majesty shines as the substratum for the variegated sketches of the world, and it is full of the essence of the outpouring of incomparable bliss.
Having restated the nature of the glorious Mṛtyujit, who embodies all deities as realized through the preceding section,
the venerable Goddess spoke, desiring to determine the rules of conduct and other requirements that are the means for attaining him:
"The most wonderful secret has been told by the God of Gods."
The God who embodies all scriptures, the solitary hero of great power.
Through the distinction between the three divisions of the Left, Right, and Siddhānta,
it is proclaimed as being joined with the Vaiṣṇava and other systems, along with its secret teachings.
For this Śiva is composed of all the gods, the conqueror of death, and all-pervading;
he is to be worshipped through many traditions according to the distinctions of one's inner disposition.
Bestowing various fruits of accomplishment through diverse ritual applications, I now wish to hear [your teaching], for a doubt remains within my heart. (16.4)
Indeed, no one other than you can be found who is capable of cutting through this doubt;
for previously, the Lord spoke of their respective individual conducts. (16.5)

How is it that the common conduct previously enjoined is revealed by the statement "consisting of all the Āgamas" as being secret? "Eka" means without a second. "Vīra" means capable of performing all actions. "Mahābala" means the embodiment of the potency of all mantras.

"Vaiṣṇava and so forth" means [the deity] is properly joined (ā-yukta) through a pervasive non-differentiation throughout the form of Viṣṇu and others—the word "and so forth" (ādi) including Brahmā, Sūrya, and the rest. "Along with the secret" (sarahasyam) means it has been proclaimed and taught according to the Kula method. "Pervasive" (vyāpaka) is the reason for this state of consisting of all the gods; and for that reason, he is Śiva.

[He is] the form of supreme non-dual bliss. "By means of traditions" refers to the forms of knowledge-yoga (jñānayoga) as taught in their respective scriptures. "Due to the difference in disposition" refers to the suitability of the devotee's mind.
By the statement "I wish to hear," the subject matter is shown separately in this verse.

In the various *saṃhitās* mentioned previously in the passage beginning with "pūrvam," [it is stated that] because the Lord is of the nature of the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānyarūpa*), he must be conceived through the universal conduct alone; the underlying intention is that no such [specific conduct] is observed at all. As for the phrase "previously enjoined" (*pūrvacodita*), it refers to what was previously taught in the ninth chapter.
"In this way, O Goddess, the omnipresent God, who possesses many forms like a gem,
is worshipped by all with the desire for the fruit of perfect accomplishment.
By such passages as these, it is stated in general terms that he is "worshipped" (*ārādhita*).
Furthermore, how is it that all [deities] are accomplished when worshipped with a single mantra? || 16-6 ||
For in various scriptures,
through seeds (*bīja*), syllabic clusters (*kūṭa*), as well as *piṇḍa* and garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*) in their entirety,
by means of the distinction between the signified and the signifier, they bestow the fruit of all accomplishments.

[The mantras] have been described: by means of *bījas* (seeds), which are vowels; by *kūṭas*, which consist of *piṇḍa-padas* (compound words); by *piṇḍas*, such as the *Navātman* and others; and by *mālā-mantras*, which take the form of an aggregate of words.

The distinction between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) is such that, from the perspective of *parāvāk* (the supreme speech), the *bījas* are predominant, while from the perspective of *paśyantī* (the visionary speech), the *piṇḍas* are predominant.
Of the *piṇḍas* by means of the middle articulation (*madhyamā-yukti*), of the *mālā-mantras* [by the same], and of the *kūṭas* by means of both the *paśyantī* and the *madhyamā*. || 7 ||
Therefore, how can a person become worthy of worship by a single mantra when there are so many deities addressed by various mantras?
Or how, through grace, can all the gods be present here? || 16-8 ||
O Supreme Lord, out of compassion for the welfare of human beings,
how is it that all the gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others— whose specific forms are not individually known— become gracious through the favor of a single general mantra?
The meaning is: how can they be pleased with human beings who do not know their specific qualities?
Moreover, having entered the Kali age, men deluded by suffering achieve success [only through this]. || 16-9 ||
Tormented by the fire of poverty, beset by the fear of various forms of death, solely intent on evil, wrathful, and excluded from purity and proper conduct. (16.10)
Devoted to violence and backbiting, and devoid of austerity and truth, they are [seized] by Yoginīs, Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, Ḍāmarikās, and others. (16.11)
O Maheśvara, tell me how living beings who are sealed by spirits, yakṣas, and apasmāras may attain success without exertion.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "Tell me the manner in which they are accomplished," meaning that method by which, through the pacification of suffering, poverty, and so forth, one attains either the supreme or the non-supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*). Purity (*śauca*) pertains to the mind, wealth, and the body. We shall demonstrate the true nature of the *śākinīs* and others later on.
To resolve this question, the Blessed Lord said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! I shall speak to you according to what you have asked.
Having thus made his promise, he speaks first with the intention of addressing that which was stated regarding the arrival of Kali.
Likewise, mortals have short lifespans, their minds struck by delusion.
Constantly delighting in wicked conduct, associating with the unrighteous, they are revilers, powerful, cruel, and brought under the sway of old age and disease. (16.14)
Devoted to wicked conduct, foolish, and always indulging in envy toward others,
they appear as if overcome by great terror and are tormented by the fire of poverty.
They were proponents of nihilism, wicked, engaged in the conduct of thieves, lacking devotion toward gods and gurus, and serving the base out of envy. || 16-16 ||
Though they performed observances such as fasting at sacred fords and various extremely difficult vows, they were all devoid of perfection and were not liberated; this is certain.

But for the sake of their deliverance, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, [I shall teach] the King of Mantras, possessed of great power, by the mere recitation, meditation, and worship of which [this is achieved]. || 16-18 ||
They shall attain the supreme state, the supreme medicine that is Nirvāṇa,
O Great Goddess, because the Kali age will become even more distressing.

The meaning is: "For that purpose, this ultimate reality (paramārtha) has been revealed by me to you through my compassion and intention from the very beginning. The word "this" refers to the form of the Lord Mṛtyujit.
And therefore, in every respect, the ultimate reality is the conqueror of death, omnipresent, and facing in all directions. || 16-20 ||
One who desires the attainment of liberation should worship Him through various modes of being (*bhāva-bheda*).
He is the one whose gates—the means of attainment—consist of the meditations and other practices directed toward various deities in all directions;
and as the Supreme, He exists through the pervasive expansion of non-dual consciousness and bliss (*cid-ānanda*) throughout all states of existence.

By means of the differentiation— that is, the shattering— of the qualities of the intellect such as passion and the like, the conqueror of death, whose nature is the ultimate reality and who is supremely worthy of being adopted, should be worshipped by the seeker of liberation. Furthermore,
he states that for one who relies upon the means consisting of fixed ritual acts, conduct and so forth must necessarily be observed.
In whichever scriptures the conduct has been described by me, [that is to be followed]. || 16-21 ||
In the various streams [of ritual practice], one should act accordingly in the specific sacrifices and oblations (*yāga-homa*);
the meaning is that a mixture of substances and so forth should not be performed, just as a mottled appearance [is avoided].

If it is argued that even a mixture of conduct (*ācāra-śabalatā*) consists essentially of non-difference from Consciousness (*cid-abheda-mayī*), then [it follows that] just like the rule of conduct...
Regarding the restriction of form, it has been said:
"What is called worship is not that firm mental state which is performed with flowers and the like;
rather, worship is the dissolution [of the mind] with devotion into the non-conceptual great void. (Viśvabhairava-tantra 147)
Thus, this alone remains. For the lord of yogins who has reached this state and constantly engages in the secret worship and other rites, there is nothing further to be done.
As it was said by our masters in their hymn:
"O Ambikā, there is indeed no praise whatsoever that does not consist of your name; alas, your body is composed of all sounds!
In every form, I perceive your presence."
And when the mind-born [passions] spread outward.
Having thus reflected that this world has arisen effortlessly within Śiva, who has quelled all inauspiciousness,
[those who are] indeed devoid of praise, recitation, worship, and meditation—
"I have not even a fraction of a moment [to spare].
For those wishing to enter the abode of non-duality, there is a rule of conduct just as there is a rule of physical appearance;
and therein too—
Since the contemplation of the potency of the mantra, which has the non-dual Supreme Lord as its cause, has been taught, what was stated previously is indeed superior.
Now, one might ask: "Since there exist other common mantras such as the *praṇava* and others, why is this [mantra] alone so preeminent?
Anticipating this doubt, with the intention that the very command of the Supreme Maheśvara is the reason here, he says:
"O Goddess, others never succeed in a general sense. (22)
However, there is authority over these three types which bestow all accomplishments;
"others" refers generally to the *praṇava*, *mātṛkā*, *māyā*, *vyomavyāpin*, *ṣaḍakṣara*, *prāsāda*, and *bahurūpa* mantras.
They may sometimes be accomplished in a general sense within the Supreme Consciousness, which is the nature of Great Being (mahāsattā) and the radiance of supreme non-duality;

however, they never become the causes for attaining that [Supreme State], but rather lead to the attainment of those specific positions appropriate to the respective deities as taught in various scriptures. The term "in a general sense" (sāmānyataḥ) is used with reference to repetition (āvṛttyā).
This is to be applied. And in this very King of Mantras, which consists of the Great Pervasion—the Self that is the nature of all things previously mentioned and yet to be mentioned—[it is said]:
"In three ways, in the three... (1.1).

Thus, since this chapter bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) upon the threefold reality whose true nature has been explained in the commentary on this very verse, its capacity to grant the aforementioned common accomplishments exists by virtue of the Lord’s command (*aiśvaraniyoga*). As was stated previously: "The Lord of Gods..."
"The Supreme is the essence of all things;
the Lord of Mantras is common to all and the designator of everything. (14.8).
Therefore, this [is the nature] of the Praṇava and other common mantras.

The Gurus maintain that because it expresses even the specific mantras of the Krama, Kula, Mata, and Trika (Ṣaḍardha) traditions, it is designated as both common and uncommon, as well as specifically particular and extra-ordinary.
Since this is so, therefore,
whether it be mixed with duality or non-duality, [the deity] will indeed be desired as the bestower of accomplishment.

Because the God is omnipresent and possesses universal form like a gem, He whose form is the universe has a cosmic body manifested through His own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*); for this very reason, even though He is the "Solitary Hero" (*ekavīra*) according to the aforementioned view, He nevertheless possesses a dualistic form that comprises the universe as assumed by His sovereignty. Even of that [dualistic form]...
Because it manifests as being attached to the wall of non-dual conscious light (*citprakāśa*),
it possesses both dual and non-dual forms; thus, being of the nature of supreme non-duality and the unsurpassed (*anuttara*), and because it is all-pervasive,
it is held to be the bestower of accomplishment (*siddhi*) within the specific Siddhānta Tantras, which consist of mixed dual and non-dual forms.
It is indeed so; the jewel here is the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
And for this reason, it is not only by means of this great pervasion of non-duality that this [practice] bestows liberation while living everywhere;
rather, when performed according to the will of the practitioner, it certainly grants supernatural powers (siddhi). || 24 ||
It certainly and definitively bestows all accomplishments. || 16-24 ||
He summarizes this as follows:
"That omnipresent deity who is all-pervading and resides within all, he is the bestower of perfection and liberation; in the ultimate sense, he is not the castes. (16–25)
Therefore, O Goddess, He should always be worshipped according to the distinction of one's inner disposition;

for it is Maheśvara— the independent, non-dual consciousness-self— who, from the perspective of ultimate reality, bestows both spiritual attainment (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*), and not the letters, because they lack the specific quality of being letters that distinguishes them from other letters.
Therefore, the Lord of Mantra— the ultimate reality which is the reflective awareness of the pure, autonomous, and vibrating consciousness—
should be worshipped according to the distinctions of one's state of being by those seeking liberation as well as those seeking worldly enjoyment. For even those seeking enjoyment,
when they engage in ritual action preceded by the reflective awareness of the non-dual abode, are not overcome by obstacles.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrīsarvācārabhaṭṭāraka*. The passage beginning with "He who is this" and so forth has already been explained previously.
Now I shall explain the sacrifice of this [deity], which may be performed according to one's desire.
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or at a crossroads;
likewise, in a forest or a delightful grove, according to the requirements of place and time.
In a place free from all thorns, avoided by wicked beings, where those who dwell in merit and dharma reside, and which is shunned by those of evil conduct; || 16-28 ||
Where the citizens are never seen intent on slander, and where those wicked men— corrupt and full of all kinds of impurity— do not even look upon it.
In that place, which is free from fear and the like, one should perform the sacrifice with the great mantra.

Sacrifice (*yāga*) is the casting of substances for the sake of a deity. "According to one's desire" means that on mountain peaks and so forth, one should act wherever there is a desire, without overstepping that desire.

"According to place and time" means by way of the suitability of place and time. "A meritorious dwelling with the righteous" is a compound [meaning] a dwelling that is both meritorious and with those most devoted to dharma. "Intermixed" refers to those born of inverse unions (*viloma*). "All intermixtures" means those for whom there is a mixing or mingling with all [types of people], such as the lowly, the most sinful, the violent, and so forth.
Calamities (ītayaḥ) refer to excessive rain and other such natural disasters.
Alternatively,
the sacrifice should be performed in the house by the teachers who perceive reality.
However, without the vision of reality, there is no teacherhood whatsoever.
And that [mantra] must be kept strictly secret, especially in rites for pacification (*śāntikarman*);
the word "especially" indicates secrecy even in the case of daily (*nitya*) rites.
He says that in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), because grace (*anugraha*) is the primary concern, there is no fixed rule;
for the mandala must indeed be constructed at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), wherever that may be.
Either in a house or on a mountain peak and so forth. || 31 ||
But for rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), he says they must be in a secret place:
"In rites for pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), worship must certainly be well-concealed with effort.
"Certainly" means having made it a certainty.
Regarding this, he states the justification: "For in the world, those intent on violence are seen to achieve success through their harmful acts. (16.32)

Since the minor [spirits] such as yoginīs, bhūtas, and piśācas—designated by the term "siddhi-hiṃsakas" (those who cause harm through supernatural powers)—are seen to be intent on violence, it is therefore appropriate that [the practice] be kept strictly secret. || 32 ||
For by them indeed are performed the pinning down of mantras, as well as their breaking, deluding, terrifying, striking, paralyzing, and immobilizing. (16.33)

Furthermore, by means of other [rites], such as making someone an enemy or even a counter-spell (*pratyaṅgira*), and causing the total destruction [of the opponent], these are performed by wicked ministers. (16.34)
In that regard:
"Having visualized it blazing intensely from the big toe up to the head,
one should cause it to enter [the body] face-down and place it in one's own *apāna* location."
Having thus visualized the target as resembling burnt wood, in the form of a flaming torch, and as having abandoned the body, the severance of the mantra is accomplished.
There shall be pinning down, as well as delusion, and likewise the loss of splendor;
there is also the severance of protection—this is the truth, there is no doubt in this matter.
"He becomes hated by all, and his mantra does not succeed"—thus, by the method of meditation; likewise:
"In the middle of the two *ka*-enclosures, one should inscribe the name of [the person]."
Outside of that is the abode of fire, adorned with eight *repha* (the letter *ra*).
Having written it, one should place the yantra within the cavity of a skull-cup joined together;
O Mahāgaurī, for whomever’s name [is thus inscribed], there shall indeed be a severance of their mantra.
"There occurs a loss of accomplishment and one becomes hated by all," and so forth, according to the method of the yantras as stated in the *Śrīkulārṇava*; likewise, [it is said] by such passages as:
"'The letter Ā is declared for cutting; the letter Ṛ for striking,' and so on."

By means of the method of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkāra*) with the forms (*ākāra*) and so forth as taught in the *Śrīmad-ucchuṣma-tantra* and other scriptures, together with the yoga residing within the body, the wicked perform this striking (*tāḍana*) and so forth.
"Pinning" (*kīlana*) is the production of a different state; "piercing" (*bhedana*) is the abandonment of the orientation toward the target (*sādhya*); "deluding" (*mohana*)...

Nirvīryīkaraṇa is the rendering powerless; jambhana is the infliction of an incapacity to perform one's functions; stambhana is the induction of immobility; and pratyaṅgiratva is the production of a contrary effect upon the user of a mantra that was intended for the subduing of spirits and other such entities.
The rest is clear. || 34 ||
Thus do the harmful ones indeed strive in ten ways;
therefore, with every effort, one should remain well-guarded upon the refuge.

One should diligently perform sacrifice, fire-oblation, and recitation in one's own home; for "hi" has the sense of "because," and it is possible to keep [the practice] secret there according to one's preference.
Moreover, this [mantra] always bestows the ultimate fruit; it is supreme, well-guarded, and conquers death.

In the mandala, on the sacrificial ground, or in the ritual jar— with a mind free from doubt and with a resolute heart thinking, "The fruit will surely arise from this"— the Lord, well-guarded within the jar and elsewhere, is eternally beloved and the bestower of desired fruits.
Moreover, a fire sacrifice performed upon a palace roof especially bestows peace and nourishment. || 16-37 ||
"So be it," [he said], with perfect secrecy and without any doubt. || 37 ||
Therefore,
O Goddess of Gods, no conceptual construction (vikalpa) should be made here.
For it is said elsewhere: "From conceptual construction, one goes to the Raurava hell."
"I see no other flaw in the mantra-practice of these ministers than this:
that such a person, though possessing such a liṅga, is merely wavering.
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, the unwavering practitioner who performs sacrifice (yāga) or fire-oblation (homa) right there obtains the fruit of all accomplishments. || 16-38 ||
But one who acts while harboring doubt should be known as a thief; he brings about the loss of accomplishment.
Such a person shall not have the authority in this Tantra of the Supreme Lord.
The meaning is that one who, with an unconfident heart, proceeds toward the Supreme Lord through deception, is bound like a thief. || 39 ||
Since it is thus,
O Goddess, he is a giver of all, a teacher who knows reality and knows the paths;
"one who knows reality" means one whose own essential nature is the self of Supreme Śiva, which is a mass of light and bliss directly realized.
Pervading the universe by means of the expansion of his power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) throughout the three times, and because he does so,
he is capable of bestowing all fruits that shine forth from his own abode.
Furthermore,
he who thus understands the pervasion according to the division of the higher and the lower— || 16-40 ||

He would be the manifest liberator, Śiva, the supreme cause; the meaning is that just as there is success (*siddhi*) for practitioners (*sādhakas*), so too is liberation (*mukti*) for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣus*), provided they are knowers of reality (*tattvavid*).
The qualification "Śiva, the manifest supreme cause" is included here because, as in the dualistic doctrine (*bhedavāda*), [the teacher] is distinct from the disciple.
This is because of the underlying intention that one should not suspect any difference between Paramaśiva and the liberated Śivas (muktaśivas).
He confirms this very point by way of the negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"But he who performs initiation without knowing the Śiva-principle... (16.41).

Those who undergo initiation with him do not attain liberation; rather, like a blind man led by a blind man, they all fall into the abyss. The word "eva" (only/just) emphasizes that this applies to one who is devoid of the aforementioned knowledge of the Śiva-principle.
It resonates with the state of not being illuminated by the light of another's eyes, even in the slightest degree.
Therefore, one who does not know the truth, even if unqualified, having entered [the path] for the sake of a livelihood, would lead both himself and his disciples into the peril of hell. (16.42)
Since this is so,
therefore the illustrious teacher who knows reality should be a bestower of everything;
he is illustrious, being embraced by the glory of liberation while living.

Furthermore, since even for a teacher who is a ritualist, activity is not appropriate without the knowledge of reality, he says: "As long as one is not a knower of reality, how could he cause [others] to perform rituals? (16.43).
The knower of mantra, in the sacrificial rite of mantra— whether for another or for oneself—
in that sacrifice of Śiva which consists of the performance of mantras whose essence is the potency of the supreme power characterized by the nature of reflecting (*manana*) and protecting (*trāṇa*),
as long as those rites such as worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), and so forth [have not been completed]...

One who knows the reality of the supreme Maheśvara as one's own self, and for that very reason knows the mantras whose essence is great potency (*mahāvīrya*) consisting of its creative vibration (*sphurattā*), being an *ācārya* in the Śaiva scripture— how could such a person cause [others] to act, how could they perform the ritual acts of mantra, and how could they employ them for another?
Regarding the phrase "or even for himself," the meaning here is this: he is not capable of accomplishing even anything for himself, much less for another.

Now, one might object: "Since initiation (*dīkṣā*) will be accomplished through the majesty of mantras, mandalas, and so forth, what is the use of the teacher’s knowledge of reality? [To this we reply:

[The objection holds] only for one whose exertion consists merely in drawing a colored mandala, performing mantra-depositions (*mantranyāsa*), reciting those mantras, and scattering sesame seeds and clarified butter.
The Great Lord dispels the delusion of living beings;
as long as the mantras are not stainless, how can there be accomplishment? (16.44)
If he becomes stainless, then the mantras residing within him become perfectly stainless;
being born from him and equal to him, they shall bestow all accomplishments.
If the teacher is stainless—

possessing immersion in the utterly pure and spontaneous bliss of consciousness that arises when the impurities of the body, the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth have been stilled— then even the mantras emerging from him, by virtue of being the essence of his power and vitality, are likewise [efficacious].
Those who are equal to him become stainless and bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*). As it is stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda*:
"Mantras are indeed instruments for the accomplishment of the work of bound souls (*paśu*);
in that regard, the teacher is the cause, for he is traditionally remembered as being the very form of Śiva. (3.160)
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Spanda*, starting from "Having ascended that" (2.1) up to "therefore these possess the nature of Śiva" (2.2).
Thus far. || 45 ||
He clarifies the statement "they are equal to that" [with the following]: "The supreme emergence of mantras occurs through the appointment of Śiva and Śakti;
since mantras bestow fruits everywhere, they are therefore remembered as 'Śivas' (Auspicious Ones). (16.46)
Therefore, all [mantras] are equal to Śiva and are eternally bestowing grace.

The application of Śiva’s power consists in being reinforced by the bliss of supreme illumination; from that, the supreme emergence of the mantras occurs—mantras whose essence is the radiant manifestation of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier—and thus, everywhere.

They are bestowers of fruits. Since this is so, they—when thus recollected and contemplated in such a form—are of the singular nature of Śiva. Therefore, by virtue of such equality with Śiva, they constantly perform grace as their habitual disposition.
"These [initiations] bear fruit only for a teacher who knows the penetration of Śiva; being of the nature of Śiva themselves, they yield results.
This connects with the subject at hand: "And Śiva, in the form of the teacher, is traditionally held to be the giver of these fruits. || 16-47 ||

The word *rūpa* (form) indicates that one should not consider the relationship of controller and controlled (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-adhiṣṭheya*) to exist between Śiva and the Ācārya. As it is said in the *Śrī Svacchanda*: beginning with "I myself am present here within the maṇḍala," it continues, "I am directly established within my own body as the agent of the acts of grace."
Thus [ends the verse]. 47.
He causes this very point to take root in his heart through his own resolve:
"O Goddess, as long as there is no mantra-master who knows reality, nor a guru, nor even a practitioner, so long [the mantra] yields no fruit; I tell you this truth. (16.48)
The practitioner bestows the fruit upon himself; by the use of the word "also," the spiritual son (putraka) does so as well.
He confirms this by stating its opposite:
otherwise, an Ācārya who is joined with worldly enjoyment does not bestow the fruit;
for one whose attachment is nourished by a body rendered helpless by the intoxication of drinking, eating, and sexual passion is no different from a bound soul (paśu).
The meaning is "thus."
Since this is so,
therefore the best among those who know reality should always [act] in all ritual actions.
In the case of the eternal [deities] and so forth. || 49 ||
Moreover,
what is gained by that [initiation] for a person who has been initiated...
he [is this].
Even a killer of a Brahmin shall become Śiva.
[The text] indicates its great power:
in whatever place one who performs this rite in such a manner may reside... || 16-50 ||
By whatever means of ritual service, by whatever distinction of state, or by the general, the particular, or the Kaulika method, O lady of good vows. (51)

He accomplishes each of those things swiftly, just as the Lord Sadāśiva does; thus, by means of the knowledge of mantras arising from the immersion (*āveśa*) into Śiva, he who performs the *śāmbhava* rite— that is,

who effects the application through sacrifice— does so according to the distinction of internal states (*bhāva*), that is, in accordance with the fitness for worshipping each respective deity to be propitiated.
By whatever conventional practice— whether dualistic, non-dualistic, or a mixture of both— he employs, he immediately accomplishes each respective desired goal, just like Lord Sadāśiva.
And for one who knows reality, there is no restrictive rule regarding the measurements of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or the mandala; thus he says:
"Whether it be square or circular, or even exceeding one cubit in size. (16.52)
Everything is accomplished by the will of the Teacher because of his knowledge of pervasion;
the Teacher’s very knowledge of pervasion is the means for achieving all success.
He demonstrates the pervasion even slightly through the meditation on the pervasion of Kuṇḍalī in the form of the power of action (kriyāśakti). || 16-53 ||
Having realized that the *kuṇḍa* is all-pervasive, the Guru indeed becomes omniscient.

By means of the pervasion of the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature consists of his own power of action (*nijakriyāśakti*), the spiritual teacher (*daiśika*), possessing immersion in Śiva, becomes the bestower of enjoyment and liberation through initiation and other rites, once he has realized the all-pervasiveness of the *kuṇḍa*.
The knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti) alone is the means to the fruit; thus he instructs through both negative and positive concomitance:
as long as one does not find the pervasion of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), so too [one does not find it] of the self (ātman).

As long as he plays like a child with the victim to be accomplished, with the sacrificial animal, and with the fetters of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), how can there be any purposeful action on his part? (16.55)
Furthermore, he who knows the Self to be of the nature of Śiva and Śakti is the bestower of all fruits, the most excellent; he is the agent, the all-knowing Śiva. (16.56)

In that regard, it has been stated that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) consists of the nature of the upward-coiling power (*ūrdhvakuṇḍalinīśakti*); of the self (*ātman*), it consists of its inherence in Paraśiva; and of the object to be accomplished—the mantra to be propitiated—it consists of the essence of the vigor of the manifestation of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*). As for the bound soul (*paśu*), however...

According to the principle stated in *Svacchandatantra* 3.13, "of that which has arisen from the mass of sounds," the nature of Śiva who has assumed limitation consists of the states of the individual soul (*āṇava*),
māyic, and karmic [impurities], such as the sense of incompleteness, the manifestation of objects as distinct [from the self], and [the experience of] auspicious and inauspicious [results].

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the nature of the contraction and intensification of the powers of will, knowledge, and action belonging to the Supreme Lord, which [corresponds to] the *saṃskāras* and the forms of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
As it has been said: "The loss of sovereignty for consciousness, and the lack of consciousness for sovereignty."
"This impurity is twofold, consisting of atoms, because it causes the loss of one's own true nature. (3-2-4).
Furthermore: "Right here, the manifestation of differentiated objects of knowledge is called *māyā*, which bestows birth and worldly experience."
"But the karmic [bond] exists when there is no awareness in the agent...
Thus, regarding the states that constitute the body of the Lord, his knowledge and action—
And in the *Pratyabhijñā*: "In the third [state], which is Māyā, those very same [qualities] are the sattva, rajas, and tamas of the bound soul. And in the *Spanda*:
"Of one who is incapable due to innate impurity... (1.9).

And so forth. Even for the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*)—known as phoneme (*varṇa*), mantra, word (*pada*), part (*kalā*), principle (*tattva*), and world (*bhuvana*)—there exists the reality of the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which consists of the manifestation of the signifier and the signified existing in the forms of the supreme, subtle, and gross. Furthermore, within that [reality], the phonemes contemplate the universe non-dually.

Mantras exist through both difference and non-difference; words exist through difference. Each preceding path exists as the pervader within each subsequent one, and each subsequent path exists as the pervaded and is included within each preceding one; thus, everything exists everywhere. Therefore:
The purification of the five other paths within the single path is taught in various scriptures.
Thus, in the *Śrī-svacchanda*: "The pervasion of the worlds within the principles (tattvas), beginning from Ananta and ending with Śiva..."
And they are pervasive, consisting of thirty-six mantra-syllables and words.
"All [principles] are included within the *tattvas* by virtue of the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
those indeed are remembered as being included within the *kalās*, such as *nivṛtti* and the rest.
(4.95)—thus it has been stated. And this has been determined by us in the *Uddyota* on that [work]. The same applies to the *maṇḍalas* and so forth.
The pervasion (*vyāpti*) which culminates in the essence of non-difference from the Supreme Lord has been demonstrated in detail in that very [work]. For this very reason:
"I myself am here, abiding within the mandala... and so forth.

Such [teachings] have been extensively taught by the God of gods in the *Śrī-Svacchanda* and other scriptures; enough said. "The task" (*kārya*) refers to enjoyment (*bhoga*), liberation (*mokṣa*), and so forth. But he who, primarily regarding himself as the "I," brings all things—mantras and the rest—unified within that "I" to the state of Śiva, [realizing them] as the very form of Śiva, whose essence is pure light...

Due to such sovereignty of His own nature, He perceives that which flashes forth as differentiated—like a city in a mirror—as being of the very form of His power; thus, He is Śiva, whose nature is non-dual omniscience and omnipotence, the supreme bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. And it was said previously:
"In beings, whether residing in oneself or others," and so forth (8.18).
Also, in the venerable *Triśirobhairava*:
"The individual soul (*jīva*) is the power (*śakti*) of Śiva himself; though she is present everywhere..."
Established upon the cognition of one's own true nature, she is auspicious through the unfolding of knowledge.

The fire, consisting of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), pervades the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) which consists of the previously mentioned power of action (kriyāśakti), according to the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader.
It must be understood by the teacher.
And such a teacher as this is the knower, the creator of all, the giver of liberation, and the guru who bestows the fruit. || 16-57 ||
The Knower is the one who knows reality; the All-doer is the self whose nature is the expansion of supreme power; he is the bestower of fruits and the giver of spiritual accomplishments. || 57 ||
Furthermore,
that teacher who performs the sacrifice transcending the six paths has become a boat in the ocean of *māyā*; he is Śiva, the protector of all.

Paramaśiva is the mass of consciousness and bliss who transcends the six paths; by the etymological derivation that "he is worshipped," he is the sacrifice (*yāga*) and the object of worship (*yājya*).
The teacher (*ācārya*) who is a guide (*deśika*) should perform sacrifice to him—he who, like a boat in the ocean of *māyā*, effects the salvation of all and is the very form of Śiva. (58)
But he who, without knowing the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*), performs a sacrifice situated within the course of time without reflection,
is not capable of liberating either himself or the Supreme Self. (16.59)

The sacrifice (*yāga*) consists of forms such as worship (*pūjā*) and fire-oblation (*homa*). Thinking that everything pertaining to the path—including the object of sacrifice, the act of sacrificing, the locus of sacrifice, and the sacrificer—is composed of duality (*bhedamaya*), he acts out of a lack of inquiry and a failure to discern reality (*tattva-avimarśa*).
The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or [he thinks] himself alone" is used to strengthen the subsequent position. (59)
And this [limited subject] does not attain perfection at all, nor is he capable of performing any action;
on the contrary, by virtue of being a limited cognizer who identifies the body and so forth as the self, he remains bound.
By that very same sixfold path, however, bondage is known as impurity (mala).
"By that very [nature]" means by the state of Paramaśiva, which has not been fully realized.
And for one in such a state,
the illusory (māyīya), individual (āṇava), and karmic [impurities] spread as the cause of bondage;
on the contrary, they spread— that is, they specifically flow forth and expand.
Therefore, neither this [disciple] nor the animal is capable of liberation while remaining there; indeed, the Guru alone is capable of it.
Remaining there, he is situated in the middle of the path; he is called "the teacher" (guru) merely by name, or else he is a burden because he consists of the body and so forth. || 61 ||
And this is logical:
the fetters situated within the path sprout from the eternal self for one who perceives a state of difference due to their being situated within the path.
Therefore, by means of the reasoning of the instruction already described, who would not be liberated from bondage after knowing the Self as that which transcends it? || 16-62 ||
Who would not be the bestower of liberation? Who does not attain accomplishment? Which mantrin would not be a giver? And who, O beloved, would not be capable in his task? (16.63)

That which has transcended the past time is of the singular nature of Paramaśiva; it is called the "Giver" because it bestows accomplishments (*siddhi*) upon practitioners, and it is called the "Effect" in such matters as protection and nourishment.

And therefore, having known that Rudra who is supreme and all-pervasive, one should become absorbed in Him. "He" (yaḥ) refers to the extraordinary one; "supreme" (paraḥ) means unsurpassed; and he is "Rudra" because he causes the dissolution (*drāvaṇa*) of all suffering (*ruj*). "Having known" (jñātvā)—this is the meaning.
Having recognized [it] as being one's own essential nature.
But that teacher of the path who knows the measures of honor and dishonor, as well as the means of valid cognition and so forth, yet does not know reality, [is truly ignorant]. (16.64)
He may be as skillful as an artisan, capable of producing various forms;
yet he does not bestow liberation, nor does he grant the fruit of spiritual accomplishment.

The measurement of the circumference and the height and breadth is *māna*, *unmāna*, and *pramāṇa*; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sequential order from one principle (*tattva*) to another is implied. "The creator of diverse forms" means that [the Lord] merely fashions various configurations, but is not a knower of pervasion (*vyāpti*). || 65 ||

Since ignorant gurus are thus to be abandoned, therefore all those who know reality should be regarded as equal to Śiva— by implication, because they abide in the meditative absorption (samādhi) of Śiva.
Although there are three types of teachers— namely, the practitioner of action (karmī), the yogi, and likewise the man of knowledge (jñānī)— so it is traditionally taught.
In various treatises on that subject.
Nevertheless,
O Goddess of gods, both ritual action and yoga have their root in knowledge and bestow their fruits;
indeed, no separate distinction is seen between knowledge, yoga, and ritual action.

Since action and yoga—which consists of its specific fruits—are essentially the expansion of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), there is no separate distinction from knowledge; rather, they appear as if distinct only by being reflected within the mirror of knowledge. || 67 ||
Since this is so,
therefore the preeminent teacher must be all-knowing; that is,
he alone who possesses knowledge— meaning he who is constantly endowed with the excellent knowledge consisting of immersion into the consciousness of another— is [the true teacher].
Among the teachers for whom karma-yoga and the like are primary, he is the preeminent teacher; he alone is the bestower of all things. As it is said in the venerable Kāmikā:
"The Guru is declared to have knowledge as his root, and he is the one who sets in motion the seven sacrificial sessions."
Thus it is said; and in the Śrīsiddhāmata as well: "But through knowledge, one becomes a great Siddha, a lord of yogins in this world."
For it is precisely because he possesses knowledge that he has Śiva as his refuge; yet, while abiding in Śiva, he is impelled by the power of Śiva. || 16-68 ||
He creates the entire universe because he is traditionally remembered as being of the nature of Śiva.

Since Śiva is his support—serving as the foundational wall upon which he relies—he is impelled by Śiva’s power and set in motion toward activities such as bestowing grace; and yet, even so, he remains in a state of union with Śiva.
According to the principle stated [in the *Vijñānabhairava*], "by means of vigilance" (vi.

bhai. 106), one who stands in Śiva—the abode of supreme consciousness—by relying upon his power (*śakti*), is possessed of that immersion; and thus, being of the very nature of Śiva, he creates the universe, which consists of the fivefold objects beginning with sound, during the states of its closing and opening.
Through its nature of dissolving the solidification of the essence of consciousness, it manifests [the world] both as differentiated and as non-differentiated.
For he is one who is proficient in the union of will, knowledge, and action, as well as in Śiva and Śakti.

The union (*yoga*) of Śiva and Śakti—whose nature is light (*prakāśa*) and bliss (*ānanda*)—is their *vīrya* (potency) through the powers of will, knowledge, and action; one who is proficient therein consists of that very immersion (*samāveśa*). 69.
Indeed, he who performs such a rite of initiation by the will of Śiva, having understood the established state of the paths (adhvan) according to the previously mentioned perspective—
that is, through the pervasive extension of the expansion of the power of action (kriyā-śakti)— [performs it] for the sake of the path that is to be pervaded.
For one who acts through the will belonging to his own self, which is of the nature of Śiva,
his inconceivable power of mantra— arising from the mouth of the Supreme Lord— is indeed [his own]. (16.70)
Whatever the Knower accomplishes by taking refuge in the power of Śiva,
that is the supreme power, the mouth of the Supreme Lord.
And this inconceivable power of mantra is accomplished for him through the influence of Śiva’s power. || 16.71 ||
Indeed, for him, the mantras are directly effective and produce immediate results.
The word "seen" (dṛṣṭa) clarifies the statement regarding rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others against poisons, spirits, planets, and so forth. || 72 ||
In an instant, he performs everything—
peaceful rites and so forth, as well as those concerning poisons and the like, such as the act of neutralizing poison; this is how it should be construed.
Now, one might object: "If he possesses the capacity for this [creation], then why was it said that it occurs 'by the power of Śiva’s energy'?
Anticipating this doubt, he states that Śiva alone is the root cause in all cases:
"Śiva is the supreme cause."
For it is he alone, when entered by various levels [of being], who performs those respective actions. As it is said in the venerable *Śrīkaṇṭhī*:
"Everything proceeds from the Lord; likewise, everything ceases in the Lord."
And therefore, he who is endowed with the power of the yoga of knowledge awakens him. || 16-73 ||
O Dear One, by the power of the mantra’s potency, he should initiate those who are to be initiated;
he awakens their own inner nature hidden within,
and through the state of being a mass of consciousness that emerges from and submerges into the body and other such things, he brings it to direct realization.

Endowed with and joined to the growth of the power of both knowledge and yoga, and therefore, by virtue of the majesty of the essence of his vigor, he certainly initiates those who are to be initiated.
He clarifies this very point through the method of explaining the etymology of *dīkṣā*:
"It leads to the destruction of the fetters (*pāśa*) and bestows the supreme state. (16.74)
By the power of Śiva’s energy, he is capable of traveling a *yojana* within a *yojana*;
for, by the power of Śiva’s energy as proclaimed,
he abides in the sequence of the *yojanikā* (unification) taught in the *Śrī-svacchanda* and other scriptures.
Since he is capable of bringing about the unification of the disciple with the supreme and non-supreme levels,
it is rightly said that he ought to perform initiation itself, which consists of the destruction of bonds and the bestowing of the supreme state that is the nature of Śiva.
"This very one has power over all the activities of the channels," he says;
"for him alone is the causal condition observed, not for anyone else. (16.75)
In the Gāruḍa, the Mātṛtantra, in the Left (Vāma) current,
the Right (Dakṣiṇa), the Eldest (Jyeṣṭha), and in the Caṇḍāsidhārā, ritual action yields manifest results.
Since for him there arises here itself a visible proof— an immediate realization consisting of immersion into Śiva—

therefore, [this applies] to the Gāruḍa in the East, to the Mātṛtantra and others in the West, to the Jayā system in the Left, to the Bhairava scriptures in the Right, and to the Caṇḍāsidhārā and others in the Upper [direction], as well as in the Jyeṣṭha.

In secret rites such as those performed for the families of the deceased and so forth, its activity—consisting of the pacification of poisons, the attainment of fortune, and various forms of grace—is directly fruit-bearing; the meaning is that it provides immediate conviction. || 76 ||
For this belongs to this person who is utterly defiled, pierced by Māyā,
attached to enjoyment through his karma, and possessed of longing. (77)
This initiation, called *kriyā* and consisting of *jñāna*, bestows liberation.
It does so by means of the two impurities—those pertaining to *māyā* and those pertaining to *karman*—which have been described as extreme defilement caused by *māyā* and *karman*.
Likewise...

This is made explicit by the statement from the perspective of the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*: "But here, desire is the impurity" (*Sva* 4.105), which describes one who is possessed of desire due to the *āṇava-mala*.
The term "called action" (*kriyākhyā*) means that its name is "action" (*kriyā*) in reality.
Considering that [the Goddess] is of the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpiṇī*), the teacher, though knowing both [knowledge and action], must abide in knowledge; as it is said elsewhere:
"There is no knowledge devoid of action, nor is there action devoid of knowledge."
The teacher, perfected through ritual action and knowledge, is the destroyer of the bonds of the bound souls.
Thus [it is said].
He states that even the activity of the *hotṛ* and other officiating priests has an internal power consisting of great discernment, which takes the form of vital breath:
"But the supreme power is *unmanā*, the *avadhūtikā* whose nature is knowledge. (16.78)

That is designated as action (*kriyā*), yet action existing in the midst of time is not [true] action. "Supreme" (*parā*) means whose nature is uninterrupted radiance; "consisting of knowledge" (*jñānarūpā*) refers to that which is called "therefore, she is supreme knowledge" (4.395).

Thus it is stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda*: "Avadhūtikā" means that in her, shaking (*dhūta*)—that is, trembling—is struck away (*avahata*); the meaning is that she is eternally risen. She is Action (*kriyā*). As it is said in the *Śrī-pratyabhijñā*:
"In this way, through the nature of the world consisting of the appearances of jars, cloths, and so forth..."
"For one who wishes to remain [in this state], it is precisely this desire that constitutes the cause, the agency, and the action" (2-4-21).
Thus,

[the world] is devoid of the permeation of the power of action consisting of such great reflective awareness (*mahāvimarśa*) as "being situated within the middle of the path," and is therefore essence-less.
The self consists of the *jāhoma* sacrifice and so forth.

Just as the act of worship has as its essence the pervasion of the aforementioned power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), so too both knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga consist of that same pervasion; thus he says:
"The power of yoga and the power of knowledge are celebrated in all scriptures. (16.79)
That power of the Supreme Lord Śiva is the remover of misfortune.
As it has been said in the venerable Gamaśāstra:
"Yoga is not something else, nor is ritual action something else; rather, it is that intellect which is ascended upon the reality-principles."
"When the latent impressions of one's own mind are stilled, that is designated as 'action'.
Thus it is said.
And because she is connected with Śiva, for that very reason she brings about bondage and liberation for men; she is not independent by her own nature. (16.80)
Because power is dependent upon the essential nature of that which possesses power. || 80 ||
Following this very principle, Śiva is the bestower of all and auspicious;
as it is said in the *Vijñānabhairava*:
"Since the non-difference between power and the possessor of power is firmly established..."
Therefore, because it possesses those attributes, the supreme power belongs to the Supreme Self.
(18) Thus.

Not only are knowledge, yoga, and action composed of Śiva and Śakti by virtue of resting upon their non-duality, but so too are the lineage of gurus beginning with Śiva, as well as the many millions of Rudras. (16.81)
That lineage of gurus, which exists through tradition solely by means of the instruction of a reliable authority (āpta),
beginning with Śiva— the Lord Anāśrita—
and consisting of [successors] such as Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Ananta, and Śrīkaṇṭha.

Likewise, there are many millions of Rudras and many millions of mantras presided over by the Infinite; all of these belong to the authoritative Supreme Śiva. That which is the instruction—the teaching concerning one’s own self—by means of what yoga or action [is it attained]?
Or, being correctly established in one's own self...

[O Goddess,] he says that the teaching of the authoritative teacher (āptopadeśa) consists precisely in the unfolding of the supreme power; for this reason, the knowledge of Śiva is always remembered as the authoritative scripture (āptāgama). || 16-82 ||

The knowledge of Śiva is the immersion into the power (śakti) of Rudra. The word "yataḥ" (from which) indicates the cause. Therefore, the meaning of the preceding verse is indeed established by this. || 82 ||
Not only is the lineage of gurus beginning with Śiva composed of Śiva and Śakti, but everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is endowed with Śiva and Śakti.
It is perfectly united with Śiva-Śakti and consists of non-duality with them. As it is stated in the Śivasūtras:
"The universe is the accumulation of His own powers" (3.30).
Summing this up, he clarifies:
"In this way, the entire world, both stationary and moving, consists of power. (16.83)
The distinction is as follows: everything from the Unmanifest (Anāśrita) down to the Earth consists solely of Śiva and Śakti;
the class of Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and so forth, consists of the unfolding (unmiṣat) Śiva-Śakti;
whereas [the levels] from Vijñānākala down to the immobile beings consist of the closing (nimiṣat) Śiva-Śakti. || 83 ||
Therefore, one who possesses power performs all actions; there is no doubt in this matter.
The class of mantra-masters and others, being permeated by the power of Śiva, are capable of accomplishing their respective tasks.
But others,
being devoid of power, do not achieve success even through hundreds of millions of sacrifices.
Through thousands of crores of recitations and hundreds of thousands of extensive fire-offerings,
the mantra-adepts [attain their goal].
Since this is so, therefore one should practice the knowledge of Śiva with every effort. || 16-85 ||
At that time, all actions indeed succeed; otherwise, they certainly do not.
The particle *eva* should be construed immediately after the word *na*.
And when he, having practiced the knowledge of Śiva, performs rites such as those for pacification, then he is a Guru. || 16-86 ||
Furthermore,
he alone is authorized for sacrifice, oblation, recitation, as well as for the sequence of painting [deities].
Thus,
having introduced the topic with "I shall proclaim the sacrifice" (16.26), [the text describes] the protection of the sacrificial house.

Having described the true nature of the Guru— who possesses the realization of pervasion characterized by immersion in the power of Rudra— and who is the essence of the potency of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) for the entire universe from the mantras down to the immobile beings, [the text now addresses] that which serves as the locus for the aforementioned worship of the Lord.
If calamities have arisen, one should undertake the sacrifice previously described. || 16-87 ||

One should begin the construction of the mandala—characterized by the previously described form and the division of the four gates and so forth—for the purpose of worshipping the Blessed One. || 87 ||
And there,
having reflected upon the goal to be accomplished, that substance was prepared with the necessary equipment—
having reflected with the intention of attaining the highest good, [it was prepared] by means of the collection of materials such as saffron, sandalwood, and incense.
For whatever goal one undertakes, a sacrifice consisting of the worship, fire-oblation, and other rites of the glorious Amṛteśa is performed.
...peace arises for him. || 16-88 ||
Calamities perish. || 88 ||
Furthermore,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds, milk, ghee, and white sugar, while reciting the name of [the person] for whom it is intended...
That person to be accomplished shall attain great peace. || 16-89 ||
With a composed mind, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) using fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) smeared with milk,

while reciting the name of [the person]... Between the worship and the fire sacrifice, one should satisfy the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*) by means of the fire sacrifice, using the name of that [person].
...for him there will certainly be peace. || 16-90 ||
If one should offer *sumana* flowers mixed with clarified butter while reciting someone's name, peace shall swiftly come to that person; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. || 91 ||
The practitioner who desires prosperity, having offered *śrīphala* fruits, attains abundant fortune.
Through the oblation of ghee and guggulu, eternal nourishment is attained. || 16-92 ||
[The attainment] of the goal is [effected] by means of what is performed by the teacher. || 92 ||
If one performs the recitation of the name of the person to be accomplished, having encased it within the *mṛtyujit* mantra,
then death shall not afflict either oneself or another.
The meaning is: of the object to be accomplished, or of oneself or another who is to be protected by means of the mantra. || 93 ||
Then, one should place [the mantra] within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus;
with the name constricted by the letters of the target (sādhya), it shall become the "Conqueror of Death" (mṛtyujit) above that.
One should place the limbs upon the petals according to the divisions starting with the southeast;
one should draw that lotus outside, complete with two sets of eight petals.
Then, one should fill [the lotus] starting from the east with sixteen digits (kalās);
outside of that, one should place a lotus endowed with thirty-two petals.

It should be written that [the letters] are to be placed starting from the east in the sequence from *ka* to *ma*, ending with *īśa* (the northeast). The limbs (*aṅga*), as described in the second chapter, are to be placed in the directions of Agni (southeast), Īśa (northeast), Rakṣas (southwest), and Marut (northwest); these are the four beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*).

The division is as follows: the *astra* (weapon-mantra) is in the four directions beginning with the east, the *locana* (eye-mantra) is on the pericarp (*karṇikā*) in front of the Lord, and [the rest] is in that lotus;
"that lotus" (*tatkamalam*) is a compound meaning "the lotus of that [Lord]. "At the end, [starting] from Īśa" means ending at the four petals situated in the direction of Īśa (the northeast).
And all these letters, obstructed by the letters of the goal (sādhya), reside within the three wheels.
In the three wheels, that is, in the three clusters of petals, the obstruction of the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished is performed as before.

And from the midst of all these petals and syllables, one should indeed restrain the name of the person to be accomplished; "restraint" (rodhana) means enclosing the syllable of the person to be accomplished.

Regarding the specific detail of the name situated within the enclosure of the mantra in the pericarp, he says: "One should place the name, situated in the middle of the *jīva*, within the pericarp. (16.98)
The *jīva* is the letter *sa*; its name is formed by that [letter] at its end. || 98 ||
One should conceive the individual soul (jīva) as being within the vital breath (prāṇa);
the letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
That [vowel] likewise, being such...

the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated between the end of the letters (*varṇa*), standing at the end of the letter *kṣa*; and in that regard, there is the phrase "situated between *ka* and *ṣa*" from another source.
The prescribed rule must be followed.
Having thus drawn a lotus containing these two lotuses within it,
one should then cause a gentle and perfectly complete mandala to be made on its exterior.
One should place the letter ṭha.
Outside of that, however, one should construct the city of Indra, fortified by the thunderbolt-wielder’s vajra.
Having thus inscribed this wheel upon a birch-bark leaf, O fair-faced one.
On a surface that is perfectly clean, free of blemishes, and smooth, [one should draw] with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron mixed with sandalwood juice.
Thereafter, the preceptor, having honored this [image] and made it grey with powdered camphor, should wrap it with a new white cotton thread.
Having placed this [substance] in the midst of honey within an earthen vessel mixed with fragrant ghee, and having set it down, one should worship it with white flowers. || 16.102 ||
Having fumigated with fragrant incense, one should worship with milk-rice mixed with ghee, various kinds of edible foods, and delicious offerings prepared in great abundance.
By means of the accumulated requisites. || 103 ||
And this is its arrangement:
one should then worship eight jars here on the outside, starting from the east, endowed with the fragrance of white sandalwood, camphor, and excellent incense. (16.104)
[One should prepare] vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or clay—exceedingly beautiful, filled with water containing jewels and endowed with all medicinal herbs. (16.105)

Having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) in sequence in their midst— [the pillars] which have roots that are not [exposed], which are very beautiful, praiseworthy, and endowed with auspicious marks.
Those whose root is not time nor the lower station; having fully worshipped them with the sounds of the *praṇava*, names, and *namaḥ* [mantras]. 106.
The command of Śiva must be given to them: "Protect the supreme sādhya.
By saying "supreme," he instructs that the procedure applicable here is not to be employed in the case of one who is unsurpassed (anuttama).
Then, one should worship at dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight.
For whomever this is performed by name, that person, when seven nights have passed, becomes a conqueror of death;
he emerges from all diseases and is freed from all defects. || 16-108 ||
One shall be liberated from all diseases and from all fevers, without a doubt; one shall be completely freed from all suffering and rid of all calamities.
And that man shall remain further, like a snake that has cast off its skin; "afflictions" refers to abdominal diseases and the like, while "diseases" refers to boils and the like.
Furthermore, O Goddess, in the worship of this wheel, if the practitioner is single-minded and devoted to that alone; || 16-110 ||
Devoted to recitation and burnt offerings, peaceful, he dwells in that place;
he is possessed of being, endowed with vigor, and joined with compassion and courtesy.

When seven nights have passed, one should forcibly bring back even those who are dead; that is, one should restore them to life. This refers to a practitioner (*sādhaka*) endowed with power who knows the potency of mantras, or a master (*ācārya*) accomplished in mantra.
And such a person [is honored] with cows, land, gold, garments, and so forth, as well as with armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments. || 16-112 ||
He should be worshipped with supreme devotion, especially through rites for peace and nourishment;
for he is indeed Śiva himself, consisting of mantra, and is the manifest preceptor.

O auspicious one, by the mere act of worshipping him, all [deities] become unfailingly bestowers of the fruits of accomplishment (*siddhi*), because— according to the reasoning previously stated— he consists of mantra and is thus permeated by the penetration of Śiva (*śivāveśa*). "All" refers to those worshipped within the *cakra*.
The mantras.

And in this regard, the doubt easily accessible to an illusory subject (māyā-pramātṛ) must be abandoned; thus he says by means of positive and negative concomitances: "My word is true, not false. (16.114)
But if the worship of the Guru is not performed, then this occurs; thus he says:
"Otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment and what has been done will indeed be useless;
even for the disciple who is to be perfected, the ritual act will destroy his stability. (16.115)
Let alone the initiates, the spiritual sons, and the practitioners; even for the master, when the task is to be accomplished,
the Rākṣasī who destroys the stability of the vision arises— meaning, due to the failure to worship the Guru—
since this is so.
Therefore, with every effort, the knower of mantras should worship the guru;
for in this way, his mantras become worshipped and bestow the fruit of all accomplishments. || 16-116 ||
The worship of a guru who knows reality accomplishes one's desired goal; may there be auspiciousness. || 116 ||
I take refuge in that eye of Śiva, through immersion in which the Guru, the Mantra, and others perform even the most difficult of actions with great ease.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Netrodyota, the illumination of the Netra-tantra, composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 16.
The Seventeenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Eyes" By means of the abundant nectar of its own light, which flashes forth with various and wondrous colors,
Victorious is the glorious Eye of the Lord, the conqueror of death and the dispeller of fear.
Out of compassion, in order to provide protection even for those within the circle,
the Blessed One said: "Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the King of Wheels, which possesses great power."

The word *atha* (now) indicates that this follows immediately after the subject matter (*prameya*) stated in the preceding section. The word *ataḥ* (hence) means: because there are many people who are to be favored, with the intention that favor may somehow be bestowed upon some of them.
In that regard,
as before, the wise one should imagine the name in the middle, ending with the word *jīva*.
Then, having placed the end of the *prāṇa* within the end of the *varṇa*,
one should place the final [syllable] outside of that, and the middle [syllable] outside of that.
First, one should then place the external [deities] upon the pericarp;
the vowels are to be worshipped on the filaments, and the limbs (aṅgas) on the petals as before. || 17-3 ||
Having drawn a vase on the outside situated in the center of both lotuses,
one who is devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, and worship should perform the worship according to the previously prescribed rule.
It accomplishes what is intended in no time at all; there is no doubt about this.

As before, the name ending in the accusative case is enclosed by the syllables of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and written above the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*), as previously described.

Because it will be stated later, "endowed with the protective syllables" (17.11), the word "protective" (*rakṣā*) is appropriate here; having placed [the letter] *kṣa*— which is internal to the *jīva* (the letter *sa*) and internal to the *prāṇa* (the letter *ha*)— at the end of the letters.

One should place [the seed-syllable] within. Then, having written the final letter *kṣa* outside of that, the middle letter *ha* outside of that, and the first letter *sa* outside of that, one should assign this to the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
On the filaments (*kesara*), one should place the vowels in order starting from the east, and on the petals, the limbs (*aṅga*) beginning with the Heart.

"As before" means in the sequence beginning with the southeast (Āgneya) and so forth. One should draw a jar on the exterior of such a lotus, having placed it in the middle of the lotus extending from top to bottom;
one who is devoted to the worship, recitation, and fire-oblation of the root mantra along with its limbs quickly accomplishes their desired goal. And here:
The meaning of the words is as previously stated: the mantra for worship and recitation ends with the word *namaḥ*, whereas for the fire-oblation (*homa*), it ends with *svāhā*.
Furthermore, this wheel bestows all peace and grants prosperity and good fortune.
It bestows longevity and vigor, destroys the disease of fever,
and brings victory to kings who are terrified by foreign kingdoms.
This protection, which destroys all calamities, must indeed be performed for the wives of kings, their sons, and for Brahmins and others in every respect.
This is clear. || 7 ||
O beloved, one should write the name in a single line with each syllable separated by an interval;
at the beginning and the end, one should place the root mantra joined with the *vauṣaṭ* exclamation.
One should worship as before with an abundant sacrifice of white and auspicious offerings;
at that very moment, one is liberated from diseases, even if already seized by death.

Having written the name such as Devadatta with the root mantra placed between each letter, and having applied the root mantra joined with the *vauṣaṭ* suffix at the beginning and end in both direct and reverse order, [one who worships] with white flowers and other offerings...
"Bhūriyāga" means that one should worship as before; thus, with single-minded concentration, one should propitiate [the deity] through worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth. || 9 ||
One should write the mantra joined with the *vauṣaṭ* syllable upon eight white directions on a beautiful birch-bark surface; in the center, however, the name is written as before.
Combined with the protective syllables, outside of that is a lunar disc;
it contains the final letter of the mantra as nectar, abiding in sixteen digits.
Having filled the maṇḍala with those [offerings], one should place the water-pot (kalaśa) on the outside;
outside of that, however, are the Moon and the Sun situated in front of Indra’s city.

One should write with *rocanā* and saffron, or with milk and sugar, in the directions— which consist of the petals of a lotus— and in the center— which is the pericarp— just as before, namely, as in the first application, encased within the syllables of the target; and on the outside, at the edge of the pericarp.
The lunar disc is the syllable *ṭha*; and the final letter of the mantra is the syllable *sa*.

"Nectar" (*amṛta*) refers to that which is pervaded by the supreme nectar previously mentioned and to be mentioned hereafter. It is situated within, and permeated by, the sixteen digits (*kalās*), beginning with *a* and ending with the visarga; it is conjoined with those digits through their connection with the syllable *sa*.

"Mandala" refers to the lunar *ṭha* syllable; the meaning is that one should draw this lotus within the interior of the jar. Outside the jar, one should place the moon and sun, represented by *ṭha* and *ḍa*, in the city of Indra—that is, in the square—arranged with the configuration of the vajra-mark. This is for the rite of pacification (*śānti*).
She who destroys previous calamities; furthermore, one should meditate upon a jar above her very head, filled with milk and flowing with nectar—this is nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite as before, he remains established in tranquility. || 17-13 ||
