The meaning is that the preceptor, established in the rite of pacification (śāntikarma), should remain vigilant. || 13 ||
And this protection for kings has indeed been proclaimed as the destroyer of all calamities;
however, while this is being performed, there is this specific distinction:
According to the ritual for the protection of kings, one should offer oblations mixed with milk.
If one offers sesame seeds mixed with white sugar, fragrant and blended with ghee,
into a fire fueled by wood from milk-exuding trees, that person shall obtain peace.
"By means of the method for protecting the king" refers to that purpose which exists as a motive present in the mind. "He" refers to the king;
furthermore, when a man is seized by time and has fallen under the power of death.
Having seen him as previously described, the sacrifice is performed in the mandala as it has been taught.
It is performed, being fully equipped with the collection of ritual substances, for the destruction of death;

this is because it belongs to this very one whose belly is the *kalaśa*, in whom the Lord of Mantras has been installed according to the stated procedure, and who is thus named the "Destroyer of Death."
And when this [mantra] is honored, one quickly crosses over death through the power of this mantra. || 17-17 ||
That very same [mantra] should be written on birch bark together with white sugar, milk, yellow pigment (rocanā), and saffron. || 17–18 ||
One should place [the vessel] smeared with honey inside a golden jar, well-concealed;
above that, a second, very beautiful [vessel] filled with milk.
Having meditated upon the flowing nectar, one should establish it for the sake of nourishment (*puṣṭi*).

"That very same" means that the wheel is indeed within the belly of the jar. By speaking thus, he indicates that this subject pertains specifically to the immediately preceding sacrifice. By stating "with milk," etc., [he refers] to the previously mentioned sacrifice.
It indicates that [the vessel] is to be prepared with rice flour. "Smeared with honey" means coated with beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*).
"Nectar" refers to that which flows in the form of milk itself, releasing it into the vessel situated below through the process of concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
The man for whose name this is performed becomes a conqueror of death through the practice of seven nights. || 17-20 ||
Likewise, his body, though wasted away, shall become full like the moon at the end of the fortnight;
he shall indeed not fall under the power of death—this is my truth, my word is not false. (17–21)
The name [of the target] should be enclosed by the syllables of the *sādhya*, accompanied by the words for protection;
one should worship the target in the center as before, and perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). || 17–22 ||

Having meditated on [the deity] by means of the name "Sādhya" as before, one performs the immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) upon the eight petals; as previously described, one effects nourishment (*āpyāyana*) by means of the King of Mantras ending with *vauṣaṭ*. || 22 ||

Having thus enveloped that which has become such with the Vāruṇa [element] by means of the Self, one should again envelop it on the outside with the remainder of the Kalās, which is complete. || 17-23 ||

One should encircle [the syllable] with the letter *ma*, which denotes the *ātman-puruṣa*; then with the letter *va* of Varuṇa; then with the letter *ṭa*, which remains as a partial unit (*kalāśeṣa*); and then with the letter *ṭha*, which is complete.
"With the water-pot" (*kalaśena*) is a corrupt reading. || 23 ||
Immediately thereafter,
outside of that [area] for Purandara, one should apply that maṇḍala within the vajra-maṇḍala, twice in each of the four directions of the field of vision.

"Square" refers to *purandara* (the city-shatterer), which is that mandala; "twice" means two times. Regarding "in the four directions," one should place a square upon the square in such a way that an eight-spoked arrangement results. And that eight-cornered mandala is situated within the center of the vajra-mandala.
Having fashioned a square mandala with a vajra, one should place [the deity] in its center. || 24 ||
And whoever this [rite] is performed for by name,
he is protected by Amṛteśa; by the use of the word "and" (ca), he is rendered immortal.
And for one who has such a goal to accomplish,
yoginīs, spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and assailants never anywhere cause him fear. (17.25)
He states another ritual application:
"One should write the name inside a jar, and that [jar] should be placed upon a lotus;
one should then draw a downward-facing lotus upon its back, as before. (17–26)
One should draw that situated upon the pericarp according to the method of facing downwards;
one should meditate on it as being completely full, with nectar flowing from every side.
One should visualize Amṛteśa entering through the aperture of the crown;
having entered the heart, he should fill all the channels.
One should write the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) upon the pericarp of the lotus inside the jar. "As before" means above the jar.

Having written that mantra of Amṛteśa located on the upward-facing pericarp with its face turned downward, one should meditate upon it as flowing with nectar in the manner of a downward-pointing drop (*bindu*). And that nectar—
One should meditate that [the mantra] of the one to be accomplished— contemplated by name and location— enters through the cranial aperture and fills all the channels (nāḍīs).
And of that...
At that very moment, nourishment arises even for a man whose body is emaciated.
Furthermore, he said:
one should write the mantra in a row, with each syllable placed in the center [of its respective position]. (17–29)
The name of the person to be accomplished should indeed be written... situated in the middle of the syllables, written between each individual mantra; its placement is outside [the mantras].
... one should write the conqueror of death in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
O Dear One, having drawn a lotus as before, one should perform the six-limbed rite as before.
Having joined [the ritual], one should worship according to one's capacity with extensive offerings as available;
by means of entirely white ritual services, this [rite] destroys all suffering. (17.31)
One becomes the foremost of mantra-holders; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having drawn a lotus, one should worship the Lord Mṛtyujit upon its petals as before, ending with *vauṣaṭ*.
Having also drawn another lotus outside of that, one should place the previously mentioned six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon its petals as before.

Having joined this wheel, one should worship it; "having drawn the lotus" is like the eye of a crow [applying to both]. By the statement "no deliberation is required here," he indicates that, as before, this results only for one who is free from doubt.
May there be auspiciousness!
We bow to the glorious Eye, which brings about the presence of Śaṅkara through the forms assumed during his play,
and which is the unimpeded protector of all.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Śrīnetratantroddyota*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 17.
The Eighteenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net.
The singular radiance of the Great Lord, whose nature is the complete enjoyment of liberation.
Victorious is that supreme, indescribable splendor of the eyes, which dispels all affliction.
In order to introduce another topic by way of restating what was previously said, the Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, you who are devoted to the welfare of all beings;
O Lord of the Suras, you are our protector and the bestower of grace upon all. (18.1)
"O Maheśāna, you have spoken of the pervasion of the mantras and the paths;
O Lord of the World, if you are pleased with me, O Master, please explain it to me. (18.2)

O Lord, the application of mantras for the purpose of ritual pinning and so forth has been indicated; however, it has not been fully explained by the God of gods as to how practitioners achieve success. || 18-3 ||
"Those employed by others—such as *kṛtyā*s, *khārkhoda*, and so forth—are destroyed.

The phrase beginning with "spoken" (*ukta*) is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. It was indicated [in the previous verse] by: "The pinning down (*kīlana*) of mantras, as well as their piercing (*bhedana*) and bewildering (*mohana*). (16.33)

Thus, in the sixteenth chapter: "By the God of Gods" means by you yourself. "In such a way" refers to the method of application, such as *kīlana* (piercing) and so forth, by which practitioners attain success, and by which the *kṛtyās*, *sākhrodakas*, and other spells employed by enemies are destroyed. For the destruction of enemies, there is the *vetālī-kṛtyā* entered into the corpse of a woman.

The connection is as follows: "Tell me about this matter"—the matter being the *yantra* known as Khārkhoda which effects death, eradication, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes images that perform those same functions.
Moreover, by the application of Pratyāṅgirā, one destroys many wicked beings. || 18-4 ||
O Mahādeva, tell me this without any doubt, however it may be.

The term *pratyaṅgirā* is a distinct word meaning: that knowledge (*vidyā*) which, directed against [an enemy], utters [curses] and contemplates the accomplishment of the fruit of base actions specifically for the sake of a base practitioner (*kṣudrasādhaka*).
By means of application; by means of practice.
To determine this, the Blessed Lord said: "Among all forms of discourse, the discourse on mantras is the highest here. (18.5)
Having understood this, O lady of excellent vows, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should apply the signs of the mantra (mantraliṅgāni).

Among all those who speak of mantras— such as those who deal with minerals, mines, and so forth— whoever is the most excellent among the practitioners of mantra, that [practitioner] is embraced and distinguished by the mantras.

Having understood those [rites] through the scriptures and having mastered them by means of the activities such as illumination (dīpana) and so forth, the mantra-practitioner who knows the reality of the tantras should employ them— that is, apply them— at the appropriate occasion.
He indicates that [the ritual consists of] illumination, awakening, striking, and consecration. || 18-6 ||
Purification, as well as the application of fuel, satiation, the state of protection, and nourishment is the ninth. (18.7)
Thus, whoever understands the ninefold mantra-discourse in its entirety understands the means for accomplishing the mantra-sādhana. || 18-8 ||
The kindling of the mantra is by means of the *praṇava* (oṃ); its awakening is by the word *namaḥ*; its striking is by the syllable *phaṭ*; its consecration is by the syllable *vauṣaṭ*;
its purification is by the word *svāhā*; and the placing of fuel is the application [of the mantra] for burning bonds, poisons, and the like that are to be consumed.

The encapsulation is performed with the syllable *huṃ*. As it is stated in the venerable *Ucchuṣma-tantra*: "O fortunate one, for the purpose of kindling, there is the joining of the *praṇava* at both ends; for awakening, there is the salutation (*namaḥ*), and likewise the *svāhā* in the stainless [rite]."
One should employ the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
one should employ it joined by *phaṭ* on both sides for the striking (*tāḍana*).
One should apply the *huṃ* syllable at both the beginning and the end to the fuel.
"Satisfying" (*tarpaṇa*) means bestowing strength; and that consists of enclosing each individual letter with the *lāṃ* syllable.
As it has been said:
"By means of the seed-syllable *lāṃ*, as well as by that which is separated by one [syllable],
the mantra becomes powerful..."

Thus [it is said]. The state of being protected (*gupti*) means guarding; and that occurs through ten thousand recitations (*ayuta-japa*) of [the mantra] encapsulated by the Lord of the Eyes (Netranātha).
As it has been stated:
"One should further recite that [mantra] ten thousand times encapsulated by Mṛtyujit."

"By reciting this according to the prescribed rule, the protection of the mantra is accomplished. Furthermore, *āpyāyana* (nourishment) is the bestowing of nourishment upon that which has regained its strength; and that is achieved by enclosing each syllable with the syllable *vām*.
As it has been said:
"By means of the syllable *vāṃ*, which is always joined with an interval of one [syllable],
the mantra shall become nourished..."

Thus: he who knows the mantra-discourse (mantravāda) in these nine ways knows that the mantras themselves are the means (sādhana), the causes of accomplishment (siddhi); he knows their practice (sādhana), which is the bringing [of them] under one's own control. || 8 ||
Furthermore, O Dear One, the elevenfold mantra must again be understood, by which,
through the correct application, the lords among practitioners attain success. (18.9)

By means of which—namely, by the elevenfold knowledge as the cause, through the correct application, that is, the employment of the mantra in its ritual function—by that, the lords among practitioners attain, that is, achieve, their desired goal. || 9 ||
Since this is so, I shall therefore fully explain that which is esteemed in all the scriptures;
therein:
The *saṃpuṭa*, the *grathita*, the *grasta*, the *samasta*, and the *vidarbhitam*.

Likewise, there is that which is "overwhelmed" (ākrānta), as well as that which has no beginning or end (anādyanta), that which resides within the womb (garbhastha), and that which is surrounded on all sides (sarvatovṛta);
likewise, there is that which is "interwoven by method" (yuktividarbha) and that which is "composed by interweaving" (vidarbhagrathita). || 18-11 ||
Thus, the eleven types of mantras are prescribed and are remembered as bestowing accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) at the beginning and end is like a "casket" (*saṃpuṭa*).
As it has been said:
"The wise one should first write the mantra, and after that the thing to be expressed (the name).
After this, he should write the mantra again; this is proclaimed as the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement).
The interweaving of the mantra syllable by syllable with each syllable of the name is called *grathana*. As it has been said: 'Each single syllable of the thing to be expressed...'"
"Encased by the syllables of the mantra, it is strung together... Thus,
the placement of the mantra in the four directions around the name situated in the center is called "grasta" (seized).
As it has been said:
"The wise practitioner should arrange the mantra above, below, and likewise across;
in the center there should be the name, and that is designated as 'seized' (grasta)."
After the mantra comes the name; "again likewise" refers to the complete characteristic.
As it has been said:
"One should first place the mantra, and after that the object of expression."
"In this manner, this [mantra] is to be applied in two ways in its entirety...
Thus, immediately after the name, the mantra is repeated once; this is *vidarbhaṇa*.
As it has been said:
"The object of expression (abhidheya) should come first, then the mantra should be applied once;
it is interlaced (vidarbhita)... Thus, if the mantra is placed by encircling the name situated in the middle, it is called "encircled" (ākrānta).
As it has been said: "The mantra, having seized the object of expression, should encircle it on all sides. When it is thus seized... [and so forth].
Thus: after the mantra comes the name, and then the mantra three times; this constitutes the beginning and the end.
As it has been said:
"One should apply the mantra three times at the end, but apply it once at the beginning."
"And in its center there should be the designation [of the name], from beginning to end...
Thus, the placement of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the four directions around the mantra situated in the center constitutes its state of being "in the womb" (garbhasthatva).
As it has been said:
"That which is declared as the characteristic for the [mantra] when swallowed is also stated for it while residing in the womb.
Thus, the insertion of the name of the object of accomplishment at the beginning and end of the mantra is "enclosure on all sides" (*sarvatovṛtatva*). As it has been said:
"Whatever form there may be in the *sampuṭa* (encased) [mantra], that same form occurs in the *sarvatovṛta* (all-sidedly enclosed)."
Thus: the fourfold insertion of the name of the mantra placed [at the beginning] is *vidarbhaṇa* (interlacing) by way of logic. As it has been said:
"The object of expression at the beginning of the mantra and so forth, joined threefold as a *saṃpuṭa* (encasement), is *vidarbhaṇa* by means of logic..."
Thus: after the name, the placement of the mantra three times is the "interlacing" (*vidarbha-grathana*). As it has been said:
"One should first write the object of expression and afterwards write the mantra three times;
this is the interlaced *vidarbha-grathita*..."
Thus they are appointed by the practitioners.
Furthermore:
the accomplished (*siddha*), the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*), the well-accomplished (*susiddha*), and likewise the state of being an enemy (*aritva*). (18.12)
Having understood everything without exception, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*).
Having divided and established the vowels— *a*, *u*, and *m*— from the syllables of the mantra beginning with the *praṇava*,
and having likewise placed the syllables of the practitioner's name beneath them:

Having counted the *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and [the fourth] by their distinctions according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā*, ending with the attainment of the mantra-syllables situated above the syllables of the name, the form beginning with *siddha* is declared according to the sequence of the mantra-syllables in the first, second, third, and fourth positions. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:
Having separated the syllables of the mantra, each provided with its vowel-mātrās and bindu,
one should likewise join the syllable of one's own name beneath it.
O Goddess, starting from the letter of one's own name up to the arrival at the syllable of the mantra, one should designate that [syllable] upon which [the breath] settles as the "āya."
I shall describe briefly that which pertains to the lines on the fingers:
on the first joint it is *siddha*, on the second it is *sādhya*,
on the third it is *susiddha*, and on the fourth it should be known as the *ari* (enemy).
"Having abandoned those that are *ari* (enemy) and *sādhya* (to be accomplished), one should bestow [the mantra] with the *cumbaka* (kisser);
for the *siddha* and *susiddha* [mantras] grant the fruits of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). (8.20.24) Thus it is said.
Furthermore,
[he taught] the rising and setting, the pervasion, the meditation, and the mudrā according to their essential nature.
He who knows this is omniscient, the doer of all, and the supreme practitioner.

"Rising and setting" refers to the expansion and the resting; "pervasion" is the vitality [of consciousness] between the heart and the station of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta); "meditation on mantras" refers to the object of the mantras; and "mudrā" is that which is appropriate to those very [mantras].
"By its own nature" means by its essential form, which consists of the nature of vigor.
In this way, O Goddess of the Gods, [it is worshipped] with all other varieties of offerings without exception.
O Dear One, the great mantras become bestowers of fruit when cultivated through these means:

namely, by the purification of the *aṃśakas* (astrological divisions) by others; by external and internal distinctions such as the rising of the *kalās* and *aṃśakas*; and by various states of being (*bhāva*) consisting of meditations and other practices following the respective deities.
Since this is so, therefore, having understood everything with all effort, one should apply oneself [to practice]. || 18-15 ||
And this conceptualization regarding the domain of this king of mantras is not like that of other mantras; thus he says:
"For this very king of mantras, there is no deliberation on distinctions, because this..."
The Supreme Lord is the nourisher of all the kings of mantras.
For, according to the perspective previously stated, the mantras have been strung together by him like clusters of jewels on a thread.
Likewise:
The mantras situated within his womb are born as bestowers of the perfection of liberation. || 18-17 ||
"This is logical," he said:
"The Supreme God is all-pervading, the source of the arising of the fruits of all accomplishments, omnipresent, auspicious in every way, facing in all directions, and imperishable. (18.18)
It is the fulfillment of all mantras, the protection that possesses strength in every direction;
it is the source of mantras, the auspicious bestower of liberation and the granting of spiritual accomplishments. (18–19)
Therefore, O Goddess, there is no further deliberation required regarding this mantra;
it has already been explained by the previous commentaries.

Since, according to the reasoning already stated, there exist procedures such as striking and swallowing [the enemy] due to the failure to understand the potency (*vīrya*) of mantras— such as their capacity to accomplish specific goals (*sādhya*) or their impurity of constituent parts— and since people are [harmed] by practitioners of corrupt mantras through the sequence of mantras, yantras, and so forth;
If the practitioner is pierced by these thousands of defects—such as being beaten, swallowed, and so forth—[he will fail]. (18–20)

Those who are seized by Vināyakas, those tormented by mental and physical ailments, those whose citizens have become disaffected, those who are without servants, those who are childless, and those who are deeply distressed; || 18–21 ||

Those whose sons have died, those whose spouses have died, those who are fearful, those whose prosperity has vanished, as well as teachers and practitioners, become averse to the accomplishment of mantras. (18–22)
Women who are sonless, unfortunate, barren, or whose husbands are hostile, as well as those joined with thousands of such other miseries and defects. (18–23)
Whosoever has seen those men in this world who are defiled by the aforementioned faults—
for them, moreover, a supreme sacrifice that brings good fortune must be performed. (18–24)
O Supreme Goddess, the Śrīyāga is performed by the practitioner with this mantra;
its form will be described immediately hereafter, for when this has been performed—
In a sacrifice performed for the sake of Mahālakṣmī, a man becomes a partaker of good fortune. || 18-25 ||
Freed from the aforementioned defects, he attains supreme bliss;
and there, at that sacrifice, having been consecrated with the water-pot (kalaśa) and having worshipped Mahāśrī, he [attains it]. (18–26)
One attains unthought-of desires comparable to those of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;

the connection [of the sentence] is that this is attained by one who has been consecrated by the preceptor after performing worship. "Desires" (kāmāḥ) are so called because they are desired; they refer to the specific stages such as those of the individual mantras and the lords of mantras (mantreśvara).
Since this is so, therefore, having understood this, the wise man should perform a most auspicious sacrifice. || 18-27 ||
This brings good fortune. || 27 ||
For this sacrifice, O Goddess, is in every way the supreme bringer of all auspiciousness;
therein—
On the previously mentioned plot of ground, which is endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Or else, in a delightful Great Lotus Grove (Mahāpadmavana) free from all thorns, well-concealed, auspicious, and well-guarded above a shelter; (18-29).
There, one should draw a square mandala on all sides; (one should cast nineteen lines from the eastern to the western direction). || 18-30 ||
The word *ti* is elided, resulting in *eṣaḥ*. The phrase *endrāvāruṇe* means that they are aligned from east to west. || 30 ||
Likewise, the southern and northern threads should be perfectly equal;
in that same manner, one should lay down exactly nineteen [threads].
When this has been done,
there [should be] eighteen parts on all four sides.
The number of squares, however, shall be three hundred and twenty-four;
likewise, in eighteen times eighteen, the number is exactly the same. Now,
And in the middle of that, one should draw a very beautiful eight-petalled lotus.
"In the eight-fold division," however, means having set aside five parts on all sides.
He asks, "How so? and says:
"...then one should divide that into four parts.
'That' refers to [the mandala] consisting of eight divisions."
And there,
the pericarp should be made in the first [circle], and the filaments in the second.
The joints are in the third [section], while the tips of the petals are in the fourth;
"in the first" refers to the section. The joints are the petals.
And one should rotate those parts into four equal circles, perfectly symmetrical and with equal divisions.
The state of being well-measured belongs to the wandering [atoms] within themselves, whereas the state of having equal parts belongs to them mutually. (34)
Then one should lay down eight lines in the cardinal directions and likewise drop them in the intermediate directions;
taking hold of the eastern direction, according to the measurement of the central line.
The petal should be situated upon the filaments;

having struck eight threads within the interval of the [original] eight threads, one should take hold of the eastern direction according to the central thread in order to produce the petals as they will be joined together according to the future arrangement.
Having divided the two side-lines from the center up to the ends of the two subsequent side-lines, one should form a petal by means of two circular rotations.
Of what kind? It is situated upon the filaments, resting as its support among the stamens.
The meaning is that it is endowed with three filaments (kesara).
Having thus established the other petals as well by means of the method of extended application (*atideśa*),
one should draw the pericarp (*karṇikā*) in their center.
He states the rationale for rotating [the lines] on both sides:
Having placed the thread situated at the junction of the petals to one side, one should rotate it.

Having placed the left hand, together with the thread, within the space between the middle and side threads, and having brought it to that very place situated at the joint of the petal, one should rotate it with the right hand on both sides— that is, along the two flanks.
In this manner, having rotated the thread, one should prepare the front leaf from both sides with two [threads];
"with two" is the specific limit.
This is extended by analogy:
"The pericarp, however, should be made yellow; the lotuses are traditionally held to be green. (18.37)
There are twenty-four variegated filaments, white, red, and yellow, according to their positions at the base, middle, and tip. (18-38)
The petals should be very white, and the circular line of the sky (the outer circle) should be one thumb's breadth in measure, white in color, and most beautiful. || 18-39 ||

The intervals between the petals are red... the lotuses and their seeds. At the base they are white, in the middle red, and at the tip yellow; thus the filaments (kesara) are to be made. "Petals" refers to those together with their tips. "Of the outer" refers to the lotus.

By saying "the spaces between the petals," he instructs that one should draw a lotus with unattached petals by means of the division of side-lines; this is done by completing it up to the sky-line (*vyomarekhā*).
Outside of that, a square should be made.
And for that purpose,
in the same manner, the white line is indeed yellow in its measurement by finger-breadths.
It should be applied on the outer edge at the end, joined with yellow orpiment, green orpiment, and so forth. || 40 ||
Furthermore,
the limbs [are formed] from the two outer portions on both sides;
"from the two portions on both sides" means from those two portions belonging to the two sides, respectively in each direction.
The meaning is "by means of four parts. The *gātrakas*—specific parts located between the corners—are to be made outside the sky-line (*vyomarekhā*).
Regarding the placement of the dust-powders (*rajonnyāsa*) on the pedestal (*pīṭha*),
he states that one should begin from the southeast corner with the various colors starting with white.
One should draw the limbs of yellow color starting from the east and so forth.

With respect to the direction facing the deity, one should perform the application of colored powders (*rajonnyāsa*) in the corners, beginning with the southeast (*āgneya*) and ending with the northeast (*īśāna*), according to the distinction of white, red, yellow, and black. In the other corners...
One should draw yellow figures representing the four directions extending through the sky.
Outside of that as well, two parts each should be erased from all sides for the sake of the walkway (vīthī). || 18-42 ||
"From all sides" means in all directions. "Vīthī" refers to the path leading to the place of worship. || 42 ||
And that [line] is to be drawn with black powder, adorned with a lotus and a conch;
for the lotus and the conch are the two insignia of Śrī.
Likewise, one should make this outer door white, with two parts on each side.
On each side, using the remaining two parts—that is, with the measurement of two squares—one should construct [the following]:

here, for the sake of the lotus, one square from the five squares on each side outside the eight squares; and for the sake of the pedestal (pīṭha), one [square]; and for the sake of the pathway (vīthī), [one square].
Since it is stated that "the pair is released," the door is indeed indicated within the two remaining squares. And as for the delineation of eighteen squares here,
it refers to the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*) numbering eighteen, which are to be purified, with the expansion of the other paths subsumed within this state.
In order to reveal the pervasiveness of the sacrifice. || 43 ||
Furthermore,
one should construct its neck with a measurement equal to the width of the street, or half the width of the street.
The term "on the side" (pārśvataḥ) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. "On the side" means on each side with reference to the central line.
"By the measure of the path" (vīthīmānena) means by two parts; however, in its entirety, it is by four parts according to the measurement of the width.
Likewise, by one part—which is half of the path—it means the neck (kaṇṭha), [measured] upwards from that point.
One should employ a specific part located above the door to act as the mandala master.
"...likewise the *upakaṇṭha* (the region near the throat) and the specific part located below the throat; likewise means that, in comparison to the throat,
it has a width of two parts on each side, and thus a total of eight parts."
One should have it made from the measurement of the cubit.
On both sides of the door, in the form of a recessed doorway arrangement, [are] the *śobhā* and *upaśobhaka* ornaments. (18.44)
One should have it made. || 44 ||

Having thus constructed the doors, one should cause three circular enclosures to be made. The western one should be left open; "the western" means situated in the western direction, facing toward the deity.
Regarding the description of the arrangement and placement of the primary and secondary ornaments, he says:
"But one should draw [them] on the two sides. (18.45)
One should [place] Śobhā and Upaśobhā, who are red and yellow in color,
at each of the four gates, arranged in upper and lower compartments.

"By means of compartments" (koṣṭhakaiḥ) refers to those which bring about the arrangement of the inverted doors. Although the number of compartments is not explicitly stated here, nevertheless, the division arises as one below and five above. || 46 ||
Then, O Goddess, one should draw lotuses and conchs on all sides at the ends of the corners situated at the flanks of the primary and secondary ornaments;
"on all sides" means on all [the corners].
Having thus completed the entire maṇḍala up to the doors,
one should then draw the lines of the earth (bhūrarekhā) all around its exterior.
The meaning is that there are five, corresponding to the number of elements (bhūta). || 47 ||
And these, according to the distinction of colors such as white and so forth,
are white, red, black, yellow, and transparent in form, by way of entering from the outside into the inside.
For those [powers] such as nivṛtti and the rest are indeed the kalās;
they are said to be the very phonemes that pervade the Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta.
For it is adorned externally with leaf-patterns, creepers, lotuses, and svastikas.
Having drawn the principal maṇḍala, one should worship Śiva in its center.
One should not draw the maṇḍala at the very outset;
rather, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) must first be performed with extensive offerings according to one's means. (18.49)
The meaning is that the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) should be performed on the preceding day. || 49 ||
For this purpose, at the very outset, a sacrificial hall should be constructed according to one's capacity and in accordance with available materials;
it should be provided with an altar and archways, and adorned with various banners. (18.50)
The banners have variegated emblems. || 50 ||
And this [residence], due to its suitability for sacrifice, is endowed with various splendors such as sandals, parasols, and beds,
as well as with various kinds of enjoyments including household utensils and other articles. (18.51)
Endowed with [these]. || 51 ||
The canopy for the sacrifice should be made high, very white, and beautiful;
one should provide a four-cornered curtain and eight lamps in the cardinal directions. || 18-52 ||
Furthermore,
one should place the fly-whisks, bells, and so forth, as well as the four mirrors, in the four directions.
Furthermore, in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
there were eight new and excellent banners, resplendent with various colors.
Likewise, eight jars— whether made of silver, copper, or even clay—
should be placed there.
And likewise, the eight oceans are to be worshipped within the jars;
[one should worship] the jars presided over by the oceans.
...endowed with all medicinal herbs. || 18-54 ||
One should worship mango sprouts accompanied by gold;
one should place eight stalks of five colors in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (18.55)
"Five colors" refers to the threads. || 55 ||
Outside of this,
the world-protectors (lokapālas) should likewise be worshipped on the cloth-paintings, remaining in their own forms; they are to be placed in the vicinity of the world-protectors.
For in this way, the form of the weapon must be fashioned all around in the ten directions.
"So be it. Accordingly, the forms of the weapons such as the vajra and others should be depicted on the cloth paintings in accordance with Indra and the other deities.
As for the "ten," Brahmā and Ananta, situated at the top and bottom, should be made with their weapons, and those stationed in the northeast and southwest corners [should likewise be depicted]. (56)
Furthermore, the gatekeepers (dvārādhyakṣas) should be placed outside of that [central area], according to the teachings of one's own tradition (svāmnāya).
They should be drawn and worshipped; "according to the teachings of one's own tradition" means in accordance with the established position of the Siddhānta.

To the right of the door are Nandin and Gaṅgā; to the left are Mahākāla and Yamunā. In the Bhairava view, however, these are reversed. In the Vāmasrotas system, as before, there are Nandin, Gaṅgā, and so forth, together with Diṇḍi and Mahodara. In the Trika system, as in the Bhairava view, there are Meṣānana and Chāgānana.

"and two more," and so forth, should be followed accordingly. Furthermore, these specific deities, beginning with the World-Guardians (Lokapālas) and ending with Trāṇa, should be depicted on the cloth-painting (paṭa), since this system is common to all. || 18-57 ||
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:

with the auspicious sounds of the Vedas joined by cries of "Victory! and "Auspicious Day!", as well as with the sounds of dance and musical instruments, and likewise with various kinds of hymns. || 18-58 ||

Being disciplined, the preceptor should be pure, skillful, and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum; he should be equipped with a clean white cloth, and adorned with a turban and finger-guards. || 18-59 ||
Adorned with bracelets and other great necklaces, and decorated with garlands and wreaths of flowers,
he was likewise accompanied by the image-bearers, the incense-bearers, and the water-offering bearers.
Endowed with all the necessary provisions and preceded by the rite of propitiation,
having worshipped the water-jar, the weapon, and the pitcher, he should perform the formal appropriation of the sacrificial field.
Afterwards, O Goddess, the best of teachers should perform the scattering of colored powders (*rajaḥpāta*).
"Pure" means one whose wealth, mind, and body are cleansed; "dexterous" means one who is diligent in worship and other rites;
and "smeared with sandalwood paste and so forth" is said precisely because he has performed his daily obligatory duties (*nityakarman*); [he wears] washed white garments.
Due to the intention of being pervaded by great light, there is the *uṣṇīṣa*, which is the binding of a turban and so forth on the head;

and the *aṅguli*, which is a finger-ring. By the term "by the *mūrtipas*," it refers to the teachers who take the form of the lords of the *mūrtis*, such as Śarva and others, who preside over the eight *mūrtis* beginning with Earth.

"Followed by the *ara*s" means that he is of one form with Maheśvara, who possesses eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*). In the passage beginning with "with vessels for the *argha*," the word "joined" (*yukta*) is to be supplied. "The collection of all requisites" (*sarvasaṃbhāra*) refers to the assembly of materials suitable for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*); "preliminary consecration" (*adhivāsana*) is the purification of the materials and so forth, performed in accordance with the requirements of the Śiva-sacrifice.

According to the rule taught in the *Śrīsvacchanda* and other scriptures, the *kumbhayāga* (pot-sacrifice) is for the purpose of completing all ritual procedures and so forth, while the *astrayāga* (weapon-sacrifice) is for the pacification of obstacles. One who has performed the *kṣetraparigraha* (appropriation of the field) has taken possession of a specific location suitable for the sacrifice; this is done by "letting the dust fall" according to the stated sequence.
Having fashioned a particular maṇḍala.
Thus, having meditated upon [the deity] in this maṇḍala with the previously mentioned form, one should worship Mṛtyuñjaya from the center.
The conqueror of death is the form of the Supreme Lord.
Moreover,
he beheld the Goddess Śrī, the Mother of the Universe, resting upon his lap—
resembling pure crystal and radiant as snow, the kunda flower, and the moon.
Resembling the moon's orb, with a luster like cow’s milk,
white as a pearl, and draped in white cloth.
Her limbs were smeared with white sandalwood paste and greyed by powdered camphor;
she was brilliantly adorned with pure pearls, moonstones, and other radiant jewels.
She was beautifully adorned with garlands and strings of white flowers and lotuses;
her limbs were as brilliantly white as the laughter of Śiva, she possessed a white smile, and she was enchanting to the mind.
She is endowed with a brilliant white crown, has one face and three eyes,
sits in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), and is adorned with a yogic band (yogapaṭṭa).
The great goddess has four arms, holds a conch and a lotus in her hands, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, is serene, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.

"Having meditated [upon her] according to the distinction of mental states (bhāvabheda) as adorned with forms and weapons—this is connected to the word 'one should worship' (yajet). And [she is] radiant and beautifully ornamented with pure pearls, moonstones, and other gems. Regarding "according to the distinction of mental states":
The practitioner is characterized by an intention colored by a specific desire. The rest is clear.
Now, regarding the limbs of the Goddess as being like those of the God, he says:
"In the same manner, one should fashion the limbs according to the procedure for Amṛteśa. || 18-69 ||
According to the principle indicated in the second chapter, by thus pointing out these specific [limbs] here,
he teaches— by implication— that these are not the limbs for all the previously mentioned deities other than these,
precisely because the Goddess herself is all-encompassing.
One should worship [the deity] who bestows all accomplishments with entirely white offerings.
Having stated the primary procedure, he describes another method:
"Or, by this very same rite, one may worship Śrīdhara together with Śrī. (18.70)
O Goddess, one should worship with devotion that which bestows the fruit of all desires;
or else, one may worship the Goddess alone with water for the feet, respectful offerings, pure flowers, and likewise with refined incense and other such items. || 18-71 ||
One should worship the Supreme Goddess, the bestower of the fruits of all accomplishments, with various auspicious foods to be licked, drunk, sucked, and chewed. (18.72)

At the conclusion of the worship, following the recitation of mantras, one should satisfy the Goddess of the gods with oblations in the fire-pit prepared as before, with a mind filled with devotion, according to the previously described rite.
The connection is as follows: by means of the oblation previously described—consisting of sesame, milk, ghee, sugar, and so forth—one should satisfy the power (śakti) of the God of gods. || 73 ||
He describes another form of the Goddess:
"Alternatively, the auspicious eight-armed Goddess holds the *cintāmaṇi* jewel in her hand; she should always carry a vessel filled with nectar. (18.74)
The goddess, who emits the moon and the sun, stands upon a white lotus;
she is further adorned by elephants and auspicious objects atop two treasure-vases.
Always worshipped and praised by the hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā,
the Great Goddess, when meditated upon and recited, bestows the fruits of both supernatural powers and liberation.

She has eight arms, characterized by holding a conch, a lotus, a boon-granting gesture (*varada*), and a fear-dispelling gesture (*abhaya*) as previously described, as well as a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāratna*), a nectar-filled jar, and the discs of the moon and sun above them. She stands upon a white lotus situated atop the treasure-vases (*nidhi*). She is adorned by auspicious elephants, who sprinkle her with water from jars held aloft by their trunks.
She is Maheśānī because she belongs to Maheśāna; for this very reason, she is worshipped by Brahmā and the others.
Indeed, it is stated in the Śrī Svacchanda Tantra that she has manifested through their respective portions and sub-portions solely through the propitiation of Him. 76.
Or else,
one should worship the beloved Goddess of the lords of gods, stationed within the pitcher,
according to the previously mentioned procedure during the auspicious sacrifice described before. (18.77)
And therefore,
having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times for Śrī situated within the pitcher by means of the previously described yoga of meditation, one should perform the consecration as before.
"As before" means according to the sequence beginning with the auspicious proclamation (*puṇyāhavācana*) and the sound of festive music.
Whatever that practitioner whom the preceptor consecrates may desire— whether it be immovable great fortune or a kingdom— that shall come to pass;
this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Moreover, having been thus consecrated, this practitioner attains terrestrial, atmospheric, and divine accomplishments, as well as auspicious lordly power.
And whatever else he may desire or seek, all that the propitiated Goddess shall grant to him.
...being well-pleased, she bestows [these].
Moreover: longevity, strength, fame, renown, intelligence, luster, prosperity, and physical form. (18.80)
Everything prospers in the house of him in whose home he is honored;
thus,
whoever has been consecrated...
O Dear One, whoever should accomplish [this] by means of the sequence of meditation and so forth as described therein, || 18-81 ||
This goddess.
He attains everything previously mentioned, and brings about peace and nourishment;
furthermore, by means of the sequence beginning with the aforementioned meditation.
But in whosever house the Goddess, depicted on a cloth, is worshipped; || 82 ||
By means of the previously described procedure, he bestows upon him every desired fruit.
Thus it is for one devoted to worship; what need is there for much speaking here? Just as deer [flee] from a lion, so do all things [flee] from him. (18.83)
All the wicked defects flee in all directions by the thousands;
what need is there for other collections of mantras or for the propitiation of deities? (18.84)

Wherever this Goddess of the lords of gods is meditated upon, recited, and well-worshipped— there, for the practitioner (the word "sādhakasya" being understood), evil spirits such as those causing epilepsy and the like, as well as defects such as diseases and misfortunes, [are destroyed].
Furthermore,
at the time of battle, she should be meditated upon as standing upon a creeper of sword-leaves.
When this is done,
it bestows victory upon him and becomes the destroyer of the enemy's pride.
And therefore:
One desiring to conquer a foreign kingdom should always perform sacrifices at the front of the battle.
At the beginning; at the start. || 86 ||
One certainly attains victory through the grace of the God and Goddess;
moreover, even one afflicted by hundreds of diseases or tormented by the defects of suffering [shall attain it]. (18.87)

Whether smeared with all kinds of evil or afflicted by sorcery, poison, and the like, [one is freed] by means of mantras, yantras, meditations, recitations, fire offerings, and [remedies for] poisons and so forth. || 18-88 ||
The connection is as follows: even he who is afflicted by diseases and the like, or by mantras, yantras, and so forth employed by others, attains victory through the grace of the Goddess. || 88 ||
Furthermore, whatever deceptive arts such as powders, ointments, collyriums, and the like, enemies may employ against either a woman or a man; [in that place, these shall not prevail]. (18.89)
When she is worshipped according to that rite, she becomes their *Pratyaṅgirā*.

[The mention of] powders and so forth is for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkāra*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and the like. "Deceits" (*kuhakāni*) refers to those mechanical devices (*yantra-kṛtya*) and such which enemies might employ; when she is worshipped by this stated method, it follows that—

Just as a poorly discharged weapon destroys its own wielder, so too the *praty-aṅgirā* rite performed against someone by deceivers and the like would become a destroyer of the very party of those who employed it.
Therefore, whoever should worship this supreme goddess with devotion, relying upon her— || 18.90 ||
The meaning is that he attains his desired object. || 90 ||
And there,
it was not seen by wicked men devoted to evil conduct,
nor by those perfected in mantras, nor by rogues, nor by all manner of thorns [of society]. (18.91)
Likewise, when well-guarded, she should be worshipped; when protected, she becomes the bestower of success.
By "rogues who have attained mantra-perfection" is meant those who have propitiated mantras for the sake of trivial accomplishments. By "all thorns" is meant Śākinīs and the like.
Thus, in this manner, [the fruit is obtained] through sacrifice, oblation, as well as recitation, through mudrās, and by means of the yoga of meditation. || 18-92 ||

He who, being well-guarded, meditates upon the Goddess shall become a possessor of good fortune; the connection [of the verse] is: "by means of the yoga of meditation," that is, he who, being well-guarded, meditates upon the Goddess through the yoga of meditation.
He establishes this very point:
"Because of this, many wicked people desire to destroy both [the body] and its pleasures. (18.93)
Others, abandoned by good fortune and oppressed by misfortune,
constantly witness sacrifices, fire-offerings, recitations, and the rules for meditation.
They produce great obstacles; therefore, the ritual procedure must be most secret.

"The wicked, the most sinful, and those devoted to trivial acts"—and by the word "and" (*ca*), [it is implied] even pleasures such as the body, wealth, and so forth. "And they see the sacrifice and the fire-oblation"—the second "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*tulyayoga*). They see [these things].
And they always produce obstacles; such is the meaning.
He concludes the stated meaning:
"That [deity] should be worshipped by the wise practitioner according to the distinction of their disposition. (18.95)
Or if the Mistress of the Gods is worshipped according to the method of the Solitary Hero,
the Supreme Goddess, being pleased, grants all desires.
By the wise one, that is, by the knower of pervasion (vyāpti); and by the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "all desires," liberation is also included. || 96 ||
She clarifies the statement "by means of a distinction of states" [as follows]:
"The Supreme Goddess is well-worshipped precisely through the distinctions of the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava Siddhāntas;
she bestows the fruit according to the different mental dispositions of her devotees. (18.97)
Moreover, just as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) in this world bestows the fruits of whatever is desired,
so too does this Mahālakṣmī bestow the fruits of all desires. (18.98)
And this is its greatness:
that gods, asuras, and humans; nāgas, gandharvas, and kinnaras; daityas along with dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas—[all these are overcome by it]. || 18-99 ||
The bhūtas, vetālas, yoginīs, mothers (mātṛs), and likewise the guhyakas;
the ḍāvis, ḍāmarikas, goddesses (devīs), sisters (bhaginīs), and likewise the messengers (dūtīs). || 100 ||
Likewise, all the lords of yoga, intensely devoted to the perfection of sacrifice,
have all become perfected ones and attained great success through the grace of the Great Siddhi.

Piśācas are those who dwell in impure places and so forth, having firebrands for their mouths; bhūtas, however, are exceedingly powerful, such as the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) and others; vetālas are those who enter dead bodies and frequent cremation grounds;
yoginīs have attained power through the practice of yoga; and mātṛs are those who constitute the retinue of Brahmā and the other [deities].

The *yogeśvaras* are those who, through yoga—that is, through identity with the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*)—are lords; they are not merely those who delight in limited supernatural powers (*mitasiddhi*).

The *yogasiddhas*, however, are those whose mastery of powers is attained through the force of yoga and who abide in those powers. The *susiddhas* are those who have acquired their respective appropriate powers in accordance with their particular internal dispositions (*bhāva*). || 101 ||
For this goddess Mahālakṣmī is of great power, the source of all accomplishments,
and the bestower of boons upon those who have taken refuge in her, her devotees, and practitioners. (18.102)
The meaning is that she bestows all enjoyment and liberation. || 102 ||
For there is indeed no other than this [Śakti] that bestows happiness upon the world;
nor are the qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, nor those others such as omniscience (*sārvajñya*) and so forth [independent of her]. (18.103)
All these are accomplished through her grace; there is no doubt in this matter.
Furthermore, this aforementioned sacrifice should be performed by one seeking liberation as a solitary hero (*ekavīra*), just as before. (18.104)
The sole object of the glorious Amṛteśa. || 104 ||
For one desiring enjoyment, he states another method for the attainment of that enjoyment:
"Alternatively, one should install the all-pervading Lord, conjoined with Śakti and accompanied by the previously mentioned requisites, in a delightful temple. (18.105)
Having established the union of power and the possessor of power according to the prescribed rule— that is,

by knowing the pervasion according to the rule— having established the union of power and the possessor of power, one attains immersion into that Śakti, which is Rudra, consisting of the equilibrium of knowledge and action.
Whoever installs the God together with Mahālakṣmī in a temple with the necessary materials—for him, whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of previous births [is destroyed]. (18.106)
O Goddess, at that very moment it perishes like a heap of cotton in a fire.
Furthermore,
as soon as he is desired, the Lord of Gods is established even by those who have been initiated.
"He rescues all his kinsmen"—
that is, he rescues all his kinsmen, such as those of his paternal lineage and so forth.
How...
"ten ancestors and ten descendants"?
The meaning is that he rescues ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants in each family line.
Furthermore, as far as the temple, the linga, the images, and the painted walls; || 18-108 ||
He enjoys that state for as long as it takes to count the atoms within stones, minerals, banners, and flagstaffs. (18.109)
Having enjoyed all pleasures—extending as far as the oceans, rivers, wind, moon, sun, and earth—within the principle (tattva) of Sādāśiva, one shall attain liberation (nirvāṇa). || 18-110 ||
The stones are those located outside the enclosure wall; the minerals are those found within the palace, such as lime and so forth;

the banners are the tridents and the like. The grammatical connection is: "as many as the number of atoms. He enjoys (*bhunakti*) means he experiences (*bhuṅkte*). The mention of "oceans" is intended to demonstrate the vastness of time. Thus it has been said:
"As many atoms as there are in the images, the lingas, and the altars," thus [it is said]. || 110 ||
He establishes the true nature of nirvāṇa through an illustration:
"Just as a river, upon reaching the ocean, becomes of one taste, so too the bound soul (paśu), having attained the state of Śiva, is liberated from the ocean of existence. (18.111)

The Sindhu is a river. "Having attained the state of Śiva" means having reached unity with Paramaśiva. The term "paśu" (the bound soul) is a statement made in reference to his prior condition. || 111 ||
Thus, the consecrator shall obtain this fruit of consecration, which consists of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus described the sacrifice and the consecration for Mahālakṣmī, [he now describes] the initiation for the rescue of the deceased.
In order to state [the following] preceded by a specific explanation, he says: "But when the king, his sons, or the twice-born are uninitiated... (18.112).
Or, O Goddess, among those who are indolent regarding their enjoyments, or those whose [practice] is obstructed by defects of karma;

and among all those who are "uninitiated" (adīkṣita), meaning they have not received initiation—including kings, their sons, and others—even though they may be initiated, because the sin of improper protection of subjects is possible for them; [and] among the twice-born.

Because even among those who have received initiation, there is no cessation of their firm adherence to caste; and because among those initiated by *sabīja-dīkṣā*—who are indolent regarding worldly enjoyment—there remains attachment to caste and enjoyment; and [finally] because there are those whose observances (*samaya*) have lapsed, either because they were intent on violating the rules or because their observances were ruined due to the obstruction of adverse fate.

It is possible that, when those very [deceased] have died and the descent of power (śaktipāta) has reached their chief kinsmen and others, the Supreme Lord is to be worshipped for the sake of initiation for the purpose of their liberation; this is the connection with the forthcoming text.
Furthermore, that which has not been performed by others, nor austerity practiced, nor meditated upon, nor established. || 18-113 ||
Even among those [who have performed rites], no sacrifice or similar act was directed toward the Supreme Lord;
yet for those who died through the downfall resulting from drowning, being bound, or being struck in the belly, there remains their residence in hell.
Furthermore, O Queen, for children, women, the elderly, and the sick, there are many causes [of death],

such as the faults of spiders, the consumption of poison, minor planetary conjunctions, being devoured by a lord, falling from a precipice, and so forth— these being the causes for children and the others.
And upon his death, falling into hell and other such fates are possible.
When all of them had died, the Supreme Lord [appeared] for the sake of their extraction and for the purpose of initiation.
The deity should be worshipped as before...

"Extraction" (*uddharaṇa*) means drawing [the soul] out from the plane of hell by means of the sequence of the yoga of the net of mantras; "for that purpose" (*arthauṃ*) means for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; initiation (*dīkṣā*) is for the sake of bestowing and exhausting those [results], for the attainment thereof.
The deity is to be worshipped with the ritual requisites as previously described.
Moreover:
"Furthermore, because of the distinction [of the occasion], an image must necessarily be made there with colored powder, resembling [the deity] and twelve finger-breadths in size. (18.116)

O Goddess, it should be fashioned from cow dung or purified with *kuśa* grass; [it may also be made] with dust or rice powder. "Silver" (*rājatā*) is a corrupt reading. "Similar" (*sadṛśī*) means similar to the corpse.
And one should not perform the ritual of *adhivāsa* (preliminary consecration) here; as it is said, "In that case, initiation (*dīkṣā*) itself is the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*)...
solely after the worship of the Lord and the fire-oblation (*homa*)."

Rising from the *mūlādhāra* and forcefully traversing the staff-like path of the infinitely extended and well-spread network of channels, it reaches the space of the nose; dispersing there, it is able to pervade the entire wheel of paths with a mass of flames, beautiful like smoke, until they have fully accumulated.
"The practice named the 'Great Net' (*mahājāla*) consists of bringing about the desired living beings after having completely covered [them].
(Tantrāloka 21.25).
Thus, by means of the "Net of Māyā" (*māyājāla*), through the contemplation of the seed-syllable of Māyā according to the logic of the tradition instructed by the Guru and others...

Alternatively: "In the middle [of the body] is the *nāda*; the neuter vowels (*ṣaṇṭhasvara*); the *avarga* [consonants]; *ka*, *ca*, *avaṅ*, and *ña*; *aṇ*, *an*, *au*; *ṭa*, *ta*; *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*; those beginning with *pa*; the eight beginning with *ya*; and the head is *mūrdhā*."

Thus, by means of the application of the net of the Mātṛkā consisting of the sixfold rotation of the neutral *nāda*, one should bring the aforementioned candidate for initiation into a state of pervasion, as it abides in the *yava*. || 18-117 ||
"By means of pervasion" (*vyāptyā*) means through the immersion (*āveśa*) into the abode of consciousness that pervades the universe. This has been stated in the venerable *Haṃsapārameśvara*:
"The worship of Śarva should take place on the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), and there is no preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) therein," beginning with these words.
I am indeed the supreme Śiva, partless, with parts, and peaceful;
I am the Supreme Self, omnipresent, and by me the entire universe is pervaded.

Thus, having entered into meditation, one should perform exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), ending with retention (kumbhaka); then, by means of exhalation, one should gradually expel everything.

At the end of the exhalation, one should again perceive within one's own heart, and then at the end of the twelve finger-breadths, one's own Śakti in the form of a sprout, moving within all the cosmic eggs.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should contemplate consciousness joined with the subtle body (liṅga),
pure and in the form of a drop of water, situated within the stream [of the central channel].
"Having seized it through its application by means of the Great Net (mahājāla) with skillful method,
one should place the captured heart, endowed with the designation of the seed-syllable.
Thus [ends verse 117].
In this manner, having brought one or many atoms, he should join them to that [image];
he should place them upon a single or multiple representation.
Then, having performed the entire purification of the paths (adhva-śuddhi) as in the case of initiation for the living, one should cast that image—
along with its crest-lock— into the fire together with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should offer oblations into the Śiva-fire.
Regarding the "joining" (yojanī) into the principle of Śiva (śivatattva),
one should unite that [soul] with the principle of Śiva according to the method of "joining" (yojanikā) prescribed in the venerable Svacchanda Tantra and other scriptures.
Thus, initiated by the initiation performed by the most excellent awakened teacher, [the disciple] shall thereafter become a partaker of union (sāyujya). || 18-118 ||
One should attain oneness with Śiva. || 118 ||
Alternatively, for the sake of favoring those people who have been mentioned, one should worship the God during a *śrāddha* or perform a sacrifice at the time of the final rites (*antyeṣṭi*).
In that regard, the procedure for the *śrāddha* according to the Siddhānta is well known; however, as for the secret procedure (*rahasyavidhi*), [it is as follows]:

The wise practitioner, having meditated upon the Guru as the nourishing power consisting of food, which takes the form of vitality, should contemplate the person to be acted upon as being permeated by that power.
"Then he should offer that aspect of his which consists of the bonds and takes the form of experience, by means of the state of oneness with the Enjoyer. In this way, the disciple becomes Śiva.
Thus, by the very method of offering the food-oblation (naivedya), the rite for the elevation of the deceased (mṛtoddhāra) and the funeral ceremony (antyeṣṭi) have been described.
Regarding the corpse, in the *Śrīsiddhā*, however:
"The last [element] should become the first; having made the last the first, the sacrifice which consists of withdrawing each one individually is considered the twofold *antyeṣṭi*."
O Dear One, when the time [of death] has been consumed by worship, meditation, and recitation,
the practitioner is liberated from the falling of the body and becomes a sky-walker (khecarī).
When an Ācārya who is perfected in reality dies anywhere at all,
no funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) is required for that pure-minded one.

"But those who have been killed by means of mantra-yoga and the like, they shall be in the hells; for them, the final rite (antyeṣṭi) must be performed here by the exceedingly compassionate Guru. Thus it was commanded. By means of the reversal of the mantra, according to the Vīrakrama, [the rite] should be performed for the two types of spiritual sons (putraka) within the covenant (samaya).

However, the intended meaning is that [the mantra does not fail] when the practitioner is diligent, nor when the Guru—who has abandoned all conceit regarding the body and is a mass of consciousness and bliss—is at the head [of the lineage]. In the *Śrīkulārṇava* it is also said: "Those men who have violated their commitments (*samaya*), or those who are haters of the path..."
But those base men who, having reached the path, nevertheless abandon it—
"Therefore, O highly fortunate one, I shall describe the funeral rites for these.
Thus, the initiation of the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi-dīkṣā*) has been taught regarding those whose observances have lapsed and so forth.
Now, he says that the act of bestowing grace upon those to be favored must be performed through the consecration of the abode of the deceased:
"O Goddess, likewise, [the body] is to be established upon a funeral pyre in the cremation ground. (18.119)
With the previously mentioned collection of materials, the Guru, according to the prior injunction,
[should manifest] the previously described terrifying form, endowed with two powers.
"In the burnt lump" means in the place where the body has been consumed by fire. "As previously stated" refers to the two powers of Bhairava, namely the thin and the thick. (120)
Alternatively, O Goddess, there are four [goddesses] situated at the sides of the central Bhairava, and then eight who were previously visualized in meditation;
these are the four beginning with Siddhā, together with the eight messengers (dūtī) beginning with Kālī, as previously described.
Having been visualized through the meditation described in the tenth chapter, they should be meditated upon and then established.
He for whom this consecration is performed attains the aforementioned fruit; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (18.121)
May it be auspicious that he attains the fortune of enjoyments for an exceedingly long time. || 121 ||
By what form indeed of the Supreme Lord, whose essence is consciousness,
do we not worship the throbbing eye that manifests for the grace of the worlds?
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the illustrious Netratantra, in the Netrodyota commentary composed by the eminent and illustrious Mahāmāheśvara teacher Śrī Kṣemarāja. 18.
The Nineteenth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Eyes. All shadows, apertures, and the like, which cause the spreading of faulty vision;
I take refuge in that in which, when it throbs, the radiance of the eyes vanishes.
Desiring to demonstrate the means for pacifying [defects] such as shadows, cracks, and the falling of glances, the Śrīdevī spoke, preceded by a summary of the chapters:
"O Lord of the Gods of gods, you have spoken out of a desire for the welfare of living beings."
The ritual procedure of Amṛteśa, moreover, is the supreme means for providing all forms of protection.
Now I wish to hear [this], for a doubt resides in my heart:
"The mothers always cast their gaze upon a human being. (19.2)
Those goddesses are indeed innumerable and endowed with immeasurable power; these most powerful yoginīs cause affliction through their shadows and their interstices. (19.3)
Exceedingly defiled, fierce, cruel, fearless, and stubborn, they were harmful to all living beings, and especially so to children. (19.4)
No number exists for them; tell me the means for that.
[The question] "I wish to hear" refers to the means for pacifying the casting of glances and so forth, which has been made the subject of inquiry.
"Casting of glances" (*dṛṣṭipāta*) is looking with the intent to kill. The "mothers" (*mātaraḥ*) are those who move on the earth and so forth. "Shadow" (*chāyā*)...

That which is given by menstruating women, women who have recently given birth, the most wicked, and others, serves as the cause for the acquisition of spirits and other beings by a praiseworthy person; likewise, crying out in the forest and similar acts [are causes].
Those who are extremely impure are tāmasas; those whose nature is characterized by intense anger are niṣṭriṃśas (cruel).
"Merciless," "firm in their commenced evil deeds," "difficult to ward off," and "cruel"— these are the [adjectives] for the planets and so forth, with a single residue (*ekaśeṣa*) applied to all.
And with the intention of revealing the true nature of shadows and so forth, he says this very thing:
"The deceptive form that is a shadow, as well as the deception consisting in the casting of a glance. (19.5)
O God, that shadow which they always produce—how many kinds is it said to be?
What is the fear regarding the falling of the gaze, or how is it averted?
"O wielder of the trident, please explain all of this in brief out of your grace.
Then, in order to resolve this matter, the Blessed Lord said: "Listen, for I shall fully declare the determination regarding the shadow."
By the word "and" (ca), [the inclusion of] the casting of glances and so forth is intended. || 7 ||
Therein, indeed, are immeasurable and infinite Mothers, most powerful;
and there are spirits of various forms, infinite and possessed of great strength. || 8 ||

The Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and whatever other violent beings there are who are firm—there is no numbering of them... [they are] immeasurable and infinite. These two expressions are stated according to the distinction between genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*). "Others" refers to the planetary spirits (*graha*) and so forth.
For these are established through a division into ten million types.
Therefore, I shall briefly proclaim such a means by which children, women, men, as well as queens and their sons, may be liberated. (19.10)
By defects such as shadows and the like. || 10 ||
Moreover,
just as those who are powerful, devoted to sacrifices and vows, whose bodies are armored with mantras, and who possess immeasurable strength, abandon [their lives]. (19.11)

"Those who abandon" refers to those such as children whom the spirits, grahas, and so forth have seized; "by means of sacrifice" means being intent on the worship of the Lord through the very method of offering up sacrificial victims (paśu). || 11 ||
For indeed, all these beings, such as the Bhūtas and others, were produced in former kalpas through thousands of various births;
they are everywhere harmful and cruel, always desiring to kill.
All the attendants of Bhairava are always intent upon performing sacrifices;
by her power they are all strong, being nourished by the strength of her splendor.
Those of great vows gratify [the deity] with the offering of great animals—that which I have made into the self-willed one (Svacchanda) in the form of Mahābhairava. (19.14)
For the sake of slaying the Daityas and for the establishment of the gods, [there were those] who were harmful;
though they were engaged in violence in some instances and even desiring to kill, they were not satisfied with that much alone and desired to slay others. This is their power (*śakti*).

The capacity for performing actions is strength (*bala*); vigor (*ojas*) is [the power of] the great vows. Those who are devoted solely to the sacrifice of the Supreme Lord are the observers of the great vows (*mahāvrata*).
Regarding this, he states the sequence of the historical narrative:
"When the gods, beginning with Indra, were oppressed by all the Daityas... (19.15).
When I was routed by the Daityas, I was then praised by them, as well as by Brahmā and various others, with diverse hymns for the sake of their welfare. (19–16)
Then, for the purpose of terrifying the Daityas and establishing the gods, that Svachanda assumed the form of Mahābhairava.
And for that purpose, the planets, spirits, and mothers were created by me;
immediately after conquering that host of enemies, they have accomplished their goal and returned to my presence.
Having arrived, they made their request out of fear of destruction:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, you have indeed been propitiated by us. (19.19)
"By the grace of the God of gods, who was pleased, perform that which must be done," he said; and then they were chosen by me. (19–20)
Seeking a boon, those of great strength requested of me, "May we be invincible"; thus, they were chosen by me upon the granting of that boon.
"May all these beings become exactly as they were created by me in the past. || 19–21 ||
From that time forward, by all those virtuous ones who had thus been chosen, the entire world— both stationary and moving,
including animals, humans, and gods— was overwhelmed and oppressed.
Therefore, certain beings of great power in heaven seek to slay the gods;
and others, being powerful, seek to slay human beings from all sides. (19–23)
Others likewise seek to destroy various beings in the animal realm;
they are said to be innumerable, for their power is immeasurably fierce. (19–24)
While things were thus situated,
I was again praised by the gods, led by Prajāpati. When—
Then all those even more powerful beings were cast away by me.
The Mothers, of fearsome form and terrified with fear, have come into my presence; all of you, who carry out my commands, why have you assembled here? (19-26)
Immediately thereafter, O Goddess of Gods, being enraged, I brought down many millions of mantras for the purpose of destroying the Mothers and the planetary deities.
By the power of Śiva’s Śakti, they are intended [to be understood] as possessing the nature of both reflection (manana) and protection (trāṇa).
And this is appropriate, as he says:
"For there are many millions of mantras; all of them have been authorized by me. (19–28)
"They have been empowered by me; since they possess supreme authority, I have thus fashioned them.
By speaking in this way, the Blessed Lord, the Lord of Uma, demonstrates his identity with Paramaśiva.
Then, immediately after my resolve, they came into my presence, terrified by the power of my knowledge. When—
Then they were scattered by me upon both the dry land and the waters.
"In the empty quarters of space" means they have been rendered fragile and liable to fall apart.
Then they,
remaining obedient to my command,
remained stationed there in that very manner.
To whom does he refer? He says:
"Some desire offerings, while others likewise desire food. (19.30)
Desirous of pleasure or desirous of killing, born of wind, born of bile, others born of phlegm, arising from the combination of humors, and spirits of various forms; (19.31)

Those desiring to consume [me] are those who crave flesh and blood; those desiring to kill are those who wish to take life. When there is a provocation of wind and the other humors (*vāta-ādi-prakopa*), they arise; however, while desire (*abhilāṣa*) is their primary motive, they do not venture to impel me by force out of fear of me.
Then those powerful ones, who abide by the constraints of the law, were addressed by me with the mantras and mudrās I prescribed, as well as through various meditations at all times.
The word "they become" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 32 ||
O beloved, when they hear that which has burst forth from the five streams, then they all flee and run away in the ten directions. || 19-33 ||
And these, O Queen, acting solely under my command and for many reasons, seek to kill men as if they were beasts;
he now demonstrates those reasons.
One who is of evil conduct, evil-souled, impure, and the lowest of men. || 19-34 ||
Due to disrespecting one's mother and father, as well as the abandonment of Vedic study, from excessive sexual indulgence with women, and especially from intoxication; || 19-35 ||

The connection with the future tense is as follows: "the *grahas* seize [them] due to sexual intercourse at the wrong time, out of delusion, fear, or likewise from agitation. [They seize] one of evil conduct (*durācāra*), who has abandoned proper behavior;
one of evil soul (*durātmāna*), who is intent on harming others; and the impure (*aśuci*), who is devoid of purity of mind, wealth, and body.

The avoidance of study is the abandonment by one entitled to study; fear produced by delusion—that is, by ignorance; and terror caused by shadows and the like; and agitation is the apprehension of danger where no danger exists.
Likewise, those who, though holding office, are devoid of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and those who indulge in sexual intercourse during the twilight periods. || 19-36 ||
O beloved, those who engage in eating, study, or sleep during the twilight hours, and those who lust after women who do not desire them or the wives of their gurus; (19-37)
The powerful forcibly destroy the wives of others;
likewise, there are others who are untruthful speakers and malevolent traitors to their masters. (19.38)
Likewise, those men who are joined with unmentioned evil deeds,
as well as by these and other such causes, are seized by the grahas.
"Desireless" means those in whom longing has not arisen. "Speaking untruths" refers to their habitual practice of lying.
"By those not mentioned" refers to such acts as killing a Brahmin; "by others" refers to such acts as betraying a friend. (39)
And women [fall] due to immorality, from eating impure things and forbidden food, as well as from hatred toward both parents and from infidelity toward their husband. (19.40)
They—referring to the planets—stigmatize those who are corrupted by other faults not previously mentioned, such as the misappropriation of deposits and so forth;
these include both the elders, such as fathers-in-law and others, as well as benefactors. "By others" refers to acts like the theft of entrusted property. "They" refers to the planets.
Likewise, [the same occurs] for children who weep and for those who keep vigil at night. || 19-41 ||
Intoxicated, fleeing, terrified, trembling, and corrupted by faults;
weeping, crying out, with disheveled hair, and dreadful. (19.42)
They were indeed defiled by the touch of wicked Pukkasa and Caṇḍāla outcasts, as well as by the touch of a corpse, by going there, and by the touch of those staying there. (19.43)

Furthermore, they were defiled by association with the wicked, by following after their talk, as well as by various impurities such as ritual uncleanness and other things that are unfit to touch. (19.44)

"Corrupted by defects" means afflicted by misfortune and the like; "cruel" means solely intent on violence. "Located therein" refers to the corpse, flowers, and so forth; [the corruption arises] from touching those. "Associated with that" refers to those who are wicked because of their connection to the corpse—namely, those appointed to play musical instruments for it—and [the corruption arises] from association with them. "News of that" is news concerning the corpse.
The connection [of the word] with that [object] is its following after it (anugama). || 44 ||
Therefore, from among those women or men— whosoever they may be— who are thus defiled by such faults as these according to their respective circumstances:
Whether it be a wicked woman or a man, having bathed, one should cause their shadow to fall [upon the image];
this applies to children, kings, their queens, and ascetics.
Then, through that very gap in the shadow, the spirits and the Mātṛs, who are exceedingly powerful,
cast their glances; for those who seek to harm seize every opportunity.
"Having found a vulnerability"—this is an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle). || 46 ||
