Moreover, these most wicked and ill-behaved ones cast fierce glances with the intent to kill the ignorant;
they are possessed by spirits and afflicted by fevers and other maladies. (19.47)
Likewise, those who are insane, evil-minded, of sinful conduct, and deeply afflicted;
those who are hungry, envious, hostile, and arrogant in their self-composure. || 19-48 ||
These and many others, having cast a terrifying glance, look upon the children and all those previously mentioned from every side. (19.49)
Having recognized that a glance has arisen from that [state], one should practice what is beneficial;
one should not delay even for a moment, for by doing so, even a small amount [of merit] is lost. (50)
The wicked do not cause harm immediately; rather, having dwelt [within], they cause affliction.

These are the most sinful ones, devoted to prohibited actions; they are of evil conduct and preeminent in their lack of discipline. The word "tathā" (so it is) is to be connected with what precedes. They are those of corrupt mind, whose nature consists of anger and the like; they are of sinful behavior.

“Liquor-sellers, fishermen, and so forth” refers to those [of low caste]. “By means of what has been done” means by means of rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and the like. “Having dwelt” means having attained a stable residence.
Since it is thus, one should not delay; rather, one should perform it immediately. || 19-51 ||
The word "tadā" means "from that"; "samācaret" means "one should perform a remedy. || 51 ||
There,
one should perform [the rite] with many highly praised medicinal herbs accompanied by auspicious items,
or else with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with mantras. || 52 ||

This bath, which generates good fortune and removes all defects and fears, should be performed with medicinal herbs such as sahadevī, balā, moṭaka, vīrā, and others; this is the procedure to be carried out.
Furthermore, for those who possess a corrupt shadow, the preceptor [should perform] the mantra-vase according to the procedure enjoined as before. (19.53)
It bestows [the fruit] immediately for all the aforementioned children and others;
"recited according to the previously stated procedure" refers to the method mentioned before, and "for the aforementioned ones" refers to kings and so forth;
it "bestows" by pouring [the water] upon the head for the sake of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Then,
it will certainly become a merit that brings immediate welfare, bestows peace, and grants nourishment— this is the understood conclusion.
For when the infinite Mothers are present there by their proximity, they immediately seek to strike [the practitioner]; at that time, one should worship the Great Mothers.

Those residing there are seen in the scriptures as the Mothers (*mātaraḥ*), who have arisen from the portions (*aṃśaka*) of Brahmī and the others. The Great Mothers (*mahāmātaraḥ*) are their mistresses, namely Brahmī and the rest. And so it is stated in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*:
"Śākinī, Dūṣikā, Cumbikā, and Patralekhikā..."
Ucchuṣmā, Nakradūṣī, and likewise Ūrdhvaniḥśvāsikā;
And now hear, O beloved, their activity regarding those who do not exhale;
among them, the Śākinīs are considered the most excellent, while the rest are remembered as even more terrible.
She who constantly discharges blood of all colors while walking or standing is known as a *dūṣikā*.
Those who taste their sons, friends, fathers, brothers, and children,
and kiss them while eating, are to be known as *cumbikās*.
Always drinking nectar by placing her face upon a leaf, she is known as Patralekhī; she is difficult to restrain and possesses great power.
Having become naked at night and having urinated while circumambulating, she should drink blood and, with her hair loose, she shall drag [the victim] away.
She should be known as Ucchuṣmikā, the heroine of the heroes, by the practitioners;
gazing at the tip of her nose, she always tastes the nectar.
She who pollutes by her cries is to be known as a *nakradūṣī*, and she who breathes upward is an *ūrdhvaniḥśvāsikā*;
she who always goes to another's house at night while naked is likewise [to be known].
"Having covered her face with a cloth and being thus downward-facing, she constantly drinks blood while exhaling from below.
Thus, the seven Mothers, beginning with Dūṣikā, are characterized as distinct from the Śākinīs; it is stated in that very same [text]:
Regarding their emergence from portions of Brahmā and the others:
"Adhaḥśvāsā is a portion of Brahmā; Nakradūṣī is Maheśvarī;
Dūṣikā is a portion of Viśākha; and Pārvatī is a portion of Vaiṣṇavī."
Patralekhī is declared to be a portion of Cāmuṇḍā, while Cumbikā is known as a portion of Māhendra, O fair-faced one; she is to be understood as having an upward breath.
"Likewise, Ucchuṣmā, who possesses a portion of Vārāhī, has been described, O Goddess praised by heroes.
Thus it was said. And that these [goddesses] are infinite is shown in that very same place by the passage beginning with, "There are three divisions of Cumbikā," and so forth. || 55 ||
One should worship the Mothers, namely: Brahmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā—the seven Mothers. (19.56)

By worshipping these seven Mothers, one becomes auspicious and shall attain the highest good (*śreyas*). The word *bhavet* is derived from the root *bhū* in the sense of "attaining," through a transposition of verbal suffixes (*tiṅ-vyatyaya*).
And this is appropriate, as he says:
"They are proclaimed to be the wombs of the entire circle of Mothers. (19.57)
As soon as they have been honored with those various kinds of offerings,
the entire assembly of Mothers becomes satisfied at that very moment.
Therefore, these seven are proclaimed as the foremost among all Mothers;
likewise, they are [worshipped] with various kinds of flowers that are white, red, yellow, and black. || 59 ||
With milk-rice, kṛsara, fish, and all kinds of linctuses and drinks;
with the four types of meat, and likewise with voracious, powerful sacrificial offerings.
Having performed worship for children, immediate well-being will come about;
with *kṛsara* (rice and peas) mixed with grains of rice and crops,
and with the fourfold kinds of food, distinguished as those from marshy regions, arid lands, water-born, and sky-born.
And for this very reason, therefore, the deities are subordinate to the principal sacrifice. || 19-61 ||
They become satisfied everywhere... when this is done, the goal is achieved;
for one shall indeed obtain immediate well-being.
Furthermore,
thirty thousand koṭis of fierce Vināyakas, whose splendor blazes like fire, were emanated by me from my own thumb.
If some man should be obstructed or overcome by them, [he would suffer]. (19.63)
In that regard, Vināyaka, the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa), is to be worshipped as the presiding deity.
The characteristic signs of one possessed by Vināyaka are as follows:
"He who emits the sound 'huṃ' and likewise throws dust from his feet [at others]..."
But he who constantly desires and grinds his teeth together;
"For this is the characteristic of one seized by Vināyaka.
Thus it is shown in the *Śrī-kriyākālaguṇottara*.
And one should worship that [deity] through the ritual procedures of another tantra and by means of the yoga of meditation. || 19-64 ||
With various and diverse *modakas*, with voracious offerings, with abundant liquors and meats, and with red flowers and ointments. || 65 ||
The practice or conventional usage of that very yoga of meditation, which belongs to another tantra or another teaching, is performed with this very mantra. || 65 ||
And in whichever place such specific deities are to be worshipped, there one should cause the garments and forms of all of them to be presented;
one should also cause gold, jewels, minerals, and lamps to be offered. (19–66)
One should cause everyone to give everything in their own respective forms;
when this is done, the practitioner is liberated from obstacles at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. (19.67)
Furthermore,
if a man is afflicted by fierce and powerful elemental spirits (bhūtagraha),
then Bhūteśvara should be worshipped according to the previously mentioned procedure.

In the *Śrītōtula*, one possessed by a spirit (*bhūtagṛhīta*) is characterized by such passages as: "And he rises up with force, powerful and having eaten much," and so forth. A planetary spirit (*graha*) is also described in that same work: "Desiring an offering, desiring to eat..."
And likewise, O Goddess, a planet has fallen, desiring to slay both humans and non-humans.
"He produces various states of being...

[Thus it is said. "By the previously mentioned procedure" means by the expansion of the potency of the mantra (*mantravīrya*) and so forth, as well as by the extensive collection of requisites such as the *bali* offering and so on.
Moreover,
whatever living beings have been brought here by various Rākṣasas will surely attain prosperity there, having sacrificed to the Lord of the Rākṣasas. (19.69)
Having been cultivated and grasped,
they all run about at night, yet each one gazes intently;
furthermore, he drinks wine and even eats his own flesh.
And Tāmra-varṇa likewise becomes a dweller in an empty village;
these are the characteristics of one seized by a Rākṣasa-graha. Thus they are described in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*. Nirṛti is the lord of the Rākṣasas. || 69 ||
Furthermore,
when a man is overcome by innumerable yakṣas,
he shall quickly attain liberation by worshipping Vaiśravaṇa.
And the characteristics of those possessed by yakṣas have been shown in the *Totula* itself: "The characteristic of one seized by a yakṣa is [the occurrence of] loud laughter and so forth.
Thus it is said.
His gaze becomes extremely fierce, and he runs about suddenly;
even while eating his food, he constantly worships the deity.
One who is fond of liquor and meat and consumes much blood—
this is the characteristic of one possessed by a yakṣa-graha. || 70 ||
Furthermore,
when the goddesses of the eight wombs are obstructed anywhere,
one should perform the Bhairava sacrifice and thereby attain prosperity. (19.71)

The eight wombs are the eightfold divisions beginning with the Piśācas; the various classes of divine wombs are the goddesses. O fair-faced one, it should be known that the Yoginīs are of the nature of reality (tattva), following the will of Śiva, possessing the speed of thought, and endowed with great power.
They all wander through the realms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
others, O beloved, are born of noble lineage, born from a womb, and born of a family.
"Those born of the *pīṭhas* and those born of the *kṣetras*, especially within the body"; likewise:
"The Yoginīs are to be known as born of the *pīṭhas*, and the deities are remembered as born of the *kṣetras*."
"The one born from the womb is said to be the embodied [form], and her divisions are indeed manifold.
Likewise:
"The heroines are born from the families of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras."
After twenty-seven years, they know that state.
"Śākinīs and Rudramātṛs born in other lineages," and likewise:
"The Śākinīs, the Rudra-Śākinīs, and others who are Śābarikas and Śivās."
And there are other yoginīs, by whom the entire world is pervaded.
The base woman always drinks the milk of living beings, drawing it out by means of her gait;
having obtained them for the sake of changing their form, she causes the beasts to fall.
She should be known as a Śākinī, always delighting in fierce places;
she knows the movements of others' minds and the transformation of forms.
She who acts out of greed for immortality should be known as a Rudra-śākinī;
those of the Śaiva sect who are likewise should be known as such, practicing in secret and delighting in the forest.
He does not cause anyone to be killed; he should taste the blood through a wound.
These others are to be known as Śābarīs, whose minds are fixed on the mantra and that [practice].
For they carry away all the five nectars and even human beings;
in an instant they roam the earth, assuming many forms.
Others, through the power of yoga, perceive the three periods of time;
those who are declared to be auspicious are devoted to mantra and meditation.

Thus, various [forms] are described in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva* by such passages as: "Likewise, those endowed with the eight qualities have boundary-pedestals (*paryantapadavedikā*)," and so forth. He is called Bhairava because he is the Lord of the entire wheel of powers (*sarvaśakticakra*).
In this sacrifice of Bhairava, an internal offering (antarbali) must be presented by all those who consume abundant food;
likewise, one who desires spiritual welfare should present an external offering in the sacred field (kṣetra). 19–72.

In the *araṇyaka* [section], there is another *bali* offering consisting of buffaloes, goats, and so forth; the *antarbali* is the *naivedya* (food offering); the *kṣetrapāla-bali* is outside; and in the forest, the *bhūta-bali* consists of buffaloes, goats, rams, and the like. Furthermore, here:
One should offer the bali-oblation with various substances such as black gram porridge, fish, and so forth;
and that [bali]...
...one should cause [the gift] to be bestowed upon all. || 19-73 ||
From the deities, yoginīs, bhūtas, and so forth. || 73 ||
And this [practice] should be performed on a riverbank, in a cremation ground, or in a forest or a circle of Mothers,
at dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight. (19.74)
It should be given to those who are strong; by that, they become satisfied.
One should always cause abundant food mixed with water to be given to them. (19.75)
"Therefore, O auspicious lady, may they all be satisfied with you; they shall unfailingly bestow the fruit of all that is most excellent, and they shall protect you like a mother. (19.76)
He explains the etymology of *bali*:
"Memory, vigor, victory, growth, body, lifespan, fame, and happiness—all these that were lost are given by means of *bala* (strength); therefore it is known as *bali*. (19.77)
And this entire ritual, ending with the offering to the *bali*, must be performed in this manner by one who has conquered death for the sake of all accomplishments.
Furthermore:
For the foolish whose selves are afflicted, being seized by the grasping at the aggregates. || 19-78 ||
Whenever women are overcome by the grasp of passion,
then Kārttikeya must certainly be worshipped according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The symptoms of the seizure of children:
"He always delights in their lap and, through association with children,
the youth himself dances and constantly plays in the dust."
Thus it is stated in that very [text]: "The previously mentioned procedure here [consists of] worship, fire-oblation, and so forth, by means of the mantra. (79)
For when this is done,
those infant-seizing spirits such as Skanda and others will quickly release them;
by the force of the word "and" (ca), the spirits that seize women during sexual intercourse are also included.
Having thus spoken specifically, he also spoke in general terms: "In whichever family one is sealed or fixed by a particular portion [of the seed-syllable], in that [family] one resides. (19.80)
By that very family [of deities] which is desired, one is liberated from all defects.

Whosoever is marked by a Yoginī, Bhūta, Graha, or the like, arising from the portion of a particular deity—whose strength is being swallowed or who is pinned down... having taken possession of the village... [one is liberated].
Once established, for him, spiritual welfare arises solely from the sacrifice to those respective deities.
Furthermore, the characteristics of those seized by planets arising from the portions of those respective deities and others are shown in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*.
He neither becomes angry nor does he rejoice, and he has no longing for food;
he does not speak anything at all, and sleep does not come upon him.
Neither urine nor excrement, nor any impurity, arises for him;
his face becomes as radiant in appearance as a lotus petal.
These are the characteristics of one seized by a celestial spirit (devagraha):
he sings, dances joyfully, and plays musical instruments with his mouth.
One who constantly delights in perfumes and garlands, subsists solely on milk,
is always of pleasant character, and never experiences aversion—
these are the characteristics of one seized by a gandharva.
He is constantly devoted to perfumes and flowers, and subsists solely on a diet of milk;
he has red eyes, casts his gaze downward, and does not bathe in rivers.
He plunges into water and always delights on the mountain;
he licks his tongue and gnashes his teeth.
For one seized by the *nāga*-graha, this is the characteristic:
he declares, "I am Viṣṇu, I am Brahmā, I am Rudra."
"I am Skanda and Viśākha; there is no one like us on earth.
Sometimes he eats food, and sometimes he does not eat at all."
He would despise the gods and he despises the Brahmins;
this is the characteristic of one possessed by an asura.
Engaged in austerity and the study of the Vedas, established in the grace of Brahman, he should always remain pure; impurity never remains with him.
He does not utter incorrect words; he studies equally with the twice-born, sings the Sāmaveda, and also recites the Ṛgveda.
"In all matters concerning the meaning of the Vedas, he constantly cites scripture;
yet he knows only what is to be known, and he runs about even while laughing—
this is the characteristic of one possessed by a Brahma-rākṣasa."

Thus, having ascertained those possessed by spirits such as gods and others by means of their characteristics, one should perform worship of the king of gods, the king of gandharvas, and so forth, here with the mantra.
Since this is so, for that purpose I have revealed all the secrets. || 19-81 ||
In this tantra, however, the nectar of all [deities] is presented according to the prescribed ritual;

for that which is the secret of all those respective deities— even the supreme non-duality— is composed of the potency of mantra, and that very nectar, in the form of the Lord of Mantra, has been [revealed] by me here through the ritual procedure.
It has been made clear.
Thus, the Mṛtyujit common to all tantras has been revealed. (19.82)
The heart of all is secret, unrevealed, and most wonderful;
its nature as the Heart and so forth is established precisely by the method already stated.
And because the manifestation of supreme non-duality has not yet arisen,
I have not been questioned by anyone...
and therefore:
...has not been told by me to anyone. || 19-83 ||
The secret...
[he states the reason for its secrecy]:
"And this tradition brings about all that is most auspicious and happiness."
"This" means "in fact"; for the particle *ca* is used in the sense of "indeed."
Since this is so, therefore those practitioners who are serene and who, being devoted, indeed worship [the deity], [attain success]. 19-84.
They are liberated from all suffering; this is my truth, not a false word.
By means of this very [practice], together with all the initiations and so forth, one's own purpose—the warding off of all suffering—is accomplished. (19.85)
The teacher, however, may cause [the rites] to be performed for his devotees, his own sons, and his own wives; and for his disciples and devotees, but he should not employ them otherwise. (19.86)

Having abandoned worldly affection and greed, one should act in this manner for the sake of devotees alone; or else, through sons and others, the devotee should have the teacher perform [the rites] regarding his own wife and so forth by means of this very [mantra].
The word "alone" (eva) expresses the majesty of this Lord of Mantras even when compared to other mantras.
Furthermore, this rite should always be performed by one desiring welfare for kings, who are the gurus of all stages of life (āśramas), as well as for their sons and wives. (19.87)
He possesses the status of a teacher to all stages of life and acts as a protector of his subjects in accordance with the scriptures.
And one should always perform this great mantra-yoga for the sake of pacification, whether it be regular, occasional, or for the fulfillment of specific desires.
Furthermore:
When the mouth has been washed, one should always apply a tilaka with white ashes.
It should be consecrated seven times for the removal of defects caused by the mother;
furthermore,
an ointment, a flower, or betel leaf may likewise be consecrated.
"Those who strike do not indeed strike him to whom [the gift] is given;
that is to say, they do not strike him at all.
Furthermore:"
And the knower of mantras should consecrate the food with this mantra.
Eating between both [rows], he partakes of immortality;
freed from all diseases, the king remains upon the earth. (19.91)

Thus, by means of this mantra— which consists of the vibration of the nature of consciousness (ciddharma) wherein the supreme nectar flows— and by meditating upon it according to the aforementioned method using the technique of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭīkāra*), the king who eats his food situated between the moon and the sun, having consecrated it, partakes of the nectar and attains immortality.
"King" is an elliptical designation.
And for him, at times of play accompanied by elephants and horses, during all games involving weapons, one should worship the *kalaśa* for the sake of protection. (19.92)
For the sake of sport, for the sake of victory, and for the sake of protection against harmful beings and the like;
during times of play— on occasions of games such as burning and so forth— for the sake of sport, that is, for the attainment of unimpeded play, [he set out] together with his elephants and horses.

By the use of the word "and" (ca), [it is implied that] one should worship the jar with this mantra for the sake of victory when the king is joined by ministers and the kingdom during occasions such as battle;
for protection during all forms of martial exercises; for the pacification of defects such as wounds from weapons;
and for protection against harmful beings and the like.
Because many wicked people desire to kill the king and others.
Therefore, protection must be performed in the form of the worship of the aforementioned water-pot (kalaśa).
By protecting all subjects in a manner that is agreeable to them, such protection becomes auspicious and brings about every form of well-being.
Thus, on occasions such as play and the like, one should worship the jar for the protection of the king who has been guarded at the head and is then asleep.
A silver vessel, joined with medicinal herbs, smeared with sandalwood and agallochum,
filled with milk and water—
[this is] the jar worshipped here.
...one should worship the supreme Mṛtyujit. || 19-95 ||

When the Blessed Lady has been thus worshipped with entirely white offerings— flowers, incense, water for the hands, and milk-rice— the Great Sleep, which causes the delusion of the world, stands before her.

One should contemplate that for the sake of the king's happiness, and for the sake of digesting food and so forth during the night, the God of Gods has initiated [these activities] after having given his command. (19.97)

One should contemplate that after the King has given his command, [the goddesses] stood before him at night and began— that is, set in motion— their activity for the sake of his comfortable sleep and for the sake of digesting his food and so forth. When this has been done, the King...
Then, he should remain awake for the entire night with sleep;
moreover,
[he is protected] from yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and the like, as well as from bad dreams arising from the mātr̥s.

Freed from fear, terror, and suffering, he may remain at ease; moreover, when the world-protectors have gone to their respective directions, he should remain for the sake of protection in the presence of the king, equipped with weapons. (19.99)
Once the water-pot has been worshipped, worship with offerings such as water for the guest (argha) and flowers should be performed.
And therefore, for a certain king purified by the descent of power (śaktipāta), the supreme enlightened teacher (daiśikottama) should constantly perform [this] in this manner. || 19-100 ||
The worship of the jar and so forth;
such a person attains what was previously described.
Enjoyment, liberation, and so forth.
And this is not impossible,
since the Blessed Lord Śiva has said:
"Furthermore..."
And in all ritual signs (nimitteṣu), one should also worship Amṛteśa.
Kāmarūpa is always that which has the form of the deity associated with the specific occasion, namely Amṛteśa.
...because one shall obtain all desires,
since it has been stated that this [mantra] is like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
He clarifies the statement "in the signs" slightly:
"for the sake of protecting the subjects and for the prosperity of the rice crops. (19.102)
For the protection of his wives, for the prosperity of his kingdom, and for the victory of the king, he should there worship the form of Indra. (19.103)
"In that context" means on the occasion of Indra’s day; the connection is that it is for the sake of the king's own victory.
Furthermore, for the sake of protecting cows, Brahmins, oneself, and one's own kin,
one should be worshipped at home on the Mahānavamī day with abundant sacrifice.
For when this is so,
one indeed attains the aforementioned perfection of longevity and health;
moreover—
The sacrifice with weapons (astrayāga) should be performed with great effort for the sake of attaining accomplishment.
On the Mahānavamī day itself. || 105 ||
For in this way, the sacrificer attains the perfection of the weapon (*astra-siddhi*) and,
through the power of the mantra, brings forth divine weapons.
And it says that the king and others obtain victory:
"The performer enjoys the fruit.
The "performer" is the one previously mentioned as the one who causes the sacrifice to be performed.
Furthermore, when a king, seized by time, has fallen under the power of death; || 19-106 ||

Indeed, when there are signs of impending death (ariṣṭa) for oneself, or for the region, or for one's children and so forth, and when all beings beginning with Brahmā face the destruction of their realm, [one should perform this rite]. (19.107)
And regarding rice and other crops, fruits, roots, and water,
as well as during famines, epidemics, and great portents— || 19.108 ||
Then the *nīrājana* (lustration) rite should be performed by the king for the increase of the kingdom.

From the words "sons and so forth," it follows that when portents occur to the king, and when there is destruction among the Brahmins and others, then by means of water— that is, the water of consecration (*abhiṣeka*)— there is the cleansing (*ajana*) of all defects.
For the purpose of warding off [the enemy], the casting [of the weapon] must be performed so as to produce a complete and radiant luster.
He begins to speak of that: having performed the sacrifice as before, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the water-pot. || 19.109 ||
How so? He says:

"Fearlessly in a secluded place at night, under an auspicious constellation and likewise in its [corresponding] *aṃśaka*, accompanied by shouts of 'Victory! and 'Auspicious Day!', and with the resonant sounds of Vedic benedictions. (19.110)
One should consecrate the king in a secluded place, free from people, as a secret location.
Then the teacher,
O beloved, should offer many oblations of perfected substances into the consecrated fire marked with the [disciple's] name, according to the rite of lustration (nīrājana).
With his mind restrained within the fire, the mantra-practitioner, intent on protection, should sprinkle many goats for the sake of satisfying the assembly of spirits.
The *nīrājana* is the production of extraordinary radiance preceded by the application of the root mantra. The formula for this is:
"May there be the *nīrājana* of [Name], svāhā. Furthermore, the compound *bhūtasaṅghaḥ* means "the spirits and the assembly";
the "assembly" (*saṅgha*) refers to the group consisting of the Mothers, Yoginīs, and so forth. || 112 ||
Thus, having set aside the ritual ending with the offering (bali),
and having ascertained an auspicious omen through the utterances of birds or by the movement of its parts,
one who sets out under the asterisms of Yakṣendra, Śiva, or Vāruṇī attains all success. (19.113)

Having ascertained an auspicious omen, a favorable moment, or a propitious time— either by consulting the tables of luminaries (*jyotirgaṇa*) or through one's own knowledge of the favorable divisions (*śubhāṃśaka*)— one should proceed from any direction other than the north, east, northeast, or west, which are presided over by the Lord of Yakṣas (*Yakṣeśvara*) and others.
The teacher who sets out together with the king intent on the conquest of the quarters becomes the bestower of all success. || 113 ||
After the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*), one should then cause the sacrifice (*yāga*) to be performed in the king’s house according to the previously mentioned procedure,
O Goddess, for seven days, which bestows success through abundant oblations.
In the phrase "by means of abundant oblation" (*bhūrihomena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). || 114 ||
And for whatever purpose one thus performs this sacrifice— whether it be for unshakable Great Fortune (Mahālakṣmī) or whatever kingdom one desires— that comes to pass.
And that king, being happy, shall attain both terrestrial and celestial perfections.
Whenever that occurs, it is known as the supreme *nīrājana*, which brings about all prosperity;
what more can be said of this?
O Goddess, it destroys the aforementioned defects; there is no doubt about this.
And one should worship this Lord of Mantras among the cows, because by doing so the herd of cattle will always increase;
and therein—
The knower of mantras, having consecrated either vermilion or red ochre with the mantra, [should apply it].
One should apply it above the horns of cows for their protection, as it conquers all defects;
furthermore,
one should worship for the protection of horses as well, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
And there, having consecrated a water-pot with mantras, one should pour it over their heads;
furthermore, white mustard seeds over which the mantra has been recited should be applied to the throat and then to the head. (19.119)
In this very way,
the consecrated *siddhārtha* protects elephants that are entirely free from all defects.
Furthermore,
one should cause this protection to be performed for all animals, beginning with goats.
It should always be employed by the king for the protection of all living beings;
the connection is that it applies to all living beings who are related to the king.
For in this way,
there shall be great peace for them, and the famine will perish in an instant.
Furthermore, in all great terrors— such as earthquakes, the falling of meteors, excessive rain, drought, and fears caused by rats and other pests— [one should recite this]. (19.122)
By flowers and the like that have blossomed out of season, by gods who have perished or been mutilated, by defects such as fever and *lūtā* (scorpions/spiders), and indeed by untimely deaths; 19-123.
If the maṇḍala has been afflicted by various kinds of sufferings, whatever faults of karma there may be, as well as the faults of the planets, [they shall be removed]. (19.124)

Likewise, disappearance, that which has arisen, the breach of mantra, and that which is free from [such faults], as well as the defects of poison from snakes and the like, and insects, boils, and so forth. (19.125)
And disorders of wind and bile, as well as all types of phlegm-related defects, hemorrhoids, eye diseases, and likewise erysipelas and other such ailments. || 126 ||
There are thousands of other diseases and humors arising from wounds and the like, as well as internal maladies such as grief and so forth that destroy the mind. (127)
When people, beginning with Brahmā, are cursed by the gods and others,
then, as before, a sacrifice must be performed for the sake of pacification.

"By the ruined" means by those [maṇḍalas] damaged by fire and so forth; "by the broken" means by those that are cracked. The connection is: "if the maṇḍala has been smelled. "Faults of ritual action" (karmadoṣāḥ) are the sufferings born of improper rites. "Concealment" (tirobhāvaḥ) is the sin arising from offenses against the deity or the guru. "A flaw in the mantra" (mantracchidra) arises from conduct not prescribed by rule.

The fault arises from the failure to propitiate the mantra. As it is said elsewhere: "I see no other defect in a practitioner during the accomplishment of the mantra than this: that he merely wavers, lacking the proper signs. Nāgas are serpents. The eruptions produced by internal insects are caused by worms.

There are insect-bites and those born from wounds arising from sores; there are internal ones resembling internal tumors. Furthermore, for the increase of the kingdom of kings, a daily fire-oblation (havana) must be performed for this King of Mantras.
By the teacher.
When this has been done by the king, the kingdom is enjoyed with ease; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. || 19-129 ||
For by the mere act of worshipping once, the malevolent spirits and others are destroyed;
they flee in the ten directions like deer before a lion. (19.130)
Furthermore, through the practice of constant repetition of these mantras, worship, and so forth, poverty is destroyed from the family.
Moreover:
In whatever country and at whatever time the knower of mantras may dwell, [he should always act accordingly]. // 19.131 //
Calamities, diseases, and indeed Khārkhoda spirits or planetary influences, as well as various Śākinīs, Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas—[all these shall not harm him]. (19.132)
Child-seizing spirits, eruptive boils, and other *vyantara* demons;
all types of poisons, famine, and the affliction of malevolent planets. (19.133)
Nothing shall prevail there due to the presence of one who knows the mantras:
the *khārkhoda* spells employed by others, mechanical devices (*yantra*), and dense *vyantara* spirits.
Therefore, such a teacher is always to be honored by all living beings and by kings alike. (19.134)
For if he is honored with incomparable gifts, worship, and respect,
then by his mere worship, all mantras are worshipped. (19.135)
Those who face him there bestow happiness; therefore, one should worship those who face him. "There" means where the preeminent teacher is worshipped.
And because the seizing spirits, who everywhere act as cutters, indeed harm the practitioner. || 19-136 ||
Therefore, water and rice should always be offered to the planets;
the meaning is that both water and rice [are to be given].
For in this way, the planets are indeed satisfied; and when they are satisfied, they do not exert their power.
And when the planets are unfavorable,
then protection must be performed by the high-souled preceptor.
Then, for the sake of determining the true nature of protection, the Illustrious Goddess said:
But this protection, O God, has been taught out of compassion for living beings. (19.138)
"What kind is it said to be? For whom is it performed?
And how?"—thus he clarifies the questions concerning its essential nature and its modes:
"The pervasive Person is indeed declared to be formless for all embodied beings. (19–139)
That embodied being, who exists both externally and internally, is indeed devoid of qualities and bodiless;
for that person who is the embodied self is, by nature, formless, all-pervasive— dwelling within and without—
and in reality free from the qualities of *sattva* and the rest, being without a body.
Then,
how indeed is its protection performed, and for what reason is it protected?
For this [Self], which is the one form of eternal, all-pervading consciousness and is partless, it is impossible for it to be an object of either injury or protection.
(140) Now, if it is argued that the Self is not protected, but rather the body—regarding that as well, he says: "Or else, how is the body, which is composed of parts, to be protected?"
It is said to be fashioned and impelled by the great elements, such as earth and the rest.

The meaning is that although it is worthy of protection because it is complete, it cannot be protected because, being composed of the elements such as earth and so forth, its destruction is inevitable. Nor is there any third thing to be protected;
he says this by asking: "How, from where, by what, or how could it be protected? and so on.
Why, O Lord, should a third person be protected, and how?
Why indeed should he be protected, and by whom? Tell me, O wielder of the trident. (19.142)
"How" means in what manner; "from what" means from what cause of fear; "by what" means for what reason—this is the meaning here.
"O Blessed One, tell me all this without exception: what is protection?
By 'this' is meant the object and the manner of protection; and what would be protection in its essential nature—this is the meaning."
To resolve this matter, the Blessed Lord said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme question; I have not been asked about it by the gods or asuras, nor by Garuḍa and others, nor by my many disciples, nor even by the sages. (19.143)

"Questioned" means a question; that which is to be questioned is the nature of the protection, yet I have not been questioned by anyone at all. "Listen to this matter"—by these words, the Goddess's knowledge of reality is praised.
And that matter regarding which you have thus asked me for the sake of a question, I shall explain to you today; listen, O large-eyed one. (19.144)
In this regard, he begins to determine the true nature of protection:
"The Puruṣa is all-pervading, subtle, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), inactive, and immovable;
therefore, He is not subject to protection."
However, the impurity is threefold: that of the individual soul (āṇava), that of action (kārma), and that of illusion (māyīya). || 19-145 ||
He possesses this. || 145 ||
And because of that connection, he is indeed impure, dependent, and powerless;
for he is not purified until there is the cessation of the three impurities. (19.146)

Since this [individual soul] is impure due to the cessation of the three impurities (*mala*), it is therefore stained because it is veiled by the impurities such as *kalā* and the rest; it is dependent because it is subject to *karman*; and it is powerless, devoid of both knowledge and agency, due to the influence of the *āṇavamala*. || 146 ||
Regarding this, [the author] asks: "How can there be a connection with impurity for this which consists of consciousness? He says: "Or how could one who is stainless be attached to enjoyments...?
How could there be a desire for impure enjoyment in one who is pure and a mass of perfect consciousness and bliss?"

Only for one who possesses the *āṇavamala*, whose nature consists of the conceit of being incomplete (*apūrṇamanyatā*) manifested by the power of *māyā*, does the desire consisting of the principle of *rāga*— in the form of "May something be mine"—
arise. Otherwise, in this regard...
...this is contradicted;
for one who is stainless cannot be attached to enjoyments.
This clarifies [the point]:
"One who is pure but an enjoyer shall not attain perfection," because:
...conceptual construction is called enjoyment. || 19-147 ||

Samsara is nothing but conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). For that which is pure, a mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaghana*), there arises the state of being a transmigrating being, whose experience consists in the perception of pleasure and pain; this experience, though ultimately unreal, is essentially conceptual construction. As it is said elsewhere: "If impurity does not exist..."
"What causes a person's attachment to enjoyment?
Thus [it is asked].
Since enjoyment, which is the essence of transmigratory existence, is not appropriate for one who is pure, therefore...
[the soul] of the bound being (paśu) is always in transmigration; and for that which is subject to transmigration and bound, purity is not possible. (19.148)

The "bound soul" (paśu) is the individual soul (aṇu) rendered ignorant by the impurity of ignorance (āṇavamala). "Transmigration" (saṃsaraṇa) is the movement from one experience to another. "Of this transmigrating being" refers to one who has been brought into the state of transmigration by the power of the Supreme Lord. 148.

Since this is so, this atomic impurity (āṇava-mala) is subtle; for it is established through its effects. From that [impurity], desire arises toward enjoyment and the like, and that [desire] is the instigator [of bondage]. || 19-149 ||
From the desire belonging to the self whose essence is *rāga*, this [self] is inferred to consist of the state of considering itself incomplete in the form of cause and effect;
as for that which is stated: "But here, impurity (*mala*) is indeed desire" (4.105).

Thus it is stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra*; therein, the *āṇava-mala* is intended as that which consists of desire for objects characterized by particularity and generality, whose nature is non-detachment and passion (*rāga*), whose essence is the conceit of incompleteness (*apūrṇamanyatā*), and which is a desire for [the cessation of] action (*niṣkarma*).

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "in enjoyment and so forth," it is meant that this applies even to the position held by the Sāṃkhyas and others, which is considered to be based on reality. || 149 ||
Having thus determined the limited soul (*āṇava*), he speaks in order to determine the dyad:

"The wise know that which has karma as its cause and results in experience—consisting of place, time, and body—as well as that which begins with *kalā* and ends with earth, as the effect of *māyā*. (19.150)
Experience (*bhoga*), which is the consciousness of pleasure and so forth, is the effect of that which is the *kārma* impurity (*mala*);

that arises from the previously mentioned causes, namely space, time, and the body. However, the thirty principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *pṛthivī* constitute the effect of *māyā*, known as the *māyīya* impurity. || 150 ||
He applies this to the subject at hand:
"In this way, the individual soul (aṇu), endowed with the three impurities, wanders in saṃsāra;
just as a silkworm firmly encloses itself within its cocoon. (151)

Just as that [cocoon] is capable of enveloping itself through its own coils, so too is this Self capable of enveloping itself within the cage of bonds; by means of its own power alone, it assumes the state of an individual soul (aṇu), according to the analogy of the silkworm, and not otherwise.

It is the state of being obstructed by the power of impurity (*mala*), which consists of the nature of a substance distinct [from consciousness]. This has been determined by us at the end of the fifth chapter in the *Śrī-svacchandoddyota*.
And therefore, as long as the powerful Lord God does not bestow his grace upon him, [he cannot succeed]. || 19-152 ||
The individual soul remains concealed by the embrace of power for as long as the Supreme Lord— having manifested the state of the individual soul through the concealment of His own power—
does not grace that state of the individual soul by the expansion of His innate power; [during that time], it remains hidden by the shrouding of His own māyā-śakti.
The sacrificial animal remains hidden.
Here, he refutes the view of the non-theists (anīśvaravādins) by first raising an objection: "Now, if there were no Lord, the entire world would be independent. (19.153)
It is accepted by the Buddhists, Mīmāṃsakas, Sāṃkhyas, and others. || 153 ||
Therefore, there would be no restriction among causes;
for, according to the doctrine that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*), anything could arise from anything whatsoever, or [arise] from what is non-existent.

Since existence as a real entity (*satsvabhāvatā*) is impossible, there would be no causal restriction whatsoever regarding what arises from what. However, this is consistent with the view of one who maintains that an entity exists solely by virtue of its own nature, independent of anything else, according to which whatever is observed immediately following another thing is of the nature of being produced by that [preceding] thing.

Even though actions are insentient and consist merely of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) residing in the self, their diversity of ripening and their status as causes of results would not be possible without the superintendence of God.

Furthermore, even in the view of those who maintain that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*), since everything exists [everywhere], nothing could ever be the cause of anything anywhere.

If manifestation and so forth belong to that which is non-existent, then there is the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) due to its cause; furthermore, even in the theory of ignorance (*avidyāvāda*), if Brahman is not the agent and ignorance is insubstantial (*tuccha*), the diversity of the world cannot be accounted for. If, on the other hand, that which appears is admitted to be non-insubstantial, then even though it is insubstantial, [the world would exist] by mere assertion.
If ignorance were a real entity (*vastu*), then the consequence of duality would follow, which is not tenable; thus, Janaka [rightly] held it to be truly unsubstantial.
Otherwise, without the power of the Supreme Lord—who is pure, autonomous, and a mass of consciousness—there would be no restriction upon causes.
And therefore...
"It would all be inconsistent"; this is the implied conclusion.
He connects the subject at hand by means of an analogy:
"Just as a certain bull is bound by a tethering rope. (19.154)
Like a bull, the bound soul (paśu) is tied with fetters— the rope and the [impurities] such as the *āṇava*— and being dependent, it is joined with enjoyments that are like mere grass.
And therefore,
there is a certain supreme subject who is the destroyer of the bonds of that object.
Just as one who is capable [is seen], so too is the Lord a bestower of grace;
Śiva, the doer of all for all, is empowered by his own power.
Regarding the phrase "of that which is to be grasped" (grāhyasya), he is the destroyer of bonds, the liberator from bonds, and like a supreme capable [master].

Only some [beings] are so, but not all; likewise, the Lord Śiva, who is the creator of all and the sovereign, is capable because he is augmented by his own power whose nature is absolute freedom (svātantrya), and thus he is the benefactor of all. || 156 ||
That power by which he is strengthened is never separated from him, just as the rays are inseparable from the sun.
Furthermore:
In fire, which possesses both heat and light, heat is never separated [from it]. (19.157)

Just as that is so, even so is that power of the Lord inseparable from Him, whose essence is Śiva; she alone is the Goddess who is the cause of the universe, though she exists in manifold forms. || 19-158 ||
He clarifies this very multiplicity:
"She exists in the form of will, knowledge, and action, according to the distinction of her functions (*kṛtya*).

Because she manifests the appearance of the world as indistinct, distinct, and so forth—being the threads that weave together the objects of desire, the objects of knowledge, and the objects of action—she is [the Goddess]."
The single power of absolute freedom exists in the form of the triad of *hā* [the subject], *ā* [the object], and *i* [the means].
And for this reason, that non-terrible will became pervasive and inherent. || 19-159 ||
The one who abides in the state of grasping is terrible, yet her nature is knowledge;
another is even more terrible than the terrible, for she is the agitator whose essence is action. (19.160)

That in which no form of terrible duality or contact exists is Aghorā; she is the Supreme (Parā), whose nature is the non-dual light of the entire universe in its subtlest state, intent upon grace, and therefore all-pervasive, inherent, and non-different from Śiva. Ghorā, on the other hand, has the form of the manifestation of both difference and non-difference.

*Parāparā*: for this very reason, she exists as one whose nature is to accept (*svīkāra*) the universe—by grasping it from all sides (*paritaḥ samantāt*) upon her own screen (*svabhitti*), even though it is not distinct from herself, as if it were distinct, in the form of its manifestation;
she is *ghoraghoratarā*, having the form of the clear appearance of the differentiation of the universe, and is therefore *kṣobhikā*, the agitator.
She is the manifestation of the impurity consisting of the grasped and the grasper, and she is the supreme form.

This very one, who reveals such non-duality, duality, and the non-duality of duality, whose nature consists of will, knowledge, and action, is the single supreme power of freedom belonging to Lord Bhairava, referred to in the scriptures by names such as Śrī Mātṛsadbhāva.
This is the protection of all beings, the protection that protects all;

because she is recognized through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), she protects all things born of transmigratory existence. Thus, this essential protection is truly well-protected by that very name.
And he says that this is logical:
"And that initiation is declared to be characterized by giving and destruction. (19.161)
For what purpose? Giving is for the manifestation of auspiciousness (śivatva), while the destruction is that of the fetters (pāśas). || 161 ||
For in this very manner, it removes all defects;
as such, its protection of the all-pervading Person is not contradictory. || 19-162 ||

"By this very [means]" refers to the form of initiation consisting of giving, austerity, and self-surrender (*dāna-kṣapaṇātma-dīkṣā*). "It is not contradictory" because it reveals the essential nature of the all-pervading individual soul (*aṇu*). || 162 ||
Furthermore, what other protection that guards all beings shall I proclaim?
He speaks of it preceded by a demonstration of its domain:
Through the cessation of the three impurities, there arises the fruit of various karmas. || 19-163 ||
That which impels the senses toward objects such as sound and so forth,
residing in the center of the heart-lotus, is the instigator of dharma and adharma.
Overcome by passion and hatred, veiled within by the threefold internal organ,
and bound by cause and effect through the instruments joined with the elements.
Bound indeed by impurity alone, hundreds and thousands of times,
through hundreds of distinctions between what ought and ought not to be done, and through the activities of merit and demerit.
One whose innate consciousness has been eclipsed is designated as a *jīva*;
its protection is prescribed by means of various extensive mantras.
Through the instruments, machines, and tantras of Śiva, the Supreme Self,
that protection of living beings is declared to be the Great Goddess Kriyāśakti.

Because of the manifestation— that is, the coming into presence— of the various fruits of karma, such as the experiences of pleasure and so forth, which is brought about by being enveloped by the three impurities (mala),
one proceeds with intense attachment toward the means of enjoyment, namely the senses such as the eyes, whose objects are sound and the rest.
And therefore, although residing within the heart, it is through the activity of the senses alone that it impels and excites one toward dharma and adharma;
for this very reason, being overwhelmed by attachment and aversion which adhere to pleasure and pain,
it is subject to the internal organs such as the intellect through its functions of determination and so forth, [and is thus manifested] by its effects.
It is bound by objects such as form and by causes situated within the category of the causal aggregate (kāraṇaskandha), namely the intellect, ego, and subtle elements; likewise,
it is bound without remainder by the thirteen instruments conjoined with the gross elements beginning with earth.

Having assumed the form of the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) and the gross body (*sthūladeha*), thus, by all this— extending down to the elements— which consists of the manifestation of objects and is a stain upon consciousness, [the Self is bound] "hundreds of times" in the form of the manifold expansion of the activity of passion (*rāga-vṛtti*). Thus.

That whose innate, natural consciousness— consisting of the nature of knowledge and agency— is obscured by activities in the form of verbal, mental, and physical operations, which give rise to innumerable merits and demerits characterized as specific things to be done or not to be done, and which has thus fallen into a state of subordination to the qualities (guṇas) such as emptiness (śūnya), is called the *jīva*.

And that which protects the individual soul—the self whose nature is consciousness and consists of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka)—along with the Supreme Self, Śiva, by means of the operations of mantra and tantra, is the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who is of the nature of the power of action (kriyāśakti); thus she is called the "mighty protection. || 168 ||
Furthermore,
there is another third protection which guards the body from all great fears.
He spoke to describe her, who removes the various fears caused by those respective [factors], such as spirits, yakṣas, and grahas: || 19-169 ||
Together with the ḍāvis and ḍāmarikās, as well as the sisters and mothers, the śākinīs and yoginīs, and those such as Mukhamaṇḍitaka and the rest. || 19.170 ||
That which certainly pacifies the fear caused by all various and exhaustive harmful beings is called the protective power (rakṣā-śakti). || 19-171 ||

The *mukhamaṇḍitakas* are specific types of spirits (*bhūta-viśeṣas*); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [beings such as] *nṛsiṃhas* and others are included. "Power" (*śakti*) is precisely what is called action (*kriyā*). The remainder has already been largely explained previously.
And therefore:
This body is born of the elements, impure, unstable, and impermanent, due to the various combinations of wind, bile, phlegm, and their disorders. (19.172)
This physical body is corrupted by hundreds of various defects; moreover, many malevolent assailants with wicked intentions seek to destroy it. (19.173)
There are beings born of wind, born of bile, born of phlegm, and born of the combination of all three;
some desire food, some desire pleasure, and others likewise desire to kill. (19.174)
And many harmful beings, desiring to return to their offspring, having reached the abode of Vāta, indeed arise from Vāta. (19.175)

Those born of *pitta* disturb their own location as well as that of *pitta*; those born of *kapha* disturb their own location; and those born of the combination of all three (*sannipāta*) disturb all locations.
They cause this agitation for the purpose of destruction; therefore, the protection of the body is necessary for that reason.
Protection through the application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and ritual practices has indeed been enjoined by Śiva. (19.177)
That [practice] which bestows auspiciousness should be performed constantly; it is the remover of both auspicious and inauspicious states.

Because it is born of the elements, it is impure; it is unstable, perishable, non-eternal, and subject to transformation at every moment; it is corrupted by the humors such as wind and so forth for all living beings.
The body is contemptible, and many harmful beings indeed injure it; these are spirits born of wind and other humors who cause madness. As it is said in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara*:
"Those born of wind, those of bile, those of phlegm, and those arising from the combination [of all three]."
Having begun thus:
"Always fond of perfumes and garlands, resorting to windy places,
he is constantly tormented by thirst and speaks very harshly."
One who constantly sleeps and likewise eats day and night—
by these signs, he should be known as one who has resorted to the pitta constitution.
But he who constantly desires and emits only froth,
being intent solely on inedible things, should be known as one who has resorted to the phlegmatic state.
Relying upon the three humors (doṣas), it manifests in various forms; that insanity (unmāda) arising from the combination of all three (sāṃnipātika) should be known as difficult to treat.
Thus they agitate and distort [the mind]; for this reason, the body is protected by her.
That protection, known by that name, has been described as having the aforementioned form; it is conducive to welfare, the very embodiment of prosperity, and the pacifier of misfortune.
Therefore,
O beloved, one should satisfy those who desire offerings with powerful and voracious beings.
And the characteristic of one desiring to return: "He who becomes agitated and looks all around,
and in whom fever, burning heat, pain, and headache arise."
"One who, hungry or afflicted by thirst, says 'Give!
Give!', should be known as one desiring an offering (*balikāma*).
Thus it is stated in that very same [text]. || 178 ||
"Those desiring to eat [the victim] seek to kill him...
And their characteristics are as follows:
'He whose eyes are red and who speaks with excitement..."
"One whose characteristic is such as this would be a planet desirous of consuming [the victim].
Thus it is stated in that very same work.
And these are destroyed through the application of mantras;
they perish by means such as striking with water consecrated by the recitation of mantras.
Those desiring pleasure [should employ] all the various tantras as well as medicinal herbs. || 19-179 ||
The minister, established in grace, should encourage them through the application of mantra;
their characteristic mark therein is that they become constantly devoted to bathing, pure, and ever-anxious.
He should always be the first to speak and should ask for enjoyments.
He is fond of perfumes and garlands, and desires clothing and ornaments;
he is always pleasant-spoken and causes no obstruction.
"He delights in female bodies and rejoices in various [objects]," so it is said.
But those who are described as desirous of killing are invincible and possess great strength.
Regarding them also, in that very same [text]:
"But he who shakes his hair and stares at the physician,
desiring to kill him..."
Thus it is said:
"One may enter fire or likewise fall into water;
one falls upon the earth through negligence, and then dances and weeps."
"This indeed is the characteristic of one who is seized by the desire to kill"—thus the characteristic was stated. They are difficult to overcome, powerful, and hard to endure. || 180 ||
Nevertheless, by the power of the majesty of the Supreme Lord’s mantra, and through the influence of Śiva’s energy, they perish here; of this there is no doubt. (19.181)
The power of Śiva and Śakti consists in being subject to their command. || 181 ||
He concludes the incidental discussion:
"Thus, this determination of the elements has been briefly stated;
however, for the benefit of living beings, the detailed account is described elsewhere. (19.182)
Except in cases such as the *Śrītōtulakriyākālaguṇōttara* and others;
for therein it says:
"Therefore, with water consecrated by mantra and joined with meditative concentration..."
"O Guhyaka, having touched him, you should say: 'Speak the truth.'"
"Who are you, and for what reason have you seized this human being?
What honor is being paid to you? Speak the truth; what do you desire?"
Speak thus to me always, remembering the word of Rudra:
having placed a cloth as an interposition, one should extend the left hand.
"One should contract [the limbs] secretly and likewise declare the truth," and so forth; there is much [to be said].
He concludes the present topic:
"In this way, protection is performed; when well-understood, it becomes well-executed."
Otherwise, however, it should be understood by the yogin here that it leads to one's own destruction.

"Thus" (evam) refers to that [knowledge] which is well-understood by way of its essential nature as the pervasion of the supreme power (parā-śakti) and so forth as previously described; by way of its subject matter, namely universal protection, protection of living beings, and protection of the body; and by way of its practical application, consisting of the performance of ritual offerings (bali-karma), mantras, tantras, yoga, and other such procedures.
If protection is performed, it shall be well-done. || 183 ||
Furthermore,
protection should be performed in many ways according to the traditional teachings;
therein:
The first is the protection of the support; the second is the protection of the seed. || 19-184 ||
The third is the protection of the fetus; the fourth occurs at the time of birth;
the fifth is the protection of the woman who has given birth; and having bathed, the sixth [rite] takes place here.
The seventh is declared for children, and likewise the eighth for men;
O beloved, I shall now fully explain these various divisions pertaining to the supports (ādhāras) and so forth.
I shall correctly proclaim and explain. || 186 ||
In this regard,
those who contemplate reality must provide the highest protection for their mother and father, because everything depends upon them.
Regarding this, he states the reasoning: "A man who is severely bitten by defects will indeed have assailants arise against him. (19.187)
They harm him who ought to be protected; therefore, one must strive for his well-being.

Faults previously mentioned by the wise—namely passion, hatred, lack of discipline, and so forth—have thoroughly bitten, or nearly touched, every person. Consequently, regarding this [person] as previously described...
For there arise those who would do him harm, and they indeed harm him; therefore, that person must be protected for the sake of his own existence and for the sake of the procreation of his lineage.
Furthermore, precisely because she is bitten by the defects, when a woman is possessed by spirits, then conception does not occur. || 188 ||
And thus, the first protection is proclaimed as being called the "support" (ādhāra).
The phrase "and thus" means "for this reason. The support consists of the parents;
because it is dependent upon them, it is the "protection of the support. He now states the protection of the seed (bīja):
For the body of all living beings consists of flesh and blood. || 19.189 ||
Then, two things must be protected by those who recite mantras;
"two" refers to the semen and the blood. The meaning is that protection of the seed must be ensured during the menstrual period.
Moreover,
there are many planetary spirits who desire pleasure and act according to their own whims.
They drink both semen and blood; when this [semen] is destroyed, how can there be conception?
Therefore, for that reason, if this is protected, conception will occur. (19.191)
"In this" refers to that which consists of semen and blood; "birth from the seed" means conception in the womb. || 191 ||
He states the third [case]:
"When the cause has arisen in the womb, the abortion must be guarded against.
Regarding the word "arisen," it means within the womb.
The fourth [verse] is spoken by those skilled in the methods of protection for women at the time of childbirth.
Protection must be practiced with effort...

the course of protection is as previously described: pervasion; therein, by those who are expert and possess stainless intellects, through the application of mantras, worship, effort, and medicinal herbs, by means of the self which is preeminent.
One must guard it with effort.
And thus...
for here, indeed, the violent do not harm;
"here" means at the time of birth.
He teaches the fifth [verse] as a protection for the newborn, for the child staying in that house until the mother has become pure after childbirth. || 19-193 ||
Until then, the defects and other evils arising from the lying-in chamber afflict [the child] if there is no protection;
therefore, it must be well-guarded by the wise with external weapons and other means. || 19-194 ||
"It must be done," meaning that it should be performed in the lying-in chamber. || 194 ||
Regarding the sixth [verse], he says:
"But at the time of the postpartum bath, powerful spirits harm either the infant or whoever is present there; therefore, one should provide protection during the bath. || 19-195 ||

And "whoever else"—meaning anyone other than a newborn infant, such as a child or another person—who stands there in that bath-house, the spirits (bhūtas) indeed harm him; therefore, one should protect [them]. || 195 ||
Regarding the seventh [day], he says:
"After bathing, during the subsequent time, the children must be protected along with their nurses.
Those children who remain after the bath are to be guarded. (19.196)
Why should the nurse be protected? He says: "The nurse, however, is the cause of that [protection] through nourishment by means of the touch of milk and so forth. (196)
Therefore, the nurse must protect the infant at the outset and thereafter;
furthermore, he must be protected at all times through the application of mantras and medicinal herbs. (19.197)
With unwearied devotion, one should perform [the rites] by means of dhāraṇās, meditations, mudrās, yantras, and incenses,
as well as with oblations (homa) made of sesame, clarified butter, and other substances, and with various auspicious water-pots (kalaśa).
Indeed, he should always be protected by means of consecrations upon his head.
That child who is worthy of protection and possesses an auspicious form must be guarded at all times with vigilance; however, one of ill birth is not so.
Furthermore,
[the mantras] are awakened, as well as those that are asleep, weeping, or consecrated.
Whether he is eating, lying down, standing, or playing; at dawn, at midnight, in the evening, or during the midday period.
At all times of the twilight, one should diligently protect the child while he is playing or wandering about.
To the question of why one should protect [the food] with effort during the twilights, he says:
"Among the gods, the asuras, the spirits, and the sisters of the Mothers. (19–20ab)
The conjunction of malevolent planets and piśācas occurs at the time of twilight;
therefore, the child must be protected during all twilights.
Thus,
whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, one is protected at all times.
He demonstrates this very point:
O Goddess, indeed, those who wish to harm will seek to kill one who is traveling here merely by seeing him.
But those most terrifying beings seal him who remains without protection;
they terrify from all sides him who is healthy yet sleeping through deception.
These lowest of seizing spirits cause terror only to one who is awake at night;
therefore, with every effort, the child must always be protected.
O beloved, one should not live by other means, but without the practice of mantras;
moreover,
a prince in particular must indeed be protected by the masters of the teachings.
He enjoys good fortune and is highly praised, being endowed with all the auspicious marks;
and because of that, he experiences his fortunes through the resulting fruits.
Having seen [the infant] with effort, even the wicked desire to kill the auspicious child.
Therefore, O Goddess, by every means— whether by continuous earth-fortifications, by the rampart-weapon (*prākārāstra*), or by various auspicious mantras— one should protect him.
Or by means of written yantras and yogas, worshipped with great effort, encircled, fastened around the neck, or bound with threads scented with perfumes and the like. (19–209)
With various kinds of incense, with worn jewels,
or even with protective *tilaka* marks preceded by the ritual waving of lights (*nīrājana*).
A child must always be protected, and a prince especially so.

The *dhāraṇās* consist of forms such as filling the *brahmadvāra* with nectar flowing from the lunar disc situated upon a downward-facing white lotus. Regarding the "worshipped [deities] of the *yantra*-yogas," and so forth.
The three qualifiers [beginning with] "clinging to the neck" are to be understood through the "crow's eye" principle (*kākākṣivat*). The *nīrājana* is as previously described.
O beloved, the king, his ministers, and likewise the queens spoke of the eighth [day] as the protection of men.
By this very procedure, they must be protected by those who are well-resolved,
because there are minor seizing spirits, elemental beings, and malicious, harmful mothers.
Unassailable by the gods, powerful, difficult to conquer, and hard to overcome, they constantly and vigilantly strive to destroy [them]. (19–213)
For the sake of pacifying them and out of compassion for living beings, there are mantras, weapons, medicinal herbs, and efforts of great power and prowess. (19–214)
For the sake of favoring mortals, all these weapons— such as the *nārāca* and *tomara* arrows— as well as the *yantras* and, by the use of the word "and," the *maṇis*, have been brought down by me.
He speaks of the distinction of this Lord of Mantras among all those mantras of immense splendor: || 19-215 ||
Strength, vigor, as well as knowledge, memory, intelligence, physical form, splendors, life-force, and sovereignty for all— this conqueror of death has been described by me.

The "of them" refers to the pervasiveness of those causes for the pacification of planetary afflictions and the like; it is unwavering memory and wisdom in the form of realization. Furthermore, according to the previously stated principle, the essence of the mantras is the Lord himself—the powerful Mṛtyujit (the Conqueror of Death)—and likewise his essential nature as the specific self that expresses the body.
He is the life-force, whose nature is speech, and who shines with the desire to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon Śrī. || 216 ||
Thus, demonstrating its distinction from all other mantras, he first describes the state of other mantras:
"Through numerous sacrifices, recitations, fire-offerings, austerity, and self-restraint, mantras and weapons are accomplished in accordance with the nature of the age. (19–217)
Likewise, in this wicked Kali age, for those most sinful and lowest of men,
those mantras may grant them success or they may not.

In the Kṛta and other ages, whatever disposition there may be—the underlying intention (āśaya) dominated by *sattva* and so forth—it is achieved through effort, vows, worship, and hardships that become increasingly greater in each successive age; the meaning is that they "come to be" or "do not come to be," implying that for the most part, they do not come to be. || 218 ||
This is the distinction of Netranātha: that for this God of gods, there is no abiding in the Kṛta or other ages;
and therefore, he is...
For those who have reached the culmination in accordance with their disposition and who practice austerities and vows. || 19-219 ||
For those who have resorted to all [various] doctrines out of a desire to conquer both duality and non-duality,
and for those possessed of misfortune and laziness whose minds are afflicted by sin— 19–220.
Because they rely solely on devotion, there is no doubt that they succeed in this;
for those whose steadfastness and state of being conform to all the philosophical systems previously mentioned, such as the Siddhānta,
even if they do not practice austerity or vows, and who have thus surrendered to all states of being.

For those who are attached to all worldly transactions and possessed of misfortune and the like, because they rely solely on devotion and act as worshippers through the pervasion of the previously determined supreme non-duality— desiring to conquer both duality and non-duality— it is here, in this very state of being alive, that [the goal] is accomplished and manifests through total immersion (*samāveśa*).
And it accomplishes the attainment of one's desired goal; there is no doubt—just as before.
And this cintāmaṇi jewel bestows every desired object just as one has thought of it. || 19-221 ||
In the same way, one who has cultivated their mind indeed accomplishes all tasks;
for one whose mind is cultivated possesses a resolute intellect.
Furthermore,
just as the sun and moon are generally illuminators in the world, || 19-222 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these sustain it in common, just as food removes the affliction of hunger.
Likewise, the Supreme Lord Śiva is all-pervading within all beings; he is free from the phenomenal world, the Lord who bestows everything upon all. (19–224)

The supreme deity who conquers death bestows all accomplishments upon everyone. "This" refers to that which begins with earth and ends with space; it is the agent. It brings about—that is, it accomplishes—the common and universal food that removes the defect of hunger. It is called "the giver of all" (sarvada) because it tears asunder the entire web of bonds.
The liberator. The remainder is for the most part already explained.
And therefore, because he relies solely upon devotion, he is intent on concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna). || 19-225 ||
He who knows this, has taken refuge [in it], and is a counselor with an unwavering mind,
obtains the entire fruit and becomes one who is secluded in all accomplishments (siddhis).

The nature of *dhāraṇā* has been shown in the eighth [chapter] in such passages as, "Dhāraṇā is the state of the Supreme Self" (81.16). The "knower" (*vettā*) is the investigator who knows the vital energy (*vīrya*).

The "one whose consciousness is unshakable" (*niṣkampacetanaḥ*) is one whose intellect is certain. "All fruit" (*sarvaṃ phalam*) refers to liberation (*mukti*), which consists of the totality of all perfections (*samasta-sampad*).
"Araha"—this is the reading; may there be auspiciousness. || 226 ||
We praise the Eye, the bestower of protection, which, manifesting the divine state of the body, is illumined by the living soul awakened through immersion in the throbbing Consciousness.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Netrodyota*, the illumination of the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 19.
The Twentieth Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net. Even those who are sealed by means of the supreme, subtle, and other yogas, [he liberates] with ease.
We bow to the eye of the Great Lord, which reveals the supreme non-duality.
In order to introduce the subject matter of the upcoming section following the aforementioned connection, the venerable Goddess said:
"Everything that was asked by me has indeed been explained by the Lord.
Now I wish to hear [more], for this doubt remains in my heart. (20.1)
How is it that the yoginīs, the mothers, and the exceedingly powerful śākinīs can, in an instant, draw away the vital breaths from another's body? (20.2)
And why are they pitiless and fierce, or what is their purpose?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this in its entirety.
"I wish to hear"—thus the Goddess desires to attain the determination of the meaning of the question's words.
By means of the expressions "how," "why," and "what," she clarifies her desire to know regarding the manner, the cause, and the purpose. || 3 ||
To resolve this matter, the Blessed Lord said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret: how they intend to take the lives [of those who violate] the command of the Lord of Beasts. (20.4)
Free from passion and hatred, and devoid of greed and delusion,
they indeed sprinkle the sacrificial animals for the sake of the God of gods.
Neither out of greed, nor for the sake of violence,
nor indeed with the intent to kill do they uphold the command of the Great Terrible Lord (Mahābhairava).
For that purpose, the animals were created by the Self-born One himself;
the animals are intended for the sacrifice to the Lord, and not otherwise. (20.7)

"By the command of their husbands"—this refers to relying upon that [command]. "Why thus? provides the reason; and by the phrase "for the sake of sacrifice," the purpose is determined. By the passage beginning with "greed and delusion," cruelty is refuted. "They sprinkle" means they prepare for an offering. "For the sake of injury" means for the sake of harm. "For that purpose" refers to the aforementioned aim.
"For the sacrifice. By the phrase "by himself," the statement "according to the Lord's command" is established as the authoritative source (*pramāṇa*). "And not" (*na ca*):
here *ca* has the sense of *eva*. || 7 ||
Therefore, O fair-faced one, for the sake of favoring those animals,
they liberate them from their sins and sever those floods of evil.
Grace is liberation; [he bestows it] upon those bound souls.
Since this is so,
there would be a constant upward movement for those sacrificial animals that have been employed;
"upward movement" refers either to the creation of the state of Śuddhavidyā and the other levels, or to liberation.
And the goddesses previously mentioned,
by the command of Śiva, unite them through the threefold yoga.
Indeed, by means of another— namely, the triad consisting of the subtle and the gross—
they join [the object] and offer it.
And since the Yoginīs join the bound souls (paśus) in this manner, for that reason... nor do they kill them there by force. || 20-10 ||
In that regard, he begins by first explaining the supreme yoga:
"The Supreme Lord is the supreme, the soul of all, infinite, actionless, stainless, all-pervasive, and the cause of all causes. (20.11)
Abiding within all beings, he is the one who effects grace for all;
he is the self of all, whose nature is supreme non-duality that does not differentiate the universe; he is infinite, being unconditioned by time;
he is actionless, devoid of sequential activity, yet his essence is radiance through the power of non-sequential action.

He is eternally united. Since impurity has departed from Him, He is indeed untouched by impurity, even though through the concealment of His own nature He brings about the manifestation of impurity. He is all-pervasive, being uncontracted in terms of space.
He is the Supreme Lord, the autonomous one. Therefore, [He is the cause] of all [beings], beginning with Brahmā and the other causal deities.
The cause is the intermediate state, whose nature is the Heart consisting of light (*prakāśa*) and awareness (*vimarśa*). As it is said in the *Gītā*:
"This Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna" (18.61).
And it is this very [Heart] that bestows grace upon all by means of the manifestation of non-difference from itself.
Appointed to that very same task, they were stainless and free from weariness.

Having attained a state of oneness, they are not separated in any way; they are joined completely and fully pervaded. And because they have obtained supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), the exhaustion based on the body, vital breath, and so forth has vanished from them; therefore, they are non-different from that [bliss].
But when that [power] is capable, they dissolve and remain in the form of will.

The stages of action are the excellences of knowledge—namely, sacrifice (*yāga*), yoga, and *avadhūtikā*—by means of the expansion of non-conceptual consciousness in the form of will. These stages of action, kindled by knowledge, culminate in the expansion of that knowledge. Sacrifice is the offering of the bound soul (*paśu*) to the Supreme Lord.
