Yoga is the attainment of identity with the Supreme Lord; those [energies] whose trembling has been struck down—that is, shaken off—by these two are thus characterized by being motionless and consisting of that very identity.
Thus,
having established themselves in that state, they apply themselves to that form for those [practitioners].
Released and become Śiva, impelled by the power of Śiva, they become stainless and take on the form of Śiva through his sovereign influence. || 20-15 ||

Those who are of such a nature are, by implication, joined to that very state; through the power of those Yoginīs, impelled and urged by the Śakti of Śiva, they become Śiva-natured, having attained the singular form of pure Śiva. || 15 ||
And therefore,
through the appropriate application [of yoga], the state of Śiva is attained during initiation by those who have been initiated while still residing in their bodies.
In that very way, indeed, through the yoga of yoga, they attain the state of Śiva.
And by means of the yoga of the yoginīs, through assuming the very form of Caṇḍīśa.
For in this way,
those [powers] manifest the purity of this aforementioned candidate, who is utterly defiled and whose nature has been obscured by impurity. || 20-17 ||

Not only for one who is merely soiled, but even for one whose form is utterly destroyed by impurities and cast down into contemptible enjoyments— such a qualified embodied being [attains] purity and the nature of the powers of knowledge and action. || 17 ||
And these goddesses, by cutting them at the root, indeed seek to destroy those three impurities;
and therefore—
For one who is free from the three impurities, the body does not grow again. || 20-18 ||
Thus,
like a lamp, there is indeed no killing of that animal for a distance of one yojana;
for the supreme yoginīs—
By means of his pervasive essential nature and the power of his own sovereign capacity.
They sever the bonds of the animal by which the body perishes;
when the body is destroyed, there is liberation, not death.
By the pervasive one whose nature is Śiva, through the power of his own manifestation as Śakti—by means of which [power], namely by this severing.
If death is not of such a kind, then what is it like? He says:
for the person who is bound by firmly rooted bonds...
The wise know that separation from the body is death. || 20-21 ||
He concludes: "In this way, however, the supreme manifestation...
Yoga is said to be the awakening through rest in the state of Śambhu."
And now the subtle [state] is being described:
he calls that the subtle, consisting of power (śakti), which is known through the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti). || 20–22 ||
Resounding with the repeated sound "arā-varā-varā," it follows the nature of the resonance;
it consists of power (*śakti*) and is primarily the vibration of consciousness (*cit-sphurattā*), rather than, as before,
consisting of repose in the Śāmbhava light, by means of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

It is reached—that is, attained—by a consciousness that has emerged through the pacification of the state of being a subject [limited] by the body and so forth. Of what nature is it? It is "resounding" (rāviṇyā), meaning it possesses a resonance consisting of the innate reflective awareness of the *nāda* (the primordial sound), which is devoid of "sound" (*rāva*)—that is, the vocalization of specific mantras. Furthermore, it is of the nature of the unfolding supreme *ahaṃ-vimarśa* (I-consciousness). Of what nature is it [that which is reached]?
He says that "knowledge" (jñāna) is the state or existence (bhāva/sattā) of the resonance of sound (dhvani-nādāmarśa); its pursuit is the attainment of identity with that.
And this knowledge, which bestows perfection upon the perfected ones, the Khecarīs worship.

The Siddhas, such as Śrī Khagendra and others, and the Khecarīs—goddesses who move through the sky of consciousness—worship [him] on all sides; that is, they manifest as being of one essence with him. || 23 ||
Although Śākta knowledge is the foundation for all, nevertheless,
the knowledge of bound souls (paśus) remains defiled, being veiled by ignorance (ajñāna).
This ignorance, produced by the power of Māyā, consists primarily in the perception of the non-Self as the Self within the Self, and [the perception] of the Self as the non-Self within the non-Self.
It consists of the conceit of self with regard to the body and so forth.
Since this is so, therefore they overcome that [ignorance] by means of their own pure knowledge, which has been awakened through the practice of yoga. 20–24.
And thus,
just as one who is awake plays here and there with one who is asleep,
or just as one might be intoxicated somewhere by the drinking of wine and spirits; (20–25)
For, due to a lack of independence, he either plays like a child or wanders about somewhere like one who is insane;
likewise, like cattle, he is impelled by that which is vigilant.

"By the Mothers, by the Guhyakas, by power, and by their own yogic strength"—here, the verb "are impelled" (*preryante*) is to be supplied by changing the grammatical number from the singular to the plural. The Guhyakas are Yakṣas, who include by implication Bhūtas, Grahas, and so forth. "By power" means by their own capacity.
And for this reason, by the power of yoga, the life-force of animals is quickly drawn away by them. (20.27)
He clarifies this very point:
that which is the supreme unmanifest, eternal, immovable, and constant—having attained that by means of the path of yoga and having entered from the body of another... (20-28)
Having become the Supreme through one's own power, one should envelop the individual soul (jīva) with the [Supreme] Life-force (jīva).
"That which... and so forth is as before. Having attained that, and having entered the supreme power consisting of consciousness by means of the path of yoga—thus [it is said].
The yogi, who has attained the perception of the entire essence of that [reality] through the practice of the *golaka* (the sphere) as revealed in the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*,
renders the power of his vital breath (*prāṇa*) independent by means of drawing it in and expelling it while his own body remains in a state of non-expansion.
Having entered the heart of the other by means of either the path from the toes, the branches, or the *brahmarandhra*, and having become the Supreme while remaining in the state of the *golaka*,
one moves about; established in the principle of *vāyu*, the principle of *vāyu* becomes accessible to the intellect.

"The intellect (buddhi) is contained within the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and that [intellect] rests upon the principle of consciousness (cittattva). According to this traditional teaching (āmnāya), when the perception of "I" has become firm in the higher [state], one should remain for a hundred measures (mātrā),
and by means of the agitation of the vital breath (prāṇa), cause that [consciousness] to be agitated.

By means of the powers of his own senses, preceded by the seizing of those [other] senses, having made the body of another— already appropriated by the power of his own self— the subject of the activity and cessation of his own movements,
he [takes] the living being as the other's *puryaṣṭaka*, [unifying it] with his own living being and its own *puryaṣṭaka* through his own power.
One should envelop and overcome [the object] with one's own vital breath (prāṇa), by means of the awakened power of Śakti.
Thus, having ascended in this manner, one should indeed enter that which resides in the heart from below and above. || 20-29 ||
Having attained oneness, one should practice equanimity therein;
then, relying upon the supreme cause, one should practice sovereignty.
Relying upon the supreme Śākta cause and seizing it through that very grasp,
one should— while practicing the thought, "Whatever I do, let him do that," and thus attaining oneness with Him— practice sovereignty; in this way, one should restrain the desire to go elsewhere.
"One should cause that which stands to move"—thus, by this sequence, one should bring it under the control of one's own will.
This very point has been stated by the Gurus: "Established therein, the yogi should eat, drink, walk, stand, and sleep, until he becomes one who has attained the fruit of all his activities."
"Then one should bring him [there], release him, delude him, cause him to open [his eyes], fill him [with power], or lead him to a distinguished place," and so forth. || 30 ||
Then,
by means of his pervasive essential nature, he should pierce power with power;
having established pervasiveness through the force of immersion (*samāveśa*), which has become his vital energy (*vīrya*), he should do so by means of his own power.
One should split that vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) and draw it away for the purpose of severance.
Having enclosed this in a seal, one should perform the severance of power (śakticcheda).
The meaning is that, having encircled [the opponent] from all sides with her own power, she should sever the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) of the other by means of the application of a knife. || 31 ||

Then, O Goddess, the knower of yoga, having resorted to the state of *sattva* which is the form of power (*śakti*), should heat [it] by means of the sun of consciousness in the form of the essence of his own *sattva*. || 20-32 ||
For, like the sun with its rays, the yogi, established in the supreme, should indeed cause [the lower state] to melt away by means of his rays.

Having resorted to and taken hold of the *sattva*— which is of the nature of power (*śakti*) and primarily consists of the power of vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*)— the yogi, by means of the cause that is the nature of the reality of the throbbing of power (*śāktasphurattātmasattārūpa*), which belongs to his own *sattva*, [should effect this].

"By means of the sun of consciousness" means by way of being formed into the form of the sun of pure awareness (*caitanya*); [the practitioner] should cause [the disciple's body] to be heated. Then, remaining right there in that supreme body, he should—like the sun with its own blazing rays of sight and so forth—melt and dissolve the rays of the moon, which are the disciple's own rays of sight and so forth, within that very same supreme body.
There too, by the power of yoga, one should unite all the objects such as sound, as well as the sense organs, within the heart.
Indeed, the elements are composed of rasa, and the qualities (guṇas) alone [pervade] everywhere;
the aggregate of the internal organs,
as well as the external and internal organs that have become objects through their relation to the Supreme, [are dissolved] by means of the aforementioned dissolution.
One should join all those elements that have become liquid and attained a state of fluidity within oneself, making them one with one's own self.
Then, having grasped that with one's own mind... || 20-34 ||
Then the yogi, having assailed the city from all sides, should enter it;
having quickly seized everything, he should swiftly bring it into his own self. (20.35)

Taking up all that was previously mentioned with the word "tat," one should, according to the perspective taught in the scriptures, emerge from the crown of the head of the person to be acted upon and enter their city— the body— with the mind; then,
having taken possession of it by means of power, that which was previously liquefied within it [should be restored].
Whatever has been gathered, all that he should quickly establish within himself. || 35 ||
Thus, by means of the application of mudrās and mantras, the yogi should bring back the life-force at that very moment.
Here, the mudrā is first the Karaṅkiṇī at the time of its own emergence from the body.

When it ascends into that body, she is Krodhanā; when it dissolves its rays and so forth, she is Lelihānā; when it emerges from that city, she is Khecarī; and upon reaching one’s own heart, she is Bhairavī. The true nature of that bond has been shown by us in the *Śrīvijñānabhairavoddyota*. As for the mantra:

The *Pañcapiṇḍakṣurikākālarātri* is designated as such; it is seen in the *Śrīpūrva* and other [Tantras] from the *Śrīguptatantra*. Through its application, the yoginīs bring back the life of another in an instant;
and therefore:
By this method, the yogi should practice yoga with subtlety.

The knower of yoga shall quickly attain all of that through subtle yoga. First, one should practice yoga according to the previously mentioned method; thereafter, by means of this subtle yoga, the knower of yoga quickly attains "all of that"—namely, the attraction of the individual soul (*jīva*) as taught in the scriptures, along with the fruits of its accomplishment.
The subtle yoga is thus fully explained. Now...
...and now the gross [body] is being described. || 20.37 ||

He says regarding that [state] "situated in the body" (*piṇḍastha*): "By means of its application, one should certainly draw forth the body. "Situated in the body" means residing in the gross body; "the body" refers to the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body consisting of eight constituents). "By means of its application" means—

One should effect the respective rites of counter-magic (*pratikṛtikarma*) through base means, such as the employment of various methods for administering poison, and thereby cause [the enemy] to be drawn in (*ākarṣayet*).
Likewise, by means of the ritual application of mantra and mudrā, and according to the prescribed rule, even with dust. || 20-38 ||

By the power of meditative yoga alone, and through the characteristics of the *chummaka* and other limbs, they cause the city of bonds belonging to the bound ones (*paśu*) to fall; of this there is no doubt.

In that regard, the method of killing (*māraṇa*) through the application of mantras is shown in the *Śrī-svacchanda*: "Bound by the King of Wrath (*Krodharāja*), it should be drawn in the center of a cloth from a cremation ground (*śmaśānapaṭa*),
using cremation ash mixed with poison and blood."
O beautiful woman, for one whose name is interwoven with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
and joined with the word "slay" (*māraya*), it is further interwoven with the names of cruel species.
"One who is well-guarded by these protections will die within seven nights. (9.64.66).
As for the procedure for the *mudrās*, it begins with the mantra tradition starting from "Vyomakuṇḍalinī," and so forth, [as seen in passages] such as:
"Having bound the seven-crested *mudrā* in the shape of a plow up to the crest (*āśikhāntam*)," and so on.
"Then the Yoginīs devour [the practitioner] after letting out a roar within the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
Thus it is shown in the *Śrīguptatantra*. Furthermore, the ritual for the dust (*pāṃsava*) should always be observed at dawn on the seventh day of the dark fortnight.
O Dear One, the Yoginī—whether steadfast or unsteady—is empowered by the strength of the performed nyāsa.
Whichever woman or even man first emerges,
with both the left and right hands [should touch] the left and right feet.
"One should cause [the victim] to grasp soil after having lifted it from the right side of the man;
by means of the *apasavya* [method], one shall always kill him in the world of Malla.
This and more is shown in that very same [text]. [This is] the power of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*).

Through the immersion (*āveśa*) of one’s own innate form as the Sovereign of Yogins (*yogīśvarī*), there arises, by way of the process of upward emergence, the capacity to draw forth the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) residing within the body of the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*). The *chummakās* are technical names according to the scriptures (*āgamika-pāribhāṣika*); for example: "The weapon (*śastra*) is that which produces division," [and] "flesh..."
"Strength-increasing [substances], kāleyaka flower, fat-cream, head-examination,
one killed by a weapon who has been obtained"— by such means [he performs] other practices mentioned in various ḍākinī-tantras.
By those marks, the branding signs, and the forcible severings of the limbs being offered as sacrifices through the methods of violent animal sacrifice.
Thus,
O Goddess, when Yoginīs become exceedingly powerful through these three kinds of yoga and seek to kill [one], then one should practice what is most beneficial.
It is stated by the scripture itself that the first type among the threefold yoga grants liberation to the bound soul (paśu);

the second and third types bestow both enjoyment and liberation, which is thus established by implication. With the intention that this is also found in other scriptural traditions, [the text mentions] in the Āgamas that which was consumed by the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśī).
The eligibility for initiation through rites such as the "resurrection of the dead" (mṛtoddhāra) and others is now stated.

The knower of mantras, by means of his own supreme nature as all-pervasive, demonstrates the conduct leading to the highest good— the immortal, supreme deity who has conquered death and faces in every direction. (20.41)
Having realized that supreme yoga and having pervaded the city of the bound soul (paśu), the mantra-practitioner,
through his power of will, presides over the auspicious life-force of those bound souls.
The wise practitioner of mantra, having understood the sequence of the yogins previously mentioned, O illustrious lady, should protect himself from all those who would cause harm. (20.43)
Having known the nature of Mṛtyujit— characterized by the aforementioned attributes according to the previously established view—

as the "knower of mantras," that is, as the essence of the consciousness of all mantras; and likewise [having known] "him" as belonging to all those previously mentioned harmful Yoginīs, meaning the Yoginīs and so forth.
Having known the supreme yoga described through the pervasion of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), the practitioner (*mantrī*)— who knows the potency of mantra and is a knower of yoga—

having pervaded the city, which is the body, of bound souls (*paśu*) by means of his own supreme nature, that is, by the aforementioned supreme meditation (*paradhyāna*), [he acts] with the power of will (*icchāśakti*), whose essence is the pervasion of the bliss of the radiance (*sphurattā*) awakened therein, for the sake of those very [souls].
Having empowered the life-force and performed the "striking" (ācchurita), one should protect it by means of the method of mantra-contemplation according to the sequence of mantras. || 43 ||

Thus, having explained the protection for those sealed by the supreme yoga through the sequence of supreme meditation, he now speaks also of those sealed by the subtle yoga through the sequence of subtle meditation:
"The subtle [protection] is by way of one's own power, through the yoga of following the wheels."
Through the previously mentioned severing of the knots and by means of subtle meditation, the knower of yoga [attains this].
One who is endowed with the power of the yoga of knowledge and is proficient in mantra and tantra shall liberate [the practitioner] from all defects; it can never be otherwise.

Having understood the subtle yoga employed by the Yoginīs, one who possesses the power of the yoga of knowledge, who is expert in the domain of mantra and tantra, whose intellect is stainless, and who is therefore a knower of mantras— one who knows the potency of the mantras pertaining to this world— such a teacher, by way of his own power, [proceeds].

By means of the previously described method of the cakras and supports, through the piercing of the knots and so forth, one should liberate the object of practice from all defects by means of the nectar of subtle meditation; however, one who is ignorant of the subtle yoga is never capable of liberating that which is sealed by subtle yoga. || 45 ||
He speaks also regarding the sealing and unsealing of the gross yoga:
"The conqueror of death, perfected in mantra, an ascetic with senses restrained, devoted to meditation and mantra, established in sattva, possessed of knowledge, and strong. (20.46)
The supreme yogi is contented, devoted to the performance of sacrifices and charitable works,
completely free from passion and hatred, and devoid of greed and delusion.
O Dear One, he shall indeed be fearless, free from hesitation, devoted to bestowing grace, and a liberator from the terrible defects previously mentioned. (20.48)

He is one who has mastered the mantra through the *mṛtyujit* mantra; he is an ascetic with a conquered mind, and therefore his senses are restrained and their longing for sense-objects has ceased. Because he knows the power [of the mantra], he is one whose mantra is perfected, yet remains devoted to recitation and meditation. Established in purity (*sattva*), he is free from doubt; possessing knowledge, he is a knower of the supreme reality.

The powerful one (balī) is one whose power has expanded through attainment; for this very reason, he is a yogi devoted to and intent upon sacrifices, charitable works, offerings, and gifts; he is free from defects such as worldly attachment; he is fearless and confident in rites such as the *bali* offering; he is a practitioner of the heroic conduct (*vīrācāra*) who is devoid of hesitation; and he is a teacher (*ācārya*) dedicated to bestowing grace.

By means of rites such as sacrifice (yāga), oblation (homa), and bali-offering, one certainly becomes a liberator from the terrible fault consisting of [the misuse of] mantras, mudrās, powders, medicinal pastes, and other such ritual applications. || 48 ||
"One should perform the practice of mantra according to this very procedure," he says;
"for he who acts otherwise will be his own destroyer, a corrupter of his own lineage, and that wicked one will certainly be cooked in hell. (20.49)
From one's own family, one falls from the stability of the portion belonging to that particular deity due to defects such as trembling; thus, being corrupted, one perishes.
As it has been said:
"I see no other flaw in the mantra-practitioner regarding the accomplishment of the mantra," and so forth. (49)
He says that even by one who knows reality, the practice of mantra should not be performed haphazardly:
"There are spirits of various forms, Mothers who are wicked and harmful, Yoginīs, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, and Piśācas who are difficult to overcome. (20.50)
Desirous of returning, desirous of killing, and likewise others desirous of devouring;
desirous of pleasure, indeed incurable, are the Skandas and other Brahma-rākṣasas.
Thereafter, those [beings] are countless and terrible; self-knowing ones who are wise regarding their own true interest should never engage in conflict with them anywhere. (20.52)

The "evil-doers and harmers" are those such as the *apasmāra* (epilepsy) spirits; the "guhyakas" are the principal *yakṣas*; the "skandas" are the *grahas* that afflict children; and by the word "etcetera," obstacles (*vighnas*) are included. Self-knowledge is the knowledge of reality (*tattva*).
The reason for not creating opposition is one's own proficiency in one's purpose.
Because they are intent on protecting their own bodies, sons, wives, and so forth, beings such as *bhūtas* and others indeed contemplate the injury of the body and its like, being [thereby] hostile.
And this practice of mantra as described should not be performed by those seeking wealth, nor by the greedy, nor by those seeking fame;
the greedy are wretched.
However, one may indeed cause it to be performed out of compassion for one's own family members, children, and so forth. || 20.53 ||
One should perform [this] for another solely out of compassion. || 53 ||
Likewise, it is always so for kings, their sons, and their wives; for:
In whatever country or kingdom one who is skilled in the application of mantras may dwell, || 54 ||
In that regard, the king is indeed the lord and always the preceptor of those in the stages of life (āśramins),
because of his proper protection of the subjects.
And for this reason, those mothers forgive one who acts on their behalf. || 20.55 ||

The terrible [spirits] become entirely pacified from the previously mentioned cruelty for one who is currently engaged in the practice of mantra. "From cruelty" refers to violence and the like; "terrible" refers to other beings such as *bhūtas* and so forth.
And those kings [propitiated them] with offerings of oblations and abundant sacrifices.
Because they truly satisfy [others], they therefore forgive everything;
indeed, those who contemplate Śiva should never engage in the recitation of mantras everywhere.
Now listen to the pacification of those terrible beings who, regarding the very subject already mentioned, destroy the body composed of the five elements by means of various methods. (20.58)

By means of the gross yoga through the gross—namely, with powders, incenses, and ointments, as well as through the application of yantras and cakras, and likewise by means of the protection of living beings and so forth. || 20-59 ||
[They were] always [accompanied] by those perfected in *dhāraṇī*, meditation, and yoga, as well as in mantras;
by those who knew the rules for *mudrās* and mantras, and who contemplated the coming and going [of breath].

In the ritual procedure for the *bhūta-tantra*, it should be performed by heroes who are knowledgeable in medicinal herbs, deeply contemplative, self-restrained, vigilant, and free from all confusion. (20.61)
By those who have bathed, performed worship, and are devoted to recitation and meditation;
by those who know the targets and their characteristics, who are free from worldly desire, and who are highly refined.
Those who seek security should practice the mantra-method and not otherwise.
"Gross yoga" refers to meditation on the forms of various deities and so forth; "powder" is that produced from various medicinal herbs;
"the application of medicinal action" is the employment of a specific single herb; and "anointing" is—

By means of sprinkling with water consecrated by the blazing mantra and so forth; a *yantra-cakra* is a collection of mantras inscribed in a specific arrangement. By the word "and" (*ca*), recitation (*japa*) such as enclosing the mantra with other mantras is included. Through these, there is the protection of the soul (*jīva*) previously determined, and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the protection of the body is also implied.

[The mantras are] for the purpose of nourishment and so forth; likewise, through yogas consisting of concentrations such as *yojanā* preceded by meditation on that [mantra], and through samādhis such as the immersion in the nectar of the perfected body (*sādhyadeha*); and through these mantras which are either perfected by recitation (*paṭhitasiddha*) or propitiated according to the ritual procedure taught in the *Kalpa*. By all these—[the preceding factors and] these [mantras].

The practice of mantra (mantravāda) must be performed by those who are the causes—namely, the practitioners who are masters (ācāryas) through their knowledge of the rituals of mantras and so forth—and not otherwise. By what kind of experts in mantras and the like?
It means by those who contemplate the coming and going [of the breath] according to the characteristics of mantra. Likewise...
By heroes who are unshakable, by those who reflect well with intellects established in reality,

by those who are self-controlled with conquered senses, by those who are vigilant and free from pride, and by those who are devoid of all impurity and devoted to the rules prescribed in their own scriptures; the target is the essential nature as it is grasped by the elements and so forth.

The "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇāni*) are the marks mentioned in the Tantras; the "Vedas" are the treatises (*śāstra*) that serve as the means for their realization. By those who know them—those who are independent, whose defects such as greed, fickleness, and pride have been exhausted, who are well-behaved and free from hypocrisy, and who are intent upon the welfare [of others]—this is the intended meaning here.
If that is performed by transgressing the prescribed order, then security itself is compromised. Thus, by these verses, the very same meaning previously stated is expressed with further elaboration.
In every respect, he states that this is the true reality here: "If one should desire the highest accomplishment, or eternal and certain liberation... (63)
The Supreme Lord has declared that the practice of mantra should not be performed for the sake of showing favor to mortals, kings, and householders. 64.

One who desires the welfare [of others] must perform [this rite] while established in the state of grace (*anugrahapada*). This is certain and definitive. It is for the sake of grace, and not for the sake of greed, honor, or the like.
By the phrase "established in the state of grace," it is meant that the preceptor (*ācārya*) must perform it only toward those who are objects of his compassion.
In that case as well,
it is said that even if one performs [the practice] at times, it does not lead to destruction if it is not done continuously; rather, it leads to ruin if one performs it constantly.
If one should do so, one perishes. || 20-65 ||
For those who are endowed with power, purified by the Śiva-sacrifices, eternally pure, free from fear, and observers of the command of Bhairava, do not tolerate [such transgressions]. (20.66)
The Yoginīs, Bhūtas, and others are eternally pure, free from passion, hatred, and the like. || 66 ||
He states the reasoning for their possession of power: "Previously, they were commanded by me through the application of mudrās and mantras;
because they wish to kill you for their own sake, they are considered powerful. (20.67)
"Commanded" means appointed for the purpose of closing the breaches caused by the previously mentioned misconduct. || 67 ||
In this regard, he recalls an ancient tradition: "In the past, by Śiva, the Supreme Self, the God beyond gods, [these beings] were created;
indeed, by this method, they roam through the ten directions. (20.68)
Possessed by that power, those exceedingly strong victors set out,
most terrible, with the prior intent to slay the gods.
By this [means], namely that which is taught in the scripture and has the nature of uprooting the Daityas. || 69 ||

And when those [demons], having been uprooted by the Daityas, were subsequently chosen by the Blessed One— though difficult to conquer and intent on slaying the gods— they became engaged in enjoying the fourteenfold creation;
at that time, they were seen by Svayambhū as before...
From that [source],
the mantras of unfailing power were emanated;
there are seventy million of them, which are mighty, self-controlled, and subduers of adversaries.
By the word "and" (ca), it is meant that the Vidyās are also masters and independent; they are the adversaries of the Bhūtas and the others.
And therefore,
for the sake of subduing those who are wicked, terrible to the world, and intent on destruction through their excessive power, and for the protection of the world— || 20.71 ||
The application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and ritual actions has been commanded by the Supreme Lord in hundreds and thousands of ways; indeed, their practice is for that very purpose.
In all the systems of mantra-discourse...
[this] has been declared regarding the subject at hand out of compassion, and only on rare occasions.
...nor otherwise by violating the command of the Lord.
For it is by following the command of the Supreme Lord that mantras, when applied to their respective objects, become powerful through His majesty and possess unfailing potency. || 20-73 ||
All the remaining letters alone are filled with that power;
by the word "that" (tat), Paramaśiva is referred to.

And because, according to the perspective previously stated, this king of mantras here—which is of the nature of Paramaśiva and constitutes the vital potency (*vīrya*) of all mantras—is called Mṛtyujit; he is the Lord and Master of all mantras. (20–74)
And no mantra or vidyā shall transgress his command;
all wicked beings flee at the mere remembrance of this Blessed One, just as deer and other wild animals flee from a lion. (20.75)
The word "knower of reality" is to be supplied as the remainder; may there be auspiciousness. || 75 ||
The mantras, the reciters of mantras, those who are to be overcome by mantras, and all mantras whatsoever—
when they are subject to his command, he conquers that inner eye of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Netrodyota*, the illumination of the *Śrīnetratantra*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja. 20.
The Twenty-First Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net.
Victorious is [He] who, through the playful movement of the oscillation of the bliss of His own vibration, [manifests all things].
Controlling the eye of the Lord, which consists of the three principles, [he realizes] the reality of mantra, whose essence is the three principles.

Regarding that which was introduced at the conclusion of the section on "all mantras," the venerable Goddess, desiring to make known the true nature of mantras for the sake of its definitive determination,
said: "O God, what is the essence of mantras, what is their form, and of what kind are they?"
What is their power, how are they capable, and by whom have they been impelled?

Who is their self—is it Śambhu, or is it the Śakti or the individual soul (aṇu)? Furthermore, what is their nature—is it formless or with form? How do they appear, and of what kind are they? Those who are formless are not seen as agents by anyone at all; even those with form, like a potter, are not the makers of everything.
They are seen. What is their power, which is eternal and which pacifies the defects that obstruct enjoyment and liberation?

In what manner are they capable? For since that which is formless, like space, lacks capability, how then can agency—which is rooted in that [formlessness]—exist? [If one argues that it exists] because of possessing a form, then [the agent] would be limited.

Since that which is impure lacks autonomy, what power could it possess? Furthermore, that which is bodiless cannot be an agent of grace and the like, nor is it logically possible for it to be impelled by the Supreme Lord. For this very reason, with what intention [could one ask] how even the formless Supreme Lord can possess power and act as an instigator? By whom, indeed?
It was stated that they were "thoroughly impelled"; the meaning is: by what means and by what agent? || 1 ||
He clarifies this point in sequence:
"O Lord, if [the elements] are of the nature of Śiva, all-pervasive, and of the form of the void, how indeed can they possess agency, given that they are devoid of action and instruments? (21.2)
Since they are formless, how can their agency be logically established?
O Lord, tell me: who performs an action without a body? (21.3)
If mantras are of the nature of Śiva, then, since they—like Śiva—are all-pervasive, consist of vibration, and are devoid of action and instruments, how can they possess agency?
Furthermore, because they are formless like Śiva, that [agency] is not tenable; for no one can produce an effect without a body.

[He] was seen performing [it]. Thus, the question of how Śiva’s status as the impeller of mantras is possible is also implied by this very [point]. And such is the view of those who know the Upaniṣads (śrutyantavid).

For they hold that agency belongs only to one who possesses qualities; thus, considering that the meditation on the Lord (īśvaropāsā) is a meditation on Brahman with qualities, [they regard the Lord] as if he were non-agent.
They maintain that non-dual Brahman is motionless, like the Puruṣa of the Sāṃkhya. || 3 ||
For the activity of any bodiless being has never been observed, O Supreme Lord.
And thus, since the bondage of the embodied soul arises from this... therefore.
...how can there be agency for one who is bound? || 21-4 ||

Furthermore, precisely because of having a body, the category of Śiva, mantras, and so forth, is considered impure; due to this impurity, it is perceived as being dependent and its power diminished. For it has been said: "The bound soul (paśu) is eternal, formless, ignorant, and inactive" (Śrī Kiraṇā). || 4 ||
Therefore, agency in all things is contradictory for one who lacks power.
Let it exist in some respect, like that of a potter-beast; what is the use of that? Thus, of what nature are they?

"What is their intrinsic nature? Of what kind are they? How are they capable? Or by whom are they impelled?"—thus the fivefold set of questions regarding the state of Śambhu has been clearly elucidated.
He clarifies the question "Of what power are they? with the following: "How, in reality, are these mantras, whose nature is Śiva, accomplished? (21.5)

The meaning is: according to the view thus stated, how can those who are in reality of the nature of Śiva—the pervasive and formless—whose essence consists solely of eternal, liberated, and pure consciousness, be accomplished [as practitioners], and how do they bestow supernatural powers (*siddhi*)? || 5 ||
Having thus conceptualized the Śāmbhava nature of the mantras, he now also conceptualizes their Śākta nature:
"If, moreover, they are of the form of Śakti... then that which is their form as Śakti, she [is the Mother]."

Whose power is it, and of what nature? To what does it belong, and what is its essential character? Power conceptualizes that very essential character; for what reason, O Lord, and what is the effect of that [power]? || 21-6 ||

Is this power (śakti) of the nature of the essential form [of the cause] together with its auxiliary factors, or is it something supersensible (atīndriya) to be inferred from its effect? And what kind of effect is that of hers?

Furthermore, it cannot be said that power (*śakti*) is an independent entity whose nature consists of its own essence and its auxiliary causes; for power is merely the capacity to act. He states this, saying: "As long as there is no possessor of power... and so forth, implying that there is no disagreement regarding the mere application of the name.
In that case... whose capacity is being enjoined? Is it being established?
For that [independent nature] cannot be established as independent without some [other entity] being already established.
But that which is to be proven by means of what is unestablished is itself declared to be unestablished;
for here, no power whatsoever exists that is devoid of a real entity.
"Those mantras are indeed of the nature of power (śakti), but [if they were] merely that, there would be a reversal.
To say that mantras are "merely of the nature of power" means they consist solely of the power of the indistinct Śāmbhava abode;
this is a reversal, a delusion, because [mantras] are like a fire which, as a substrate (dharmin), must be established by something else.

No independent power (śakti) whatsoever is established as existing apart from its nature as properties such as combustibility. Nor is it logical to claim that the possessor of power—the substratum—is established by that very power, which consists of the capacity to act; for without the establishment of a substratum, there is no establishment of power, and without the establishment of power, [there is no establishment of the substratum].

The establishment of the substratum [is impossible], for this results in mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). As they say: "That is unestablished which is sought to be established by means of that which is itself unestablished. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a supersensible power (*śakti*) existing apart from a potent object; thus, even mantras do not possess [intrinsic] power. He speaks next to analyze the state of being atomic (*āṇavatva*):
Moreover, if the mantras consist of atoms (aṇu) and possess the form of a physical body, [then... || 21-9 ||
In that case,
those who are renowned as being of the nature of the Self are neither impure nor powerful;
and thus it is.
Who can wash away the impurity of another who is himself impure? 21-10.

Only those that are stainless are capable of purifying what is stained, not those that are themselves stained; and mantras, due to their possession of the āṇava-mala, are indeed stained, just like the individual soul.
And thus, O Supreme Lord, the individual (āṇava) mantras are not indeed independent;
for those that are individual are neither independent nor pure. Therefore, how could they render other [mantras] independent?
Or rather, how could they accomplish what is impossible to accomplish? This is the remaining intention.
To the objection that these must therefore be something else entirely, he says: "The existence of a continuum of real entities apart from the three principles is contradictory. (21.11)
In the Āgamas it is stated that nothing exists without the three principles (tritattva), nor does anything arise without being of the nature of the supreme subject and object. || 11 ||
Therefore,
for the sake of wishing well for living beings, it is precisely reasoning (*yukti*) that must be stated here—
reasoning in the form of correct investigation— as to how this is logically established.
It is that which brings conviction to the hearts of all. As it is stated in the *Saurabheya*:
"That reasoning (*yukti*) which consists solely of the activity of consciousness (*cidvyāpāra*) is the means of proof in every case;
whether regarding worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) or liberation (*mokṣa*), one should therefore hold fast to it."
Thus [it is said].
Nor should it be said that if mantras are not logically tenable when analyzed by reasoning, they should therefore not be accepted;
for powerful mantras are seen which cannot be overcome even by gods and asuras. (21.12)

Because they bestow grace upon all, the mantras beginning with Catuṣkalanātha are givers of everything, omnipresent, and auspicious; they are indeed experienced as bestowing the attainment of the removal of suffering and liberation.
Thus it is.
In brief, O Mahādeva, tell me my doubt.
O Lord of the universe, there is no other whatsoever who is superior to you.
O Great Lord, O Master, tell me everything if you are pleased with me.
O Mahādeva, tell me this doubt briefly within your own self; determine the object of my uncertainty.
Since there is no one else more excellent than you who can provide a definitive resolution, therefore, speak everything exactly as it was asked. 14.
Having heard this, the Blessed Lord said:
"Aha! This question is profoundly secret; indeed, I have never been questioned by anyone in this way.
Yet, I have always set forth everything that is to be known within all the scriptures."
But those who are utterly deluded and perpetually shrouded by illusion do not perceive it.

The question you have asked is exceedingly profound; indeed, I have never been questioned about it by anyone. Whatever I must say on this matter, however, has already been stated in all the scriptures.
People are perpetually shrouded by illusion; even when the truth is spoken, they do not grasp it due to their aversion.

You, however, although you have realized the true essence of the scriptures, desire to reveal them solely out of compassion for deluded beings—this is the underlying intention. As for me, I have not been questioned by anyone.
Regarding the reading "coditāstu mayā sarve" (but all were urged by me), I was not questioned by anyone;

rather, I was questioned by all others, such as Kumāra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth. Although they were urged and awakened by me in various scriptures, they did not understand [the truth], whereas you have done so through your knowledge of reality.
The meaning is that this question has been posed in a concealed manner.
Now he resolves the question:
"Without the three realities, it is not proper to speak of a mantra as a real entity. (21.16)

For mantras have the nature of protecting through reflection; although they may reside in the categories of the atoms of power whose true essence is the power of knowledge and action, because power is not distinct from that which possesses power, they are also Śāmbhava—this is the meaning. || 16 ||
In this regard, he states the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpīya*):
let the present section on mantras be set aside for now.
The entire world, being devoid of reality (*tattva*), is not established.

Reality is Supreme Śiva, whose nature is the luminosity of consciousness that is transparent and autonomous. And it is precisely that [Reality] which is the establishment of the universe, because for that which is non-luminous by nature, establishment as such is impossible without the nature of luminosity.
Thus, precisely because its nature is the light of the consciousness of another,
everything whatsoever that is perceived here is constructed from the three principles.

For the Supreme Light, through its own transparency and autonomy, manifests the universe— consisting of the objects of desire, knowledge, and action— as if it were something external, even though it is not distinct from itself, upon the ground of the three principles whose true nature is the powers of will, knowledge, and action.
Just as in the stages beginning with Paśyantī, the individual soul [perceives] the sequence of the signified and the signifier.
In the manner thus described,
O Goddess, no entity whatsoever exists apart from the three principles;
therefore, everything— both the supreme and the non-supreme— is comprised within these three principles.
The higher path is pure, while the lower is impure. || 18 ||

And thus, these mantras, which possess immeasurable power, should be known as being of the nature of Śiva, consisting of Śakti, and likewise atomic (āṇava); for they exist through the division of the three principles (tattvas). || 21-19 ||

They are established in the powers beginning with the Supreme Lord’s will (icchā) and take on forms such as Śiva; therefore, they possess immeasurable luster (ojas), which is the state of being unimpeded in their capacity for universal grace and other such acts. || 19 ||
To explain in detail this nature of the universe as consisting of these three principles, he says:
"The Supreme is the essence of all, pure, beginningless, the cause, and eternal;
it is immeasurable, indefinable, incomparable, and free from affliction. (21.20)
It is without appearance, supremely peaceful, devoid of all limbs, all-pervading, auspicious in every respect, and endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
It is completely filled with a mass of consciousness, delighted by the bliss of its own inherent joy;
it is beyond [worldly] bliss, free from conceptual construction, devoid of ritual conduct, and imperishable.

Non-duality, free from conceptual construction, a mass of consciousness that removes the impurities of the mind, pervading both the conscious and the unconscious, it is to be known as eternally manifest and unsurpassed. (21–23)
Unchanging, supreme, eternal, stainless, and free from affliction;
devoid of all points of comparison and divested of all states of being.
Beyond all forms and parts, immovable, eternal, and all-pervading;
omnipresent, abiding in all states of being, and established within all creatures.
Residing in the hearts of all beings and impelling all things,
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, nothing whatsoever is seen that is devoid of Him.
Therefore, that one Supreme Lord is all-pervading and the universe itself;
he is omniscient and eternally satisfied, for his consciousness is indeed beginningless.
The Great Lord (Maheśvara) is independent, possessed of unimpaired power, and of infinite power;
and the will of that Great Lord is in no way to be conceptualized.
Because it is immeasurable and beginningless, how and by whom can it be perceived?
For it is understood through inference based on its effects and through the investigation of its actual nature. (21.29)
His activity is his supreme power, which should be understood as being inseparable from him, like the rays of the sun or the heat of fire. (21.30)
She brings joy to all, auspicious, and follows the will of Śiva;
she possesses his nature, is peaceful, and is characterized by eternal grace.
All this is indeed an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of that [Supreme Reality], for it cannot arise from anything else.

The Supreme Abode should be known as characterized by such attributes as being the Self of all; its power called Will (*icchā-śakti*) is inferred from such effects as the emergence of the universe, and the effect likewise belongs to that very [power].

The Lord’s supreme, non-dual power is indeed non-distinct [from Him]. Therefore, the essential meaning here is this: all of this is a *vivarta*—an appearance as a manifold nature—of the Supreme Lord’s power.

As for the word-meaning: "the supreme" (*param*) refers to that which is most excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*), the primordial reality (*prakṛta*) known as Mṛtyujit, which is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*).

That [consciousness] is such that its very nature (*svarūpa*) consists of all that; it is "pure" because it is not covered by any of those [phenomena]. Having made certain—that is, having ascertained with certainty—that it is the unmoving source which brings forth the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth, even though that universe does not exceed its own [conscious] wall, appearing as if it did; and having established it as beginningless and the primordial ground of all—

The reason is this: for this Supreme Light, which is the Great Light, no cause whatsoever is established that is distinct from its own independent conscious manifestation. As it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: "That which is non-existent is non-existent;
it is not logical for the non-existent to have the nature of existence. Furthermore, there is no purpose in saying that even the existent acquires existence anew."
"In the world, the relation of cause and effect belongs to that which revolves within;
its being perceivable by both types of sense organs is due to the power of some [unseen principle]. (2.4.3.4).
Precisely because it is the cause of the universe, it is immeasurable. Therefore, it is of such a nature as this.

It is impossible to point out or to express. And thus it is "beyond comparison" (anaupamya); that is to say, there exists no other thing with which it could be compared, because nothing exists apart from it.
It has emerged from "mere appearance" (ābhāsa), meaning from a slight manifestation; it is not like the limited consciousness (saṃkucitacit) which is merely a slight [manifestation].
The meaning is that it shines. Because the universe abides in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with it, all differentiation has subsided;
thus, it is supremely peaceful. Furthermore, unlike the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, the universe there does not even exist as a mere conceptualized part;
therefore, it is said to be devoid of all parts. It is all-pervasive and auspicious in every respect.

By the phrase "by what form indeed is the doer of good not pervasive? it is made clear that [He] pervades both the conscious and the unconscious; by the phrase "omniscience and so forth," meaning "the omniscient one who is eternally satisfied," etc., [He is shown to be] a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*), which means a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*); and by the phrase "His own bliss," as follows:

Light is said to be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*); likewise, it is that whose bliss is its own, independent of anything else, consisting of the wonder of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). It is thus enriched by bliss, yet unlike sensual pleasure, it is not to be grasped or reflected upon by a subject. Bliss has emerged from it.

Since the aesthetic delights (*camatkāra*) are delimited [by them], it has emerged from conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), ritual practices (*ācāra*), and phonemes (*akṣara*). The phoneme (*akṣara*) is the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of the essence of the expressive mantra (*vācaka-mantra-kalā*). It is devoid of mental construction (*kalpanā*), non-dual (*advaita*), free from opposites, and unsurpassed—the non-dual mass of consciousness (*cidghana advaita*). And therefore:

It is that which effects the pacification of the impurity (*mala*) of those living beings—that contraction (*saṃkoca*) consisting of the concealment of one's true nature (*svarūpa-gopana*) arising from the power of *māyā*. It is eternally risen, ever-shining. It is supreme (*para*), from which all modifications (*vikāra*)—such as birth, existence, transformation, and so forth, pertaining to the entire world—have departed.

It fulfills all desires; it is eternal, unconditioned by time, stainless, untouched by the impurity of *āṇava*, free from affliction, and devoid of the adventitious stains of *māyīya* and *kārmika*. Since it is non-dual, there is no similarity with anything else such that it could serve as a comparison;
likewise, there exists nothing whatsoever that can serve as its analogy.

It is devoid of all states of being and all attributes of the intellect; it stands transcending the formal aspects (*rūpakalā*)—that is, the manifest forms (*svarūpa*)—of all the principles (*tattva*) beginning with earth. It is immovable and eternal, as before. It is the pervasive Lord (*vibhum īśvaram*), for it goes everywhere.
It is "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*) because it causes [beings] to go and because it sustains them; here, the root *gam* is used with an implicit causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇic*).
It abides in all states of existence, both insentient and sentient, for without it, their existence would be impossible.
This very point has been made explicit by the passage beginning with "situated in the heart," meaning that it resides in the hearts of all beings.

The meaning is that, while abiding as the internal vitalizing principle within the state of the subject (*grāhaka-pada*), it impels all things, culminates in the respective effects of those objects of perception (*grāhya-kārya*), and bestows the agency of the perceiver (*grahītṛ-kartṛtā*). Therefore, nothing is seen devoid of it, because that which is manifest is one with its manifestation. Since this is so:

Therefore, by stating that the all-pervading Lord—that which is the universe—is the one, non-dual Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the nature of supreme non-duality (*paramādvaita*) is established. The attributes such as "omniscient" and so forth have already been explained previously. Thus, the power of the Lord known as Will (*icchā-śakti*) is of this very same nature. From the perspective of its effects...

Thus, that [power] of the Lord of Consciousness, the agent, which consists of His capacity, is inferred precisely from such activities as the creation and dissolution of the world. As it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"Power is the essence of the entity, whose difference is superimposed due to the difference in its effects."

Thus, that very possessor of power (śaktimat) has as his effect that supreme, non-dual power; that is to say, it consists of the power of knowledge whose nature is manifestation, because it is that which is manifested. For this reason, it is indeed non-different [from him], just like the rays of the sun and so forth. It is only in such a form that this [power] has vibrated into existence.

She brings joy to all and is the cause of the descent of Śiva’s power (śivāveśa). For this reason, she is called Bhadrā, the auspicious one, because she exists in accordance with the will of Śiva as previously described. Furthermore, because her very nature is such, she is peaceful and changeless; and for this very reason, she is eternally bestowing grace. And all—

This universe is fashioned by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); it is the manifestation (*vivarta*) of that very power whose nature is the appearance of the universe, existing in its diverse forms. Therefore, it cannot arise from anything else, because nothing else exists apart from being created by that power. As it has been stated in the *Śivasūtras*:
"The universe is the accumulation of His power" (3.30).
Also, in the *Śrīsarvamaṅgalā*:
"His powers are the entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power."
Thus [it is said].
Thus,
the supreme Śakti is with bliss (sānandā), while the supreme Śiva is without bliss (nirānanda).

She who exists with intense joy along with bliss is "sānandā" (blissful). He whose bliss consists of the complete repose in the state of great aesthetic flavor (*mahāsāmarasya*) is "nirānanda" (beyond bliss). || 32 ||
And because of the very intensity of bliss (*ānanda*), the power (*śakti*) manifesting itself takes the form of the appearance of the six qualities, such as omniscience; thus he says:
"And those qualities such as omniscience which belong to Śiva, the Supreme Self..."
They are Śākta; they are not seen as anything else, for there is no other possible explanation.

The meaning is that when the supreme power (paraśakti) assumes the form of knowledge, preceded by will (icchā), these qualities—such as omniscience and so forth—are manifested; therefore, they are indeed powers (śākta).
Thus, in this way, Śiva is indeed one, and Śakti likewise is eternal and one;
established in non-dual identity, she alone is the unified totality.

That which is non-dual (advaita) is that which has duality as its counter-correlate; she whose nature is established by that [non-duality]. She is the collective whole, whose essence is the aesthetic harmony (sāmarasya) of the entire universe without exception.
To the question of how she remains undifferentiated even while existing through the manifold variety of qualities such as omniscience, he says:
"This [power] of Śiva is of the nature of will; it is indeed undivided and faces in all directions.
From its attainment of a slight swelling [of manifestation], there arise the qualities of omniscience and so forth. (21.35)

The meaning is that the Supreme Power (parā śakti) itself, having attained the nature of the powers of knowledge and action through a slight swelling [of consciousness], abides in the form of omniscience and so forth.
Therefore it is said:
"When that very same one, being of the nature of knowledge, fully awakens [the soul], then awakening—which is indeed beginningless and infinite—is remembered as the supreme knowledge. (21.36)
Known as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), she is the locus of qualities such as omniscience;
when she is independent and unimpaired, she is the action (*kriyā*) whose form is that of the instrument (*karaṇa*). (21.37)

O Maheśvarī, that Mātṛkā, which consists of the forms of sound such as *sphoṭa* and so forth, and is divided into eight types according to color and form, is designated as the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). 21.38.

That supreme power called Action (kriyā), which embodies the entirety of speech, is indeed that very same aforementioned Supreme Power (parā śaktiḥ). For when it brings about awakening, that single power alone is designated by various forms according to the limiting conditions (upādhi) of its respective functions. This is because awakening is indeed [the essence].
That supreme knowledge which is devoid of beginning and end because it is not delimited by space, time, and so forth—
this very thing is known and celebrated as the Supreme Power (parā śakti), renowned as the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). And for this reason,
she is remembered as the locus of the aforementioned qualities such as omniscience, since [these qualities] are inseparable from the power of knowledge.

When that very same supreme power (*parā śakti*), having assumed the state of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), becomes independent at the beginning of the creation of the universe—and for this very reason remains forever with its power undiminished—then she alone takes on the form of the instruments (*karaṇa*). [She is] the one who possesses the qualities known as omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, and infinite power.

And when that same supreme power, having taken hold of the stage of the power of knowledge, becomes independent at the beginning of the emanation of the universe, then she herself, being always of unimpaired power, becomes the nature of the instruments.

Being of the nature of emanation (*nirmāṇa*), she is called the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Anticipating the objection—how can the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), which is itself non-successive, take the form of successive action?—he says "in the form of phonemes" (*varṇa-rūpa*) and so forth. For consciousness (*bodha*) has as its ultimate reality the power of self-reflection (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose essence is the vibration of freedom (*svātantrya-sāra-sphurattā*); otherwise, this [consciousness] would not exist.

Since it is untenable for [the self] to be the agent of cognition or the knower of the self, its state is merely that of bearing a form, which is equivalent to being an insentient object like a crystal and so forth. Furthermore, even the emergence of a form and such is untenable, because the cause thereof—which is distinct from consciousness—is unestablished due to its non-manifestation; thus, it is consciousness [that is established].
The true nature of agency consists precisely in the self-reflection of "I," which is the form of the supreme Word vibrating as both self and other. And it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"The wise know that the essential nature of manifestation is self-reflection. (9.5.11)

Thus [it is said], and also in the *Vākyapadīya*: "Consciousness (*citi*), whose nature is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), is the supreme speech (*parā vāk*)," and so forth. (9.5.13) Also in the *Vākyapadīya*.
"If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from consciousness,
then manifestation would not be manifest, for it is that [nature] which performs reflective awareness. (1.125)
Thus, the supreme power of speech (*vāk-śakti*), whose essence is the sovereignty of consciousness, consists of sound (*dhvani*)—
the nature of which is subtle and gross phonemes beginning with *paśyantī* and ending with [spoken speech]— and is described as: "Resonance (*ghoṣa*),
roar (*rāva*), tone (*svana*), sound (*śabda*), and that which is called the *sphoṭa*, is indeed sound (*dhvani*)."
"The humming sound (jhāṃkāra) and the cawing sound (dhvaṅkṛti)— these eight sounds are proclaimed.
According to this view stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda*, [the first resonance] has the luster of a blazing fire,
then the brilliance of split bell-metal, then resembling a bamboo flute, and like the sound of a female bee.
He who has entered all the tantras, resembling the fifth tantrika.
"Like a bell, like a cloud, and like a string struck by the wind—
the sound is to be heard in ten ways, becoming progressively more subtle.
According to this principle stated by our Guru, the pervasion of the eightfold sound consists of the fifty phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*.
In her non-lordly (abhaṭṭāraka) form, she is the mother of the entire world—both pure and impure—consisting of all mantras and the like;

she is the unknown Mother, Mātṛkā, the Supreme Goddess, the power of action (kriyāśakti). And this very same [power], though without sequence, becomes sequential action through its manifestation as the totality of speech, consisting of both the signified and the signifier.
It is said: "As it has been stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*:

'The agency of worldly action is possible only through the power of time; it is not at all possible for that which is eternal, such as the power belonging to the Lord, which is like that of the Lord himself. (2.1.2)
Thus [it is said].
Thus, that which consists of the very sequence manifested by its own freedom is called "action" (kriyā); it is born from a single, non-dual nature.

Arising from her own nature, having that nature as her object, self-existent, and proclaimed by herself as auspicious (*śivā*), she is the Supreme Lord’s power (*pārameśvarī śaktiḥ*)— though she is essentially one and non-dual— yet, being colored by the sequence according to the perspective thus described, she is called "action" (*kriyā*). And she does not arise merely from some other nature.
Thus, she is not born from any other nature; rather, her emergence is from her own nature alone—she is such that the surging forth of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) arises from her very essence.
In this way, her sovereignty is demonstrated both through negation (*vyatireka*) and affirmation (*anvaya*).
Although she surges forth as the self-nature of the universe, she remains "by herself" (*svataḥ*) established in her own form. And yet...

She is not merely covered by the universe, but rather she is self-proclaimed and self-luminous; for this very reason, she is that [reality] in whom all existents—beings, objects, and universal categories—are non-different from herself. Furthermore, she is *svā* (one's own), because she is the self-nature of the universe through the manifestation of its particularities. And therefore, she is *śivā*.
She is of the nature of Śiva, whose essence is a pure and spontaneous light. As it is said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:

"That which is this intuitive flash (*pratibhā*), colored by the succession of various objects, is the cognizer whose nature is non-successive and infinite consciousness; he is the Great Lord. (1.7.1)
Thus [it is said].
This clarifies that this power of agency is not at all distinct [from the self]: "Nor indeed is this power said to be separate from the agent. (21.40)

For the word "hi" has been displaced in the sentence structure. Since the state (*bhāva*) of an independent agent (*kartṛ*)—that is, its very nature (*svarūpa*)—is agency (*kartṛtva*) when other attributes are excluded; and since that very thing is called power (*śakti*), capability (*śakana*), or capacity (*sāmarthya*), which is not distinct from the possessor of capacity (*samartha*); therefore, this [power] is not something separate.
As it is said in the venerable *Vijñānabhairava*:
"Since the non-difference between power and the possessor of power is firmly established, therefore, because she possesses his attributes, the Supreme Power belongs to the Supreme Self. (18)
Thus [ends the section]. 40.

Now, if Śiva, being possessed of power, manifests as the form of the universe, then—since he would be subject to modification—he would become a material cause (*upādāna*) like the principle of *māyā*; consequently, there ought to exist another agent (*kartṛ*) who acts as the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) presiding over him. Thus...
"In order to bring about the means for enjoyment for this one who desires enjoyment, the King of Mantras,
having agitated (or entered) Māyā with his powers, brought forth the universe"— thus,
according to the principle established in the venerable *Pūrva* [Tantra], by that agitator.
Anticipating the doubt that [the Lord] must be conceived as being like some infinite deity (anantabhaṭṭāraka), he says:
"Since Śiva is perfectly complete, independent, and all-pervasive, who could be the agent or who the disturber? Therefore, there is non-duality in Śiva. (21.41)

According to the principle that "His powers are the entire universe, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power," because the Lord Mṛtyujit— Śiva, who is the self of the universe, the perfectly full, the mass of consciousness and bliss— is independent due to His perfection and is the sovereign, all-pervading, and omnipresent one.

Who is the agent, and who is the agitator? None at all, because there exists nothing other than the state of Bhairava, which is autonomous consciousness. Since this is so, therefore, within Śiva—the venerable Lord Śiva—there is non-duality (*advaitatā*), that is, the nature of supreme non-duality; for there is not even the name of duality.

This has been stated by the venerable Bhagavān Kātya in the *Śrīpūrvavārtika*: "Since pervasiveness is established, there is non-difference from that [Bhagavān] on the part of the universe, because difference would be contradictory. Since the Bhagavān’s nature is consciousness (*cit*), and he is not limited by spatial dimensions or the properties of the objects of cognition (*cetya*), his pervasiveness is established as far as it extends. By this very fact—
Since [the Self] is woven across and through both the interior and exterior of everything—from the atom to the infinitely great space and so forth—how can there be any distinction?
Because distinction is contradicted by that very all-pervasive reality, there is non-difference between the universe of the conscious and the unconscious and that [Self].
Thus, that which constitutes His omnipotence by virtue of being the self of the universe is metaphorically designated as "Power" (śakti).
By means of that [power], He effects creation, maintenance, and indeed dissolution. (21.42)
The Blessed One performs everything, both concealment and grace.

That which is the Blessed One’s possession of all powers is his very power, his sovereignty; by virtue of his own sovereignty, the Blessed One is the power of the universe. As it is said in the *Śivasūtras*:
"The universe is the accumulation of His power.

(3.30). It is "designated metaphorically" (upacaryate), meaning it is spoken of as distinct from Śiva; however, no real ontological distinction between the world and Śiva’s power—or even between that power and Śiva—is possible. As it has been said:
In the *Pratyabhijñā*, it is stated: "Power (*śakti*) is the essence of the category [of reality] whose distinctions are superimposed due to the difference in effects.
And by means of that power, which is non-different from Himself, the Blessed Lord performs everything. This very point...
This is made clear by the specific statement: "Perform the fivefold [process] beginning with emanation."
He demonstrates this very point through its divisions:
"By the power of action (kriyā-śakti) he creates, and by the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) he maintains the stability of the world. (21.43)
He performs withdrawal by means of Rudra-śakti, concealment by means of Vāmā, and grace by means of Jyeṣṭhā; there is no doubt in this matter.
The power of the Possessor of Power is indeed one; it is spoken of in the forms of Jyeṣṭhā and the others due to the differentiation of its functions. Thus he says:
"Since a fivefold function of Śambhu is observed in the world—namely, that which is being done and that which is to be conceptualized—that is the activity of the Omniscient One. (21.45)

Since the activity (*kṛtya*) to be performed in the world is seen to be carried out in five ways through the distinctions of creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth, therefore the movement (*viceṣṭita*) or vibration (*spandita*) of Śambhu is described as being differentiated by means of the powers (*śakti*), such as Jyeṣṭhā and the others. || 45 ||
Thus, from whatever source it may arise, this power is inferred to belong to Śiva alone;
for the power that consists of manifestation arises from everything that appears, and belongs to the Lord Śiva, who is the manifestor.
It is inferred and ascertained of the conscious self alone, and not of anything else whatsoever.
Since the supreme power of the Lord alone is the cause of every effect, therefore the infinite individual souls (ātmanu) are indeed obstructed by impurity (mala). || 21-46 ||
They have been favored by the supreme will of the Supreme Lord;

yet, being obstructed by the *āṇava* impurity—which consists of the contraction of the power of *māyā* determined previously—they have been made to harbor the conceit of thinking themselves incomplete. For this very reason, they are the infinite *āṇava* selves (*ātmāṇava*). And these...
Favored by the supreme will of the Supreme Lord, they have attained non-difference from the Supreme Lord.
Thus, Śiva, Śakti, and likewise the Self—these three principles constitute the unsurpassed reality. || 21-47 ||

According to the perspective already stated, Śiva and Śakti possess supreme excellence; however, even though the Self appears contracted, it possesses superiority because its nature as the cognizer consists solely of the light of consciousness. || 47 ||
Thus, the venerable Lord Paramaśiva, having manifested as the triad of principles known as Śiva, Śakti, and Ātman, once again, by virtue of His absolute freedom,
appears in three forms: the God Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha (Brahmā).
He performs a sixfold creation, which is further divided into four types.
The one who possesses the threefold nature is the single Trimūrti; the term "creation" is intended as an indicator for both maintenance and dissolution. (48)
He demonstrates its sixfold nature and its fourfold division:
"O Goddess, [the beings] are those of the hungry ghosts, hell-beings, animals, gods, sages, and humans; likewise, they are born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, and from a sprout. (21.49)
Indeed, by His power and through His sovereignty, the Blessed Lord creates everything.

The creation of ghosts and hell-beings is characterized by darkness (tāmasī); the creation of animals, birds, reptiles, and other lower beings is characterized by a slight reduction of darkness; and the divine creation is characterized by goodness (sāttvikī).

The silent one consists of *rajas* and *sattva*; the human consists of *rajas* and *tamas*. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "First, he creates a *tāmasī* creation, intensified by *tamas*:
the various forms of hells, and indeed the bound souls (*paśu*) ending with the immobile."
Through the entry of *tamas* and *rajas*, he would again create human beings;
and through the entry of *rajas* and *sattva*, he would create the lords of the best of sages.

"Having cast off sleep and being fully awakened, the Lord of the World, permeated by *sattva*, shall create the gods along with the world-protectors according to the previous arrangement. Thus, humans and the like are born from the womb (*jarāyuja*); birds and the like are egg-born (*aṇḍaja*); [and] sweat-born (*svedaja*)...
Mosquitoes and the like; plants are born from sprouts; but sages and gods are for the most part born of the mind.
From that sovereignty which is omnipresence by virtue of power in its nature as absolute freedom.
He establishes this very point:
"The deity is the efficient cause, just as the sun is for the action of a gem. (21.50)
But that *upādāna* (material cause) is power (*śakti*) agitated through *samavāya* (inherence).
It is an auxiliary cause by mere proximity, not by entering into activity;
it is called the "cause" (*kāraṇa*) because it brings about [the effect] by its own power, and the "agent" (*kartṛ*) because the universe is manifested by it—this is the Lord (*deva*).

The Supreme Lord is the true essence of illumination and the rest; and His very own supreme power (*parā śakti*) is the material cause (*upādāna*). Through inherence (*samavāya*), because He abides in a state of equilibrium with Śiva, that power becomes agitated, becoming conducive to the production of the entire universe, and assuming a state of slight swelling (*kiṃcid-ucchūnatā*).

It has taken recourse to an equal level. Just as the sun is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and the action of a gem is the material cause (*upādāna*)—meaning, for instance, in the production of fire—this is the illustration.
This very equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti, though non-different from itself, is indeed different.

In accordance with the principle taught in the *Śivasūtras* and other texts—namely, "The universe is the accumulation of His own power"—He unfolds the world; He does not depend on anything external, nor does He act out of any desire for a specific purpose. And by this much alone...

The relationship between the example and the illustrated is established through specific cases such as the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*) and so forth, rather than by a universal rule (*sarvasarvikayā*), whereby there might otherwise be a sense of difference or insentience (*jāḍya*) between Śiva and Śakti, as in the case of the sun and other objects.
He clarifies that very point: "Just as the great sun-crystal gem [blazes] through contact with the rays of the sun. (21.51)
It radiates its brilliance excessively, yet there is no desire on the part of either;
upon seeing a magnet, iron performs its action.
In neither case is there any desire; rather, Śiva is the cause.
"Of both" refers to the sun-crystal and the fire-crystal. "Action" refers to that which consists of vibration.
"Of both" refers to the magnet and the iron. He is the cause merely by his presence, through his own power alone.
It causes the universe to unfold.
Surely, since there can be no restriction of place, time, or nature for things that lack a cause, there must necessarily be some regulator for the sun-gem and so forth.
True, there is one; however, it is this:
Because of its subtlety, that which impels those two would not be perceived.
The meaning is "the Supreme Lord" (parameśa), because of His subtlety—that is, because He is unknowable. || 53 ||
Such a cause for the entire world has not been experienced;
and this is logical, because if the Supreme Lord were the cause of the universe and were directly perceived,
He alone would be determined to be the impeller of even the sun-gem and other such things, yet He is not so perceived.
Because the experiencer is of a single nature.
"But is it not the case that 'Indeed,
no entities have ever been made objects by anyone apart from cognition;
therefore, it is concluded that cognition has attained the nature of the object of knowledge'?"

Thus, according to the principle taught in the *Kālikākrama*, it is experienced that the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) alone is the cause for the manifestation of the universe, just as the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is the cause for its creation. Therefore, how can it be said that "the unexperienced is not the cause"?
This is true: the power, as it flows outward, is experienced as the manifester of the universe; however, internally—
However, he states that the universal cause—the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti—cannot be delimited by the aforementioned reasoning:
"That Śakti, moreover, is perceived as the material cause (*upādāna*) everywhere. (21.54)
Just as everything appears fully accomplished through the power of action, the state of the agitated and the agitator is not perceived by anyone at all. (21.55)
The wise know that cause to be [the state of] agitation arising from conjunction;
it is clearly manifested and experienced. In this very context, the example is provided by the word "just as.
"Everything" refers to jars, cloths, and so forth. This is the relationship of the agitated and the agitator between Śiva and Śakti.

The first vibration (spanda) is that which is appropriate for the manifestation of creation and so forth; and because it is "inherent" (samavāyāt), meaning through its state of equilibrium (sāmarasya), it is "agitated," pulsating with the fitness for the manifestation of creation and so forth. The wise ones are Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananteśa, Sadāśiva, and others. It is "caused" by its own power, meaning it is manifested by this [vibration].
Considering the universe as the cause, they know the agent [of creation] and realize him through immersion (*samāveśa*).
As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "Without desire, he creates the entire world, both moving and unmoving."
O lady of excellent hips, having effortlessly agitated the sky with your own splendor.
