"But that [state] is called 'grasping' (upādāna) when it is agitated by the coming together [of the elements].
(11.3.4). Also, in the *Śrīśrīkaṇṭhī*: "Everything proceeds from Īśvara."
Thus [it is said].
In this case as well, Śarva would create all this, both moving and unmoving, by means of his power, even without desire. (21.56)

Because it is completely full, he has no desire whatsoever—that is, no longing for any fruit—thus, by his own sovereignty (*svasvātantrya*) alone and not out of desire, he acts through power; he does not depend on material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth, as is the case with a limited Lord (*bhedaiśvara*). As it has been said: "That power is indeed the material cause. (21.54)

Thus: "all that is moving and unmoving. The intention is that the Lord creates and manifests through the diversity of concealing His own nature the entire multitude of living beings—both the unmoving and, as it were, the moving—all of whom are of the nature of Rudra and the kṣetrajña; it is not, however, that they are established from beginningless time. || 56 ||
He applies this to the subject at hand: "In the manner thus described, all mantras are born of the three principles (tritattva);
they are called Śiva, they are of the nature of Śakti, and likewise they are of the nature of the Self. (21.57)
The three natures are taught everywhere as being powerful;
they are always all-pervading, possessing all forms, and existing in every way. (21.58)
Since, according to the view stated above, Paramaśiva alone manifests the universe upon his own screen by means of his own power (*svaśakti*),

therefore the mantras arise within the three principles (*tattva*) beginning with Śiva— bearing the names of Śiva and so forth, possessing the nature of Śiva and so forth, and likewise endowed with all capacities and powers— but not in the manner [of other systems].
Those of deluded intellect [argue]:

"Śiva is one and changeless, and his Śakti is likewise; therefore, those two are not capable of existing in manifold ways, or else they would be subject to modification due to being devoid of consciousness. (Nā.)
Thus, not perceiving the sovereignty of Śiva, they say that mantras depend solely upon atoms. || 58 ||
Śiva indeed is the beginningless abode, eternal, primordial, and immovable;
this has already been explained at length.
And when that [wind], O Goddess, spreads forth at will without delay, || 21-59 ||
Then, that power of his called *icchā* (will)— supreme, subtle, *unmanā*, and of the nature of Śiva—
having transcended the mind, becomes an uninterrupted, self-luminous vibration.
And it is this very [power] that, when it agitates its own self which is mere existence, causes agitation. || 21-60 ||
This Śakti, who exists throughout all the paths, has been described as being in equilibrium;
she embraces the universe, and having withdrawn it, creates it once again.

Existence-in-itself (*astitvamātra*) is the nature of Great Being (*mahāsattā*) whose essence is luminosity; therefore, when Śakti agitates that Self—which is otherwise undisturbed and incapable of any threading together—She vibrates as the very act of weaving the entire universe from the Void (*śūnya*) and the Beyond-Void (*atiśūnya*) down to the Earth (*dharā*). At that time:

Having ascended to the level of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), she is called *Samanā* because she consists solely of the subtle weaving together of all objects of thought and the acts of thinking. For this very reason, she exists throughout the entire path (*adhvan*) and flashes forth as the primordial act of mental projection;
consequently, she embraces the universe. And this embracing of hers consists in the fact that she withdraws it [into herself].
By immersing itself in its own non-dual nature, it creates through the manifestation of emptiness;

it projects [the world] as "this-ness," by virtue of being the form of the Great Creative Power (*mahāsṛṣṭiśakti*), which internally contains the entire manifold of the creation and destruction of the universe.
The meaning is that it "throbs. This very point is further illuminated by the word *punaḥ* (again), signifying that she creates after repeatedly withdrawing [the universe].

By the term "having withdrawn," the stage of the Earth, which is pervasive throughout the Void and the Beyond-Void (*śūnyātiśūnya*), is expressed; whereas by the term "creates," the stage of Power (*śaktibhūmi*) is indicated. || 61 ||
When it is said that the third [power], called Kuṇḍalā, is also figuratively designated as such,
by the term "called Kuṇḍalā," there is the manifestation of her nature as being internally empty and externally characterized by a state of dependence.
It has been shown that she is all-pervasive and embraced here; she alone is thus metaphorically designated and so spoken of.

And this very power called Unmanā, which has manifested as the nature of the powers Samanā and Vyāpinī through the threading together of all existence and non-existence and by virtue of being the self-luminous manifestation of the generality of existence and non-existence—
that same power, desiring to manifest the universe consisting of the signified and the signifier, [assumes] the form of Śakti.

He says that it first vibrates in the form of sound (*dhvani*), because it consists of the nature of disregarding the commonality of both the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) which have been embraced [within it]:
"When the *sphoṭa*, in the form of sound, [emerges] from the body of Śiva due to *adṛṣṭa*... (62).
Spreading with extreme velocity and filling the world with its sound,
that resonance is declared to be Sadāśiva, the Lord of the gods of gods.
The *sphoṭa* is the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), so called because from it the entire multitude of sounds (*śabdagrāma*) bursts forth—that is, is manifested.
For this very reason, it is of the nature of resonance (*dhvani*), its essence being that of sounding.
It arises from the Supreme Sound (*paranāda*), which is of the nature of reflective awareness (*āmarśa*), from the Seer who is invisible due to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and whose form is one.

It flows forth with extreme velocity from the nature of Śiva, which is a mass of light and bliss, like the uninterrupted roar of a rushing river. Of what kind? Filling the entire universe with its resonance—the final *nāda* in the form of the resonance of a bell—and assimilating it to itself through reflective awareness (*āmarśana*). That very [state]...

The Lord Nāda is the nature of the light of supreme consciousness (*paracit*), whose essence consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the non-artificial identity (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "I" and "this. This is the intention behind the statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Sadāśiva.
By the expression "it spreads forth," he indicates that this very power of supreme speech (*paravākśakti*) of the Supreme Lord manifests as such.
And here, even the end of sound (nādānta) has entered.
Now, that sound which, having traveled along the path, comes to rest without being obstructed—
she is renowned as Nirodhinī, the obstructress of all the gods. (21.64)
The venerable Lord Nāda, who has traversed the paths, is all-pervasive, unceasing, and unstruck, wherein he comes to rest;

by immersing himself in his own pervasion, he causes the lower pervasions to emerge. This is the celebrated mantra-power known as *Nirodhikā*. Of what nature is it? It is the "obstructor" (*nirodhikā*) of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā.

"By pervading upwards, she is the Sustainer; as it is said in the venerable Svacchanda: 'She who restrains the gods, beginning with Brahmā, and the lords of the deities, is declared to be Nirodhikā. (10.1223)
Thus [ends the verse]. 64.
He states that the very non-manifestation of the non-difference from Paramaśiva is the cessation of Brahmā and the others:
"The majesty of the state of Maheśvara does not function for one who is [otherwise] obstructed.
Therefore, he says that the diversity of those situated therein exists solely through the non-manifestation of non-difference.
Indeed, countless millions of mantras are established therein.
Furthermore, what do those who have entered that [state] obtain? Indeed,
those yogins who have entered that state which brings about cessation obtain that very thing, and nothing else.
"Upward" refers to the pervasion of non-differentiation; the word "that" (tad) should be applied by repeating it [in each case].
And this mantra-kalā, which consists of mere sound and is called *ādāntavyāpti-irodhikā*...

[is] the bindu, and Īśvara is remembered as [the state] beyond it; having opened the plane ending with Śakti by means of the pervasion of the supreme power, the power of will (*icchāśakti*), from the level of *samanā*.
By the pervasion of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), she unfolds the predominance of the power of action (*śakti*);
having obstructed the state of being composed of the reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) that is non-different from all denotators—
which is manifested through the pervasion of the internal resonance (*nādānta*) by means of the nature of mere sound (*dhvanimātra*).

It assumes the nature of the Bindu, which consists of the Lord whose essence is the reflective awareness of the unity between "this-ness" and "I-ness," and whose form is the manifestation of the non-difference of all that can be expressed as a totality.

And it does not assume the nature of the *bindu* immediately upon the appearance of the words that cause cessation; rather, in the interim, when the nectar of Śiva, the cause of emanation, falls upon the crown of the head. || 21-66 ||

Through that, there should be a swelling [of energy], which is known as the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra). Tending toward reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), consisting of the power of sound (*nādakalā*) whose denotable object is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and having resorted to the state of cessation (*nirodhinī-pada*) by means of the obstruction of its own existence, it desires to emit the state of the Bindu, whose nature is the realization of non-difference from all denotable objects.

The intended meaning is that, first of all, it assumes the state of the "half-moon" (*ardhacandra*), in which the signified object (*vācya*) is slightly emerging and predominates. As for the literal sense: the "nectar" (*amṛta*) belonging to Lord Sadāśiva, whose nature is *nāda*, is the creative potency (*sṛṣṭivīrya*) consisting of the manifestation of the clearly evident "this-ness" (*idantā*) of that which is to be created.
When [the Bindu] falls upon the head of the multitude whose nature is the existence of the universe, and first unfolds from the arising of the Bindu,

then that constituent of Mantra is called the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra), because through it nourishment occurs for one who has ascended to that stage; for she who is of the nature of the Bindu is the creative power in the form of the full moon.
The state of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) arises.
And for these [energies], as they ascend from the position of the half-moon and the bindu,
there is the withdrawal (saṃhāra) of all beings; however, for those descending downward from the nāda, it is the creation.
...and indeed the very cause of creation.

Thus, when the power of action (kriyā-śakti) consisting of the *bindu* has become manifest, he speaks in order to show the state of the mantras where the signified and the signifier have become distinct:
"For here, the letter *ma* is indeed Rudra, the supreme conjunction of phonemes."

This *bindu*, manifesting as a state of differentiation, first becomes the form of the letter *m*, which is the awareness (*amarśa*) of the individual soul (*puruṣa*) resting upon *māyā*. And here, it should be understood that Rudra is the presiding deity. Furthermore, this letter *m* [is distinguished] from the letters *a* and *u* with respect to the *praṇava* under discussion.

In comparison with other mantras, however, the conjunction of phonemes (*varṇa-saṅghaṭṭa*)— which is the locus of rest— is superior, more excellent, pre-eminently elevated, and situated above even other phonemes;
for the phonemes associated with the *piṇḍākṣara* (the seed-syllable) assume the capacity to denote their respective *tattvas*.

As long as they have not entered into the state of the sound of the syllable *A* characterized by a protracted (*pluta*) utterance that pierces the knot of *māyā*, so long do they not enter into the pervasion of the *bindu*, which consists of the consciousness that knows the non-differentiation of all objects of knowledge. Furthermore, up to the end of the protracted vowel, there exists the reality of the long, short, and their respective phonemes and denotations; thus, there is a conjunction of phonemes.

And thus, the previously mentioned power (śakti), having become the support of the knot of māyā and having attained the form of the constituent part of the mantra consisting of the letter A, exists as the self of the entire universe.
When it attains stability, facing itself as the cause of emanation, || 21-68 ||

The syllable *U*, known as *Pratiṣṭhā*, is Viṣṇu himself manifest. Regarding the phrase "turned toward itself" (*svonmukham*): having turned [the consciousness] toward itself—that is, toward its own nature as consciousness—this is stated because the state of stability (*sthitidaśā*) is primarily characterized by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and because the means of knowledge consists of consciousness permeated by the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Therefore...
Thus, [the Lord] is the cause of the state of emanation (sṛṣṭi) in which the object of knowledge (meyapradhāna) predominates.

For it is precisely the manifestations (ābhāsas) existing within consciousness in the form of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), when being reflected upon as distinct, that are emanated as objects of knowledge (prameya). And in this regard: "Due to the conjunction with the movement of the fish, the fish residing in the throat..."

Thus, according to the view stated by the venerable Mīnākula, consciousness—which has established its footing within the cavity of the throat through oscillation between the prior and posterior limits—is said to be the constituent part of mantra known as *ukāra*. It consists of the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) whose nature is the object of knowledge (*meyātman*) emerging forth;
and it resides in the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā].
It is that in which the enumeration— the manifestation— of the twenty-three principles beginning with *āba* and ending with *prakṛti* is contained within the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*; for this very reason,
it is directly [the state] because of being the awareness (*amarśitva*) of the venerable Lord Viṣṇu, who consists of the consciousness of persistence presiding over that plane.

Viṣṇu, speaking thus to her, instructs her that she must understand that the predominance of the state of withdrawal (saṃhāra-daśā) belongs to the *m*-portion (*makārakalā*), and that the seven principles beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā are subsumed [within it], as well as the pervasion of the *vidyā*-portion (*vidyākalā*), and so forth.
Then, having descended from the throat, when consciousness has reached the heart-lotus, the all-pervading Lord, for whom everything is accomplished, [attains] cessation within the *praṇava*.
The supreme abode called *akāra* is Brahmā, who is seated upon the lotus;

it is the cessation (*nivṛtti*) resulting from the withdrawal of the creation of the principles down to the element of earth (*pṛthvī*). Therefore, because this [element] is the limit of the *praṇava* in the descending order, *akāra* is its manifestation (*ākhyāna*) on all sides (*āsamantāt*); thus, that is the supreme abode called *akāra*.

Because by means of it the supreme abode is praised (*nūyate*) intensely, lauded, and contemplated as non-different from it, even the letter *A*, which is a single part of the *praṇava*, is the supreme abode of the *praṇava* according to the principle: "Even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its universal form. Thus, [the letter *A*] is the supreme abode of the *praṇava*.

This is indicated by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And that which is this nature of the letter *a* is called Brahmā and Kamalāsana (the Lotus-seated One), because it denotes the form of Brahman, because it is the reflective awareness (*āmarśa*) of consciousness primarily characterized by emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and because it is mounted upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
Just as with the *dvādaśānta*, it is entirely appropriate to call the heart the "supreme abode" (*paradhāma*), because it is full consciousness.
Thus, in this manner, this creation of mantras belongs to Śiva, the Supreme Self. || 21-70 ||

From the passage beginning with "For Śiva is indeed beginningless" (21.59) up to the end of "the great power called Kuṇḍalinī" (21.62), [the reality] exists as the nature of the *śivatattva*; from *nādānta* up to *bindu*, it exists as the nature of the *śaktitattva*.
The creation of mantras from the letter *ma* to the letter *a*, as the very essence of the self, has been described.

Having thus described the creation of the Great Mantra whose essence is the *praṇava*, which consists primarily of the *paśyantī* speech resulting from the intervention of others, he now describes the creation of the *mātṛkā* with the *madhyamā* speech as primary.
Then, through its eightfold division, that supreme, subtle power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), which consists of the fifty phonemes, the wise know as *Mātṛkā*.
(21.71) Its eightfold nature arises from the division of the classes (*varga*), while its form of fifty arises from the division of the individual phonemes belonging to those classes.

And because differentiation is predominant in it, its predominance of speech (vāk) should be understood. Even so, because it encompasses the entire range of the signified and the signifier, it is supreme and full;
yet, because it differs from the phonemes perceivable by the ear produced by Vaikharī, it is subtle.
Because she is the cause of the birth of all that is expressed and the means of expression, the Mātṛkā is the Unknowing Mother.
The wise are those possessed of the knowledge of the Mātṛkā, according to the status of the Śiva Sūtra: "The awakening to the wheel of the Mātṛkā" (2-7). || 71 ||
Furthermore, this Blessed Lady, being of the nature of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*) through her predominance of non-duality,

is the source (*yoni*) of all mantras, abiding everywhere like fire in the friction-stick (*araṇi*). Thus, since the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) has been introduced, although the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *praṇava* [is to be discussed].

Although it was stated in reverse order (*prātilomyena*), nevertheless, in the forward order (*ānulomyena*), the *praṇava* draws [the energy] from the heart to the *dvādaśānta* through the process of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*) during the state of differentiation (*bhedadaśā*), according to the verse: "The *praṇava* encompasses everything; by means of its parts (*kalābhiḥ*), one should contemplate Śiva. (22.14).

Having uttered that [syllable] according to the principle to be stated in the passage, "The letter *a* and the letter *u*" (22.21), one should descend from the *dvādaśānta* to the heart by means of the nectar of Śiva, through the cultivation of each respective location according to the method already described.

Having created the unsurpassed stage by perceiving that very universe— which has the form of the first sprout of the expansion of Mātṛkā, who encompasses everything without exception after having flooded the entire world— as being rendered fit for the offering in the Great Sacrifice through the consecration of the sprinkling of supreme nectar; that same universe...
Having offered [the offering] into the supreme abode through the reflective awareness (*amarśa*) of the utterance of the second seed-syllable,

one [dissolves it] into the third seed-syllable within one's own abode— the nature of which is light and bliss, consisting of non-difference from Unmanā and Supreme Śiva, whose essence is the state of equilibrium between the upward and downward [movements] of the entire process of emanation and withdrawal within the nature of Agni and Soma.

"One should rest through stability," he says; [thus] one offers the incomparable nectar joined with emission, which possesses the power of the two seeds through the two feet. (21.72) The potency of the two seeds is here indicated by the two quarters of the verse. (21.72)

Since it is thus, therefore that Lord of the Gods, Amṛteśa, is both transcendent and immanent (*parāpara*). The word "this one" (*asau*) refers here to the King of Mantras. He is both transcendent (*para*) and immanent (*apara*), and thus "transcendent-and-immanent" (*parāpara*); this is according to the principle of *tantra* (multiple meanings).
Its nature as the universal self has been stated.
Furthermore,
because he delivers one from death, he is called Mṛtyujit (the Conqueror of Death).
He is remembered as Bhairava because of his sustaining (*bharaṇa*) of the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) of the process (*prakriyā*).

Within the process—the systematic sequence of the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with the *pura*—the "eggs" are the egg of Brahmā, the egg of Prakṛti, and the egg of Māyā-śakti; [he is so called] because of his sustaining of these.

Because of the act of assimilating [them] into one's own self. Having thus explained the nature of the Lord of Mantras residing here as being in the form of Amṛteśa and others, he begins to carry forward the topic at hand: that all the mantras under discussion consist of the three principles (tritattva).
All such mantras as these are remembered as possessing immeasurable splendor.
O beloved, they exercise authority over the entire world; they liberate beings from saṃsāra and unite them with the supreme Śiva.

Because they possess the nature of protecting through reflection (*manana*), they are known as *mantras*. The word "thus" (*evam*) refers both to the Lord of Mantras previously mentioned and to his potency (*vīrya*). Therefore, all [deities] such as Amṛteśa and others who have been mentioned are, according to the principle established previously, primarily composed of that potency.

The mantras possess light that is immortal, indestructible, and the essence of supreme nectar; therefore, because their nature is the radiance of consciousness (*cit*), they exercise authority over the creation and other processes of the universe.

Primarily, however, they perform the grace (*anugraha*) directed toward the individual soul by means of liberating it from its bonds and manifesting its Śiva-nature; thus, according to the etymological derivation (*nirukta*).
They are called *mantras* because they possess the quality of protecting through reflection.
Since this is so, therefore mantras are omnipresent and exist at all times, born from the three principles (tritattva). || 21.76 ||
Being of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, they possess eternal grace;

because they lack limitation like the *kṣetrajña*, they are omnipresent and all-pervading; because their agency is not obscured like that of the *vijñānākala*, they are bestowers of everything, and they possess eternal grace.
Because they consist of the nature of Śiva, Śakti, and the Self, they are born—that is, they are manifested—within the three principles (tattvas).
Moreover,
through the power of Śiva and Śakti, they bestow auspiciousness and remove inauspiciousness.
"Those who perform restraint and favor, and who bestow auspiciousness and remove inauspiciousness"—this is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa). || 77 ||
For those possessing the knowledge of yoga, however,
[the mantras] grant results merely upon being known, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation; thus,
he elucidates the nature of mantras as consisting of Śiva, Śakti, and the Self through their differentiation.
That which constitutes their state of omniscience and indeed their omnipotence.
That state of Śiva has been fully described as the possession of all powers due to its universal nature.
The state of being power (*śaktitva*) is the capacity to act as the agent of all things.
Power (*śakti*) is that by which something is made possible; it is autonomy (*svātantrya*).
That very [power] manifests as the agency that bestows grace upon all, granting fruit everywhere. || 21-79 ||

The expression "the state of bestowing fruit" refers to the fact that [the Lord] bestows fruit everywhere—in each respective instance—with respect to reality and so forth; thus, this is an indication where the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary focus.
The nature of the self is its essential form, which is traditionally taught as a threefold means of accomplishment:
mantra, meditation, and likewise mudrā.
Whatever is the essential form of a particular means of accomplishment—namely, the propitiation of the deity of the mantra—that [is its nature].

The atomic nature (*aṇutva*) of mantras consists of their threefold selfhood, because they have as their means the recitation of mantras, meditation, and *mudrās*, which depend upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the body (*deha*). As it is said in the *Śrīpūrva* [Mālinīvijayottara-tantra]: "Recitation, the instruments [of speech], and meditation... (2.21), and so forth.
And this threefold means of accomplishment is enjoined by the scripture. (21.80)
And he shows these three in detail:

initiation, the consecration of the maṇḍala, sacrifice, and likewise recitation; the performance of fire-offerings, as well as drawing [the maṇḍala], and the practice of meditation and concentration. (21.81)
The binding of mudrās, as well as yoga, worship, and the unification of ritual action;

initiation (dīkṣā), the maṇḍala, and the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) consisting of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and so forth—this is the collective summary. The "drawn" refers to the yantra. This concludes the expansion of the mantra. [Now follows] dhāraṇā.

The elaboration of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-prapañca*): the binding of mudrās is for the sake of the yoga of one-pointedness of mind; since yoga culminates in unification (*yojanā*), this is described as the elaboration of mudrās. The elaboration of the triad consists of the unification of ritual action (*kriyaikatā*), which takes the form of the conjunction of mantras, the conjunction of the channels (*nāḍī-saṃdhāna*), and the process of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*).
Having thus established that mantras consist of the three principles (tattvas), he concludes: "In this way, the mantras have been fully explained; they are authoritative everywhere. (21.82)
In accordance with the three principles, [this applies] to both enjoyment and liberation, and also to enjoyment; may there be auspiciousness!
That which, through its utterance and pervasiveness, by virtue of resting in the supreme state,

bestows both enjoyment and liberation; that peerless non-duality which is the eye for the protection of the world, the sovereign of all subordinate wheels, and the supreme nature of the three principles belonging to Īśa.
That which consists of the nectar of supreme awakening is victorious.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Netrodyota*, composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja, on the *Śrī Netratantra*. 21.
The Twenty-second Chapter:
"The Illumination of the Net.
Destroying duality with the surging streams of the essence of one's own supreme self-luminosity.

We praise that indescribable eye of Śarva, the lord of all mantras, which, having poured forth everything without remainder, emits it as the fire of Supreme Śiva and causes it to manifest as the vibration of the unity of light and bliss.

Although the reality of mantra (mantratattva), which was introduced at the beginning of the preceding section, has become intermingled in the interim with infinite objects of knowledge, the Goddess spoke in order to bring it to a conclusion.
Indeed, countless millions of mantras of immeasurable power have been spoken by the God; they are all-knowing, all-pervading, and always auspicious. (22-1)
All [of them] are praised as sovereigns of all, and each is authoritative in every respect;
yet among all of them, how is it that one is superior and more powerful? (22.2)
O Supreme Lord, how is the King of Mantras the supreme conqueror of death?
A doubt has arisen in my heart; O God, tell it to me. (22-3)
"How was the true essence of the previously mentioned mantra taken away from me by the Lord?
I wish to hear that today, for my curiosity is indeed great. (22.4)

O Lord of the Heart, O Sovereign of the Heart, O Self! It is because of the greatness of this mantra—whether it be deficient or excessive—that you have stated in the scriptures that almost all ten million mantras [are contained within it].
Therefore, the doubt has arisen in me as to how this King of Mantras can be superior; for that reason...

Speak; utter a definitive statement, for I desire to comprehend with a mind that grasps the essence that very reality of the Mantra previously described—which was taught for many purposes—now that it has been obscured by being mixed with the expressions of various objects of knowledge. In this matter, which is the quintessence of all things, my [desire] is exceedingly great.
"This is the curiosity," [he said]. || 4 ||
Questioned by the Goddess, Bhairava said:
"Listen; I shall fully declare that which resides as a doubt in your heart—this complete teaching is the final resolution."
Thus it is said:
"For indeed, all the innumerable millions of mantras are each presided over by their respective deities. (22.5)
And they are the manifestations of Śiva’s power, endowed with all powers;
they all bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, augmented by the strength of their own respective powers.

Although he is augmented by the power and majesty of sovereignty— the strength of his own Śiva-nature— nevertheless, [the author] begins to state that this Lord of Mantras possesses a specific distinction.
But the Supreme God is indeed peaceful, endowed with immeasurable qualities;
He is Śiva, the soul of all, pure, perceivable through contemplation, and unsurpassed. (22.7)
The Supreme Lord is their ultimate support, all-pervasive,

the deity whose true nature consists of luminosity and other qualities; he is supreme and unsurpassed, tranquil due to the cessation of duality, endowed with immeasurable attributes such as non-dual omniscience and so forth, and is the self of all.

She is the one who has embraced the forms of duality, non-duality, and supreme non-duality; she is pure, unobscured even within the state of universal identity, perceivable through contemplation, and self-luminous due to her density of consciousness.
She is the support of those mantras, which are manifested by her very self in such a variety of ways.

It consists of the foundation of the illumination of others; although it is called "supreme" (*parama*) because, according to the aforementioned view, even their power (*śakti*) is its support, nevertheless, the meaning is that this is the most excellent resting place even for that power. For this very reason, it is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*).
The Supreme Lord is autonomous in the manifestation of those respective mantras, as well as in their conjunction and disjunction;
for this very reason, there exists nothing else superior to Him,
who is such a being here, consisting of the essence of all vital powers (*vīrya*) previously introduced as the nature of the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*).
The meaning is "Lord of Mantras. And this has already been largely determined previously.
And therefore, they have arisen by His will and are impelled by His power. || 22-8 ||
All [mantras] become fruitful everywhere, for they are properly impelled by His power—the flash of His sovereignty—and are appointed to [tasks such as] bestowing grace;
therefore, mantras that are authoritative in all respects certainly yield their fruits. The particle *eva* is used out of its usual order.
Although all mantras are generated and employed by Śiva and Śakti, nevertheless, this [mantra] possesses a greatness that distinguishes it from others; thus he carries forward the subject at hand:
"That which is the supreme abode, Śiva, the dwelling place of all. (22.9)

From this very source have arisen the mantras of unfailing power. From the first chapter onwards, that which is the supreme abode of Śakti— the form of Mṛtyujit, the great universal essence consisting of consciousness and bliss— is itself of the nature of Śiva.
Because consciousness alone is the support of the universe, since nothing whatsoever manifests apart from its nature as consciousness;
for this very reason, and not from anything else—for there is no existence of that which is other than it because it does not manifest—the mantras [exist].
By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that the entire universe, beginning with Māyā, arises from this very substratum, and thus the mantras possess unfailing power.
The sequence is also broken.
And that is logical, because there must be an eternal, unimpeded leader who governs them. (22.10)
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, the protector, the savior, the auspicious one—he provides protection for all and delivers those whose minds are terrified. || 22-11 ||
Existence (*bhava*) is necessarily pervaded by all directions and times, yet it remains untouched by them;

it is the regulator and the employer of these mantras. It is the swift leader, manifesting externally through mere will alone and bringing [all things] into the state of one's own self. And for this reason, it is also the primary leader (*nāyaka*).

"Unassailed" (*anupaplava*) means that one has emerged from the impurities such as those of the individual soul (*āṇava*); and since they have emerged from that [source], it should likewise be understood as "devoid of conceptual proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*) and "without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*). Here, "proliferation" (*prapañca*) refers to the manifold diversity of the world, and "appearances" (*ābhāsāḥ*) refer to limited manifestations of light. "The protector" (*trāyaka*) is the one who provides all protection; "the savior" (*tāraṇa*) is the liberator.

And therefore, Śiva—the Lord Mṛtyujit, whose nature is that of the supreme Śiva consisting of ultimate bliss—is [the protector]. This very point is made clear by the half-verse beginning with "etadeva trāṇam" (this alone is protection). *Trāṇam* means protection for those whose minds are terrified and who fear *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, this is the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) of Netranātha through the correspondence of its syllables and phonemes.
As it is said:
"Because it leads one to the state of liberation and delivers one from great fear, it is called 'Netra' (the Eye) due to its leading and its protecting. (22.12)
Furthermore,
this life-force is proclaimed to be the eye among all beings;
just as the eye reveals the nature of forms, so does this.
Because it illuminates everything without exception, the eye is said to have become the eye; therefore, it is the life-force of all beings.
And it is stated in the venerable *Pratyabhijñā*: "Knowledge and action are considered the life-force of living beings. (1.1.4)
Thus, this Lord is the Supreme Sovereign of the entire collection of mantras, like their master. || 22-13 ||
And this has already been determined previously. || 13 ||
Having thus stated the distinction of this Lord of Mantras from other mantras by means of general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), he speaks also by means of phonemic pervasion (*akṣaravyāpti*):
"The *praṇava* is the vital breath of living beings; it is established as their life."
The Praṇava grasps everything; through its parts, one should contemplate Śiva.
One offers the sixfold great path, established upon the state of the six causes, all of it by means of the Vidyā, impelled by the syllable *juṃ*. (22.15)
That which is one's own essential nature, self-cognizable, characterized by perfect contentment,
the support for all states of immortality, and the supreme Śiva accompanied by the emission (visarga).
It is full and uninterrupted by means of that full oblation;
it is the utterance of one's own self, abiding in its own nature, consisting of its own form, and arisen from itself.
And that supreme power is one, consisting of will, knowledge, and action;
by means of it, the omnipotent Śiva is said to eternally create. (22.18)

For all living beings, for all that possesses life, the *praṇava* alone is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of the nature of the universal vibration of the common reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which is unstruck (*anāhata*) and the primary assumption of the means of knowledge regarding all objects of cognition; for without it, neither cognition nor action is possible.
For when this [Self] exists, their life—consisting of the movement of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth—attains a firm foundation; otherwise, it would remain unstable, like the blowing of a bellows.
Even though it is of such a nature, this [Self], having internalized everything without exception...

By means of the powers (kalā) beginning with *ā* and *u* which are about to be described, having manifested them separately through his own sovereignty, he grasps them by means of those very powers through the method of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), assimilating everything up to the level of *Samanā*.
He should then contemplate Śiva through the function of the Supreme Speech (*parāvāc*). And furthermore—
One should contemplate [the universe] according to the perspective described in the twenty-first chapter and, by way of the process of descent (*avaroha*), cast it into the end of the heart;

one should then render the entire universe drenched with that supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*). In this way, the sixfold path (*ṣoḍhādhvan*)—consisting of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*pura*), and so forth—is made into a lake by the sprinkling of the nectar of Śiva.

That very *praṇava*, which is the previously mentioned form of the first commitment (*abhyupagama*), abides as the six-footed bee within the causal chain beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śiva; impelled by the power (*śakti*) whose primary function is knowledge (*vidyā*) in the form of the syllables of the middle mantra, it proceeds through the method of ascending and descending within the central abode (*madhyadhāma*).
He offers oblations and casts [the offering] into the great fire of the supreme abode (*paradhāma*).

Furthermore, that which is called by such terms as "nature" (*svarūpa*) and so forth, previously determined, is the abode of Śiva known as Paramaśiva, a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*); it is "with emission" (*savisarga*), meaning it is in a state of aesthetic fusion (*samarasa*) with the power of *unmanā*, whose essence is supreme autonomy.

By means of that nectar of Śiva’s bliss, obtained through the support of the logic of the third seed-syllable, there arises within one's own very nature— rather than elsewhere— the Supreme (Parā) consciousness, which consists of the state of equilibrium among the triad of powers beginning with Will (icchā), which is self-arisen, self-luminous, and its own utterance (uccāra),
by way of the logic of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṃ-vimarśa). Not...

Abiding within the Self, which is slightly contracted in its powers of will, knowledge, and so forth, there exists that very one supreme power, the venerable Parā-bhaṭṭārikā, who is the essential nature of one’s own Self, the Lord of Consciousness;
she alone is that by whom the universe is filled— that is, brought to the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with Paramaśiva and His Power.
Through that perfect *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation) perfected by such realization, the entire universe offered into that fire of consciousness becomes,

without interval, the all-pervading whole— an identity of aesthetic relish (*sāmarasya*) consisting of the supreme power and its possessor, whose nature is the essence of all flavors. Thus, the practitioner who has attained the supreme abode through the method of mantra-recitation is directly [one with it].
"The one possessing power is Śiva alone" is what is traditionally taught; thus, there is a connection with the preceding term.
He clarifies the statement “the *praṇava* grasps” [as follows]:

[It grasps] that which is connected to the syllables of the *udgītha*, consisting of principles (*tattva*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and words (*pada*), as well as the worlds (*bhuvana*), the *kalās*, the mantras, and the six causes themselves. (22–19)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva,
and Śiva—
because he is sung of as being present above all and as the primordial source everywhere, the Praṇava is called the Udgītha.
Within that stainless, imperishable abode of such a nature, the six paths and the six causes are interconnected, embraced within, and established.
And for this reason:
"But due to incapacity regarding the [first] six, there is dissolution in the seventh by abandoning the six. (22.20)

The meaning is that, by means of one's own non-failing power whose nature is the radiance of the Other, through the relinquishing of the six paths and their causes, one must come to rest at the end of the utterance of the *praṇava* in the seventh [state], the supreme abode which transcends both paths and causes. || 20 ||
He analyzes this very [Oṃ] according to the sequence of the manifestation of the kalās of the Praṇava:
"The letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the Bindu;
the Ardhacandra, the Nirodhī, the Nāda, and indeed the Nādānta. (22.21)
*Kauṇḍalī*, *Vyāpinī*, and *Samanā* are the *sāmaya* [elements].

*Kauṇḍalī* is an epithet for *Śakti*. Thus, these eleven components of the mantra, whose true nature has been previously determined, are the *sāmaya* elements that are to be abandoned. This is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda*:
"O beautiful lady, the infinite web of bonds extends as far as the realm of Śamana. (4.432)
Beyond that is the partless reality of the Self (ātmatattva), as well as Śakti and likewise Unmanā.

That, together with its manifestation, having emerged from the sphere of conceptualization extending up to the level of *samanā*, at the conclusion of its utterance, is the pure reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which, though free from obscuration, has not yet fully blossomed into the pervasion of Śiva and Śakti; that indeed is it.
But [it is] the nature of omniscience and so forth, which emerges as non-differentiation through the power of *unmanā*;
this very pair of objects of knowledge, because it has not yet attained rest in Paramaśiva, is accompanied by manifestation and possesses an extremely subtle contraction. As for that...

That supreme, unsurpassed reality, which is without manifestation (*nirābhāsa*), illuminates the state of being both transcendent of and identical with the entire universe extending to the limits of space—
as previously explained, "without manifestation" means as before.
Thus, by means of the method of ascending step by step through the abandonment of the six, the seventh is declared to be the supreme dissolution, the abode of dissolution (layamālaya).
By abandoning the six previously mentioned paths and causes, there is the seventh, supreme abode (*dhāman*).
It is called *laya* because everything dissolves and vibrates within it; and it is called *ālaya* because one merges into it, attaining supreme equanimity. || 23 ||
He clarifies the statement beginning with "layam" (dissolution) as follows:
"In that state, all are indeed dissolved; by His grace they become equal to Him.
Strengthened by His power, those possessed of Śakti (the Śāktas) truly become fully perfected. (22–24)
The meaning is that, precisely because they are augmented by that power (śakti), the Śāktas are indeed identical with it. || 24 ||
Therefore, I shall here declare the sequence of their dissolution,
by which sequence those [elements], beginning with the cause (kāraṇa), [dissolve].
...they dissolve, O beautiful goddess.

That sequence of denotations beginning with the letter *ta* consists of the deity to be denoted, its locus, its presiding Brahman, the *kalā*, that which is to be presided over by it, the *tattva*, and so forth.
He indicates the vowel *a* together with the consonant *ñca*; it has Brahmā as its deity and extends through the heart along the path. (22–25)
One should contemplate [the deity] endowed with eight digits within all living beings;
it is the abode whose essence is the reflective awareness of the letter *A*, whose nature is the consciousness of emanation, presided over by the deity Brahmā,
extending from the big toe up to the heart.

One should contemplate [the Self] as endowed with the eightfold *kalā* of Sadāśiva-Brahmā, which will be described later and which presides over the Earth-principle (*pṛthvī-tattva*) that contains within it the entire manifold expansion of infinite worlds; [one should contemplate this] within all living beings, [according to the teaching]:
"O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the very heart of all beings, causing all beings to revolve."
"Mounted upon the machine by means of Māyā" (Bhagavad Gītā 18.61);
according to this principle, He brings about their manifold creation of consciousness, consisting of both conceptualization and non-conceptualization.
He indicates the kalās of Sadyojāta by name:
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Dhṛti, and Svadhā. (22–26)
These [five] kalās of Sadyojāta remain pervading the western [face].
The "western" refers to the face of Śrī Sadyojāta which encompasses the pervasion of the earth;
because he is the cause of maintenance (sthiti), his powers possess names appropriate to that function.
Now, he demonstrates the expansion of the deities and so forth signified by the vowel *u*, preceded by the non-grasping of the *kalās*:
"Dust, protection, pleasure, that which is to be guarded, desire, thirst, intellect, and action. (22–27)
Vṛddhi, Māyā, Nāḍī, Bhramaṇī, and Mohanī—
these are indeed the kalās of Vāmadeva, established within the Vaiṣṇava portion.
That [space] is pervaded as far as the throat; these waters remain pervading it.

Because the venerable Vāmadeva is the agent of emanation (*sṛṣṭikārin*), thirteen powers are appropriately designated. Among these, in the *Śrīsvacchanda*, only one, Manonmanī, is recited as belonging to the Vṛddhikāya.

Only this much difference is observed: [the term] "vaiṣṇavāṃśe" refers to that portion of the Lord known as Viṣṇu, who presides over the category of Prakṛti and whose nature is the consciousness of maintenance (sthitisaṃvit).
And all of this is internally embraced by the letter *U* through the method of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Likewise, he stated that what is indicated by the syllable *ma* consists of darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), hunger, sleep, death, illusion, fear, and old age.
These are indeed the digits (kalās) of Aghora, established within the portion of Rudra.
[The space] is pervaded as far as the end of the palate...
because Aghora is the agent of withdrawal (saṃhāraka), its time and its corresponding designations are such. "Within the portion of Rudra" means—

The meaning is that these are the eight kalās of the venerable Lord Rudrabhaṭṭāraka, who is a portion of the Blessed One, whose nature is the consciousness of the destroyer, who is to be contemplated through the digit of the letter *ma*, and who presides over the Māyā-tattva that pervades the palate and the end of the nose.
And this, according to the established nature of reality, is the supreme fiery pervasion. || 22-30 ||

"In accordance with the principle taught in the *Śrī-Svacchanda* and other scriptures, 'As far as the pervasion of the *kalās* extends, so indeed does that of the *tattvas*' (5.13), the intention of the 'excellent state' is that it consists of the essential pervasion of *vidyā* and *kalā*;
above this, in the middle of the eyebrows..."
Cessation, stability, knowledge, and likewise tranquility—
these indeed are the kalās of the Puruṣa, established within the Lord.
Relying on the enclosure of Vāyu, they blaze forth as far as the Bindu;
indeed, because of the universal nature (vaiśvātmya) of the Lord Puruṣa, they encompass the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti and ending with Śānti. Thus, the Lord is that which contemplates the Bindu.

The meaning is "the venerable Lord (Īśvarabhaṭṭāraka)," who is the presiding authority over the principle of Īśvara. They are "radiant" because they have attained a state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) and are thus luminous.
And this state, through the persistence of the five digits (kalās),
is the state of peace known as the Fourth (turya).
Now, above this, beginning from the forehead...
...we declare [it] in the *Nādanta*. || 22-32 ||
The object of knowledge consists of the mantra. || 32 ||
And this state called Nāda is the pervasion (vyāpti) belonging to Sadāśiva; it is named Vyoma and has the nature of emptiness.
The meaning is that its essence consists of the pervasion of the supreme void.
Tārā, Sutārā, Taraṇī, Tārayantī, and Sutāriṇī. || 22-33 ||
These digits (kalās) are known to extend up to the end of the fourth state (turyānta), ascending to the station of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta).
Indeed, these five digits of Īśāna are of the nature of the causal [principles].

The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because. Since these are indeed portions (*kalā*) of Īśāna, they consist of the forms from the Fourth (*turya*) up to that which transcends the Fourth (*turyātīta*). Furthermore, because they deliver one from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), they possess names such as *Tārā* (the Savior) and others appropriate to them; being of the nature of the Cause (*kāraṇātmikā*), they are the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for performing the five cosmic functions.
Thus,
this gross path born of Brahman has been fully described;
for "Brahmans" refers to Īśāna and the others, and "elements" refers to space and the rest.
It consists in the pervasion by the conceptual proliferation (prapañca) of that very [object].
Now, I shall describe the subtle path as it truly exists, which is indeed included within this very [system]. || 22-35 ||
He begins to speak of that which is called the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), which floods the head of the *bindu*;
O Maheśvarī, that is declared to be the nectar of power (*śaktyamṛta*) joined with the digit (*kalā*). (22–36)
It is said:
"When the nectar of Śiva, the cause of emanation, falls upon the crown of the head, there shall be nourishment by means of it... (21.66).
Thus, in this case. || 36 ||
This [deity] displays the digits (kalās):
Jyotsnā, Jyotsnāvatī, Suprabhā, Vimalā, and Śivā. Indeed, these are the half-moon digits, established in the state of omniscience.
Bound by the veil of ignorance yet adorned with tens of millions of mantras, they abide as the very nature of the power of action—pure and auspicious. (22-38)
The meaning is that they are established in that state which is omniscient (*sarvajña*), having its nature and its grace.

Furthermore, these [energies] consist of the expansion of the quality known as omniscience; because the half-moon is characterized by the predominance of light, these powers of it are also appropriately designated by names such as "moonlight" (*jyotsnā*).

They are surrounded and connected by the protective enclosure formed by the *vidyās* and *mālā-mantras*; they are adorned with tens of millions of mantras in the form of *kūṭākṣaras* and so forth, which, because they effect emanation, are of the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). Nevertheless...
They are stainless because they are not defiled by activity; they are auspicious because they are inclined toward bestowing grace. || 38 ||
Now, above this are these [energies]: Rundhanī, Rodhanī, Raudrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā;
for these are the Nirodhikā-kalās, which obstruct all the gods. || 39 ||
They are eternally satisfied, highly fortunate, and of the nature of the Vāmā-śakti;

they are the obstructors even of all beings from Brahmā downwards who have not received the descent of the supreme Śakti, and they are named Anurūpa, Rundhanī, and so forth, as they stand as adversaries to the immersion in the states of Nāda and the rest.

However, for those purified by the supreme descent of power (*para-śaktipāta*), these [energies] are designated as "awakening of knowledge" (*jñāna-bodha*) and so forth, because they cause the destruction of darkness through the awakening of gnosis. Because they obstruct the downward and upward movement of both the awakened and the unawakened, the energy (*kalā*) called "the eternally satisfied" (*nityatṛptikā*) is that which pervades the qualities (*guṇa*).
Because they are presided over by Vāmā, these powers (śaktis) have her very nature.

Now, following that, he describes the powers (śaktis) with their appropriate designations in the state of Nāda, which consists of supreme luminosity and is characterized primarily by reflective awareness (vimarśa): "Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā. (22–40)
These digits (kalās), which arise from Nāda and move upwards, are endowed with autonomy; they abide both in the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala).

These [energies] are known as having the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and are bestowers of omniscience. The upward-moving energy (*ūrdhvagāminī*), which resides in the state of the end of sound (*nādāntapada*), is indicated by the plural number because it is adorned by the entire series of powers. Those whose arising and manifestation (*ullāsa*) occur within *nāda*, the abode of *nāda*, are [the energies] in the manifest (*sakala*).

In the *nāda*— which possesses the power of the eightfold sound beginning with *ghoṣa*— the stages ending with *mocikā* reside; but in the *nādānta*, which consists of nothing but the most subtle vibration (*susūkṣmadhvanimātra*) and is partless (*niṣkala*), the practitioner is engaged in entering the state of Śakti, which is dominated by the upward-moving power of will (*icchāśakti*).

The division is that Śakti is the bestower of entry into that [state]. By the statement "endowed with sovereignty," he shows their manifestation as the expansion of the quality of autonomy (*svātantrya*). By saying they are "of the nature of the power of knowledge" (*jñānaśakti*), he indicates that [the powers] up to the *nirodhikā* belong to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), while above the *nāda* is the power of will (*icchāśakti*).
He indicates that the pervasion belongs to the capacity (śakti), and so forth.
Beyond this, there are indeed Sūkṣmā and Susūkṣmā, who arise from the nectar of immortality. || 22-42 ||
And they are indeed renowned as all-pervasive, resting upon the principle of Śakti;
because their connection with power is unimpaired, they are presided over by the power of consciousness (cicchakti).
For these [energies], though consisting of pure consciousness (cinmātra), are observed to reside within the principle of Śakti;
because the Earth element is dominated by the power of will (icchā-śakti) and is subtle in comparison to the powers of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) and the rest,
the energies belonging to that [Earth] are also subtle, and due to the excellence of that subtlety, the predominance of the touch of bliss (ānanda-sparśa) arises.

Because it bestows that [state] and because it effects pervasion (*vyāpti*), it has such names as "Subtle" (*sūkṣmā*) and so forth. It is specifically known as "Pervasive" (*vyāpinī*); situated above the station of Śakti which is located at the upper part of the *brahmabila*, it remains at the very limit of the skin. The "Principle of Power" (*śaktitattva*) pervades two locations called Śakti and Vyāpinī, but not...
The station of Śakti itself belongs to Vyāpinī, because she rests upon the Void and the Great Void that lie above the plane of Śakti.
And these [stations], although they are essentially pure consciousness (cinmātra) precisely because they are presided over by the power of consciousness (cicchakti),
appear as if they possess a slight degree of objectivity, since they consist in the non-recognition (akhyāti) of the identity with that [consciousness] which is produced by Mahāmāyā.
They have attained the state of being pure consciousness itself, characterized by primordial awakening that surpasses the power of ordinary cognition.
Now, demonstrating the pervasive powers (*vyāpinī-śakti*), he reveals their omnipresence by means of the term "power" (*śakti*):
"The pervasive one, whose form is space, infinite, and designated as 'the Lordless' (*anātha*). (22.44)
O Maheśānī, the *kalās* of Vyāpinī are remembered as being without support (*anāśritā*).

They are designated thus because of their pervasiveness (*vyāpti*), their formlessness (*anākṛtitva*), their lack of limitation by time (*kālānavaccheda*), and because they have no other master (*ananyasvāmikatva*) and no other support (*ananyāśrayatva*). The term "Vyāpinī" refers to the state of *śūnyātiśūnya*. And of these—

By virtue of its previously described nature as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it possesses the character of being the manifestation of the multitude of qualities known as primordial awakening (*anādibodha*).

Then, by means of the statement in the *Śrī Svacchanda*— “Now, above the plane of Vyāpinī, in the abode of Samanā, there is the consciousness of form, which is the pacifier” (4-394)— the Lord reveals the powers of Samanā that have been indicated therein.
The omniscient one, the all-pervading, the difficult to attain, the sacrificial flow, the desirable, and fortitude. || 22-45 ||
And these are known as the *samanā* [kalās], remembered as the digits of Śiva;
because they are the knowledge of the pervasion of everything up to the end of the *vyāpinī*, because that pervasion is difficult to attain,
because they grant repose at the morning twilight (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*), because they are desirable, and because of the aforementioned support of the universe.

Because they bring about the state in which the entire universe consists of nothing but thought, these are the *kalās*, the powers (*śaktis*) of Śiva— the venerable Lord Paraśiva— who presides over the Śiva-tattva.
And these, presiding over the power of will, are the bestowers of the accomplishment of will. || 22-46 ||
Resting upon the Śiva-principle, they possess the luster of a perfectly full ocean;
they abide in infinite power, subtle and exceedingly pure. (22.47)
Because the pervasion of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) culminates in this [state], these [energies] abide presiding over the power of will;

and therefore, for one who worships this plane, they bestow desired objects by mere will, their light and radiance being like that of a perfectly full ocean, since they encompass the entire universe up to the level of the Pervasive One (*vyāpinī*).
Therefore, their state is as if established within an abode of infinite power (*ananta-śakti*), and they consist of the manifold expansion of the qualities known as infinite power.

Thus, they abide in the following locations: the Half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the Obstructress (*nirodhikā*), Sound (*nāda*), the End of Sound (*nādānta*), Power (*śakti*), Pervasion (*vyāpinī*), and Equalization (*samanā*).

It has been taught that the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) consist of the expansion of the sixfold group of divine qualities (*bhagavadguṇaṣaṭka*) known as omniscience, contentment, sovereignty, the power of the obscured, beginningless consciousness, and infinite power; thus they are called "subtle" (*sūkṣmā*).

The meaning is that they have attained an ever-increasing subtlety; "extremely pure" refers to the *śakti-kalās* in comparison to the *nāda* and *nādānta* stages. Even more pure than those is the *vyāpinī-kalā*;

however, these [present kalās] are even purer still, because their nature consists solely in the cessation of the mental activity (*manana*) directed toward the pervasive object of contemplation up to the limit of *vyāpinī*.

At the end [of the phrase] "stainless" (*nirmalāḥ*), their stainlessness is relative; however, in reality, even though this entire section has been reduced to the nature of mere contemplation (*manana*),
it consists of the supreme triad of principles known as Mantra, Śuddhātman, Unmanā, and Paramaśiva.
Since it consists of these [elements], how could there be absolute purity? || 47 ||
As it was said:
"O lady of excellent limbs, the infinite web of bonds, up to the level of Samanā, is traversed by the six causal stages, according to their gross and subtle divisions. (22.48)
From the *samanā* level up to the *akhyāti-asūtraṇa*, this entire path constitutes a "net of bonds" (*pāśajāla*).
This is appropriately pervaded by the "planes" (*pada*)—that is, the points of rest—of the six causes beginning with Brahmā.
Coarseness belongs to the bonds ending with *nāda*, whereas subtlety belongs to...
"Of those beginning with Śakti and ending with Samanā. || 48 ||
He recalls the meaning already stated: "Indeed, [the reality] from Śakti up to Samanā is the domain of subtle consciousness,
accessible only to the most eminent yogis."
Now, in order to demonstrate the supreme state of the three principles (tritattvī), wherein the pervasion of bonds has been stilled, he says:
"But above that is the supreme, peaceful, immeasurable, and untainted [state]. (22.49)
"O Goddess, having known the supreme triad of principles, the Guru liberates [the disciple].
'Having known' means having entered into [them]. As it is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda*: 'Abandoning mental activity, one should unite [the disciple] through pure awareness alone.'"
Then the bound soul (paśu), liberated from the ocean of existence, attains the state of Śiva. (4.437)
He shows the three principles through their differentiation:
therein, this stainless Self is established upon the support of its own power. (22.50)
Pervaded by knowledge and action, consisting of pure consciousness alone, without support, transcending the state of all objective existents, and devoid of all sense organs. (22.51)
"In that place" means at the level of *samanā*. Having emerged from the impressions of the *āṇavamala*—which consists of the contraction limited by *samanā*—he is stainless.

And because he is thus properly established in his own support, which is the nature of his own power (*śakti*), it is stated by the phrase "pervaded by knowledge and action" that his power consists of knowledge and action. He is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone, and not...

He whose self is the Supreme Śiva, who is autonomous and a mass of consciousness and bliss, is called *anuplava* because he "floats after" (*anu-plavate*), meaning he flows forth immediately following the *āṇava-mala*. He has thus emerged from the *kārma* and *māyīya* impurities. Since he has transcended the abode of all objective existents (*sarva-bhāva-pada*) ending with the level of *Samanā*, therefore—
It is devoid of all internal and external sense-faculties, transcends them, is beyond their range, and has the nature of self-luminosity. || 51 ||
Thus, this self, being stainless and having the nature of a crystal, is established within its own self;
it is stainless and has the nature of a crystal because of its capacity to reflect the universe, due to its transcendence of everything up to the level of *samanā*.
The Self is established within its own self.
For him who has crossed beyond the noose of the limit of the samana and remains there, that power acts as his benefactor.
O Goddess, as long as [this state] does not arise, the Self is indeed not Śiva.

Even for one established in the plane of the pure three principles (tattvas) and so forth, as long as that supreme power called Unmanā— the bridge, which brings about grace through her own immersion— does not manifest, so long...
Even though he abides in the state that transcends the universe, he is the Self alone, and not Śiva. As it was said previously:
"Those who say [this] do not find anyone other than the Supreme Śiva."
"Those who worship the self do not go to the supreme state in Śaivism. (8.30) Thus it is said.
And this is logical, because even though he has ascended to that state,
being slightly expanded and pure...

[he remains] Śiva as distinct [from the Absolute], consisting in the non-apprehension of identity with Supreme Śiva arising from the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the pacification of the bonds up to the level of *samanā*.
It is slightly extended because of its subtlety (ūpatva), and it is pure because it has transcended even the level of *samanā*.
This [verse] illustrates by means of a primary example:
"Or as the lotus by the rays of the sun" (22.53).
As long as everything has not been manifested, [the teaching] remains somewhat brief.

In the case of the illustrated reality (*dārṣṭāntika*), Supreme Śiva occupies the position of the sun. Manifestation (*udbhāsana*) is the illumination through non-difference from oneself by virtue of being preeminent.
Having thus spoken by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), he also speaks by way of positive concomitance (anvaya):
"Just as a lotus blooms in an instant through contact with the rays of the sun. (22–54)
In that same way, the Self is indeed Śiva, who is grasped on all sides by the power of Śiva. "Union" means an embrace on all sides; "grasped" means supported by one's own immersion [in Him].
And this Śiva indeed becomes endowed with qualities such as omniscience, just as [previously described]. (22.55)
It is without appearance, supremely peaceful, indeed beyond discursive thought, and unsurpassed;

it possesses qualities such as omniscience attained through immersion in the state of Śambhu, and for that very reason, because the latent impressions of the body and so forth— which serve as the seeds for re-emergence— have dissolved, it is said to be "just like Śiva."

But when the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the body and so forth have dissolved, according to the principle previously stated, he himself is the supreme Śiva who is without manifestation (*nirābhāsa*);
thus the meaning has been explained.
He clarifies this very point: as long as it has not attained fullness, so long is it said to be "with appearance" (sābhāsa). || 22-56 ||
But when that whose nature is power is extended forth with his entire being, then he is grasped by the Supreme, who consists of that very expansion. (22.57)
O Goddess of the gods, he indeed becomes Śiva in every respect through non-differentiation.

He is "with manifestation" (*sābhāsa*) because he exists with a slight radiance through the vision that has been determined; the ablative case here is used in the sense of "having taken [something as a basis]" (*lyablope pañcamī*), meaning "having resorted to that Śiva," by one who partakes in non-difference from Him.
When he is grasped by the expanding power of the Transmental (unmanā-śakti), which consists of outward radiation,

and has attained identity with his own Self through that self-absorption, then he is truly one alone, by means of the supreme non-dual vision— which is entirely undivided and distinct from the limited Śiva-hood arising from the perception of duality.
He becomes that supreme Śiva. As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*:
"Joined to that supreme reality and endowed with qualities such as omniscience, O Goddess, he becomes one with Śiva, entirely without distinction" (4.402).

Thus, having realized that the very nature of the supreme non-duality— which is unconditioned and consists of immersion into Paramaśiva— is joined with the ascent and descent through the central channel, one always effects the true state of being a mantra for all mantras. (22–58)
The meaning is that for one endowed with this knowledge, mantras truly become mantras.

For one who knows the potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*), all mantras abide in power (*śaktistha*) and bestow power (*śaktida*); they grant the fruits of both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
Power is *unmanā*. "Bestowing power" means unfolding supreme autonomy (*parasvātantrya*); and therefore, according to one's desire, [they grant these fruits].
They bestow enjoyment, liberation, or both.
When the practitioner of mantra does not perceive these two paths of emanation and withdrawal through both negative and positive concomitance, [he attains stability]. (59)
Mantras whose forms are subject to rising and setting yield little fruit;
even when recited, meditated upon, or worshipped, they bestow neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation.
Impelled by the command of Śiva, they bestow only slight fruit;
however, when the practitioner of mantra truly knows the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of all things], || 22-61 ||
Then, by means of the rising and setting of those mantras of immeasurable power,
they become my servants, carrying out my commands.
And these [powers] become manifest before the practitioner in another existence.
He does not find [the goal], for he does not enter the central channel; thus, for the mantra-practitioner, this is merely a name.
According to the stated condition, there are the sequences of descent and ascent, which are the processes of emission and withdrawal.

In the phrase "in the form of rising and setting," the word *ya* is elided, [and thus it refers to] Īśvara. By the ascending order (*ārohakrama*), the heart is the abode of rising and the *dvādaśānta* is the place of setting; by the descending order (*avaroha*), the reverse occurs. This has been stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda-tantra*, in the section on recitation (*japa-prakaraṇa*).
Those desiring liberation should perform the recitation (japa), which is equal to the vital breath, while remaining established in the day;
that indeed should be known as the withdrawal (saṃhāra), which bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva.
When the sound, having reached the sky, turns back again,
that should be known as the night, until it has returned to the heart.
"This creation has been fully described as that which brings about the arising of the fruits of all attainments" (2.140–142).
Because they yield only small fruits, they grant only slight results, but not enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).

And in the granting of even slight fruits, the command of Śiva alone is the cause. The space between the heart and the *dvādaśānta* is the station of the mantras. Their emergence (*udaya*), setting (*astamaya*), and form (*rūpa*)—that is, the form as it is being uttered within the interval between the prior and posterior limits—is the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). [The state of] servitude...

The state of being impelled toward the performance of actions as desired, as well as the manifestations of immersion (samāveśa) that appear before the practitioner in other existences, within the midst of saṃsāra, and upon the various planes of experience for those specific principles (tattva)— these become the causes for the bestowal of liberation once the enjoyments have been experienced.
He applies this to the subject at hand:
"Thus, permeated by the command of Śiva, they have become Śiva and bestow Śiva. (22.63)
By the power of this mantra of Śiva, the Supreme Self, they become free from exertion, untainted, and without further rebirth. (22.64)
The command (*ājñā*) of the Lord Amṛteśa, of Mṛtyujidbhairava,
and of Śiva is the supreme power (*parā śakti*) whose nature is radiant vibration; by means of that [power],
which consists of vitality and is the very essence of the power of this mantra, they are possessed and become one with it through contact (*lepāt*).

They have emerged from the *māyīya* impurity, which is characterized by the manifestation of distinct objects of knowledge arising from the residual traces (*saṃskāra*) of the *āṇava* impurity consisting of that very degree of contraction, and from its subsequent flow; and for this reason, they have become Śiva.
Thus, as stated, having known reality through the sequence beginning with the rising [of consciousness], they are those from whom all exertion has departed.
They bestow auspiciousness and grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation. The words ending with "Bhairava" have already been etymologically explained.
He concludes the meaning of the tantra:
"But he who always understands the distinction between the higher and the lower... (22.65).
He shall attain the state of Amṛteśa before long; there is no doubt in this matter.

He who, through the vision of meditation upon the supreme, the subtle, and the gross, attains the specific distinction of this Lord of Mantras—whether it be the supreme, the intermediate, or the lower—he indeed reaches identity with Him.
And therefore, those who have taken refuge in this mantra become ones who have accomplished their purpose. || 22-66 ||
Because of the attainment of liberation while living in another body.
Moreover, one who is intent upon propitiating this mantra shall obtain whatever fruit he desires through whatever disposition,
for by resorting to anything with devotion in the hope of attaining a particular result, he shall surely attain that very result. (22.67)
"By whatever means" refers to forms such as duality and non-duality; "whatever" refers to enjoyment, liberation, and so forth; and "whatever" refers to deities such as the venerable Sadāśiva.
And one should not have any doubt here due to the inherent deficiency of the illusory subject; thus he says:

"This is true, as it has been fully explained by me to you, and not otherwise. By saying "by me to you," he suggests the appropriateness of the speaker and the questioner. As it has been stated elsewhere:

"The connection [between these] is exceedingly difficult to establish. Thus [it was said]. Therefore, O Goddess, regarding this great scripture which is a compendium of the essence of all streams, you have urged me to speak for the sake of bestowing grace upon all. (22.68)
Through this cryptic question, I have revealed all of that to you;
because of its supreme excellence,
this ritual procedure, which is difficult to find on earth, has been declared in brief.

And this [attainment] is not for those of evil character, nor for the wrathful, nor for the lustful, nor for those intent on reviling their gurus, nor for those who disparage the mantras of the gods and so forth. (22.70)
[This refers to] those who are nihilists (*nāstika*) and deceitful (*śaṭha*), excluded from the dharma of ritual action (*kriyādharma*).

"Deceitful" means having base attachments. Those for whom the performance (*kṛta*) or practice (*karaṇa*) consists of things external to the dharma of ritual action—such as the worship of the Blessed One—and takes the form of indulging in sense objects and the like.
Thus, having set aside those who are unworthy— those whose power-descension (śaktipāta) has not occurred and who have not undergone examination—
this [teaching] is to be given to one's own disciples and one's own sons, and not otherwise.
[This applies] to one's own sons who have been initiated, who possess devotion, who worship the Guru, the Deity, and the Fire,
who are worthy of being instructed by oneself, and who are disciples who have not merely been taught mantras,
but are themselves initiated and endowed with devotion and other such qualities.
This should indeed be given to such persons for their propitiation; it must be revealed in accordance with reality.

One should not grant [the teaching] to one who is worthy of instruction, yet whose discernment has not fully blossomed, or to one who lacks the necessary wealth, without first performing the initiation of the pledge (*samayadīkṣā*)...
"O Goddess worshipped by heroes, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas..."
Eunuchs, women, Śūdras, and whoever else seeks that same goal.
"At the time of initiation, one should not investigate; one should deliberate regarding the bestowal of knowledge, for the Guru is rooted in knowledge and is the initiator of the sevenfold sacrifice.

According to this principle stated in the venerable *Kāmika*, even to one who has been thoroughly tested and possesses wealth and garlands for the sake of manifesting devotion to Śiva, [one should not grant initiation without deliberation].

Or rather, that procedure must indeed be imparted to one who has received the initiation of the established convention (*samayadīkṣā*), but never without initiation. And it is stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*: "There is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śiva without initiation," beginning with this and continuing until: "even the eligibility for mantras and liberation [are not attained]."
"By means of Śiva-initiation. (4-6-8) Thus [it is said].
............and even toward that which is unpleasant. || 22-72 ||
"In every way, it must not be given at all"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.

To one who is unworthy, even if they be one's own dear son or wife, the supreme wealth belonging to the Supreme Lord—which removes the misery of saṃsāra—such as gold, garments, and so forth, must never be given; this indeed is the command of the Supreme Lord.
By stating "ājñā" and so forth, he commands that one should protect this pledge in every respect.
Otherwise, however, there is immediate danger; thus he says:
"O Goddess of the Gods, because the fall of the body occurs through the violation of the command. (22.73)
Thereafter, one should carry out the command. || 73 ||
He speaks even of one who does not protect [the preceptor] and for whom no karmic obstruction is seen:
"If he ever gives [to the preceptor] out of delusion, affection, or a desire for wealth..."
"He who transgresses this command goes to a terrible hell"— this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
"It is gone" means "it is led"; here the root *gam* is used with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). || 74 ||
Thus, considering the command of the Blessed One to be inviolable, one shall attain perfection by observing it, O Supreme Goddess;
for one who enjoys the supreme wealth of knowledge through the very observance of the command, [all powers] are held within the palm of the hand.
There is no cause for wonder regarding these accomplishments.
And because of its protection, O Goddess, the Supreme Lord becomes the Conqueror of Death.
Through the practice of immersion into the supreme abode of the venerable Lord Mṛtyujit, the lord of yogis becomes that very form itself; may there be auspiciousness!
He whose opening and closing of his eyes manifests all manifestation and so forth, who is the dispeller of the darkness of dualistic vision, and who is delighted by perfect non-duality;
he who elevates the minute to his own abode and protects the great from fear.
We bow to that supreme eye of Śiva and Śivā, which is of the nature of radiance and possesses all powers. || 1 ||
It is white through the manifestation of the universe; red through its own radiance by virtue of that awareness;
perfectly white-and-black through the relishing of that [awareness]; and black through the swallowing of it.
Furthermore, due to the unity with the wheel of light, it is neither white, nor black, nor both.
Neither red nor yet non-self, this eye of the Lord triumphs.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Netrodyota*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrī Kṣemarāja, on the *Śrī Netratantra*. 22.
From you, the darkness of night subsides and the world awakens; your eyes always bestow fruitfulness upon both the existent and the non-existent as they are correctly established.
Yet you do not consider yourself so, being like a pig, an owl, a hide, or a sparrow.
This fault of yours, O radiant one, is a poison for their eyes, which are of such a nature. || 1 ||
He is the hero who utterly destroys the enemy that is saṃsāra; he is the refuge for heroes;
he is the assembly of venerable teachers beginning with Śrī Rāma, as well as his other disciples.
Bhaṭṭa, Raktika, Garbheśa, Keśava, and others have already composed works on this subject;
therefore, only a small portion of it has been illuminated by me here.
This radiance of the eye has arisen, swelling with the nectar of supreme non-duality, dispelling the darkness of the distinctions proclaimed by those who follow the path of mere conformity.

Having reflected upon his own incomparable and perfect ripening from the honey of the speech of the venerable Abhinavaguru, Kṣemarāja—within the lotus of the illustrious Uccaiḥśravas, which possesses the beauty of blossomed flowers— [The remainder of the verse continues: ...having entered the interior of the lotus of the illustrious Uccaiḥśravas, which possesses the beauty of blossomed flowers, [he has composed this work]. (Note: The provided fragment ends mid-sentence; the full verse concludes with *praviśya* or similar, indicating he has entered that inner space.)
He expounded this treatise on the essence of fragrances.
This entire worldly existence has been swallowed up; the impurities of karma and māyā have dissolved;

a state of dense bliss has been attained; what more can be said? The supreme light has been realized by those whose awakening was gained through the savoring of the rasa of the hymn to the glorious Netramahēśvara.
We remain unrestrained in the stainless expanse of the sky-like heart. || 6 ||

That which they call the eye of Śaṅkara, which expands everything and ordains the path, and by whose delineation it fashions everything as if inscribed with a thread— that very eye, consisting of consciousness, is present here.
Victory to the third eye, which is light itself and filled with supreme bliss. || 7 ||
Thus ends this treatise named Netroddyota. A.
This work is by the illustrious Kṣemarāja, who is solely intent on tasting the pollen from the lotus feet of the great devotee of Maheśvara, the venerable Abhinavagupta; may there be auspiciousness!
